entries.headline: Puppet Enterprise report-deserialization RCE is on CISA KEV; upgrade to 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 or 2026.0.1
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-115731 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-115731, Puppet Enterprise before 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 and 2026.0.1: deserialization of a crafted agent report gives code execution as the Puppet service user to any holder of a CA-signed agent certificate, and unauthenticated where the CA autosigns; CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.4)

CISA added CVE-2026-115731 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-17 on evidence of active exploitation, naming no actor or victim (CISA, 2026-11-17). The flaw sits in Puppet's report-processing code as used by Puppet Server: a client that holds any CA-signed agent certificate can run arbitrary code on the server as its service user by sending a report with a crafted rich-data type in a PUT request, and where the certificate authority autosigns requests without strong verification an unauthenticated network attacker can first obtain such a certificate (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03). The CNA scores it CVSS 4.0 9.4 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03) and Red Hat CVSS 3.1 9.9 (Red Hat, 2026-11-03).

The discoverers at Neodyme call the bug authenticated in the strict sense, because it needs a valid agent certificate, and say it allows code execution on the management server in a default configuration (Neodyme, 2026-11-03). The OpenVox advisory of the same day includes a full trigger event and says autosign is common in enterprise deployments and that code execution as the puppet user gives access to the CA signing key (OpenVox, 2026-11-03). Puppet's 2026.0.1 release notes list the flaw among the fixes in Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1 (Puppet, 2026-11-12), and the EUVD record names 2025.12.1 and 2023.8.13 as the fixed releases of the other two lines (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03); OpenVox fixes it in server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 (oss-security, 2026-11-03), and Vox Pupuli says open-source Puppet will not receive any more updates (Vox Pupuli, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
A Puppet Enterprise or OpenVox server below the fixed releases that accepts agent connections; the reachable condition is a CA-signed agent certificate, which an outsider obtains where the CA autosigns without strong verification, a setup the OpenVox advisory calls common in enterprise deployments (OpenVox, 2026-11-03).
Detection
On the Puppet server, PUT requests to the agent report endpoint from hosts that enrolled recently, newly signed certificate requests that nobody approved, and child processes of the server's service account. Huntback's access-log sequence is a PUT to the certificate-request path from a non-agent address, a GET for the same name within a second or two, then a PUT to the report path (Huntback, 2026-11-20). A server that untrusted clients could reach before the upgrade should be treated as having exposed its CA signing key, since code execution as the puppet user reaches it (OpenVox, 2026-11-03), and the upgrade does not undo a key that was copied.

Huntback, which runs decoy servers, reports that on 2026-11-19 one decoy received the whole chain from one address in 1.47 seconds: a certificate request for a generated node name, a fetch of the signed certificate 1.4 seconds later that tests whether the CA autosigns, and a report upload carrying a type definition with a Ruby method annotation. Huntback calls it a check for vulnerable servers: the decoy returned no marker and Huntback does not tie it to the exploitation CISA holds evidence for (Huntback, 2026-11-20).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade now and, until then, avoid autosigning certificate requests without strong verification (Red Hat, 2026-11-03). The 2026.0.1 upgrade changes auth.conf wildcard matching, so a rule for *.example.com no longer matches example.com itself and rules that relied on that need review (Puppet, 2026-11-12).
Improvement20 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-intelsummaryaffected_productscvessourcesactionsbodyentities

The same Perforce advisory fixed a second flaw, CVE-2026-115732, an authorization bypass in the certificate-name matching of Puppet's authorization library, scored CVSS 4.0 9.0: a CA-signed certificate whose name extends or shortens an authorised host name is authorised as that host (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03). Neodyme's example is that an attacker who got a certificate for evil.target.lab.local can authenticate as target.lab.local, then fetch that host's catalog, which can carry configuration files with database credentials and API tokens, push spoofed facts and add exported resources (Neodyme, 2026-11-03). Where the CA autosigns, such a certificate can be requested for a name that does not exist yet, and OpenVox says autosign is not the default but is common in real deployments (OpenVox, 2026-11-03); NCSC.ch adds that in Puppet Enterprise the bypass also enables CA administration and remote command execution on managed nodes (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).

The fix is in the same Puppet Enterprise builds and in Puppet Core 9.1.3 and 8.22.2 (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-18); OpenVox ships it in OpenVox Server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 (OpenVox, 2026-11-03) and in OpenVoxDB 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 (oss-security, 2026-11-03). CISA's catalog entry covers only CVE-2026-115731 (CISA, 2026-11-17); NCSC.ch labels the pair actively exploited with a proof of concept available and lists a community report as an additional source (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19), while the report The Hacker News quotes describes a CVE-2026-115731 intrusion, so exploitation of CVE-2026-115732 itself is not established (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). NCSC.ch's temporary measures are to disable certificate autosigning, enforce strong request validation, audit the issued certificates for colliding names and review the CA configuration for signs of compromise (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).

Improvement22 Nov 2026 14:56 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodycves

OpenVox's advisory for CVE-2026-115731 lists two packages: OpenVox Agent up to 9.2.0 and 8.31.1, fixed in 9.3.0 and 8.32.0, and OpenVox Server up to 9.1.0 and 8.17.0, fixed in 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 (OpenVox, 2026-11-03). OpenVoxDB's fixed versions, 9.2.0 and 8.18.0, are in OpenVox's release notice (oss-security, 2026-11-03).

Update27 Nov 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsourcing_notesourcesevidenceactionsbodyupdated_at

Huntback, a research firm that runs decoy servers, captured the whole exploit chain on one Puppet Server decoy on the morning of 2026-11-19, in 1.47 seconds from one address (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The chain is a bare certificate request for a generated node name, which a CA that asks for a shared secret or other proof would refuse, a fetch of the signed certificate 1.4 seconds later without polling, which answers 200 only where the CA signs automatically, and a report upload whose wrapper is ordinary and whose event carries a type definition with a Ruby method annotation (Huntback, 2026-11-20). Huntback reads it as a check for vulnerable servers: the decoy signed the certificate, accepted the report with a 200 and returned no marker, and the same address had tried exploits for four other products in the previous ten days (Huntback, 2026-11-20). A scout from a different address had probed the status service and the CA paths about two and a half hours earlier without asking for a certificate. Huntback's advice is to list the signed certificates (puppetserver ca list --all) and account for every name, to refuse at a reverse proxy any report containing RubyMethod, since no agent sends a type definition in a report, and to keep TCP 8140 closed to networks that are not agents'; none of this is vendor guidance (Huntback, 2026-11-20). The capture is a single source and Huntback names no actor or victim.

entries.headline: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, 3.3.14 fix seven memory flaws; Veria's Rails exploit not found yet: update the interpreter
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-132825updatedNATOA2

Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14: seven memory-safety flaws in the regexp engine and string case conversion, three rated Critical by the project, with proofs of concept for code execution; Veria Labs says Rails and classic Sinatra are exposed by default and announces a public Rails exploit for 25 November 2026 (CVE-2026-132825, CVSS 3.1 7.4)

The Ruby project released 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 on 2026-11-18 to fix seven vulnerabilities in the regexp engine and in string case conversion, and says it is aware of proofs of concept that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution (Ruby project, 2026-11-18). NCSC.ch lists three as Critical, a one-byte heap overflow in case conversion of strings in single-byte encodings such as ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, a double free in regexp compilation and a heap overflow from an integer overflow in regexp compilation, and the rest as High or Moderate (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19); the project's advisory for the first confirms it can write one byte past the output buffer (Ruby project, 2026-11-18). Affected are Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 and 4.0.0 to 4.0.9, and Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and unfixed (Ruby project, 2026-11-18).

NCSC.ch says Rails and classic-style Sinatra are exposed to the case-conversion overflow in their default configuration (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19); watchTowr reports no exploitation as of 2026-11-19 (watchTowr, 2026-11-19). Veria Labs, which says it found the flaw independently and first demonstrated code execution, calls it Ruby2Shell, says it is reachable without authentication on Rails and classic Sinatra and that plain Rack and other frameworks are not exposed by default, and announced a proof of concept for remote code execution on stock Rails for 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix; its page, blog feed and GitHub organisation showed no release on 2026-11-27 (Veria Labs, 2026-11-19). Moritz Sanft, a co-discoverer Veria names, writes that a plain Rails application is enough to be exploitable and that OpenAI sent the Ruby maintainers working exploit proofs on 2026-11-07 (Durendal, 2026-11-19). GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.6 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.21.11 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.20.13 (GitHub, 2026-11-22) and 3.19.17 (GitHub, 2026-11-22) carry the Ruby fix, although Veria's table, last changed on 2026-11-21, still shows 3.22.5 and earlier unfixed; it lists Chatwoot (4.20.1), GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject and the Discourse base image as patched, and the Ruby advisories name no product, so the vendors' own advisories decide for each (Veria Labs, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-132825 names the case-conversion overflow and is scored CVSS 3.1 7.4 with a local attack vector and high complexity (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-19); the Ruby announcement says CVE identifiers were requested and none was assigned at publication, so the other six flaws are known by GHSA id (Ruby project, 2026-11-18).

Exposure
Ruby 3.3, 3.4 and 4.0 below the fixed releases that run Rails or classic Sinatra, or any application that passes untrusted text to a case-changing method or compiles untrusted regexp patterns; the interpreter version is shown by ruby -v, and self-hosted products that bundle Ruby carry their own fix timeline (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Crashes, segmentation faults and abnormal restarts of Ruby application workers that coincide with requests carrying long single-byte-encoded text or unusual regexp parameters, and a shell or network tool spawned by a Ruby worker process.
Defender takeaway
Update the interpreter, not the gems, rebuild container images and restart workers, since exploit proofs exist and Veria's proof of concept may appear at any time; until then NCSC.ch's temporary measures are to avoid compiling regexps from untrusted input and, for the case-conversion flaw, to convert input to UTF-8 so the vulnerable path is not reached (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).
Update22 Nov 2026 04:32 UTCrun 2026-11-22T0355Z-intelaffected_productsentitiessourcesevidenceactionsbody

GitLab released 19.6.1, 19.5.8 and 19.4.10 on 2026-11-20 as a critical patch release for self-managed installations, with CVE-2026-132825 as its only security fix; GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already patched (GitLab, 2026-11-20). The fix is a patch to Ruby: official Linux packages and container images already carry it, while a self-compiled installation must rebuild Ruby 3.3.14 or 3.4.13 or a later release of the same series, and the release also covers the other flaws in the Ruby advisory (GitLab, 2026-11-20). Veria Labs' software table now lists Chatwoot 4.20.0 and earlier as fixed in 4.20.1, leaving GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 and earlier as the one product shown without a fixed release, and its proof of concept for stock Rails is still announced for 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix (Veria Labs, 2026-11-19).

GitHub's release notes list the Ruby update as a critical fix in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.6 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.21.11 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.20.13 (GitHub, 2026-11-22) and 3.19.17 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), all dated 2026-11-22, with application-level mitigations where an update was not immediately possible; they name no Ruby version or CVE. Veria Labs' Rails proof of concept was announced for 2026-11-25 or later; its page, blog feed and GitHub organisation show no release as of 2026-11-27, which does not show that no exploit exists. Sanft writes that Rack's multipart method override and a field charset reach the vulnerable case conversion in a plain Rails application, and that OpenAI sent the Ruby maintainers working exploit proofs for the case-conversion and an integer-overflow flaw on 2026-11-07; the second flaw is limited to Rack 3.2.1 and earlier (Durendal, 2026-11-19).

actions: Copy the application and network logs of every self-hosted Zammad instance, then upgrade it to Zammad 7.2.3, the critical security update of 2026-11-11 that supersedes 7.2.2, and add the Remote-User header-clearing line next to X-Forwarded-User in its nginx or Apache2 configuration (the Docker images apply it automatically); a 6.5 instance that cannot be upgraded yet gets the 6.5.5 emergency fix from Zammad's new 6.5 package repository, and an older instance that cannot be upgraded goes offline.

On every instance that was internet-reachable on 6.3.0 to 6.5.4 since 2026-09-21, run DIVD's log-check script, and treat a hit, or any DEB or RPM host where code ran as the zammad account, as compromised, rotating every credential its database held (mail-channel passwords, OAuth client secrets and refresh tokens, API tokens) and revoking cloud OAuth tokens as well as isolating the host, because DIVD's forensic report shows the attacker read those tables and network isolation does not revoke tokens.

entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-102489 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-102489 / CVE-2026-102490, Zammad helpdesk: a session-hijack remote code execution and a zammad-to-root escalation, both reported exploited since 21 September; 7.2.2 fixes the root flaw on DEB and RPM installs

DIVD, the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure, says attackers first reached its systems on 2026-09-21 and that they got in through two zero-days in Zammad, the customer-service ticketing software (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09), which together allowed session hijacking, remote code execution and privilege escalation from the Zammad user to root "in seconds" (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09). DIVD's forensic report says the attacker went on from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence inside one VLAN, by ARP poisoning and forged administrator session tokens, and took credentials, about 41,000 ticket titles and volunteer contact data (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24). DIVD assesses the attack as driven by AI agents, because the attacker's scripts carry notes in which the agent justifies its own actions (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09), and its forensic report says the attacker likely used ARTEX and names no actor (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

CVE-2026-102489 is a session hijack that leads to remote code execution as the zammad user in versions 6.3.0 to 6.5.4; the defect is also present in 7.0.0 to 7.1.3 but DIVD says it is not exploitable there because of environment conditions (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01). NCSC-NL describes it as exploitable by an attacker who has not logged in (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30), while DIVD's CVE record scores it CVSS 4.0 8.7 with passive user interaction (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-09-29). CVE-2026-102490 lets the local zammad user escalate to root, in all versions including the latest alpha according to DIVD's case page (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01) and in DEB and RPM (packager.io) installations only according to Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-08 (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), and DIVD scores the pair 9.4 when chained (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-09-29). NCSC-NL states both flaws have been actively exploited since 2026-09-21, rates likelihood and damage as high, said then that Zammad had released an update for the first flaw only and that the second "is not yet fixed" (translated from Dutch) (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30). DIVD's case page instead lists patch status Available, recommends upgrading to Zammad 7 or taking Zammad offline, and says it is scanning for and notifying owners of vulnerable instances (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01).

Exposure
Self-hosted Zammad. The code-execution flaw needs a version from 6.3.0 to 6.5.4 per DIVD and NCSC-NL (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01; NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30), and Zammad says only 6.5 and older are exploitable and 7.0 and later are not affected (Zammad, 2026-10-01); the root escalation was reported by DIVD as present in every version from 1.5.0 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01), while Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-08 limits it to installations from the DEB and RPM packages (packager.io), says every released packaged version was affected and says installations from source or the official container images were not (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08); Zammad assesses it as a local privilege escalation that needs prior access to the server (Zammad, 2026-10-05), so it matters as the second stage after the code-execution flaw or any other foothold as the zammad user. Zammad says SaaS customers need take no action for 7.2.1 because their instances are already patched (Zammad, 2026-10-06), and the 27 advisories of 2026-10-06 list affected versions up to 7.2.0 (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06); the two critical ones concern the public sign-up form and accounts with multi-factor authentication configured that never completed email verification (Zammad advisory GHSA-79wh-8g2f-xj2c, 2026-10-06; Zammad advisory GHSA-f3qr-94c2-7mx2, 2026-10-06).
Detection
Web and application logs on the Zammad host. DIVD links a log-check script for the code-execution flaw that searches the Zammad application and nginx logs for error lines carrying session material, a cookie value or a client list, and says to look for unfamiliar processes and files as well (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-01; DIVD log-check script, 2026-10-01). Horizon3's public exploit shows the flaw from the attacker's side: a single request to the /ws WebSocket endpoint makes the server return an error carrying every active user's session cookies, so those error log lines are the trace, and an administrator session obtained that way can install a package through the admin interface that writes a template over the password-reset email view, so unexpected packages and overridden view templates in the application directory are the follow-on artifact (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). The forensic report adds traces: a mail-view template override or a file written through the package-upload endpoint, a setuid copy of bash, a root-run systemd loop and cron entries that run text files dropped in the web-served directory, ARP-cache changes on the application servers, and remember-me tokens in the Confluence and Jira databases that no login issued (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24). Updating to 7.2.2 closes the escalation but does not show whether it was already used: Zammad's advisory says an attacker holding a foothold as the zammad account could have reached root within seconds (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), so on any host where code ran as that account, look for new root-owned files, services and processes as well. More generally, updating does not show whether an instance was already compromised: NCSC-NL asks operators to copy application and network logs before installing the update so the second flaw's use can be investigated later (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to Zammad 7.2.3, which supersedes 7.2.2 as a critical security update (Zammad, 2026-11-11), after saving the logs: 7.2.2 fixed the root escalation on DEB and RPM installs (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), 6.5 and older receive no regular security fixes (Zammad, 2026-10-01), with 6.5.5 as an emergency fix for the code-execution flaw on 6.5 only where upgrading is not yet possible (Zammad, 2026-10-15), and 7.2.0 is affected by the advisories published on 2026-10-06 (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06); treat any internet-reachable instance on 6.3.0 to 6.5.4 since 2026-09-21 as possibly compromised, including the ticket data and anything the host can reach, since NCSC-NL says an attacker can take over the system, read, change or delete data and use it for further attacks (NCSC-NL, 2026-09-30), and treat a DEB or RPM host where code ran as the zammad account as possibly root-compromised, since the upgrade does not undo an escalation already made; keep restricting access to the underlying server to trusted administrators, as Zammad advises (Zammad, 2026-10-05), and keep Zammad behind authentication or off the internet; the forensic report asks for deny-by-default segmentation even inside one VLAN and for TLS on database links, because its intruder moved from Zammad to Jira and Confluence in the same VLAN (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).
Update04 Oct 2026 04:43 UTCrun 2026-10-04T0405Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CISA added both CVE-2026-102489 and CVE-2026-102490 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-02 and describes them as chainable (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-02). Zammad published its own statement on 2026-10-01: exploitation of CVE-2026-102489 is "only possible on Zammad 6.5 and older, because of the runtime environment those versions use", those versions no longer receive security fixes, Zammad 7.0 and later are not affected, and the code is hardened in 7.2.0, the current stable release (Zammad, 2026-10-01). For CVE-2026-102490 Zammad says "DIVD has not given us any technical details about this vulnerability", so it cannot confirm the flaw, its scope or the affected versions, names no fix, and disputes DIVD's handling of the disclosure, citing a report to Zammad on 2026-09-24 and public scanning and disclosure on 2026-09-26 (Zammad, 2026-10-01). Zammad also says it first received a report about CVE-2026-102489 in August 2026 and analysed it then, which is before the exploitation DIVD dates to 2026-09-21, so the vendor may have known of the flaw before it was exploited (Zammad, 2026-10-01).

Update06 Oct 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-10-06T0405Z-intelsummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Zammad published its own security advisory for both CVEs on 2026-10-05 (Zammad, 2026-10-05). For CVE-2026-102490 it now says it has received DIVD's technical details and is analysing the issue as a high-priority item, assesses it as a local privilege escalation that cannot be exploited remotely on its own because an attacker would need access to the underlying server beforehand, and says the issue is related to a confirmed vulnerability in packager.io and that its team is working on a solution (Zammad, 2026-10-05). The advisory names no fixed release for it. Zammad recommends that administrators still on 6.5 or older update immediately, since those versions no longer receive security updates, and that access to the underlying server be restricted to trusted administrators (Zammad, 2026-10-05).

Update07 Oct 2026 04:52 UTCrun 2026-10-07T0404Z-intelheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Zammad released 7.2.1 on 2026-10-06 as an important security update that addresses critical vulnerabilities, with no action needed for SaaS customers and an immediate upgrade advised for self-hosted installations (Zammad, 2026-10-06). The release comes with 27 security advisories published the same day, rated by Zammad as two critical, twelve high, ten medium and three low (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06); every affected range ends at 7.2.0 and none carries a CVE id yet (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06). 7.2.0, the release Zammad recommended on 2026-10-01, is therefore affected itself.

The two critical advisories: the public sign-up form accepted account fields it should have ignored, so an attacker without any account could register on an email address they did not own, have that account treated as already confirmed and add it to any organization, then read and reply to other customers' tickets in those organizations, with a second flaw letting a customer change fields of another customer's ticket in the same organization (Zammad advisory GHSA-79wh-8g2f-xj2c, 2026-10-06); and the email-verification flow established a fully authenticated session for an account that had never completed email verification and had multi-factor authentication configured, without the second factor, which needs possession of the account's verification email but no password and carries the account's permissions up to administrator (Zammad advisory GHSA-f3qr-94c2-7mx2, 2026-10-06). Among the high-rated advisories are a remote code execution through a template sanitizer bypass in automation configuration, a session identifier disclosed in an authenticated configuration response that enabled off-host session takeover, and a second-order SQL injection in ticket overview sorting (Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06).

No source reports exploitation of any of the 27 flaws. Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-05 still says its team is working on a solution for CVE-2026-102490 and none of the 27 titles names that flaw, so whether 7.2.1 closes the exploited root escalation is not stated (Zammad, 2026-10-05; Zammad advisory records, 2026-10-06).

Update08 Oct 2026 04:57 UTCrun 2026-10-08T0404Z-intelheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Horizon3 published a reverse-engineering of CVE-2026-102489 on 2026-10-07, with a proof-of-concept repository (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). Zammad keeps the state of every connected WebSocket client, including the session Cookie header, in a class-level registry that is passed to every event; a single request to the /ws WebSocket endpoint carrying the event name base makes the dispatcher instantiate an event class that has no implementation, and the resulting error message, which includes the object's full representation, is returned to the caller together with the cookies of all active users (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). With a leaked administrator session an attacker writes files into the application directory through the package installation endpoint, overrides the built-in password-reset email view with a malicious template and triggers a password reset for any user, which executes the template as the zammad user (Horizon3, 2026-10-07).

Horizon3 says it believes the privilege escalation is CVE-2026-102490, that it remains unpatched, and that it is withholding those details (Horizon3, 2026-10-07). Horizon3's write-up names no Zammad version; Zammad's advisory of 2026-10-05 says CVE-2026-102489 is exploitable only on 6.5 and earlier (Zammad, 2026-10-05).

Update10 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Zammad released 7.2.2 on 2026-10-08 as an important security update that addresses a vulnerability affecting only DEB and RPM packages built with packager.io; SaaS customers need take no action and self-hosted installations are told to upgrade immediately (Zammad, 2026-10-08). Its GitHub advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq describes a local privilege escalation to root: services started as root and executed files that the unprivileged zammad account owned and could write before dropping privileges, and that account could write to the installation directory, so an attacker already running code as zammad could have reached root within seconds because the services restarted automatically whenever they stopped; installations from source or the official container images were not affected and every released packaged version was (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08). The advisory record lists CVE-2026-102490, names 7.2.2 as the patched version and versions up to 7.2.1 as vulnerable (Zammad advisory GHSA-p97w-927q-8vxq, 2026-10-08), and DIVD's case page says Zammad has fixed the first flaw in release 7.2 and the second in release 7.2.2 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-10-09). Zammad's advisory page of 2026-10-05 still says its team is working on a solution (Zammad, 2026-10-05), so the vendor's own pages disagree on status. As of 2026-10-10 nothing had changed for the code-execution flaw: it stayed exploitable only on 6.5 and older, which received no security fixes.

Update20 Oct 2026 08:40 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0835Z-auditactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessummary

Zammad released 6.5.5 on 2026-10-15 as an exceptional security release for the unsupported 6.5 series: it hardens the WebSocket server code to address CVE-2026-102489 and is meant for customers who cannot yet move to a supported version (Zammad, 2026-10-15). It is available only through a new package repository that administrators must switch to before updating, and Zammad says it is a temporary measure that does not extend the 6.5 support lifecycle; 6.5 users who cannot upgrade to 7.2.2 yet are told to install it immediately, and every self-hosted installation is still told to upgrade to 7.2.2 as soon as possible (Zammad, 2026-10-15). The release notes name only CVE-2026-102489 and do not say whether the 6.5.5 packages also carry the root-escalation fix that 7.2.2 brought to DEB and RPM installs (Zammad, 2026-10-15). The release is for the 6.5 series only, so 6.3 and 6.4 installations, which DIVD lists as vulnerable (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-09-29), still have to be upgraded.

Update20 Nov 2026 05:14 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-inteltechniquessourcesbodycvesactionsheadlinesummary

DIVD completed its forensic investigation and updated its case file on 2026-11-18 (DIVD, 2026-11-18). It says that after obtaining root the attacker used AI agents to continue the attack, which it infers from the volume of payloads and the comments in the attack scripts (DIVD, 2026-11-18), and that the attacker was mainly interested in credentials, all of which have been rotated (DIVD, 2026-11-18). The credential material it touched was a GitLab personal access token that could not reach the internal GitLab, a Slack API key without read permission and the OAuth tokens of two shared mailboxes, used to send test emails with no mailbox-content compromise observed; only the host carrying Zammad was compromised at root level, and because direct outbound traffic from it was impossible the extraction from the ticket system was selective, about 41,000 ticket titles and a limited set of older conversations (DIVD, 2026-11-18); DIVD says its Jira and Confluence environment was also compromised, with 207 volunteer email addresses, two phone numbers and seven profile pictures taken (DIVD, 2026-11-18). DIVD says its alert arrived quickly but it took 19 hours to initiate the first response, and that there is plenty of room for improvement (DIVD, 2026-11-18). Separately, Zammad released 7.2.3 on 2026-11-11 as a critical security update that addresses several vulnerabilities, so 7.2.2 is no longer the build to install, and it requires an nginx or Apache2 configuration change that clears the Remote-User header next to X-Forwarded-User, which the Docker images apply automatically (Zammad, 2026-11-11).

Update27 Nov 2026 04:56 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

DIVD published the forensic report on its September breach on 2026-11-25 (DIVD CSIRT blog, 2026-11-25), written by Merlon Security with NVISO's analysis of the Google Workspace side. It says the attacker likely used ARTEX, on the basis of 990 scripts and 3,259 output files, scripts commented in an LLM style, an API token named artex- plus a number and a Zammad administrator account named artex.ops, ARTEX strings in an e-mail subject and the numeric job IDs that ARTEX's intents use; it names no actor (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The chain at behaviour level: the attacker probed the perimeter from 07:40 UTC on 2026-09-21; an administrator logged in to Zammad at 18:53 and the WebSocket flaw yielded that session cookie 1.3 seconds later; the replayed session wrote a file through the package-upload endpoint at 19:06 and a malicious Ruby mail template as an override of a mailer view at 19:27, which a user-creation request rendered, giving code execution as the zammad user at 19:27:58. Command and control ran through a Zammad API endpoint, with files staged in the web-served directory and fetched back through the egress proxy because direct outbound traffic was blocked. Root followed through the second flaw: a service that runs as root read configuration from a directory the zammad account owned, and a dropped file plus a kill of the web worker, which the supervisor restarted, gave root by 19:46 and left a setuid copy of bash (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

From the Zammad host, in the same web-application VLAN as Jira and Confluence, the attacker sniffed passively from 21:19 and from about 01:37 on 2026-09-22 ran ARP-poisoning scripts, reaching a man-in-the-middle position between Confluence and its PostgreSQL database at 02:27. The link was unencrypted, so it read the database protocol, learned the schema from captured traffic and injected its own SQL into live connections, writing a remember-me session token of its choosing for an administrator into Confluence's token table and presenting it at 08:49; Jira followed through its OAuth tables and a replay of remember-me tokens at 14:08. The report says TLS on the database links would have stopped the injection, asks for deny-by-default micro-segmentation inside the VLAN and says a containerised Zammad would have prevented the root step (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Persistence was a new Zammad administrator account and API tokens, a root-run systemd loop with Restart=always and cron entries that run text files dropped in the web-served directory, and an edit of Zammad's Google sign-in initializer that switched the access type to offline and added the Gmail scope, which captured nothing because no user signed in while it was live. Credentials taken included the hosting provider's mailbox password in cleartext, OAuth tokens for the two shared mailboxes, the database password, an Elastic credential and Jira's OAuth consumer private key and password hashes. NVISO says the content of the two shared mailboxes up to the credential and session resets must be considered potentially compromised, and that tokens were re-issued after the network isolation, so network isolation alone does not revoke cloud OAuth access (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The alert fired at 19:43 UTC on 2026-09-21. A volunteer first looked at it at 03:04 on 09-22, 7 h 21 min later; the CISO was informed at 15:06, 19 h 23 min after the alert; and isolation completed at 23:24, 27 h 41 min after it (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Contradiction: DIVD's case page says "it took us 19 hours to initiate our first response on 22 September 2026" (DIVD, 2026-11-25), while the report says "The first response to these alerts was observed on Sep 22nd 2026 at 03:04 UTC", 7 h 21 min after the alert, and puts the CISO notification at 15:06 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24). The case page's own metrics table lists a mean time to acknowledge of 07:20:51 ("Time between first alert and SOC pickup") and a mean time to respond of 19:16:51 ("Time between first attack and formal response"), the same 7 h 21 min the report gives for the first look and about the 19 hours of the prose, so the two documents use "first response" for different intervals (DIVD, 2026-11-25). The report counts about 39 hours of actor interaction in the cloud, to 08:33 on 2026-09-23 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Builds on: BSI flags 13 vulnerabilities patched in Zammad 7.1, admin privilege escalation in a DACH…

entries.summary: DIVD, the Dutch vulnerability-disclosure CSIRT, says attackers entered its network on 2026-09-21 through two Zammad flaws it calls previously unknown: CVE-2026-102489, a session hijack leading to code execution as the zammad user in versions 6.3.0 to 6.5.4, and CVE-2026-102490, a local escalation from that user to root. NCSC-NL states both have been exploited since 21 September and CISA listed both in KEV on 2026-10-02; Zammad says the code-execution flaw is exploitable only on 6.5 and older, and Horizon3 published the root cause and a working exploit for it on 2026-10-07. Zammad 7.2.2 (2026-10-08) fixes the root escalation, which affects only DEB and RPM (packager.io) installations, Zammad 7.2.3 of 2026-11-11, a critical security update, supersedes it, and 6.5.5 (2026-10-15) is an emergency fix for the code-execution flaw in the otherwise unsupported 6.5 series; 7.2.1 (2026-10-06) had fixed 27 newly published advisories in 7.2.0 and earlier, two rated critical, none with a CVE id and none reported exploited. DIVD's forensic report of 2026-11-25 says the attacker likely used ARTEX and moved from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence by ARP poisoning and forged administrator session tokens.
entries.title: CVE-2026-102489 / CVE-2026-102490, Zammad helpdesk: a session-hijack remote code execution and a zammad-to-root escalation, both reported exploited since 21 September; 7.2.2 fixes the root flaw on DEB and RPM installs

updates.summary: CISA added both CVEs to its KEV catalog on 2026-10-02, and Zammad's own statement of 2026-10-01 says the code-execution flaw is exploitable only on 6.5 and older (which receive no security fixes), that 7.0 and later are not affected and 7.2.0 hardens the code, and that it cannot confirm the root-escalation flaw because DIVD gave it no technical details. Zammad also says it first received a report about the code-execution flaw in August 2026, before the exploitation DIVD dates to 2026-09-21.

Zammad's own advisory of 2026-10-05 says it now has DIVD's technical details for CVE-2026-102490, assesses it as a local escalation that needs prior access to the server, ties it to a confirmed vulnerability in packager.io and is working on a solution; no fix is named yet. Zammad advises restricting access to the underlying server to trusted administrators.

Zammad released 7.2.1 on 2026-10-06 with 27 security advisories, two rated critical (a public sign-up path to other customers' tickets and a multi-factor bypass in the email-verification flow), all affecting 7.2.0 and earlier; 7.2.0 is therefore no longer the release to install. None of the advisories carries a CVE id, none is reported exploited, and no source says whether 7.2.1 fixes the exploited root escalation CVE-2026-102490.

Horizon3 published the root cause of CVE-2026-102489 and a working exploit on 2026-10-07: a single unauthenticated WebSocket request makes Zammad return an error carrying every active user's session cookies, and a leaked administrator session writes a mail template through the package installation endpoint that runs code as the zammad user. The exploited flaw now has a public exploit, and Horizon3 says the root escalation remains unpatched.

Zammad 7.2.2 (2026-10-08) fixes the local escalation from the zammad account to root that no vendor fix covered before, in DEB and RPM (packager.io) installations only; installations from source and the official container images were never affected. The exploited code-execution flaw and its public exploit are unchanged.

Zammad shipped 6.5.5 on 2026-10-15, an emergency release for the unsupported 6.5 series that hardens the WebSocket server code against the exploited code-execution flaw CVE-2026-102489; it installs only from a new package repository and does not extend 6.5 support. Zammad still tells every self-hosted installation to upgrade to 7.2.2, and the 6.5.5 notes do not mention the root escalation.

DIVD completed its forensic investigation: the attacker, who used AI agents after reaching root, was mainly after credentials (a GitLab token, a Slack key and shared-mailbox OAuth tokens); about 41,000 ticket titles and a limited set of older conversations left the host, and the first response started 19 hours after the alert. Zammad's release 7.2.3 of 2026-11-11, a critical security update, supersedes 7.2.2 as the build to install.

DIVD's forensic report of 2026-11-25 says the attacker likely used ARTEX and moved from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence by ARP poisoning an unencrypted database link and forging administrator session tokens, took credentials from Zammad's database, and kept cloud OAuth access after network isolation. The alert fired 7 h 21 min before a volunteer looked at it and 19 h 23 min before the CISO was informed; containment finished 27 h 41 min after it.

ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that as early as September 2026 Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, used the agentic penetration-testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations across many industries, government and military among them; ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent LLM system that runs a penetration test from reconnaissance to exfiltration with little human involvement (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Microsoft says ARTEX accelerated the abuse of compromised applications already granted access to Microsoft 365 tenants, and most targeting failed, yet several cases went from first targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Expel saw Storm-0940 infrastructure scan a customer and, from 2026-10-13, abuse its Okta self-service registration with no ConnectWise application involved: the attacker created five accounts, enrolled Okta Verify on three of them about a minute after activation and ran a password spray that Okta ThreatInsight blocked (Expel, 2026-10-21). Expel says the shared source address is its only link to Storm-0940, and the activity alone does not prove ARTEX was used (Expel, 2026-10-21). CrowdStrike saw another actor use ARTEX against South Korean financial institutions from late September; Recorded Future tracks it as TAG-217 (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-07; Recorded Future, 2026-10-16).

Wiz tracked an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors in October 2026, focused on identity providers and Microsoft 365 integrations; most attempts failed and none of the techniques is novel (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
Microsoft 365 tenants with applications already granted access, whose abuse ARTEX sped up (Microsoft, 2026-10-21); Entra and Okta sign-in, which the sprays target (Wiz, 2026-10-22); and any Okta org with self-service registration enabled, where not using ConnectWise does not exclude exposure (Expel, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In every identity provider's authentication logs, bursts of failed logons and lockouts spread over many accounts; in the Okta system log, newly self-registered accounts that enrol Okta Verify and start single sign-on within minutes; and in the Entra audit log, credentials or certificates added to applications that nobody on your team created and any application that assigns itself a directory role (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21). A clean audit log is not proof of no access, because Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record (Expel, 2026-10-21). In web access logs, Wiz points to source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes found only in those files, and in sign-in telemetry to a new user agent per burst at a one-second cadence (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Wiz also reports that ARTEX and Cairn write a numeric intent ID into names the agent creates (ARTEX i<N>, a per-installation counter unreset by default; Cairn i001, reset per project), visible in AWS role session names, SSM comments, tags and Azure resource names; pair it with an anchor (Wiz, 2026-11-25).

Triage: Python and curl user agents match common legitimate automation, so Expel treats them as supporting evidence only, and on the two ConnectWise applications Huntress reviewed, which call Graph with a .NET SDK, a Python user agent is the anomaly (Expel, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Expel's reading is that the framework adds speed, not a new vulnerability, so the levers are identity controls: least privilege on multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants, alerting on credential additions and privileged role assignments by applications, and a review of self-registered Okta accounts since 2026-10-13 (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21).
Improvement24 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_note

Wiz Research reports an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors throughout October 2026, focused on Okta, Entra and Cognito and on Microsoft 365 integrations, with most attempts failing (Wiz, 2026-10-22). It describes the log signatures of the agent: source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes that appear only in those files, fabricated OAuth callback values, unsigned JWTs tried against more than 60 SSO route variants in two minutes, account-recovery and sign-up calls, and password-spray bursts of 20 to 60 minutes against Entra and Okta with a unique user agent per burst and a median gap of one second between attempts (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Wiz says chaining, automatic adaptation to rate limits and blocks, and tests against heavily scrutinised Microsoft OAuth flows separate the agent from a human operator (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Update27 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-27T0256Z-intelevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Seoul Metropolitan Police announced on 2026-10-26 that it referred a 32-year-old gang leader to prosecutors on 2026-10-23, with six accomplices investigated without detention, for taking 8.2 million personal-data records and internal files from more than 90 organizations since September 2025, among them cram schools, hospitals, golf courses, universities and large-company affiliates, and for sending extortion e-mails (Yonhap, 2026-10-26, translated from Korean). BleepingComputer, citing local media, reports that the group demanded 360 million won (about USD 270,000) in 38 of the incidents in exchange for not leaking the data, that the police say the leader used the ARTEX framework, the same system used in the attacks on South Korean banks, and that he moved from conventional tools to AI utilities in late August 2026 (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-26). Yonhap counts 60 of the victims as hacked with AI and describes the system as the AI autonomous penetration-testing system used in the recent financial-sector data thefts without naming it, so the ARTEX name is BleepingComputer's (Yonhap, 2026-10-26). No encryption step is reported, and the police say AI lowered the barrier to entry and call this the first arrest in Korea in a large-scale hacking and personal-data theft case that exploited generative AI (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-26). The framework is therefore in use by a financially motivated criminal group as well as by the state-aligned actor Microsoft describes; no source reports a Swiss victim.

Update01 Nov 2026 03:29 UTCrun 2026-11-01T0256Z-intelheadlinesummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_note

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant report that since late August 2026 they have seen threat actors operate ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and possibly custom harnesses inside Mandiant incident-response engagements, with agents carrying out significant parts of the attack lifecycle such as lateral movement, database exploitation and exfiltration preparation (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31). They say ARTEX has been adopted since late August by financially motivated extortion groups and suspected PRC-nexus clusters, whose operations affected organizations in government, technology, chemicals and materials, and manufacturing in the United States, and that the campaign Wiz tracks, which GTIG tracks as UNC7228, overlaps with Microsoft's Storm-0940 and dates back to at least August 2026 (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31). The original ARTEX repository was taken down by its creator in October because of abuse, but community forks keep the framework in circulation, including a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31). ThreatBook's own launch release presents Artex Pro as an extension of the open-source Artex, developed as a personal project by the product lead of its RedAgents platform (Macau Business, 2026-10-16).

In several cases the operators handed ARTEX compromised credentials and told it to run the later stages. GTIG's log signature for the agent is execution in bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds, error-driven retries and forensically noisy trial and error; in one case, given valid credentials, the framework used an application's SQL API to point the MySQL general log at a web-accessible .jsp path and then ran SELECT statements carrying script tags, likely intended to write web shells under somewhat-incremental file names until they ran cleanly (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31).

Update07 Nov 2026 03:50 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_note

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that Storm-3358, a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organisations in Southeast Asia and a smaller number of large financial organisations globally, began using ARTEX against the financial sector in October 2026 (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). Microsoft says the cluster combines ARTEX with conventional automated tools to scan internet-facing systems, exploit flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery, and install the open-source remote access tools WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2, which ARTEX agents download with netcat and curl (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). Microsoft's tell for an agent on a scanned system is "a wide variety of requests in a brief time", retries of variations on one technique and a move to next-stage actions at machine speed; ARTEX by default drives Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients and headless Chromium through Playwright, and blocking their default traits will not stop an agent, which "will quickly change them" (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). In Microsoft's testing, honeypots, decoys, tarpits and fake wins helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets, with no figures given (Microsoft, 2026-11-06).

Check Point Research counts 2,557 systems that host or hosted ARTEX panels, 1,608 of them live and public, and ten that exposed the full database; in those ten consoles the operators set a goal and then "barely interacted with their agent fleets" (Check Point, 2026-11-05). The campaigns it reads are opportunistic crime, not espionage: iOS signing certificates from grey-market shops, a cryptocurrency-service campaign and game-account credentials. In the signing-shop campaign the agents got in through hardcoded administrator passwords in JavaScript bundles, missing API authentication, command injection, insecure direct object references, weak administrative credentials and template injection (Check Point, 2026-11-05). Check Point does not name Storm-3358.

Update08 Nov 2026 14:11 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditsourcessummary

CERT-EU, the cybersecurity service of the EU institutions, says it has seen several threat actors use ARTEX to automate their campaigns in recent weeks and has observed AI-driven activity against its own constituency that highly likely involved ARTEX; it assesses that the framework's public availability will likely accelerate adoption, notes that the public versions are independent forks since the original author withdrew the repository in October, and maps the activity to active scanning, tool acquisition and exploitation of public-facing applications (CERT-EU, 2026-11-05). Its guidance adds one point beyond limiting exposure and isolating management panels: keep non-severe findings in the remediation cycle, because AI-enabled tooling can chain minor misconfigurations into higher-impact attack paths (CERT-EU, 2026-11-05). In Switzerland, Roman Hüssy, co-head of GovCERT at the Federal Office for Cybersecurity, said at Gohack26 that no case in which autonomous AI agents hacked someone had been reported to the office so far, while AI makes attacks easier and more convincing (translated from German) (Netzwoche, 2026-11-02).

Update16 Nov 2026 04:29 UTCrun 2026-11-16T0356Z-intelheadlinesummarytechniquessourcessourcing_note

The FBI's FLASH of 2026-11-13 (TLP:CLEAR) adds a US authority's account of ARTEX use. It says a variety of malicious actors have used the framework since at least August 2026 against organisations in financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal services, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours (FBI, 2026-11-13). The original repository was withdrawn on 2026-10-08, but forks, archived copies and a commercial version keep the framework available, and researchers identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November (FBI, 2026-11-13). The FBI says ARTEX excels at finding and exploiting peripheral systems that get less security attention: partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee applications, legacy services and third-party integrations (FBI, 2026-11-13).

The FBI's table of observed activity lists these further steps. Initial access came through unsigned SAML assertions, XXE, SSRF, anonymous file upload, hard-coded administrator passwords in single-page-application JavaScript bundles, stolen VPN configurations and leaked credentials, cross-account cloud trust abused from an external partner tenant, and compromised third-party vendor credentials used across trusted B2B federation. Persistence used JSP and PHP web shells (one route was MySQL log poisoning), Kudu administrative APIs to run commands, and credentials added to existing OAuth applications. For privilege escalation and internal discovery the agents used Kerberoasting, DCSync, resource-based constrained delegation abuse and a cloud metadata query through XXE, ran iterative PowerShell enumeration against domain controllers (over 110,000 Active Directory objects), read LAPS passwords and inventoried Windows hosts without a particular EDR sensor; attempted lateral movement to domain controllers by pass-the-ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay and pass-the-hash was blocked by endpoint protection. Theft preparation used database queries, mass blob reads, custom boot scripts via EC2 instances and new 100 GB volumes, with command output sent to rotating webhook endpoints, and command and control ran through residential proxies, Tor, Chisel and SoftEther (FBI, 2026-11-13).

Telemetry the FBI lists: unexpected outbound calls to LLM API endpoints (to be read alongside other suspicious activity), high-frequency sequential enumeration against login and search endpoints, Azure Resource Manager deployment-validation dry runs across many resource types, IAM permission tests with DryRun flags and sub-second test blob writes and deletes, credential additions to applications and service principals in the Entra audit log, and .aspx or .jsp files in unexpected web-application paths (FBI, 2026-11-13). Its recommendations: inventory every internet-facing application including the peripheral ones named above, restrict Kudu/SCM endpoints, cloud administration, hypervisor and backup interfaces to trusted networks or dedicated administrative paths, and disable basic publishing authentication where it is not required. For every Microsoft 365 tenant where an affected ConnectWise application is or was authorised, it asks for a review by application ID of activity from at least 2026-10-01 and says not to delete the enterprise application before evidence is preserved (FBI, 2026-11-13).

Update20 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-intelsourcesbody

The European Commission confirmed on 2026-11-19 that an AI-generated cyber campaign hit its internal systems: its spokesperson said the incident was detected on 2026-10-22 and confirmed on 2026-10-26, that several applications were taken offline as a protective measure and most are restored, that there is no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole and that it is not aware of a ransom request, and the Commission names no tool or attacker and declines to attribute or size the campaign (European Commission, 2026-11-19). POLITICO, citing an anonymous EU official, reports that CERT-EU detected earlier this month that international hackers used ARTEX, that the staff HR platform Sysper and the medical-reimbursement system MyPMO were disrupted for more than 10 days, and that investigators have not yet established whether staff data was compromised (POLITICO, 2026-11-19). The dates differ: the Commission says detection was on 2026-10-22, while POLITICO's official places CERT-EU's finding of ARTEX use earlier in November, and the sources do not reconcile them. The Commission has not confirmed the ARTEX link (European Commission, 2026-11-19), and the reporting does not establish whether ARTEX provided entry or was only used to find weaknesses (Cyber Security News, 2026-11-19).

Improvement22 Nov 2026 15:01 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditbody

Who is exposed, by source: Microsoft ties ARTEX's speed-up to Microsoft 365 tenants whose applications already hold access (Microsoft, 2026-10-21); Wiz saw the sprays go after Entra and Okta sign-in, hitting hundreds of users, mainly software engineers (Wiz, 2026-10-22); and Expel's case needed only Okta self-service registration, so not using ConnectWise does not exclude exposure (Expel, 2026-10-21).

Update26 Nov 2026 05:05 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelheadlinesummarytagsentitiestechniquessourcesevidencebodyupdated_at

Microsoft's defender guide of 2026-11-25 says it has observed state-sponsored and financially motivated actors such as Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon integrating ARTEX into their tooling (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). For Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet the basis is Microsoft's report of 2026-10-29, which says it has identified both using ARTEX since late October 2026 and says that human operators likely continue to direct intent and objectives (Microsoft, 2026-10-29); the guide gives no campaign detail for Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, which The Record describes as Chinese state-backed groups (The Record, 2026-11-25). The Record also reports that The New York Times and Nextgov said ARTEX was allegedly used in attacks on the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (The Record, 2026-11-25). Nextgov, citing people familiar with the matter, says ARTEX is believed to have been used in the breach of an unclassified CIA and ODNI system for analyzing public and commercially available information and in an intrusion into the Defense Department's Cyber Defense Command, which one of its sources called low-impact, and that it is unclear who carried out the CIA and ODNI breach or whether information was taken (Nextgov, 2026-11-24).

Microsoft says ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November and began offering commercial access to an ARTEX Pro (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). ThreatBook's own launch release of 2026-10-16 already lists Artex Pro as an extension of the open-source Artex, developed as a personal project by the product lead of its RedAgents platform, and says the open-source edition was converted to closed source on 8 October 2026 after attackers misused it (Macau Business, 2026-10-16); GTIG lists ARTEX PRO among community forks, whereas ThreatBook's release presents it as the vendor's own extension, so the sources differ on whether it is a fork.

Microsoft says ARTEX can drive virtually any model, including open-weight and guardrail-stripped ones, and can switch models when one fails, so its activity is not necessarily constrained by any single provider's safety controls or visible in any single provider's telemetry; it adds that ARTEX introduces no new techniques and does not obfuscate by default, and calls behavior the most durable signal: a wide variety of requests in a brief time, retries of technique variants and next-stage actions at machine speed (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). Its detections, by telemetry class: on web servers, web-server processes (w3wp.exe, php-fpm, httpd or apache2, Java application servers) starting shells, script files created in web-accessible or upload directories, including files a database server process writes after its log file was pointed at a web directory, several short-lived web shells with incrementing names, and rapid reads of /etc/shadow, .env files, private keys and cloud credential files; in access logs, a client requesting 100 or more distinct paths with 50 or more client errors in one minute; in Entra sign-in logs, one address attempting service-principal sign-ins for three or more applications within an hour with both failures and successes, where a success after an invalid or expired client secret error warrants immediate investigation; in the audit log, one identity adding application credentials and assigning roles or permissions within an hour, and in one case an application assigning itself Global Administrator; and on egress, reverse shells and requests from servers to webhook and file-sharing services, where Microsoft's lever is to restrict outbound connections from web servers (Microsoft, 2026-11-25).

Microsoft's thresholds are defaults to tune: exclude build and automation servers that run shells under Java or Node.js, review file names because content management system updates also write script files, and do not alert on default curl, Wget, Python or headless Chromium user agents alone (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). Service-principal sign-ins are logged separately from interactive ones, so an empty hunt proves nothing where they are not collected (Microsoft, 2026-11-25).

Update27 Nov 2026 04:54 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_notebodyupdated_at

Wiz Research shows how ARTEX and Cairn leak their intent numbering into victim logs. ARTEX draws intents, facts, findings, hints and digests from one counter per installation that is never reset by default, so intent numbers climb across runs and targets and consecutive ones are rare, and it puts the number in its working directory, its session name and its prompt; Cairn formats zero-padded counters per object type and resets them for every project (Wiz, 2026-11-25). The numbers surface wherever an API takes a name or comment: AWS role session names, SSM command comments, KMS key descriptions and aliases, security-group rule descriptions, Azure run-command, VM and app-registration names, and the error message of a denied call (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Wiz uses them to link activity across rotating residential-proxy addresses and victims, to separate installations and to read scope from a jump far larger than the activity in one victim's logs, and cautions that hits are tool markers and pacing clues, not operator fingerprints: unrelated installations collide in the same ranges and operators reset or parallelise (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Google's report of 2026-10-31 had already seen incremental numeric markers in ARTEX file names, account names, passwords and e-mail subjects without being able to explain them (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31).

Wiz's account of ARTEX-Harvester ties it, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organisations between late October and mid-November, clustered by a distinctive boto3 build, the cross-victim intent counter and proxy-pool overlap, and warns that activity labelled ARTEX comes from multiple unrelated operators; these two posts do not mention Storm-0940 (Wiz, 2026-11-23).

Huntback reads an exposed ARTEX console whose workspace holds a South Korean university, where the numbering also leaks onto the victim, with a local administrator account named after an intent number. Single sign-on accepted a stored password hash as the password, a Microsoft 365 password-reset bridge ignored the old password, and a password-grant token, which involves no browser and no second factor, carried Global Administrator from 18:47:53 UTC on 2026-11-16; student-style accounts were then created and licensed and a further account was made Global Administrator (Huntback, 2026-11-24). Huntback says a Conditional Access policy requiring multi-factor authentication for every user and blocking legacy and non-interactive password sign-ins would have stopped the token request, names no actor, and says its detection queries were not run against a live workspace (Huntback, 2026-11-24).

DIVD's forensic report on its own September breach says the attacker was likely using ARTEX and that ARTEX's intents are numeric job IDs included in all input and output (DIVD, 2026-11-24).

actions: Take the management interface of every PA-Series and VM-Series firewall and Panorama off the internet now by restricting it to a jump box or trusted internal addresses, because Palo Alto reports active exploitation against internet-exposed management interfaces, and install the hotfix PAN-SA-2026-0015 lists for your maintenance release (12.2.4-h3; 12.1.4-h15, 12.1.7-h15, 12.1.10-h6; 11.2.4-h25, 11.2.7-h25, 11.2.10-h19, 11.2.13-h6, 11.2.16-h3; 11.1.4-h40, 11.1.6-h42, 11.1.7-h14, 11.1.10-h38, 11.1.13-h18, 11.1.16-h6; 10.2.7-h41, 10.2.10-h45, 10.2.13-h29, 10.2.16-h14, 10.2.18-h15), which includes the PHP2Shell fix and fixes the kernel flaw as well.

Rotate the directory bind account, HA replication keys, certificate private keys and device authentication keys of every PAN-OS firewall and Panorama that was reachable from the internet while unpatched and shows a PHP web shell or a tunnel, because the chain Dream Research recovered harvested exactly those from rooted firewalls, and the hotfix does not remove a web shell or tunnel already in place.

entries.headline: PAN-OS management interfaces rooted via PHP2Shell and a kernel flaw, both exploited per Palo Alto: hotfix, then check
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-109618 +2exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Panorama: the PHP2Shell flaws affect every release below its train's hotfix through the management web interface, and Palo Alto reports active exploitation against internet-exposed management interfaces; all twenty hotfixes are out

Palo Alto Networks' advisory of 2026-10-21 lists PAN-OS 12.2, 12.1, 11.2, 11.1 and 10.2 and Panorama as affected by CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the unauthenticated PHP remote-code-execution flaws (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21) (PHP, 2026-10-21). Only the management web interface is affected; the GlobalProtect portal and gateway and the captive portal are not (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).

The advisory says active exploitation has been observed against the management interface exposed to the internet (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-28). Dream Research reports that a custom PHP2Shell build for the PAN-OS management web server, chained with the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 to turn the web server's unprivileged context into root in one unauthenticated HTTPS request, rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). On the second of two firewalls of a US government-affiliated organization (the first crashed) it added a reboot-persistent reverse SSH tunnel and, through it, ran the same chain against the organization's internal firewall management server, decrypted the directory service account's password from the device configuration, enumerated the Active Directory and attempted a password spray and backdoor accounts, which Dream cannot say succeeded (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). Unit 42 says it independently verified the attacker's tooling and results and that customers who applied the available patches are not affected (Unit 42, 2026-10-29); Dream relays that Unit 42 tracks it as CL-UNK-1280, a Chinese-speaking attacker in UTC+8, while Dream names none (Dream Research, 2026-10-29).

All twenty hotfixes are released (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-30). Palo Alto's bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 of 2026-11-24, labelled Informational, says exploitation of the kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 has been observed against internet-exposed management interfaces and that the only known way to exploit it is PHP2Shell first, so a PHP2Shell hotfix protects against that chain; it lists a later hotfix in every train that also fixes the kernel flaw, to install at the next maintenance interval where management access is restricted and immediately, with access restricted, where it is internet-reachable (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).

Exposure
Every PAN-OS firewall and Panorama appliance below its train's hotfix through its management web interface; it is reachable from the internet where the management port, or a dataplane interface with a management profile, answers from outside the administrator range (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).
Detection
In management-plane web access logs, very large multipart POST requests from outside the administrator range (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). A hotfix does not remove an attacker already in: on an interface that was internet-reachable and unpatched, look for a PHP file nobody deployed in a web-reachable directory of the management web server, a systemd service or rc.local entry that starts scripts from a hidden directory under /usr/local/lib, and outbound SSH from the management plane; in directory logs, bulk LDAP enumeration and password-spray bursts against all users, launched from the firewall management server (Dream Research, 2026-10-29).
Defender takeaway
Move management access behind a jump box or trusted internal addresses, as Palo Alto recommends (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-27), and install the hotfix for your maintenance line. An interface that was internet-reachable and unpatched is a possible root compromise until those checks are clean; where a web shell or tunnel turns up, rotate what the device held: the directory bind account, HA replication keys, certificate private keys and device authentication keys (Dream Research, 2026-10-29).

Dream Research updated its report on 2026-10-29 to say that the affected devices run Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS; the operation it had described with an unnamed vendor rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers, and Unit 42 says it independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed the reported results (Dream Research, 2026-10-29; Unit 42, 2026-10-29). Dream's recovered artifacts show web shells left on 24 firewalls, 22 of them parked with nothing further done, and a boot-persistent tunnel into the internal network of a US government-affiliated organization that it assesses is likely still active (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). Unit 42 says customers who applied the available patches are not affected and that the management interface is not exposed to the internet by default (Unit 42, 2026-10-29). Dream also says the management web server fronts the GlobalProtect portal, which Palo Alto's advisory lists as not affected (Dream Research, 2026-10-29; Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-30). Palo Alto Networks published bulletin PAN-SA-2026-0015 on 2026-11-24 at 23:10 UTC (its timeline's initial-publication entry; the page header reads 2026-11-25), titled "OSS CVEs Fixed in PAN-OS" and labelled Informational with a zero CVSS block; its exploitation-status block reads "Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet" (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24). CVE-2026-46300 is the Linux kernel flaw Dream Research chained with PHP2Shell, so the vendor now itself states exploitation of the second half of the chain that Dream Research described; CISA's catalog has listed the kernel flaw as exploited since 2026-10-28 (CISA KEV, 2026-11-25). It has no workaround section and no affected-product table and says nothing on Panorama, Prisma Access or Cloud NGFW for this flaw; its mitigation is restricting management access to trusted internal addresses (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-11-24).

entries.headline: Mitel MiCollab AWV flaws exploited pre-advisory per Accenture APEX, CISA lists them; patching alone does not evict
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-133323 +4exploitedupdatedNATOA2

Mitel MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier, MISA-2026-0012: an unauthenticated blind command injection in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing component (CVSS 3.1 10.0) and four more flaws there, one an XML injection that can run commands (9.0); CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133303 lead the five assigned CVE ids, patch KB000129195, Accenture APEX Labs reports exploitation before the advisory and CISA lists all five as exploited since 2026-11-25

Mitel's advisory MISA-2026-0012, first issued on 2026-11-16, covers five flaws in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier; Mitel tracks them by internal ids and, since its revision 2.0 of 2026-11-24, lists the CVE identifiers against them (Mitel, 2026-11-16); MITRE published the record for CVE-2026-133323 on 2026-11-19 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-19). MTLVULN-1864 lets an unauthenticated attacker conduct a blind command injection through insufficient parameter sanitization and is scored CVSS 3.1 10.0 with changed scope; MTLVULN-1862 lets an unauthenticated attacker leverage pre-staged malicious content for an XML injection that could run arbitrary commands, scored 9.0 with high attack complexity (Mitel, 2026-11-16). Three further flaws are rated Medium: an unauthenticated arbitrary file upload through weak file-type validation (MTLVULN-1861, 5.3), unauthorized access that needs a system-generated random identifier or pre-staged content (MTLVULN-1863, 5.9) and an authentication bypass (MTLVULN-1877, 5.3) (Mitel, 2026-11-16). Mitel says exploiting them together can significantly amplify their impact (Mitel, 2026-11-16).

Accenture APEX Labs reports exploitation before the advisory: web-shell activity at one victim before 23:00 UTC on 2026-11-15, root within about 30 minutes, and the credentials stored for MiCollab's LDAP connector used against a domain controller 32 minutes after the first request (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24). The internet-facing reverse proxy at that victim did not stop it, and APEX does not say which of the five flaws were used (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24).

The fix is a patch for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18), delivered through knowledge-base article KB000129195 on Mitel's customer portal, or an upgrade to a later release that Mitel does not name; Mitel's partners can supply it to customers without portal access (Mitel, 2026-11-16). Mitel's July advisory named 10.3 (10.3.0.18) as the release that fixed its earlier AWV command injection, so a system moved there in July is inside the new affected range (Mitel, 2026-07-22). CERT-FR lists the advisory on 2026-11-17 (CERT-FR, 2026-11-17); BSI's revision of 2026-11-25 rates it critical, says active exploitation was reported and describes a remote anonymous attacker who can manipulate files, run code with the service's rights and bypass security measures (BSI, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier whose AWV component external users can reach, including through a reverse proxy or MiVoice Border Gateway web proxy, which APEX says cannot be assumed to protect it (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24); Mitel assesses only supported versions and states no branch before 10.3 (Mitel, 2026-11-16).
Detection
Child processes of the AWV service, new files in the component's upload paths and unauthenticated requests to conferencing endpoints that carry shell metacharacters or XML payloads, which follow from the command-injection, upload and XML-injection mechanisms the advisory names (Mitel, 2026-11-16). APEX adds POSTs to AWV CGI scripts from unfamiliar sources followed by requests for new files in the web pictures directory, the LDAP connector account authenticating to many domain controllers, and system logs that suddenly shrink (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24).
Defender takeaway
Apply the patch now; where that waits, restrict external access to the AWV component, the mitigation Mitel names (Mitel, 2026-11-16). APEX says patching alone will not close an intrusion that started earlier, and the actor filtered local logs: image the server first, compare its logs with proxy and WAF logs, and treat a suspected compromise as a directory compromise by resetting the LDAP connector account and Kerberoastable service accounts (Accenture APEX Labs, 2026-11-24).
Improvement20 Nov 2026 05:11 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-inteltitlesummarycvessourcesbodyentities

MITRE published CVE records for all five flaws on 2026-11-19, which Mitel's advisory page did not yet list on that date.
