entries.headline: Danfoss AK-SM 800A: six unpatched pre-auth RCE flaws, Strict mode does not remove them; France blames IRGC
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-129713 +4exploitedupdatedNATOA2

Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised in France, at least six more European countries and Switzerland, with France blaming the IRGC unit Shahid Kaveh for the October campaign; Midnight Blue reports six unpatched pre-authentication flaws in AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2

Coopérative U, Intermarché and E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP on 2026-10-12 a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems (AFP, 2026-10-12). CERT-FR knows of numerous compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers and of Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16); NCSC Switzerland rates the activity actively exploited (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). On 2026-11-09 France's foreign ministry attributed the 11 to 12 October campaign, and only that campaign, to the Iranian unit Shahid Kaveh (French foreign ministry, 2026-11-09).

Midnight Blue reports six pre-authentication remote-code-execution stack overflows in every Danfoss AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2 (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11). Danfoss assigned CVE-2026-129713 (CVSS 9.3) to an unauthenticated stack overflow in AK-SM 8xxA firmware 5.4.0 and earlier, fixed only in a coming 5.5.x, without saying if it is one of the six (Danfoss, 2026-11-20). CCB says the research also finds a flaw in session control, so Strict mode does not remove the risk (CCB, 2026-11-12). BSI reports exploitation attempts against two Copeland XWEB EVO flaws (translated from German) (BSI, 2026-11-17).

On 2026-11-02 refrigeration failures reached retailers in at least six more countries (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-02) and the first German cases followed (heise, 2026-11-03); SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known Swiss cases, at a butcher in Köniz and three Volg stores (SRF, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
A Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC refrigeration controller, or a Copeland or Dixell xweb unit, whose management interface is reachable from the internet, legacy units above all, since Danfoss told AFP that most affected units no longer receive updates (AFP, 2026-10-12); the six new flaws are reported for the AK-SM 800A (CCB, 2026-11-12). BACS says Switzerland is affected too and that the controllers also run in butchers, restaurants, pharmacies, doctors' practices, laboratories and farms, many of whose operators do not know they are reachable from the internet (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10).
Detection
On the controller, defrost, setpoint and account changes outside a maintenance window, and defrost duration, which Le Monde reports the attackers lengthened from one hour to eight (translated from French) (Le Monde, 2026-10-12); in firewall, provider VPN or ISP logs, inbound connections to the management interface from addresses other than the contractor's. Midnight Blue says an attacker with code execution could hide the activity from any system logs (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11), and CSIRT Italia says to check actual temperatures and alarms with instruments independent of the supervision platform (CSIRT Italia, 2026-11-04).

Triage: a defrost cycle is normal; BFMTV reports that installations can be programmed for two hours of defrost per 24 hours, whereas the reported attack is a continuous forced defrost at a 50-degree setpoint (translated from French) (BFMTV, 2026-10-12).

Defender takeaway
Take any Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC, Copeland xweb or Dixell xweb management interface off the internet and restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network, as CERT-FR advises (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). For the AK-SM 800A, patching and Strict mode do not close the exposure: CCB calls updating, new passwords and Strict mode insufficient on their own (CCB, 2026-11-12), while BSI asks operators to take internet-reachable devices offline and, on suspicion of compromise, to change all credentials (translated from German) (BSI, 2026-11-17). The legacy AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 have no fix and accept documented default credentials (CVE-2026-127057); Danfoss says to move to the AK-SM 800A (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13; Danfoss, 2026-11-20).
Update14 Oct 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryregionsentitiesaffected_productssourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesactionsbody

CERT-FR revised its alert on 2026-10-13: the list of compromised remote controllers now includes Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb besides Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, campaigns against these devices are probably still ongoing, and an unpatched end-of-life unit kept on the internet is very likely to be compromised, so a factory reset alone is insufficient (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). NCSC Switzerland published advisory 13054 on 2026-10-13 with the exploitation status Actively Exploited. It lists the Danfoss AK-SM 800 (end of life, no longer patched), the AK-SC 355 (phased out, no longer patched) and the current AK-SM 800A series when it runs outdated firmware, says no fixes exist for the two older models and that Danfoss urges replacing them, and says the attack could affect other sectors, such as healthcare for specialized cooling equipment, so organisations should check whether affected devices are in use (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). Danfoss told Cooling Post that the AK-SM800 was declared end of life in 2021, that the AK-SC355 was phased out in 2016, and that the affected AK-SM800A systems ran outdated firmware (Cooling Post, 2026-10-12). Blick reports that Migros uses the same Danfoss refrigeration systems in a limited number of Swiss stores and sees no sign they were targeted, and that Aldi, Lidl and Coop say they are not affected (Blick, 2026-10-13); as of 2026-10-14 no source reported a Swiss victim. The advisory relays a six-step CERT-FR sequence (limit access to trusted addresses, factory reset, apply all fixes, rotate passwords and secrets, review accounts, reconfigure) and lists filtering to trusted addresses as a temporary measure (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13), whereas the revised CERT-FR page puts removal of internet exposure first, accepts source-address filtering only as an emergency stop-gap and lists no secret rotation or account review (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).

Improvement15 Oct 2026 03:49 UTCrun 2026-10-15T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Censys, which scans for Danfoss StoreView control panels, says Danfoss has not confirmed the initial access vector and points to three AK-SM 800A flaws that Danfoss patched more than a year earlier: CVE-2025-41450 (March 2025), which Censys describes as letting an unauthenticated actor log in as an administrator with a code computed from the current calendar date, and CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452 (August 2025), which it says let authenticated users run commands and disrupt the management interface (Censys, 2026-10-14). Censys maps the firmware by build: below 4.2 carries all three, 4.2.4 fixes only the date-based login and still carries the two later ones, and 4.3.1 or later fixes all three (Censys, 2026-10-14). Its scan counted 1,825 exposed StoreView panels in France on 2026-10-11 and 537 on 2026-10-14, a fall of 71 percent, with builds below 4.2, build 4.2.4 and builds from 4.3.1 leaving at about the same rate, which it reads as operators taking controllers off the internet rather than patching them (Censys, 2026-10-14). Outside France the count fell from 1,166 to 966, and in ten of the twelve countries with the most exposed hosts more than 60 percent of the hosts run a build below 4.3.1, led by Poland at 81 percent and Romania at 80 percent (Censys, 2026-10-14).

Update18 Oct 2026 03:33 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelsummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

CERT-FR's alert now has a third version, dated 2026-10-16 and listed on the page as an update of the recommendations; the page does not show which sentences changed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). Its current text separates the two cases. For every unit it asks to remove the internet exposure of the affected units and of any unit on a public IP address, and to check the insurance contract conditions before cutting the data uplink to the refrigeration contractor (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). For a unit not known to be compromised it then asks to check the whole configuration, notably the defrost ranges; for a compromised Danfoss unit it says to restart the equipment or otherwise restore it with a factory reset, and then to reconfigure it for service (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). In both cases access returns only through a secure VPN or protected network, with source-address filtering for the contractors an emergency measure and not a lasting one, and the maker's practices apply (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). The alert still says campaigns are probably ongoing, still names no flaw or entry vector, and gives the risk as not specified by the vendor (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16).

The alert's documentation section links an operator guide from Dixell France (Copeland) (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16). The file at that address was replaced on 2026-10-18; its current text is Copeland's bulletin of 14 October 2026 followed by Dixell France's own complement (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). That complement says XWEB PRO and EVO ship with the same factory account, Admin with the password Admin, advises keeping the original Admin password sealed or in a password manager and not using it daily, gives each user a named account with an expiry date for an external contractor's account, and requires remote access through an encrypted VPN, with no port forward or DMZ and no remote-control software such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer on a site PC that stays on (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). CERT-FR does not say how the attackers got in, and SecurityWeek writes that neither Danfoss nor French authorities have tied the attack to the flaws Claroty disclosed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-16; SecurityWeek, 2026-10-15).

Correction19 Oct 2026 04:06 UTCrun 2026-10-19T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The Dixell France guide that CERT-FR links was replaced on 2026-10-18, the file's date on the vendor's server, and now opens with Copeland's own security bulletin dated 14 October 2026 (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). The bulletin acknowledges the vulnerability on a generation of XWEB EVO controllers that is no longer marketed and has reached end of life, says to remove every XWEB EVO from the public internet immediately and then look for suspicious activity from the local network, and says XWEB EVO no longer receives security patches, while XWEB PRO is the supported platform and must not be exposed to the internet either (Dixell France, 2026-10-14). For an XWEB EVO that may have been accessed it gives a procedure: isolate the unit, restore the latest backup made before the access or otherwise check the users and profiles, set new passwords, check the alarm categories and recipients with a test alarm, and restore the device parameters from backup files or, without one, read each device's parameters and check setpoints, alarm thresholds and defrost parameters; it also says to check the product temperatures in the cabinets directly, since altered setpoints or alarm thresholds can compromise food safety (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).

Le Monde reports that besides raising the defrost temperature to 50 degrees the attackers lengthened the defrost operation from one hour to eight so that alarms trigger late, which delayed interventions and amplified the damage (translated from French) (Le Monde, 2026-10-12). SecurityWeek relays that detail and adds that the Paris prosecutor's office said the attack caused fires as well as food losses, that the Finance Minister put the number of affected supermarkets at about 700 of roughly 10,000, and that investigators are reportedly puzzled by the lack of a claim of responsibility or a ransom demand, citing Reuters (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-15). Cybersecurity Dive had already reported that a Copeland spokesperson confirmed the vulnerability was found in discontinued end-of-life controllers (Cybersecurity Dive, 2026-10-15).

Update25 Oct 2026 03:37 UTCrun 2026-10-25T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

ANSSI's director general, Vincent Strubel, told the French Senate foreign-affairs committee on 2026-10-21 that the attack rested on elementary security flaws, starting with refrigeration equipment directly on the internet and administered without particular protection, and weak passwords, and he dismissed analyses that tied it to vulnerabilities researchers had published over the previous two years (Public Sénat, 2026-10-21). Le Monde Informatique reports the same hearing and adds that the systems were reachable without a firewall or network segmentation and that the management interface was protected only by weak passwords (Le Monde Informatique, 2026-10-22). Neither outlet reports evidence beyond the testimony, and ANSSI names no actor; the account sits against Copeland's acknowledgment of a vulnerability in its end-of-life XWEB EVO controllers and the earlier report, from a person close to the Prime Minister, that ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in a Danish company's software (AFP, 2026-10-12), and no source reconciles them; the two outlets also differ on the date and the count, Public Sénat giving the night of 12 to 13 October and more than 700 supermarkets, Le Monde Informatique the night of 11 to 12 October and at least 300 Intermarché and Netto shops. Le Monde Informatique adds that ANSSI can alert and advise but has no means to impose connection rules on retailers (Le Monde Informatique, 2026-10-22), and Public Sénat reports that ANSSI ran a rapid check with health-sector players because laboratories and pharmacies that store vaccines use the same kind of refrigeration equipment (Public Sénat, 2026-10-21).

Forescout's Vedere Labs says on 2026-10-22 that the access vector, exploited vulnerabilities, attacker infrastructure, persistence and responsible actors in the French incidents remain unconfirmed, and that the reported changes, made in rapid succession, used ordinary supervisory functions (Forescout, 2026-10-22). Its tracking of hacktivist groups counts over 20 claimed attacks on refrigeration systems since January 2026, the most active being the pro-Russian groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) through internet-exposed human-machine interfaces, and its count of exposed services is 12,976 observations on 6,017 public addresses in 99 countries, with 3,762 exposed Danfoss StoreView observations on AK-SM 800A units, 80 percent of the 4,697 StoreView observations, on firmware older than 4.3.1 (Forescout, 2026-10-22). Forescout adds that the manufacturers' documentation presents internet remote maintenance through port forwarding as a supported option, so the exposure is not only an accident of configuration (Forescout, 2026-10-22).

Update02 Nov 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-11-02T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencebody

Reuters reported on 2026-10-29, citing four officials, that the Pentagon is treating the late-August freezer failures at military bases across the United States as a suspected hack (Reuters, 2026-10-29). On Reuters' own review of the bases' social-media posts at least six commissaries were hit, and in at least one case the cooling units' temperatures were raised overnight instead of the units stopping; Fort Huachuca said its freezer "went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food" (Reuters, 2026-10-29). A Cyber Command unit and the Army Criminal Investigation Division's Cyber Field Office are involved, and one official said the investigators are in touch with their French counterparts about the French attack; Reuters could not establish whether Danfoss or any other controller brand was in use at the bases, nor how far the investigation had got or who might be responsible (Reuters, 2026-10-29).

Nextgov reported on 2026-10-30, citing two people familiar with the matter, that US officials suspect Iran-linked hackers, that the intrusions began around late August, that how the intruders got in is not clear and that the assessment may change (Nextgov, 2026-10-30). No official has attributed the activity on the record, and the sources give no technical evidence for the suspicion. The only stated link between the two cases is the investigators' contact, and Reuters notes that the French attack, like the Fort Huachuca failure, raised temperatures instead of switching units off (Reuters, 2026-10-29).

Update03 Nov 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-11-03T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

On 2026-11-02 refrigeration failures struck stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia, and Finland according to The Guardian; BleepingComputer counts more than 115 affected stores from company statements and says it is unclear whether they were hit in a coordinated attack, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-02; The Guardian, 2026-11-02). Sabcobel's chief executive says the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode (The Guardian, 2026-11-02) and, per BleepingComputer, that the attacker used the same vulnerability as in France (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-02); Euronews names Danfoss as the software supplier in both incidents and quotes it saying customers who had not updated their software were affected (Euronews, 2026-11-02), and in Estonia attackers reached the control computer of an older Danfoss system with outdated software (translated from German) (Tagesschau, 2026-11-02). CyberInsider nonetheless states that the manufacturer, controller models and initial access method of the new wave remain unknown (CyberInsider, 2026-11-02), so the vendor of the Belgian and Swedish sites is not independently confirmed. Coop Switzerland told 20 Minuten that corresponding attempts were registered without success, and Migros reports no indication of an attack (20 Minuten, 2026-11-02). The head of Sweden's national cybersecurity centre says it is working on incidents around the country and that Sweden has quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices (The Guardian, 2026-11-02).

Update04 Nov 2026 03:30 UTCrun 2026-11-04T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebodyactions

The first German cases followed on 2026-11-02: heise reports that the cooling systems of an Edeka market in Reisbach, Lower Bavaria, were heated to 50 degrees overnight into Monday and that the police have not confirmed a cyberattack as the cause, and WDR quotes a division manager at a CAP supermarket in North Rhine-Westphalia saying the actual attack hit the firm that maintains the cooling plants remotely, which is the operator's statement and not an authority finding, and Rewe's head office confirmed to WDR a cyberattack aimed specifically at the cooling-system supplier Danfoss, whose technology only a few regional Rewe stores use (translated from German) (heise, 2026-11-03; WDR, 2026-11-03). SentinelLABS' assessment of 2026-11-03 says responsibility for the European incidents has not been publicly established, calls Russian-aligned disruptive groups one credible hypothesis based on precedent, and says shared maintenance access deserves scrutiny (SentinelLABS, 2026-11-03). Le Canard enchaîné reports that Coolworld, a company that maintains refrigerated storage containers for the French blood service, was hacked overnight on 1 to 2 November and that cold rooms held at minus 30 degrees were programmed to reach 110 degrees; the blood service says an on-duty technician saw the temperature rise and acknowledges that frozen plasma intended for transfusion was among the products, and the Health Ministry says there was zero operational consequence because the situation was spotted (translated from French) (Le Canard enchaîné, 2026-11-03). The 110 degrees is the programmed set-point and not a measured temperature, and no source names the equipment, the vendor or the access method, or ties this case to the Danfoss and Copeland controllers.

Update05 Nov 2026 04:02 UTCrun 2026-11-05T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysectorssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The French blood service EFS confirmed on 2026-11-03 that on 2 November a refrigeration-equipment supplier suffered a cybersecurity incident that affected the supervision and control installations of cold rooms at three EFS sites, with temperature and defrost thresholds raised to very high values (translated from French) (EFS, 2026-11-03). EFS says its own monitoring and alarm systems identified the anomalies quickly, the affected equipment was brought under control without impact on the products or neutralised, the products stored in those cold rooms were transferred preventively to other installations, and no health impact or loss of blood products is to be reported; it names no supplier and gives no temperature figure (translated from French) (EFS, 2026-11-03).

BleepingComputer, heise and SRF identify the supplier as Coolworld, and SRF reports that the attackers reportedly entered through its remote maintenance (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-04; heise, 2026-11-04; SRF, 2026-11-04). Coolworld's statement of 2026-11-04 says the incident involved remote monitoring software, that the vulnerability reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier outside its control and that a limited number of its units were affected; it does not say that attackers exploited that component (Coolworld, 2026-11-04). BleepingComputer's account reads it the other way, saying Coolworld says the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party component, which the statement does not state (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-04). No source names Danfoss, Copeland or Dixell equipment for this case.

ENISA, the European Commission (DG CNECT), Europol's EC3, the EU CSIRTs Network and EU-CyCLONe issued a joint statement on 2026-11-04: since 11 October 2026 several commercial refrigeration systems and similar devices have been hit in a number of EU Member States, a new wave occurred on 1 to 2 November, affected Member States are investigating and issuing guidance, and organisations are advised to take immediate action to mitigate exposure in the affected systems; it names no product, actor or count and does not mention Switzerland (ENISA, 2026-11-04). CSIRT Italia's bulletin of 2026-11-04 extends its call to every operator of cold-chain technology, whatever the sector, to apply its earlier measures urgently, removing direct internet exposure of administrative and control interfaces and verifying that operating parameters and alarms are intact first (CSIRT Italia, 2026-11-04). Its bulletin of 2026-10-13, re-issued on 2026-11-04 as version 1.2, asks operators to limit supplier access to authorised resources and periods, to require multi-factor authentication on remote access, applied on the mediating system when the device cannot do it, and to check actual temperatures and alarms with instruments independent of the supervision platform (CSIRT Italia, 2026-11-04). The BSI had urged operators of networked freezer controllers to disconnect them from the internet or at least secure and patch them (heise, 2026-11-04).

Update06 Nov 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-11-06T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known attack of this kind in Switzerland: the butcher Lüthis Fleischwaren in Köniz, canton Bern, told customers that manipulation of the electronic control of its cooling and freezer systems caused considerable temperature deviations, the owner told SRF he found 50 to 70 degrees in the freezer, and the firm disconnected the installation from the network and closed the branch (translated from German) (SRF, 2026-11-05). Keystone-SDA adds that the shop can probably only reopen on 20 November and that the Bern cantonal police were briefly informed on Monday and had received no complaint yet (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). Volg says three of its stores noticed that parameters in the cooling shelves had been changed (SRF, 2026-11-05). No source names the controller make, the access route or a maintenance provider in the Swiss cases; Keystone-SDA notes that operators can supervise cooling plants centrally over the internet and that the butcher apparently has such an installation, which is the agency's inference and not the owner's statement (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). BACS told Keystone-SDA that it does not comment on specific incidents and has received one reportable notification about a cyberattack on commercial refrigeration so far, and it stressed that voluntary reports are welcome at any time (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). Blutspende SRK Schweiz told Keystone-SDA that no attacks on Swiss blood-donation services are known to date (SRF, 2026-11-05).

On the same day CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT published a joint fact sheet on malicious cyber activity against industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide: the actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, through authentication bypass, arbitrary code injection or weak configurations, with loss of visibility into current temperatures as a further effect (CISA, 2026-11-05). It names no vendor, CVE, victim or actor; its mitigations include keeping controller panels off the internet, allowlisting the devices and IP addresses that may change settings, defining reasonable setpoint limits for downstream devices with alerting on deviations, and collecting network traffic between OT assets where logs are not available (CISA, 2026-11-05).

Update07 Nov 2026 03:53 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_note

NCSC Switzerland edited its advisory on 2026-11-06 with the reason "added Swiss incidents, Copeland/Dixell XWEB and healthcare attacks" and states that "The public information reviewed does not establish a common attack method across these incidents or confirm exploitation of the specific Danfoss CVEs listed above"; it lists CVE-2025-41451, CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41452 as "alleged as potentially related" (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). Its checklist asks operators to review refrigeration management systems across all relevant operations, "including equipment managed by external service providers"; to remove direct internet access to management interfaces and provide remote access through a secure VPN; to check temperature settings, defrost schedules, alarm thresholds, notification recipients and user accounts, verify actual temperatures and test alarm delivery; and to apply current firmware and plan to replace equipment that no longer gets security updates (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). For a suspected compromise it says "A factory reset alone is insufficient if the system remains vulnerable and directly accessible from the internet" (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13).

Ransom-ISAC published the event log of a Copeland XWEB Pro controller, reportedly on firmware 1.9.0 and reachable through a public address, compromised on 2 November: two Administrator sessions from different external addresses read parameters across 31 devices, then made 588 writes across 26 devices in about six minutes, which Ransom-ISAC reads as scripted or bulk programming rather than manual edits, and 155 further writes across five cold rooms, moving setpoints to 110 and 150 degrees C and recording keypad-lock, alarm-mute and defrost commands (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06). The post says the controller still used its default Administrator credentials, publishes no evidence for that statement, says the log cannot show how the attackers got in or what temperatures were reached, and says it has no evidence linking the case to NoName057(16), Z-Pentest Alliance or the French attacks (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06). Its suggested alerts are more than about 20 parameter-write events a minute from one account, writes to more than three devices within five minutes, and keypad-lock, alarm-mute or defrost commands that do not come from the scheduler (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06).

Unit 42 counts over 5,000 internet-exposed devices across countries from the manufacturers CERT-FR names on 5 and 6 November, and for France alone 1,853 in the first half of October, 558 in the second half and 316 in the first six days of November, and says the claims of NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance remain unverified (Unit 42, 2026-11-06). The counts do not show which versions are vulnerable.

Update10 Nov 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagsentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

France's foreign ministry said on 2026-11-09 that, following the investigation, France is able to attribute the destructive actions of the night of 11 to 12 October to Iran, carried out by the cyber-offensive unit Shahid Kaveh, affiliated with the electronic and cyber centre of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and calls it the first cyber-offensive campaign run purely for sabotage on French soil (translated from French) (French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, 2026-11-09). The report of the C4 crisis cell, which CERT-FR published, words the case as a bundle of indicators that names the Revolutionary Guard as sponsor and Shahid Kaveh as executing unit (translated from French) (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09). The indicators it lists are attack infrastructure also used in the same period to reconnoitre Schneider Electric equipment, use of the FOFA scan tool, which it says the unit habitually uses, relay of the attack on the unit's CyberbanNews outlet from 13 October, and traces of Farsi in the attack infrastructure (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09).

The same report says the unit is known mainly through hacktivist personas, CyberAveng3rs among them, and the CyberbanNews outlet, and that it has held scripts since at least June 2024 to scan, access and control Schneider Electric, Siemens and Rockwell industrial equipment; in April 2026 it was seen using Modbus on TCP port 502 for mass reconnaissance of Schneider Electric systems, including in France (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09). The C4 links to the same attack the concurrent targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at small hydroelectric installations in France, with moderate effects on the targeted equipment (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09). Industrial controllers of that class, reachable on Modbus, belong in the same internet-exposure check as the refrigeration controllers.

The attribution covers the French campaign of 11 to 12 October. Sekoia's honeypots recorded unauthenticated requests to the controllers' xml.cgi endpoint from 26 addresses, password spraying of the Supervisor and admin accounts and, on 2026-11-01, an attempt to use a non-public flaw that renames an account by its numerical identifier; Sekoia says the evidence shows similarities between the October and November waves that suggest they may share an actor, and that it assesses the NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance claim with doubts (Sekoia, 2026-11-10). Reuters reports that the Paris prosecutor's office said it had requested international arrest warrants against the leader of Shahid Kaveh and his two deputies, and that it could not establish exactly how the French made their determination (Reuters via NBC News, 2026-11-09). NCSC Switzerland's advisory still says the public information does not establish a common attack method across the incidents (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13).

Update11 Nov 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencebody

BACS published a public warning on 2026-11-10, which repeats the earlier warning of the Cyber Security Hub advisory cited above; it says the attacks of recent weeks show that Switzerland is affected too and that it is repeating its warning because the systems are widespread among small and medium-sized businesses (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10). Per BACS, attackers reach management interfaces that are directly reachable from the internet and then change temperatures, defrost cycles, alarm thresholds or notification settings remotely, which can spoil food, medicines and other temperature-sensitive goods; it names the end-of-life AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355, the current AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family when it runs outdated firmware, and Copeland and Dixell XWEB.

What is new is the wider population: BACS lists butchers and food producers, restaurants and hotels, pharmacies, doctors' practices and laboratories, logistics and warehouses, industry and farms among the users, many of which do not know their cooling plants are reachable from the internet or run by an external provider, and it repeats what the Hub advisory already said, that security updates fixing the known flaws are available for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family and that newer firmware activates additional protections and enforces encrypted HTTPS communication (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10). It recommends identifying the controllers, those run by contractors included, installing vendor updates, restricting unsupported systems to trusted networks or a VPN, reaching them remotely only through one centrally managed access point with default passwords replaced, and replacing end-of-life products; it names no attacker, no exploited CVE and no count of Swiss victims.

Update14 Nov 2026 03:55 UTCrun 2026-11-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagssourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Midnight Blue published on 2026-11-11 a report on six pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaws in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A, which it says it found within an hour of manual investigation and which affect all versions up to and including 5.3.2 (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11). It says the exploited application runs as root, that the controller does not use the processor's secure-boot features, which makes malicious firmware that survives a factory reset or bricks a device feasible, and that the strict session-control mechanism also has at least one trivial pre-authentication memory-corruption flaw; it recommends against spending scarce effort on patching and in favour of reducing exposure (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11). At that date no CVE identifiers existed yet and technical details were withheld during coordinated disclosure with Danfoss (Midnight Blue, 2026-11-11).

BSI's first notice of 2026-11-13 (version 1.0, since revised), criticality 3 (Orange), listed no fixed version, said nothing was known about active exploitation and warned that the report may give attackers enough hints; its worst case is a remote attacker loading malicious firmware that leaves the devices unusable until they are replaced or restored by hand (translated from German) (BSI, 2026-11-13). CCB's advisory of 2026-11-12 relays the research, says no patches were available and that removing direct public internet exposure must not wait for them, and says Strict mode does not eliminate the risk because the research identifies a flaw in the session-control mechanism itself (CCB, 2026-11-12). heise reports that BSI told it that it does not want to rule out vulnerabilities in firmware 5.4.0 of 12 November either (heise, 2026-11-13). Danfoss's advisories page lists no advisory on the six as of 2026-11-14 (Danfoss, read 2026-11-14), and the readme for software release 5.4.0 says an update from 4.x leaves the security settings unchanged and names no vulnerability (Danfoss, read 2026-11-14). BACS's statement of 2026-11-10 that updates fix the known flaws (BACS, 2026-11-10) predates the report and does not address these six.

Update21 Nov 2026 04:39 UTCrun 2026-11-21T0355Z-intelsummarytechniquescvessourcesevidencebody

Danfoss published two advisories on 2026-11-20. DSA-2026-12-01 assigns CVE-2026-129713 (CVSS 9.3) to a stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the AK-SM 8xxA series, firmware 5.4.0 and earlier: crafted HTTP or HTTPS POST requests cause memory corruption and a web-server restart and, in Danfoss's words, hypothetically arbitrary code execution with web-server privileges, with no authentication; the fix is an announced 5.5.x release that is not yet published, Danfoss will remove the option to disable Strict mode, and its mitigations are no internet exposure, access only through a VPN or protected network, Strict mode and strong passwords (Danfoss, 2026-11-20). DSA-2026-12-02 assigns CVE-2026-127057 (CVSS 9.9) to default or known passwords on all versions of the legacy AK-SC 355 and AK-SM 800, which shipped with default credentials documented in the product manual; Danfoss's remediation is to replace the fleet with the AK-SM 800A series (Danfoss, 2026-11-20). Neither advisory reports exploitation in the wild or says whether CVE-2026-129713 is one of the six flaws Midnight Blue reported. BSI's warning, now at version 1.1 (2026-11-17), reports sensor-observed exploitation attempts against two Copeland XWEB EVO flaws (translated from German) (BSI, 2026-11-17).

Improvement22 Nov 2026 14:59 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditbodytitle

The early report that ANSSI had found a flaw in the vendor's software comes from a person close to Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who told AFP that the agency had identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor" (AFP, 2026-10-12).

Update26 Nov 2026 05:06 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelsummarytagscvessourcesevidencebodyupdated_at

CISA added three Danfoss AK-SM 800A flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25 (CISA, 2026-11-25): CVE-2023-25914, a path traversal that could let an attacker read system files of the underlying server through the XML interface, CVE-2023-25915, an improper input validation that could let a remote attacker run arbitrary commands, and CVE-2025-41450, an authentication bypass that generates a web report exposing internal IP addresses, usernames and store names (CISA KEV catalogue, 2026-11-25). CISA names no campaign, actor or victim and cites Danfoss's advisories as the vendor source for them, so no source ties the listing to the October and November attacks. The catalogue's description of CVE-2025-41450 as a web-report disclosure differs from Censys's account of a date-derived administrator login (Censys, 2026-10-14).

Danfoss's advisory for the two 2023 flaws lists AK-SM 800A software below 3.3 as affected, fixed by software 3.3, scores them 7.5 and 9.8 and does not state whether authentication is needed (Danfoss, 2023-08-21); the discoverer Synacktiv calls CVE-2023-25914 unauthenticated and says CVE-2023-25915 needs authentication, and has described the pair as a chain since 2023-10-31 (Synacktiv, 2023-10-31). CISA's ICS advisory of 2026-11-24 covers CVE-2026-129713 only, scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8 and says no known public exploitation specifically targeting the vulnerabilities it covers has been reported to CISA (CISA, 2026-11-24).

entries.summary: Coopérative U, Intermarché and E. Leclerc confirmed a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems overnight on 11 to 12 October 2026, a remotely forced defrost at hundreds of French stores, and on 2026-11-09 France's foreign ministry attributed that campaign, and only that campaign, to the Iranian unit Shahid Kaveh. More followed: more than 115 stores in at least six more countries and the first German shops on 2026-11-02, altered cold-room settings at three sites of the French blood service through a supplier, and, per SRF on 2026-11-05, a Köniz butcher and three Volg stores in Switzerland. CERT-FR reports numerous compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers and of Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb, and NCSC Switzerland rates the activity actively exploited. On 2026-11-11 Midnight Blue reported six pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaws in all Danfoss AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2, and on 2026-11-20 Danfoss published CVE-2026-129713 (CVSS 9.3, an unauthenticated stack overflow in AK-SM 8xxA firmware 5.4.0 and earlier, fix only in an announced 5.5.x) and CVE-2026-127057 (CVSS 9.9, default credentials on every legacy AK-SC 355 and AK-SM 800, no fix); CCB says updating, new passwords and Strict mode are insufficient, so removing internet exposure comes first, and BACS's statement of 2026-11-10 that updates fix the known flaws predates the report and does not cover the six. CISA added three older AK-SM 800A flaws (CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915 and CVE-2025-41450) to its exploited-vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25 without tying them to this campaign.
entries.title: Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised in France, at least six more European countries and Switzerland, with France blaming the IRGC unit Shahid Kaveh for the October campaign; Midnight Blue reports six unpatched pre-authentication flaws in AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2

updates.summary: CERT-FR revised its alert on 2026-10-13 to add Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb to the compromised controllers, says campaigns are probably still running, and says a factory reset alone is insufficient on an unpatched end-of-life unit. NCSC Switzerland published an advisory rating the activity actively exploited and naming the current AK-SM 800A on outdated firmware, and Danfoss says that is the case for the affected current units. Blick reports that Migros uses the same Danfoss systems in a limited number of Swiss stores and sees no sign they were targeted.

Censys's exposure report of 2026-10-14 points to three published 2025 AK-SM 800A flaws that Danfoss patched more than a year earlier and gives their firmware boundaries (4.3.1 or later fixes all three; Danfoss has not confirmed the vector), and shows exposed French controllers falling about 71 percent in three days with patched and unpatched builds leaving at the same rate, which Censys reads as operators taking units offline rather than patching.

CERT-FR's alert has a third version dated 2026-10-16 whose guidance differs for compromised and uncompromised units: the whole configuration, defrost ranges included, is to be checked, and a compromised Danfoss unit is to be restarted or otherwise factory-reset and reconfigured, with a caution to check insurance conditions before cutting the contractor's data uplink. The Dixell France operator guide that the alert links says any XWEB PRO on firmware 1.12.1 or earlier must be updated without delay, that XWEB units ship with a factory Admin account, and that remote access must go through an encrypted VPN; neither document names an entry vector.

The Dixell France guide that CERT-FR links was replaced on 2026-10-18 and now carries Copeland's own bulletin of 14 October 2026, which acknowledges the vulnerability on a discontinued, end-of-life generation of XWEB EVO controllers, says to remove every XWEB EVO from the public internet at once, gives a restore procedure and says to check product temperatures in the cabinets directly; the earlier statements about XWEB PRO firmware 1.12.1, a CISA advisory and a March 2024 bulletin are no longer on that page and are removed. Le Monde's report that the defrost operation was lengthened from one hour to eight so that alarms trigger late, and SecurityWeek's figure of about 700 supermarkets, the prosecutor's report of fires and the absence of a claim or ransom demand, are added, with Cybersecurity Dive's report that Copeland confirmed the flaw was found in discontinued controllers.

ANSSI's director general told the French Senate on 2026-10-21 that elementary flaws were exploited, starting with controllers directly on the internet, administered without particular protection, and weak passwords, not vulnerabilities researchers had published, so a firmware update alone does not close the exposure. Forescout, on 2026-10-22, counts 12,976 exposed service observations in 99 countries, 3,762 exposed Danfoss StoreView observations on AK-SM 800A units, 80 percent of the 4,697 StoreView observations, on firmware older than 4.3.1, and over 20 hacktivist-claimed refrigeration attacks since January 2026, and says the French access vector remains unconfirmed.

Reuters reports that the Pentagon treats late-August freezer failures at at least six US military commissaries as a suspected hack, with Cyber Command and Army investigators in touch with their French counterparts, and Nextgov adds that two people familiar with the matter say US officials suspect Iran-linked hackers; neither says how the intruders got in, and no official has attributed the activity on the record.

The attacks returned on 2026-11-02 across Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia, and Finland per The Guardian: BleepingComputer counts more than 115 stores and says it is unclear whether the attacks were coordinated, Sabcobel says its sites were hit through the same vulnerability as in France, Euronews names Danfoss as the software supplier in both incidents while CyberInsider says the manufacturer and access method of the new wave remain unknown, and Coop Switzerland says attempts against it failed.

The attacks reached Germany: heise reports an Edeka market in Reisbach whose cooling systems were heated to 50 degrees overnight into 2 November, WDR quotes a CAP supermarket manager saying the attack hit the firm that maintains the cooling plants remotely and reports that Rewe's head office confirmed an attack aimed at Danfoss; SentinelLABS says responsibility has not been publicly established; and Le Canard enchaîné reports that cold rooms of a contractor of the French blood service were programmed to 110 degrees overnight on 1 to 2 November, with no source tying that case to these controllers.

The French blood service EFS confirmed that an incident at its refrigeration supplier on 2 November altered the temperature and defrost thresholds of cold rooms at three of its sites, caught by its own alarms with no loss of blood products, so the case no longer rests on Le Canard enchaîné alone; ENISA, the European Commission, Europol and the CSIRTs Network advised organisations on 2026-11-04 to take immediate action, CSIRT Italia issued cold-chain measures, and no source ties the blood-service case to the Danfoss, Copeland or Dixell controllers.

SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known cases of the refrigeration attacks in Switzerland, a butcher in Köniz whose freezer reached 50 to 70 degrees and three Volg stores with changed cooling parameters; BACS has received one reportable notification about an attack on commercial refrigeration, and CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT published a joint fact sheet on refrigeration and cold-chain controllers that names no vendor, CVE or actor. No source names the controller make or the access route in the Swiss cases.

NCSC Switzerland updated its advisory on 2026-11-06 with the Swiss incidents, Copeland and Dixell XWEB and healthcare, a four-point checklist for refrigeration management systems across all relevant operations, supplier-managed equipment included, and the statement that the public information does not establish a common attack method or confirm exploitation of the Danfoss CVEs it lists. Ransom-ISAC published the event log of one internet-reachable Copeland XWEB Pro compromise (743 parameter writes in two administrator sessions, default credentials claimed without published evidence), and Unit 42 counts over 5,000 exposed devices across countries on 5 and 6 November and a falling count in France since October.

France's foreign ministry and the C4 crisis cell attributed the 11 to 12 October refrigeration-controller campaign to Iran on 2026-11-09, naming the Revolutionary Guard unit Shahid Kaveh, and the Paris prosecutor requested arrest warrants against its leader and two deputies; the French documents cover that campaign only, and the later waves and the Swiss cases are not attributed in them.

BACS published its own public warning on 2026-11-10: it says Switzerland is affected and that the controllers also run in butchers, restaurants, pharmacies, doctors' practices, laboratories, logistics, industry and farms, many of whose operators do not know their plants are reachable from the internet, and it repeats that security updates for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family exist and that newer firmware enforces HTTPS.

Midnight Blue reported on 2026-11-11 six pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaws in all Danfoss AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2, with no CVE identifier, no fixed version and no known exploitation (BSI); CCB says updating, new passwords and Strict mode are insufficient and removing internet exposure comes first, and BSI will not rule out flaws in firmware 5.4.0 (heise).

Danfoss published CVE ids for two controller flaws: CVE-2026-129713 (CVSS 9.3, unauthenticated stack overflow in AK-SM 8xxA firmware 5.4.0 and earlier, fix only in a coming 5.5.x) and CVE-2026-127057 (CVSS 9.9, documented default credentials on every legacy AK-SC 355 and AK-SM 800, no fix). BSI's version 1.1 warning reports exploitation attempts against two Copeland XWEB EVO flaws.
The early report that ANSSI had found a flaw in the vendor's software comes from a person close to the French Prime Minister, quoted by AFP; the campaign reached at least six more European countries.

CISA added two 2023 Danfoss AK-SM 800A flaws, CVE-2023-25914 (file read through the XML interface) and CVE-2023-25915 (command execution), and the 2025 authentication bypass CVE-2025-41450 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2026-11-25 without naming a campaign; no source ties the listing to the refrigeration attacks. The 2023 flaws are fixed in software 3.3, and CISA's advisory for CVE-2026-129713 says no known public exploitation specifically targeting that vulnerability has been reported to it.

entries.action_label: 1Password breach via an employee GitHub account…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: 1Password breach via an employee GitHub account exported customer records; vaults not affected
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

1Password: an attacker used an employee's corporate GitHub account to push malicious code to backend services that downloaded administrative data about a subset of customers, and copied private-repository source code and reached the CI/CD system; vaults were not affected

1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 that on 2026-11-19 it began investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account (1Password, 2026-11-25). The attacker used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data about customers; the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the CI/CD system, which holds infrastructure secrets, and 1Password rotated every credential that may have been exposed (1Password, 2026-11-25). It says the actor had stolen a token and that vault contents, the keys that protect them, account recovery keys and its apps and browser extensions were not affected (1Password, 2026-11-25).

The records taken for a subset of users, whose size is not stated, are names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, tokens embedded in certain emailed invitation, SCIM Bridge and Hosted Provisioning, and account-recovery links, and non-secret internal metadata (1Password, 2026-11-25). Those tokens complete an invitation or recovery only together with an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which 1Password has lengthened from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters, and it says it found no evidence of account takeover with the exposed tokens; its advice to customers is caution about phishing that mentions invitations or account recovery, that it will never ask for the account password or Secret Key, keeping both safe, and reporting suspicious messages to its support address (1Password, 2026-11-25). BleepingComputer adds that the harvested name and email list is useful for such phishing (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
Any organisation with 1Password accounts, since users' names, sign-in addresses and identifiers were in the copied records, and especially one using SCIM provisioning or account recovery, because tokens in those emailed links were among the data; 1Password says it notified a small number of users with pending invitations or recoveries directly (1Password, 2026-11-25).
Detection
In the identity provider's and 1Password's administrator audit records, invitation, provisioning and account-recovery events since about 2026-11-19 that no administrator or user requested; in mail-gateway logs, inbound mail that imitates 1Password invitations or recovery messages with real tenant or user details; and user reports of recovery codes nobody asked for. These checks are analysis from the data classes the post lists, which publishes no indicator.

Triage: a legitimate invitation or recovery message follows an administrator's or user's own action; one that arrives without it is the signal.

Defender takeaway
1Password's own advice covers phishing caution, never sharing the password or Secret Key and reporting suspicious messages, and BleepingComputer says it is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-25); the action is to warn users about phishing that mentions invitations or account recovery and to watch for unrequested provisioning events. For your own pipelines the mechanism is one employee source-control identity that could push to backend services and reach CI/CD, so require review on the deploy path and alert on pushes and workflow changes made with employee tokens.

The attacker also copied private-repository source code and reached the CI/CD system, and 1Password rotated every credential that may have been exposed. 1Password says vault contents, vault keys and recovery keys were not affected and the exposed tokens need an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which it lengthened; it does not say how the account was compromised or how many customers are affected.

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: SEPPmail 15.1.2 fixes unauthenticated GINA account takeover (9.3) and ten more flaws; update the gateway
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-130637 +10NATOA2

SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway before 15.1.2: an unauthenticated template injection on the GINA login page can read and take over any GINA account (CVE-2026-130637, vendor score 9.3) and ten more flaws are fixed in the 2026-11-24 patch release; no exploitation or workaround stated

SEPPmail's revision history lists patch release 15.1.2 of 2026-11-24 with eleven security fixes, each marked as affecting versions before 15.1.2 (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The worst is CVE-2026-130637 (vendor score 9.3): request values reflected on the GINA login page were processed by the template engine, which could let an unauthenticated attacker read attributes of any GINA account and take it over, and the fix stops expanding request values as template placeholders. Two further rows score 9.2: CVE-2026-124840, where a session created by answering the security question was also accepted by the registration and settings workflows, so an attacker who knows the security answer could replace the password, and CVE-2026-124843, where a hard-coded fallback secret was used if the appliance's key material could not be loaded, which could let encrypted Large File Transfer attachments be decrypted outside the appliance (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24).

The remaining rows are CVE-2026-124844 (8.7), unauthenticated GINA uploads that were never removed and could fill the disk; CVE-2026-124838 (8.5), a configuration-service socket open to every local user; CVE-2026-124842 (8.3), an unauthenticated GINA request that reset the password of a registered account without the security question; CVE-2026-124839 (7.7), a crafted GINA account address that reached a shell command in a maintenance script at start, with elevated privileges; and four rows at 6.9 to 6.3 covering unescaped LDAP filter values (CVE-2026-124841, CVE-2026-124836), a crafted DKIM signature that injects forged Authentication-Results later covered by the gateway's ARC seal (CVE-2026-124837) and a GINA domain lookup that falls back to the default domain settings (CVE-2026-124845) (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The page names no exploitation and no workaround, and does not say whether the 15.0 branch, whose last release is 15.0.7, is affected.

Exposure
A SEPPmail Secure E-Mail Gateway before 15.1.2 whose GINA web interface is reachable from outside; the revision history says release 15.1.0 added support for restricting the file types that external communication partners can upload through GINA, which shows external recipients use it (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24). The page does not state the CVSS vector of any score.
Detection
In GINA web access logs, login-page requests whose parameters carry template placeholder syntax, unauthenticated password-reset requests for accounts that are already registered, calls to the registration and settings workflows that follow a security-question recovery, and bursts of unauthenticated uploads; in the gateway's audit log, GINA password changes without the usual recovery sequence. The fixes do not undo an account already taken over, so review GINA password-change and sign-in history for the period before the update. These checks follow from the mechanisms the vendor names; the page publishes no indicator.

Triage: an unauthenticated password reset on a GINA account that is not yet registered is legitimate, since the fix keeps it for unregistered accounts only; the same request taking effect on an already registered account without the security-question step is the abuse (SEPPmail, 2026-11-24).

Defender takeaway
Update every gateway on 15.1 to 15.1.2 and, for gateways on the 15.0 branch, ask SEPPmail whether these flaws apply, since the page does not say; where GINA is internet-facing, give the update priority within the regular cycle, because the template injection and the unauthenticated reset need no login, and review GINA account changes made before the update.

Builds on: SEPPmail gateway: unauthenticated sender reaches root RCE or file access; fixed in 15.1.1…

entries.action_label: Okta: AI agents sign up with mail.tm; its rotating…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Okta: AI agents sign up with mail.tm; its rotating domain will very likely outdate blocklists within weeks
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Okta Threat Intelligence: AI agents register on Auth0 tenants and Okta organizations with disposable addresses from the mail.tm service, whose single rotating mailbox domain makes blocklists very likely stop matching within weeks; ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and pentestcode each picked it at run time

Okta Threat Intelligence reports that since June 2026, and at scale through October and November, AI agents have registered accounts with disposable email addresses on Auth0 tenants and Okta organizations that allow public self-service registration, activity Okta calls almost certainly malicious and that customers often reported alongside attacks on their applications (Okta, 2026-11-23). The addresses mostly belong to the mail.tm family, a free receive-only service whose API needs no account or key and lets a script create a mailbox, obtain a token and poll for one-time codes (Okta, 2026-11-23). In tests by the P0 Labs team of Permiso, which Okta acquired on 2026-08-26 (Okta, 2026-07-30), the ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and pentestcode frameworks each picked mail.tm at run time, and in a data set containing attacker tooling mail.tm appeared on 80 percent of the attacker hosts where disposable email was found (Okta, 2026-11-23).

mail.tm exposes only one active mailbox domain at a time and replaces it periodically, so a blocklist built from earlier domains will very likely stop matching within weeks; Okta's Auth0 telemetry shows sign-ups tracking the domain the API currently returns, and the attackers' domain changed around 2026-10-30 when the API response did. Agents also used mailinator, guerrillamail and emailnator, and at one target an agent moved to another provider when blocked, which Okta reads as agents treating disposable mail as an interchangeable capability. Okta says the use always occurred within a short window of other agentic reconnaissance and intrusion attempts against the same entities (Okta, 2026-11-23). Bot detection and CAPTCHA generally stopped the October mail.tm sign-ups before email verification, but Okta warns agents can solve challenges and commonly register by calling the Auth0 Authentication API directly, which can skip protections applied in Universal Login (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
An Auth0 tenant or Okta organization that allows public self-service registration. For workforce users Okta says self-service registration is a prerequisite for many of the attacks it describes and should be disabled or restricted (Okta, 2026-11-23).
Detection
In identity-provider registration telemetry, sign-up events whose email domain belongs to a disposable provider's currently active mailbox domain, kept current by polling the provider's public domain endpoint instead of a static list, as Okta advises (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Triage: the discriminator Okta supports is context: a disposable-domain sign-up read alongside other agentic reconnaissance or intrusion attempts against the same entities, not the domain alone (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Defender takeaway
On Auth0, block sign-ups through the API while allowing Universal Login and block disposable domains with Actions; on Okta Workforce Identity, disable or restrict self-service registration. Treat a disposable-domain sign-up as a prompt to look for other agentic activity against the same estate, since Okta says it gives a heads-up to look for successful intrusion attempts, and do not rely on CAPTCHA alone (Okta, 2026-11-23).

Builds on: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names… · ARTEX in AWS: CloudWatch log searches for secrets, Cognito self-sign-up for credentials; hunt… · Elastic: CyberStrikeAI against AWS, six medium or low alerts joined only by source IP; alert on… · Barracuda: an unretired vendor cloud key led an ARTEX-consistent intruder across ten accounts… · Unit 42: AI agents behind web shells in 10+ campaigns; hunt 1.4 s command gaps and…

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: Splunk Enterprise: unauthenticated REST bypasses accept an empty pass4SymmKey (CVSS 9.4, 9.1); set the key, upgrade
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-76536 +3NATOA2

Splunk Enterprise SVD-2026-1103: two unauthenticated REST API authentication bypasses that accept an empty shared secret (CVE-2026-76536 in the cluster configuration endpoint, CVSS 3.1 9.4; CVE-2026-76535 in RapidDiag task collection, which runs searches as an authenticated user, 9.1) and three more unauthenticated rows at 7.5; fixed in 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12 and 9.4.17, no exploitation reported

Splunk's advisory SVD-2026-1103 of 2026-11-18 fixes 38 flaws in Splunk Enterprise, two rated Critical and unauthenticated (Splunk, 2026-11-18). CVE-2026-76536 (CVSS 3.1 9.4) lets an unauthenticated user use an empty clustering shared secret to read and modify clustering configuration through the cluster configuration REST endpoint on a standalone instance with clustering turned off, and CVE-2026-76535 (9.1) lets an unauthenticated user run arbitrary SPL searches through RapidDiag task collection as an authenticated user, because Splunk Enterprise accepts an empty shared secret on those requests (Splunk, 2026-11-18). Three further unauthenticated rows are rated 7.5: CVE-2026-131192 gives access to live event data from the indexing pipeline on a standalone instance or a search head that is not an indexer cluster member, on an empty shared key, and CVE-2026-131190 exposes RapidDiag process metadata and a log file inventory through endpoints that accept a factory-default shared key, and a third lets an unauthenticated user crash the Splunk daemon through the S2S data-forwarding receiver, for which Splunk lists no workaround (Splunk, 2026-11-18).

Splunk lists fixes in 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12 and 9.4.17, with CVE-2026-76536 and CVE-2026-131190 not listed for the 10.6 branch (Splunk, 2026-11-18). For CVE-2026-76535 Splunk says to set a non-empty pass4SymmKey in server.conf, using the same value on each node that participates in the service, and restart; for CVE-2026-76536 the workaround is a strong, unique pass4SymmKey of at least 12 characters in the [clustering] stanza of server.conf, standalone instances included, followed by a restart; CVE-2026-131190 is closed by turning off or removing the RapidDiag app (Splunk, 2026-11-18). The advisory does not say any flaw is exploited; NCSC-NL rates the likelihood medium and the damage high (NCSC-NL, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
A Splunk Enterprise instance whose pass4SymmKey is empty or unset (for CVE-2026-131190, one that accepts RapidDiag's factory-default key) and whose management REST API can be reached by an untrusted host; Splunk does not say an empty secret is the default on a stock install, so the effective value in server.conf is the thing to read on each instance, and Splunk Cloud impact is not addressed in the advisory.
Defender takeaway
Set a non-empty pass4SymmKey on every Splunk Enterprise instance now, since that is the workaround for the two Critical rows, and take the upgrade at the next window if the management API is internal; instances reachable from user or internet networks are the ones to do first.

entries.headline: Rejetto HFS pre-auth session forgery reaches code execution and is exploited since 2026-10-02; update to 3.2.1
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-61500exploitedupdatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-61500, Rejetto HFS < 3.2.1: predictable session-signing PRNG lets an unauthenticated attacker forge admin sessions to RCE (CVSS 9.3)

VulnCheck disclosed CVE-2026-61500 in Rejetto HFS (HTTP File Server) 3.0.0 through 3.2.0 (VulnCheck, 2026-07-13), fixed in 3.2.1 on 2026-07-13 (Rejetto, 2026-07-13). The headline flaw, CVE-2026-61500 (CVSS 4.0 9.3, CWE-338 weak PRNG), derives the session-cookie signing key from JavaScript's non-cryptographic Math.random() and leaks outputs of that same generator to unauthenticated clients on the login endpoint; an attacker who collects a small number of login responses can reconstruct the generator's internal state, recover the signing key and forge a valid administrator session cookie, reaching full admin access and code execution through HFS's built-in server_code configuration feature, with no authentication or user interaction (VulnCheck, 2026-07-13). Exploitation is reported: VulnCheck warned on 2026-10-02 of small-scale reconnaissance against CVE-2026-61500 that hit its canaries (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-05), and GreyNoise observed an actor forge the admin cookie on an unpatched HFS server from 2026-10-02 and keep it as a relay (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
Any internet-reachable Rejetto HFS 3.0.0 through 3.2.0 (VulnCheck, 2026-07-13); GreyNoise saw an unpatched server taken over from 2026-10-02 (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).
Detection
In HFS request logs, the recovery-then-forge sequence shows as a short burst of repeated login requests immediately followed by an authenticated, admin-privileged session, then privileged actions such as server_code edits, command hooks or an SSH key appended to root's authorized_keys from that session, with a forged cookie carrying a flag that lets it work from any source address (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

Triage: a genuine admin login issues a Set-Cookie from the server before any privileged action; a forged session presents a valid-looking admin cookie the server never issued and is typically preceded by a cluster of login probes used to recover the generator state, either signal alone is weak, the sequence is the tell.

Defender takeaway
Treat any internet-reachable HFS instance below 3.2.1 as possibly compromised now that exploitation is reported, and upgrade to 3.2.1; the primitive is a forged admin cookie, not a memory-corruption craft, so weaponisation is cheap.
Update25 Nov 2026 04:48 UTCrun 2026-11-25T0356Z-intelactionsbodycvesentitiesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

GreyNoise reports that an actor it tracks as GT13 exploited CVE-2026-61500 on an unpatched Rejetto HFS server from 2026-10-02: repeated login requests gave it the generator state, it forged an administrator cookie that carried a flag letting it work from any address, and it then used HFS command hooks to append an SSH key to root's authorized_keys and kept the server as a relay for an intrusion campaign against Check Point management servers (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23). VulnCheck had warned on 2026-10-02 of small-scale reconnaissance against the flaw that hit its canaries (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-05). entries.headline: vCenter auth bypass exploited since September; Metasploit module in public review: patch to 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 or 8.0 U3m
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-123890 +4exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-123890, VMware vCenter Server: an unauthenticated authentication bypass in the Directory Service gives an administrator session; GTIG reports the suspected China-nexus actor ARMORY CASTLE exploited it from early September, Broadcom lists no workaround; first fixed in 8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200 and 9.1.1.0200, with 9.1.2 and 9.0.2.0300 now superseding the 9.x builds (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

Broadcom's advisory VMSA-2026-0009 of 2026-11-19 fixes CVE-2026-123890, an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter that needs only network access (CVSS 3.1 9.8), with no workaround; it does not state exploitation (Broadcom, 2026-11-19; Broadcom, 2026-11-19). Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus actor, exploited it from early September 2026 with its BONESAW utility, in one intrusion (GTIG, 2026-11-19); BleepingComputer notes Broadcom has not confirmed it (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-19), and CISA listed the flaw as exploited on 2026-11-20 (CISA, 2026-11-20).

The cause is a session-key disclosure over DCE/RPC in the rpc_srp_verifier service on TCP 2012: the SRP key getter checks neither that the caller authenticated nor that it owns the verifier, and the RPC context handles are predictable UUIDv1 values, so an attacker needs only network access to TCP 2012 and an existing SSO principal name (Rapid7, 2026-11-24). Rapid7 chained the administrator session to a root shell on vCenter 8.0.2.00400 and describes a Metasploit module for the whole chain that sits in an open public pull request (Rapid7, 2026-11-24; Metasploit pull request, 2026-11-20). In GTIG's intrusion the actor forged administrator SAML assertions after extracting the SAML signing key, switched SSH on through the appliance management API and reached ESXi hosts, where it planted an authorized_keys entry and extracted domain data from Windows guest disks (GTIG, 2026-11-19).

Fixes for this flaw: vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5; vCenter 7.0 has no public fix (Broadcom, 2026-11-19). VMSA-2026-0011 of 2026-11-24 fixes a second Directory Service bypass, CVE-2026-123903, in 9.1.2 and 9.0.2.0300, so 9.1.1.0200 and 9.0.2.0200 leave it open while 8.0 U3m and 5.2.5 cover both (Broadcom, 2026-11-24).

Exposure
VCenter 7.0, 8.0, 9.0 and 9.1 before the fixed builds; the prerequisites are network access to TCP 2012 and a valid SSO principal name, and GTIG's actor reached vCenter from an internal Linux appliance, so exposure does not require an internet-facing vCenter (Rapid7, 2026-11-24; GTIG, 2026-11-19).
Detection
In network telemetry, repeated calls to operation 1 of the SRP helper interface on TCP 2012 with no RPC authentication verifier and context UUIDs that differ mainly in their timestamp fields (Rapid7, 2026-11-24), and sweeps of ports 2012, 5480 and 9080 from a Linux appliance that is not a management host (GTIG, 2026-11-19); in appliance logs, a database-transfer grant in the vmdird log, the SSH-settings request and a new local administrator in the vAPI endpoint access log and the SSH enablement itself in the appliance management log, then an SSH login followed by sudo (Rapid7, 2026-11-24); on ESXi, vpxuser or root logins, a new authorized_keys entry and a hidden directory on a VMFS volume (GTIG, 2026-11-19). A forged SAML session looks like an administrator session, and because BONESAW extracts the SAML signing key the compromise check covers SSO and local administrators, signing material and ESXi keys from early September on (GTIG, 2026-11-19).

Triage: a connection to TCP 2012 or an administrator SRP login alone proves nothing; the signal is the call pattern and log sequence above (Rapid7, 2026-11-24).

Defender takeaway
Treat the update as an emergency change and move 9.x vCenter straight to 9.1.2 or 9.0.2.0300, which cover this flaw and the second bypass; until then GTIG's hardening guidance drops inbound TCP 2012 from non-allowlisted addresses, tested first because the port carries SSO traffic (GTIG, 2026-11-19; Broadcom, 2026-11-24).
Improvement22 Nov 2026 14:57 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditaffected_productsbodycves

CISA listed CVE-2026-123890 as exploited on 2026-11-20 (CISA, 2026-11-20). GTIG ties the SSH enablement to the appliance management API, describes the Directory Service database being pulled through the directory service's RPC interface and the master key and credential file being read over SSH, and names no log in which those reads appear (GTIG, 2026-11-19). Broadcom lists VMware vSphere Foundation among the impacted products as well (Broadcom, 2026-11-19).

Update25 Nov 2026 04:46 UTCrun 2026-11-25T0356Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessummarytagstitle

Rapid7 published its technical analysis of CVE-2026-123890 on 2026-11-24: the SRP key getter checks neither authentication nor verifier ownership and its RPC context handles are predictable, the chain reaches a root shell on vCenter 8.0.2.00400, and a Metasploit module that does the whole chain is described (Rapid7, 2026-11-24). That module is in an open public pull request to Metasploit (Metasploit pull request, 2026-11-20). Broadcom's VMSA-2026-0011 of 2026-11-24 fixes a second Directory Service authentication bypass, CVE-2026-123903, in vCenter 9.1.2 and 9.0.2.0300; 8.0 U3m and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5 already carry that fix, but 9.1.1.0200 and 9.0.2.0200, the builds named above for this flaw, do not (Broadcom, 2026-11-24).

entries.headline: Broadcom VMSA-2026-0011: second vCenter auth bypass and ESX I/O filter RCE, all 9.8; the earlier fix does not cover 9.x
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-123903 +3NATOA2

VMSA-2026-0011, VMware vCenter and ESX: a second Directory Service authentication bypass in vCenter (CVE-2026-123903) and two I/O filter service flaws in ESX that give code execution from network access (CVE-2026-123910, CVE-2026-123911), all CVSS 3.1 9.8; no workaround for vCenter, fixed in vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m, no exploitation reported

Broadcom's VMSA-2026-0011 of 2026-11-24 fixes 23 flaws across vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools and Avi Load Balancer, rated Critical, and Broadcom's questions and answers treat the critical issues as an emergency change (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). CVE-2026-123903 is an authentication bypass in vCenter's VMware Directory Service, CVSS 3.1 9.8, reachable with network access to vCenter and no credentials, with no workaround; Broadcom calls it a new and distinct issue from the exploited CVE-2026-123890 in the same component (Broadcom, 2026-11-24; Broadcom, 2026-11-24). CVE-2026-123910 (heap out-of-bounds write) and CVE-2026-123911 (use-after-free) are flaws in the ESX I/O filter service, each 9.8 with network access to the host, and CVE-2026-123912 is an out-of-bounds write in the XHCI USB controller that gives code execution as the VMX process to an administrator inside a virtual machine, CVSS 9.3 in Workstation and Fusion and 8.4 in ESX (Broadcom, 2026-11-24).

Fixed builds: vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m, VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x through 5.2.5 (KB88287), with no public fix for vCenter 7.0 or ESX 7.0; ESX ESXi-9.1.2.0-25946735, ESXi-9.0.2.0200-25953133 and ESXi80U3m-25926933; Workstation and Fusion 26H1u1 (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). Broadcom says a vCenter on 8.0 U3m from the earlier advisory needs no further update but vCenter 9.1.x does, and for 9.0.x the fixed version in the new advisory (9.0.2.0300) governs, so 9.1.1.0200 and 9.0.2.0200 do not carry the fix (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). For ESX 8.x only, KB463535 restricts TCP 9080, where the I/O filter service listens, to the vCenter address; Broadcom says limiting access to the service resolves only a small portion of the issues in the advisory and may affect cluster operation, and tells customers to apply the updates (Broadcom, 2026-11-24; Broadcom, 2026-11-24). Broadcom's release notes disagree with its response matrices in places: the vCenter 9.1.2 notes list only four vCenter CVEs, not the authentication bypass that the matrix says 9.1.2 fixes (Broadcom, 2026-11-24), the 8.0 U3m notes list only the earlier exploited flaw (Broadcom, 2026-11-19) and the 9.0.2.0300 notes list ESX flaws (Broadcom, 2026-11-24), and the questions and answers score CVE-2026-123912 at 8.5 for ESX where the response matrix prints 8.4, and Broadcom names the advisory as the source of truth for affected versions and patches (Broadcom, 2026-11-24). Neither the advisory nor the questions and answers say any flaw is exploited, and no source reports it as of 2026-11-25.

Exposure
Any vCenter Server reachable over the network, with the build shown in the appliance's version summary, and any ESX host whose I/O filter service port is reachable; on ESX 8.x that service listens on TCP 9080 and KB463535 says only vCenter should reach it.
Detection
Broadcom publishes no indicators. Flows to TCP 9080 on ESX hosts from any address other than the vCenter Server are outside the pattern KB463535 describes, and administrator sessions or account changes on a vCenter that was reachable before patching deserve the review described for the earlier Directory Service bypass.
Defender takeaway
Treat it as the emergency change Broadcom describes: move vCenter and ESX to the builds above, re-patch any 9.x vCenter that stopped at the earlier advisory's build, and keep management interfaces and the ESX I/O filter port off untrusted networks until then; vCenter 7.0 and ESX 7.0 have no public fix and Broadcom directs extended-support customers to its support, so isolation is the interim lever there.
