entries.headline: Unit 42: AI agents behind web shells in 10+ campaigns; hunt 1.4 s command gaps and ===[Title]=== headers
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Unit 42: more than ten campaigns in July to September 2026 ran autonomous AI agents from web-shell footholds on vulnerable web applications, with a command-gap median of 1.4 seconds, ===[Title]=== script headers and 40 to 100 unique Base64 payloads per session

Unit 42 tracked more than ten global campaigns between July and September 2026 in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents, against sectors including government, logistics, manufacturing, agriculture and education. Every campaign began with a web shell deployed through a vulnerable web application, typically supplied by the human operator, after which the agent did reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement; Unit 42 names no product, CVE or flaw class for the entry vectors and says the novelty was speed and efficiency, not technique (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

The traces: a median gap of 1.4 seconds between commands once an agent took over, against 23.9 seconds in the human phase of a subset of attacks; about 800 unique commands in 140 minutes in one case; section headers such as ===[Title]=== in shell commands and scripts in every campaign and step-by-step reasoning notes in more than half; 40 to 100 unique, target-tailored Base64 payloads per session; and no compiled implants, the arsenal being in most cases simple single-use scripts such as PHP web shells, PowerShell WMI backdoors and Python credential harvesters. The agents probed defences: the same find command ran on six endpoints excluding three security vendors, and one agent applied strace to the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint daemon (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

The Copy Fail exploit recurred across several organisations; in a different attack sequence an agent tried the public PwnKit and CVE-2024-1086 binaries, then wrote custom C on the target and rewrote the exploit in Python, and Unit 42 saw agents try five techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed. In one AWS case it switched to IMDSv2 token acquisition after IMDSv1 was blocked and enumerated 20 services across eight regions; in another it pushed web shells to more than 40 locations on a Windows IIS server within 26 minutes, and Unit 42 describes another agent that found a vendor's GitLab credentials on a victim's web server and tried to brute-force access to that GitLab instance, exploiting no GitLab flaw (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

Unit 42 found no behavioural marker tying the activity to a model or framework; a command-and-control address in one campaign also hosted a CyberStrikeAI instance, from which it infers the orchestration platform (Unit 42, 2026-11-24). ReliaQuest saw a credential-gated CyberStrikeAI login page on a staging host and could not determine whether the tool played a part (ReliaQuest, 2026-10-07).

Exposure
Internet-facing web servers that host a vulnerable web application; Unit 42 does not name the applications.
Detection
In process-lineage telemetry, shells and scripts spawned through a web shell's sh -c interface in bursts seconds apart, with ===[Title]=== headers or reasoning-style comments and many unique Base64 payloads; the same enumeration command across hosts excluding security-product directories, and tracing of the endpoint-security daemon; on cloud workloads, a switch to IMDSv2 token requests after IMDSv1 is blocked.

Triage: Base64 commands and reconnaissance appear in human-operated intrusions; Unit 42's discriminators are the volume and uniqueness of payloads, the command cadence and the headers, which it says rarely appear in human-operated attacks except with pre-coded scripts.

Defender takeaway
Hunt web-server hosts for these traces, looking for volumes of single-use scripts rather than malware families, and close the web-tier entry first; enforce MFA, sign-in rate limiting and source-address restriction on services whose credentials sit on web servers, as Unit 42 advises for GitLab.

Builds on: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names… · Elastic: CyberStrikeAI against AWS, six medium or low alerts joined only by source IP; alert on… · ReliaQuest: AI agents took a Tomcat server to SYSTEM in under a day through an exposed… · BACS: five confirmed AI-agent attacks in Switzerland, three on critical infrastructure…

entries.headline: GT13 holds Check Point management servers at 22 organisations; patching does not evict it, check audit logs
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-16232 +1exploitedNATOB2

GreyNoise GT13: an unattributed actor that GreyNoise believes used LLM tooling held persistent access to at least 24 Check Point Security Management servers at 22 organisations, government among them, using CVE-2026-16232 and a Rejetto HFS relay hijacked through CVE-2026-61500

GreyNoise reports an intrusion campaign it tracks as GT13 against Check Point Security Management servers: at least 22 organisations and 24 servers, confirmed activity against the Check Point servers from 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-02 and the actor's relay observed from 2026-10-02, victims in 17 named countries and territories (Germany, Austria and France among them, Switzerland not named) and sectors including government, financial services, energy and transportation (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23). GreyNoise could not determine when or how the actor first reached the Check Point servers, only that it did so before compromising the Rejetto HFS server it used as a relay; it does not attribute GT13, cannot judge motive and believes that the actor used LLM and agentic tooling (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

The actor ran a script for the SmartConsole authentication bypass CVE-2026-16232, purportedly adapted from the Metasploit module, to launch more than 100 management tasks, among them copying the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, minting a certificate and unloading security policies, which would disable the firewall (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23). Check Point confirmed the use of CVE-2026-16232 and called the flaw and its protections not new (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-24); the fixes are Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator R82.10 from Take 36, R82 from Take 118 and R81.20 from Take 158, and exploitation needs internet access to the management server with no restriction on Trusted Clients (Check Point, 2026-09-24); Check Point's disclosure table scores the flaw 9.3 and lists exploitation against a handful of customers with a specific configuration (Check Point, 2026-07-22). The relay was taken over by forging an HFS session cookie after recovering the signing key from login responses (CVE-2026-61500, HFS 3.0.0 to below 3.2.1) (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23; VulnCheck, 2026-07-13).

The actor planted an SSH key on its relay, and GreyNoise concludes from scp deliveries that each compromised device holds the matching private key; it also ran Nmap and a Chisel reverse proxy, used at least 30 Python scripts with victim-themed credential lists, and probed NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, vCenter, Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and domain controllers without any stated success. A bulk certificate task to 24 servers failed on each; GreyNoise notified victims directly or through government partners and expects the campaign to be ongoing (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
Any Check Point Security Management or Multi-Domain Security Management server on R82.10, R82, R81.20 or an unsupported earlier train, below the fixed Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator, whose Trusted Clients list was unrestricted, reached from the internet or from a compromised internal host.
Detection
In management-server audit logs, SmartConsole sessions authenticated by "Password based application token", which Check Point says to treat as suspicious and check for an unrecognised administrator name or address (Check Point, 2026-09-24); script-run, certificate-management and policy-unload events; outbound SSH or scp from management servers to the relay and other non-administrator hosts; unfamiliar SSH private keys and a registration in /etc/ld.so.preload, which GreyNoise says may indicate an implant; tunnelling-tool process creation. A server patched later still needs this check, reaching back to at least early October, since the actor held persistent access and copied the internal CA.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator and restrict Trusted Clients now, then treat any server with an unexplained application-token login as a compromised management plane: review policy changes and rebuild trust where the internal CA or stored credentials left.

entries.headline: Project Zero: one-bit change loads untrusted .NET assemblies past UMCI; fixed in October, PPL bypass expected to remain
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-108398 +1NATOB1

Project Zero: clearing one COFF header flag makes .NET Framework 4 load an untrusted assembly past Windows code-integrity checks (CVE-2026-108398, fixed 2026-10-13); the same behaviour defeated VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (CVE-2026-87268) and is expected to remain a protected-process bypass

James Forshaw of Google Project Zero published a write-up of a code-integrity bypass found re-examining VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (Project Zero, 2026-11-23). On .NET Framework 4 the runtime first maps an assembly as an image section; if that fails with a bad-format error it falls back to a flat, data-only mapping that .NET can still run, so protection code that checks the loaded image section never sees it. A check meant to stop the fallback when code integrity is enforced tests the Windows lockdown policy for inequality with the configuration-code-integrity value, which is exactly what Windows 11 S Mode returns (User Mode Code Integrity on, Dynamic Code Security off), so it passes. Clearing the executable-image flag in the COFF header of a managed assembly, one bit with no checksum fix-up, and loading it through a .NET Framework 4 command-line utility without administrator rights ran arbitrary code under User Mode Code Integrity; it only seems to work on .NET Framework v4 (Project Zero, 2026-11-23).

Forshaw presented it at 44Con before reporting it in late September 2026, so Microsoft treated it as a zero day; CVE-2026-108398 was fixed in October 2026 by correcting the policy check (Project Zero, 2026-11-23). Microsoft rates it Important, not exploited (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-10-13).

The same behaviour defeated VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (CVE-2026-87268): an AnyCPU .NET assembly made its image screening return the bad-format status, the flat fallback loaded the unmodified assembly, and a current-user COM registration brought it into a hardened process; VirtualBox fixed it by never returning that status and by adding a COM option that disables current-user hive lookups. Against protected processes, hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads gave code execution as a protected process light without administrator rights; Microsoft's servicing criteria place such bypasses out of scope and the policy fix does not change that, so Forshaw expects it to remain bypassable (Project Zero, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
Windows hosts that rely on App Control for Business or WDAC user-mode code integrity as an application-control boundary without Dynamic Code Security (Project Zero, 2026-11-23), and Windows hosts that run Oracle VM VirtualBox 7.2.16 or likely earlier builds (Oracle, 2026-09-15).
Detection
The post says protection code that checks the loaded image section does not see this load (Project Zero, 2026-11-23); from that and the shown method, look at process creation of the .NET assembly-registration utilities with an unregister option against a file in a user-writable path, current-user COM registrations for the .NET runtime, .NET assembly loads with no matching image load, and managed assemblies whose COFF header lacks the executable-image bit.

Triage: developers and installers run the registration utilities legitimately for their own signed COM assemblies from build or Program Files paths; the discriminators are an unsigned or modified assembly, a user-writable path and a current-user COM registration on a host enforcing user-mode code integrity.

Defender takeaway
Confirm the October 2026 .NET Framework update (4.8.1 at build 4.8.9363.0, 4.8 at 4.8.4811.0, 4.6.2 to 4.7.2 at 4.7.4150.0) on every host that enforces user-mode code integrity (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-10-13) and do not treat protected process light as a boundary against local code that can run .NET Framework 4 assemblies; Dynamic Code Security blocks the behaviour but is off by default, disables loading assemblies from byte arrays and can break applications (Project Zero, 2026-11-23).

Sources: Google Project Zero (James Forshaw) · Microsoft MSRC · Oracle (Critical Security Patch Update, September 2026)
entries.summary: Google Project Zero's James Forshaw shows that .NET Framework 4 falls back to a flat, non-image mapping when an assembly's executable-image header flag is cleared, so protection code that expects to check the loaded image section never sees the load, and that the code-integrity policy check meant to stop the fallback passes on Windows 11 S Mode, letting an untrusted assembly run under User Mode Code Integrity. Microsoft fixed it as CVE-2026-108398 in October 2026 (Important, CVSS 3.1 8.8, publicly disclosed, not exploited); the same behaviour bypassed VirtualBox's Windows process hardening (CVE-2026-87268) and gives code execution as a protected process light, which Microsoft's servicing criteria treat as out of scope.

entries.headline: Symantec: 41 AI-authored PowerShell modules ran under an IIS web shell and exfiltrated through DNS lookups
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Symantec: 41 likely AI-authored PowerShell modules ran under an IIS web shell at an African stock exchange for just over three minutes, hunting secrets in SYSVOL, shared folders, SharePoint, SCCM and TFS, testing them against financial APIs and returning the output as hex-encoded DNS lookups to a public out-of-band testing service

Symantec's Threat Hunter Team found a toolkit on a stock-exchange web server in an African country: 41 PowerShell modules ran under a web shell inside the IIS worker process between 08:44 and 08:47 UTC on 2026-09-20, a new module every few seconds (Symantec, 2026-11-19). The modules profiled the host and its IIS sites and hunted for secrets in the domain's SYSVOL share (Group Policy Preferences password fields), shared policy folders, web roots and deployment directories (hard-coded passwords, AWS keys, connection strings in .xml, .json, .env and web.config files); they also searched SharePoint for the keywords aws, credential and password, queried SCCM for the machine a given user last logged on to, listed Team Foundation Server projects and probed a PostgreSQL instance and a SQL Server. Four modules tested a guessed password, a reused bearer token and several API keys against the exchange's investment API and a securities-depository gateway (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Every module hex-encoded its output into 50-character chunks and resolved each as a DNS name under unique subdomains of a single token on a public out-of-band testing service, so the data left as DNS lookups; Symantec calls this rarely seen, cannot see the collector and does not know whether any credential or key worked (Symantec, 2026-11-19). Its case for AI authorship is uniformity: the same error handling in every module, the DNS loop copied byte for byte into all 41, generic variable names and a deliberately invalid test credential; it calls no signal conclusive (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Symantec attributes six persistence implants on the same server to Witchetty (LookingFrog), a China-linked espionage group, with high confidence, the earliest evidence dating from April 2026, but does not attribute the toolkit to any group; it names three explanations: Witchetty with new tooling, a second operator using the same access, or an unrelated actor. The way in is not stated, a web shell under the IIS worker process suggests a vulnerability may have been exploited, and Symantec found no evidence of privilege escalation or data theft (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
A Windows estate with an IIS server whose worker account can read secrets: Group Policy Preferences passwords in SYSVOL, credentials in web.config and deployment folders, and reachable SharePoint, SCCM and TFS servers (Symantec, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Repeated short-lived PowerShell jobs started within seconds with the IIS worker process as ancestor; DNS egress from a server-class host to long hex-looking labels under a public out-of-band testing service; reads of SYSVOL policy folders and of web.config and .env files by the web-tier account; SCCM, SharePoint and TFS queries from a web server. Symantec says the uniform scaffold and the copied DNS loop are what defenders can look for (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Triage: out-of-band testing lookups are normal from a vulnerability scanner or penetration-test host; the discriminator is a production web server issuing them from PowerShell children of the IIS worker process.

Defender takeaway
Hunt web-tier servers for PowerShell spawned by the worker process and for server DNS egress to out-of-band testing services; remove Group Policy Preferences passwords from SYSVOL, move secrets out of web roots and shared folders, rotate any found there, and keep the web-tier account away from SCCM, TFS and SharePoint (Symantec, 2026-11-19).

Builds on: Symantec: AI-assisted retailer intrusion pivots through SolarWinds Orion's bundled RabbitMQ…

entries.headline: F5 BIG-IP: six unauth CVSS 9.8 TMM overflows, fixed only by engineering hotfixes; check iRule and APM use
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-123637 +5NATOA2

F5 BIG-IP: six unauthenticated stack overflows rated CVSS 9.8 (CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-116953, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805) crash TMM and may allow code execution where an iRule command or APM policy is configured; fixed only by engineering hotfixes, no exploitation reported

F5's security notification of 2026-11-18 lists 22 advisories, 10 of them for NGINX; six BIG-IP flaws among them let an attacker without credentials crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM), disrupting traffic until it restarts, and F5 says they may also allow remote code execution (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). All six are stack-based buffer overflows in the data plane, which processes almost all of BIG-IP's network traffic, rated CVSS 3.1 9.8 and CVSS 4.0 9.3; the management side is not exposed, and watchTowr's Sina Kheirkhah reported four of them while F5 found the other two (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). BSI CERT-Bund's advisory, which lists only the APM flaw CVE-2026-123637, says a remote, anonymous attacker can execute arbitrary code (translated from German) (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-23), and NCSC-NL, whose advisory also covers six lower-rated BIG-IP flaws, rates the likelihood medium and the damage high (NCSC-NL, 2026-11-19).

Each flaw needs a specific configuration on a virtual server: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic (CVE-2026-116953); an HTTP profile with an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address (CVE-2026-120285) or MR::message route (CVE-2026-120292); an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic (CVE-2026-120722, BIG-IP DNS) or PEM::subscriber on client traffic (CVE-2026-121805, BIG-IP PEM); or an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents (CVE-2026-123637, APM only) (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, for some of the six, BIG-IP CNF are affected as well, and F5 checks only versions still in technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).

No scheduled release is listed as a fix and F5 lists no workaround: the fixes are engineering hotfixes, which F5 says do not receive the QA of scheduled releases, and a system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from F5 support (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18). None of F5's advisories says the six are exploited, and they differ from CVE-2026-94127, the APM flaw F5 disclosed on 2026-09-22 that was later exploited (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).

Exposure
A BIG-IP on the 21.1, 17.5 or 17.1 branch (BSI's product tree lists builds before the hotfix builds) whose virtual servers use one of those iRule commands or APM policy agents (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-23; The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).
Detection
TMM process terminations and restarts and core files in the BIG-IP system logs, tied to the virtual server that carries the affected iRule or policy, follow from the stated impact (traffic disrupted until TMM restarts); no source describes a successful code-execution chain or a post-exploitation artefact (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).
Defender takeaway
An unauthenticated remote crash of the traffic plane, with possible code execution, can be reached only on the configurations above, so inventory those first and apply the engineering hotfix instead of waiting for a scheduled release; a system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from F5 support (The Hacker News, 2026-11-18).

BIG-IP 21.1, 17.5 and 17.1 are affected, no scheduled release carries the fix and F5 lists no workaround, so the fix is an engineering hotfix from F5; none of F5's advisories says the flaws are exploited.

entries.headline: N-able Mail Assure SSRF CVE-2026-134624 is on CISA KEV after a hosted-cloud breach; revoked tokens need reissuing
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-134624exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-134624, N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts before 20261121.1943: a server-side request forgery in the LDAP-sync connection check, disclosed after a breach of N-able's hosted cloud, is listed by CISA as exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.3)

N-able disabled access to the portal and API of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, the email-filtering service it runs for managed service providers, on 2026-11-16 and confirmed two days later that it had been attacked: the intruders hit a web server and likely accessed certain credentials stored there, while email delivery kept working (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-23; The Hacker News, 2026-11-23). On 2026-11-22 N-able said it had remediated the identified vulnerability, restored the dashboard and APIs as of 2026-11-21 23:45 UTC and published CVE-2026-134624 (N-able, 2026-11-22).

The flaw: the LDAP-synchronisation connection check that runs when a relay is configured did not restrict its destination, so an authenticated API user can make the server connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, learn which are reachable and send crafted data to internal services; builds before 20261121.1943 are affected, N-able scores it CVSS 4.0 9.3 and does not claim code execution (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23; GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-11-22). CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-23 (CISA, 2026-11-23). N-able says exploitation was confined to a single N-able-hosted server and that monitoring since remediation found nothing further; it has not said whether this flaw was the attackers' way in, and it has engaged an independent forensics team and promises a root cause analysis within two weeks (N-able, 2026-11-22; The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).

N-able's response included taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' API and OAuth tokens and resetting local users' passwords; it says it found no evidence that customer data, tenants' mailboxes included, was compromised and that the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
The Hosted Cloud is already patched and there is nothing for its customers to install; exposure runs through the MSP or hoster that serves the tenant, whose scripts and integrations stopped working when the API and OAuth tokens were revoked (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23). SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware and the incident statements describe only the Hosted Cloud, so its operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943 (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).
Detection
Management-plane and API audit logs for LDAP-synchronisation connection checks whose target is an internal address or a non-LDAP port follow from the stated mechanism; on the tenant side, unexplained authentication failures from integrations after the token revocation. N-able says mail flow continued throughout, so mail-flow telemetry is not expected to show the intrusion (N-able, 2026-11-22). The Hacker News notes that it is not known whether credentials the intruders may have reached were actually taken (The Hacker News, 2026-11-23).
Defender takeaway
Nothing to patch for Hosted Cloud customers; re-issue the integrations that lost their tokens, confirm the fixed build on any Local Cloud, and treat the root cause analysis due around 2026-12-06 as the point to re-check scope (N-able, 2026-11-22).

Sources: N-able (Mail Assure Incident Update) · SecurityWeek · The Hacker News · GitHub Advisory Database (N-able CVE record) · CISA (KEV alert)

entries.action_label: Azure APIM Classic secrets exposed and exploited…
actions: On every Azure API Management instance, read the gateway RuntimeVersion as NSM describes (0.52.x is patched from build 31936, 0.53.x from build 31938, and v2 or Consumption-tier patterns are not affected) and, whatever the result, rotate every named value, backend credential, identity-provider client secret, subscription key and token the instance held, plus the Key Vault secrets it references, then review the Activity, gateway, Key Vault and service-principal sign-in logs for use of the old values, because NSM says to assume secrets and named values are exposed and Microsoft's notice says Classic instances were exposed before Microsoft identified the issue on 2026-11-18 and mitigated it on 2026-11-19.

entries.headline: Azure APIM Classic secrets exposed and exploited; NSM: assume compromise, rotate every token and secret
entries.html:
HIGHexploitedNATOA2

Azure API Management Classic: a flaw let an unknown actor take secrets, named values and tokens from APIM instances; Norway's NSM names Equinor and Skagerak Energi among those hit and tells every APIM user to treat secrets as exposed and rotate them after Microsoft's 2026-11-19 mitigation

Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said on 2026-11-20, in a post updated on 2026-11-23, that an unknown actor has actively gone after access tokens, secrets and named values in Azure API Management (APIM), that Equinor and Skagerak Energi are among the organisations hit, and that the flaw also affects several sectors in Norway and beyond its borders (translated from Norwegian) (NSM, 2026-11-20). NSM says it is still uncertain how widely the flaw has been and is being exploited, and that it has no indication so far that compromises or attempts have affected deliveries at Norwegian organisations (translated from Norwegian) (NSM, 2026-11-20).

Microsoft's customer notice, read by SecurityWeek, says Microsoft discovered the issue on 2026-11-18 and closed the access path the next day, and that an unauthorized party could have used it to reach secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the issue; exposed data can include secrets stored as named values, client secrets for identity providers, subscription keys and tokens for APIM's direct management APIs, and instances on the v2 tiers are not affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-23). SecurityWeek adds that Microsoft noted Classic tiers that do not follow its documented security guidance are affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-23). Equinor reported its attack on 2026-11-17, said on 2026-11-19 that it did not appear to target Equinor specifically and on 2026-11-20 that the attack had been stopped (Equinor, 2026-11-20); Skagerak Energi reported a possible attempted attack on 2026-11-18 and said operations and production were not affected and there was no indication that information had left (Skagerak Energi, 2026-11-18). No source says how the flaw works, who the actor is or how many tenants lost secrets.

NSM tells every APIM user to assume that secrets and named values are exposed and to rotate all tokens and secrets, to map what sits behind each instance to judge the potential scope, and to check whether the instance has been updated (translated from Norwegian) (NSM, 2026-11-20).

Exposure
NSM's guide reads the RuntimeVersion from the gateway's internal-status page: 0.52.x is patched from build 31936, 0.53.x from build 31938, lower numbers are still vulnerable, and patterns such as 0.53.4608.0 are v2 or Consumption tier and not vulnerable; an organisation whose instance is not updated is asked to contact the vendor, and one that sees signs of compromise to contact NSM (translated from Norwegian) (NSM, 2026-11-20).
Detection
An independent practitioner's hunting map, which is not a confirmed attack chain, points to the Azure Activity log for secret-list requests and configuration changes, APIM gateway logs for newly seen subscription identifiers and tracing requests, developer-portal audit logs to see whether an unused portal is in use, Entra service-principal sign-ins for use of the app credentials APIM held, Key Vault audit logs for reads of the secrets APIM references, and Microsoft Graph activity logs; calls to the retired direct Management API do not appear in the Activity log (Anders Kristiansen, 2026-11-21). Credentials lifted from APIM can be used against outside services, and the damage depends on each credential's permissions (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-23).
Defender takeaway
Patching is not the end: treat every APIM instance as having lost the secrets it held, rotate them all and then hunt for their use; the practitioner guide also advises switching off the retired direct Management API and closing an unused developer portal (Anders Kristiansen, 2026-11-21).

entries.headline: Entra Connect Health API flaw exploited: admin email addresses read; Microsoft warns of targeted phishing
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Microsoft Entra Connect Health: an API flaw present from 2026-07-23 was exploited to read tenant metadata including administrator and technical-contact email addresses; Microsoft fixed it server-side on 2026-11-19 and warns of targeted phishing

Microsoft told tenants through Azure Service Health, from 2026-11-20, that a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API, introduced on 2026-07-23 and found on 2026-11-09, was exploited for unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21). Connect Health is the cloud service that lets administrators monitor the health of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Entra admin center (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21). Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on 2026-11-19, concluded its investigation on 2026-11-20 and found no unauthorized configuration change, although the flaw could in principle also have changed Connect Health monitoring settings (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21; Netzwoche, 2026-11-23).

The exposed data are the email addresses of tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts, tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country and region codes, Entra licence tiers and directory-synchronisation status, Connect Health onboarding status, and an expired agent-registration certificate for an internal Microsoft service decommissioned in late 2024; Microsoft says passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology and Azure subscription data were not exposed (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21). Microsoft has not said who exploited the flaw, how many tenants are affected or when the attacks began; more than a dozen administrators reported receiving the notice, and some managed service providers received notices for several customer tenants (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21).

Exposure
Any tenant that received the Azure Service Health notification; Microsoft says the flaw needs no software update or other customer remediation (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21).
Detection
The leaked data cannot be recalled, so the signal is the follow-on: mail-flow and helpdesk telemetry for phishing or social-engineering messages aimed at the exposed administrator and technical-contact addresses, and Entra sign-in and audit logs for privileged accounts and for changes to Connect Health settings; Microsoft advises reviewing the Connect Health configuration and the Entra audit and sign-in logs, and its PowerShell script shows the current values of the exposed metadata types, not what was accessed (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21).
Defender takeaway
Treat the exposed administrator and technical-contact addresses as targets of tailored phishing and social engineering, tell those people, and enforce phishing-resistant MFA on privileged accounts; there is nothing to patch (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-21).

entries.headline: BabidiGhost AI agent targeted 50+ organisations, mostly in Belgium, France, Switzerland; MFA and allow-lists held
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOC2

BabidiGhost: a jailbroken Hermes-based AI agent run against more than 50 targets, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland, exported an insurer's customer database and 13 municipalities' archives through public flaws and exposures; MFA, IP allow-listing and server-side validation stopped it

SOCRadar recovered the exposed home directory of a hijacked French staging server and reconstructs a nine-day operation, 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-14, in which a low-skill French-speaking operator, BabidiGhost, typed plain-language orders to a jailbroken Hermes-based AI agent that wrote the scanners, exploits and exfiltration scripts (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20). The agent targeted more than 50 organisations and datasets, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland; of 14 analysed in depth, two were breached and three partly breached; SOCRadar says every successful intrusion used an exposed, unpatched analytics tool, a readable secret, a weak password or an unauthenticated endpoint, with no zero-day (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

An internet-facing, unpatched Metabase vulnerable to CVE-2023-38646 let the agent in; it then ran commands on the server beneath the dashboard, read cloud database credentials from the container environment, exported the customer database and planted a database trigger that relaunched its implant on every new record. A shared IT provider's storage-management interface was exposed to the internet and a weak administrator password opened it, giving 23 archives of about 8.6 GB from more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies; SOCRadar says this one server drives Belgium's share of more than half of the targets and names no Swiss municipality. Against banks the agent mapped the attack surface through certificate logs and a sign-in error oracle confirmed 48 valid corporate accounts, while a crawler swept Swiss websites for IBANs, email addresses and phone numbers. TOTP second factors, an IP allow-list and server-side business validation stopped the same agent (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

Its model API key was revoked on 2026-11-14, but a PowerShell beacon and a C# backdoor posing as a Windows Update service, persisted through scheduled tasks and a Run key, kept calling home until 2026-11-15, and stolen archives had gone out through Telegram (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

ZATAZ reports that the BlackHatSect0r handle, whose toolchain SOCRadar says the agent runs, rents a jailbroken agent (ZATAZ, 2026-11-23) and offers a bank-phishing platform with templates for 81 banks in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, 28 of them Swiss including UBS, PostFinance and Raiffeisen; ZATAZ names no Swiss victim (ZATAZ, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
The gaps used were internet-facing analytics tools, storage-management interfaces at shared IT providers, unauthenticated API routes, sign-in flows that reveal whether an account exists and secrets readable from a web application's environment (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).
Detection
Egress or proxy telemetry showing a server calling a model-provider API or the Telegram bot API without a business reason; on Windows, a Run key and scheduled tasks for a service posing as Windows Update, unexpected Defender exclusions and outbound TCP to port 8443; on PostgreSQL, triggers nobody created. SOCRadar's hunt window is 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-17, and revoking the model key did not remove deployed implants (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

Triage: the Hermes Agent directory and its SOUL.md exist on every Hermes installation; they matter only when SOUL.md carries the jailbreak strings SOCRadar's rule matches (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

Defender takeaway
Patch Metabase and take analytics tools, storage-management interfaces and unauthenticated API routes off the internet, keep secrets out of runtime environments, and verify the controls that stopped the agent (TOTP, IP allow-listing, server-side validation) at the shared IT providers that hold municipal data (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

Sources: SOCRadar Research · ZATAZ

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Kaspersky: ShadowCloud's GitDoor and GraphDoor hide C2 in GitHub and Microsoft Graph, planted via a MeshCentral agent
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Operation ShadowCloud: Kaspersky's GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors hide command and control in GitHub, Microsoft Graph with SharePoint, and Ably against government networks in Asia and Africa, delivered through an abused MeshCentral agent and DLL sideloading

Kaspersky GReAT describes Operation ShadowCloud, an intrusion set identified in early 2026 that abuses the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two new backdoors, with victims in Asia and Africa primarily in the government sector (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). The entry point is unknown: the first observed step is a MeshCentral agent launched inside a Taiwanese organisation, with evidence pointing to reuse of a prior infection on the network (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Through the agent the operators drop a legitimate binary, a malicious loader DLL and an encrypted payload file named config.ini, so the legitimate program loads the loader when it starts; hosts include a Sandboxie launcher, an OpenJDK launcher, a Python application and Sysinternals ZoomIt started as a service (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Sophos, which tracks the Sandboxie sideloading as BRONZE SANDCASTLE and which Kaspersky says covered a fragment of this campaign (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17), saw victims between August 2025 and August 2026 in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia and likely the Republic of Korea (Sophos, 2026-10-20).

GitDoor uses GitHub as its command channel: it opens and labels an issue through the GitHub API, writes victim data to a private repository and reads commands and plug-ins from a public one, authenticating with a personal access token (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). GraphDoor requests a token for an attacker-registered application with the client-credentials grant from Microsoft's sign-in endpoint, then writes encrypted data to files named like JavaScript source maps in a SharePoint document library through Microsoft Graph (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Both download plug-ins on demand and run shellcode in memory, among it Mimikatz and a browser-cookie stealer, with plug-ins for keylogging, screen capture and proxying through a modified Erfrp client or Ably (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17; Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Kaspersky says it lacks sufficient information to attribute the activity and reports overlaps with the Chinese-speaking groups FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle, which on several victim systems shared staging directories with GitDoor (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
Windows servers and workstations in networks that let non-browser processes reach GitHub, Microsoft's sign-in and Graph endpoints and Ably over HTTPS, and where a MeshCentral agent is not a tool the organisation deploys (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17; Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).
Detection
In endpoint inventory and process telemetry, MeshCentral agent processes and services that IT did not deploy, and a legitimate program (a Sandboxie start binary, an OpenJDK launcher, a Python host, ZoomIt) loading a DLL from the folder where an encrypted config.ini sits, as in the first instance Kaspersky shows, in system32 (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). In network and identity telemetry, a non-browser process requesting an app-only token from Microsoft's sign-in endpoint and then writing files through Microsoft Graph to a SharePoint site outside your tenant, and a process other than a git client or CI runner calling the GitHub API to open issues, label them and write repository contents with a personal access token (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17; Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

Triage: MeshCentral is legitimate software, so the agent alone is not the signal; the signal is an agent no administrator deployed that drops a legitimate binary, a DLL and an encrypted config.ini side by side (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

Defender takeaway
Hunt now for MeshCentral agents nobody deployed and for that binary, DLL and config.ini triad, and baseline which processes on servers and workstations legitimately call GitHub, Microsoft Graph and Ably, because both backdoors hide their command channel in that traffic and Kaspersky found the entry point unknown (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

The operators sideload a loader DLL into a legitimate program beside an encrypted config.ini, and the backdoors take commands through the GitHub API (GitDoor) or Microsoft Graph and SharePoint (GraphDoor), with Ably as a further channel. Kaspersky does not attribute the activity and reports overlaps with FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle; Sophos tracks a fragment as BRONZE SANDCASTLE.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Ghostscript CVE-2026-125396: print jobs, Roundcube attachments and upload forms reach the sandbox escape; update
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-125396NATOB2

CVE-2026-125396, Ghostscript before 10.08.0 (Upload2Shell): a font-loader use-after-free breaks the -dSAFER sandbox, and pwn.ai reaches it from an anonymous print job, a viewed Roundcube attachment and public WordPress upload forms; fixed since 2026-09-08, no exploitation reported (CVSS 4.0 8.5)

Artifex fixed CVE-2026-125396 in Ghostscript 10.08.0 on 2026-09-08 (The Hacker News, 2026-11-22). The CVE record says the .putgstringcopy procedure in the font loader calls the privileged .forceput operator without checking operand types, so a crafted PostScript or PDF document triggers a type error, recovers .forceput through a custom error handler and causes a use-after-free across save and restore that executes arbitrary code; VulnCheck scores it CVSS 4.0 8.5 with a local attack vector (VulnCheck, 2026-11-09). pwn.ai's writeup of 2026-11-21 shows the flaw is reachable from the network because applications pass untrusted files to Ghostscript indirectly, through ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips or a print filter, even when the file is named like an image or a PDF (pwn.ai, 2026-11-21; The Hacker News, 2026-11-22).

pwn.ai ran a command as the rendering account through an anonymous IPP print job to a shared CUPS queue on Debian 13 (as the lp user), through an emailed attachment declared as a JPEG but holding PostScript that a Roundcube 1.7.2 user only had to view, with a permissive ImageMagick delegate required (as www-data), and through public WordPress upload forms in Forminator, a public PDF field storing to the Media Library, and in Essential Addons for Elementor, a public registration widget with an upload field (pwn.ai, 2026-11-21). WordPress closed its own upload path in 7.0.4 on 2026-08-12 under CVE-2026-65640, a different point in the same chain (The Hacker News, 2026-11-22). No source reports exploitation, and the one published proof-of-concept file shows only the core memory trick and fails on 10.08.0 (The Hacker News, 2026-11-22).

Debian's tracker lists fixed packages for bookworm (10.0.0~dfsg-11+deb12u9), trixie (10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u2) and unstable (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-11-23). pwn.ai records Ubuntu fixes for seven releases in USN-8949-1 of 2026-10-21, a notice that predates the CVE assignment and carries no CVE number, and, as of 2026-11-12, Amazon Linux fixes pending and several SUSE branches affected or in progress (pwn.ai, 2026-11-21). Updating the host does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application (The Hacker News, 2026-11-22).

Exposure
Ghostscript before 10.08.0, or a distribution package without the backport, on a host that renders untrusted files: a mail server that thumbnails attachments, a CUPS server with a shared queue that takes jobs without credentials, or a web server with public upload forms that build image previews (pwn.ai, 2026-11-21). Read the package version, and note that a distribution backport can fix the flaw under an older version number (pwn.ai, 2026-11-21).
Detection
A shell or other unexpected child process of the Ghostscript renderer running as the web-service or print account is the sign of success, since the proof ran its command through Ghostscript's pipe device (pwn.ai, 2026-11-21). Delivery looks like a mail attachment or upload whose declared type or extension (image/jpeg, .jpg, .png, .pdf) holds PostScript, or an anonymous Print-Job request to a shared CUPS queue (pwn.ai, 2026-11-21). In one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell (The Hacker News, 2026-11-22).
Defender takeaway
Update Ghostscript wherever untrusted files reach it, mail, print and upload servers first and bundled container copies included; until then require authentication on shared print queues and limit the file types image processors accept (The Hacker News, 2026-11-22).

entries.headline: GL.iNet GoodCloud exploited: the cloud fix leaves routers and KVMs infected; install the model's security firmware
entries.html:
NOTABLEexploitedNATOA2

GL.iNet GoodCloud: an exploited cloud remote-management flaw installed malware on routers and Comet KVMs; the cloud fix does not clean infected devices, the vendor's firmware is the clean-up, and RemoteToHome finds that clean-up partial

GL.iNet says it identified on 2026-11-20 a vulnerability in its cloud remote-management services that an unauthorized party exploited to access some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices and install malicious software; the cloud-side fix blocks new infections but does not remove malware from devices already infected (GL.iNet, 2026-11-20). BleepingComputer names the service as GoodCloud and reports that GL.iNet has not said how the flaw worked or how many customers are affected (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-22).

BleepingComputer's analysis of the installer script found that it replaces the netstat utility with a script that hides the attacker's server from connection listings (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-22). RemoteToHome Consulting, which manages many of these routers, reads the entry point as the router's GoodCloud client passing a value from a cloud message to the shell as root without checking it, and says GL.iNet has not confirmed that reading; on GL-AXT1800 and GL-MT6000 units it opened a root reverse shell (RemoteToHome, 2026-11-23). It also finds an older persistent backdoor that GL.iNet's check does not detect and that may not be tied to the November attacks, and BleepingComputer reports malicious files with December 2025 timestamps, so infection may predate 2026-11-20 (RemoteToHome, 2026-11-23; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-22).

GL.iNet lists stable security firmware for each exact model, routers from 4.7.14 to 4.11.1, and says it removes the identified malware without a factory reset and with settings kept (GL.iNet, 2026-11-20); the Comet KVM builds are 1.10.3 and, for the RMQ1, 1.8.7 (RemoteToHome, 2026-11-23). RemoteToHome reports that the clean-up is one short script that does not examine the settings an upgrade keeps, and advises reinstalling with Keep Settings switched off for any device that shows a sign (RemoteToHome, 2026-11-23). GL.iNet's own notice says its quick checks may not detect every affected device (GL.iNet, 2026-11-20).

Exposure
The GL.iNet router and Comet KVM models on the vendor's list; RemoteToHome's check applies to devices that had the cloud service switched on (RemoteToHome, 2026-11-23). GL.iNet says an unlisted model is not necessarily unaffected (GL.iNet, 2026-11-20).
Detection
On the device, a running process whose command line mimics the cron daemon with an argument pointing at a hidden file in /tmp is GL.iNet's published check (crond -i /tmp/.log, found with ps | grep tmp over SSH or in the LuCI process list) (GL.iNet, 2026-11-20). RemoteToHome did not find that process on any router it examined although other signs were present, and lists instead outbound nc sessions running an interactive shell and, surviving a restart, an empty state file in /etc dated 2026-11-20 or later on a router that does not use AstroWarp (RemoteToHome, 2026-11-23).
Defender takeaway
Find every GL.iNet router and KVM your organisation or its remote and branch users run, check each one and capture the process list, connections and firewall rules before any restart or upgrade, because some traces exist only in memory and GL.iNet says to install the firmware even when its checks find nothing, then install the security firmware for the exact model and treat any device with a sign as compromised: reinstall with settings discarded, and rotate every key, password and VPN profile stored on it, removing its peers on the server side, because RemoteToHome says cleaning or reinstalling does not take back what a root shell could read (RemoteToHome, 2026-11-23). For a KVM, also examine the computer it controls, which GL.iNet is still assessing (GL.iNet, 2026-11-20).

entries.action_label: Timeroasting leaves no logon event; Huntress shows…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Timeroasting leaves no logon event; Huntress shows the signal that holds is a host requesting another account's RID
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Huntress on timeroasting: the unauthenticated MS-SNTP sweep that harvests crackable MACs for computer and trust accounts leaves no logon event, Defender for Identity raised no alert in its tests, modern Windows sends an extended authenticator Huntress now has a cracker for, and the signal that holds is a host asking a domain controller to sign for an account other than its own

Timeroasting abuses MS-SNTP, Microsoft's authentication extension to NTP: a client names an account by its RID, and the domain controller answers with a MAC computed with that account's password-derived key, without the client authenticating first; the reachable accounts are computer and trust accounts, and the MAC is then cracked offline with no further contact and no lockout (Huntress, 2026-11-19). Huntress names the crackable population as image-built or never-rotated machines, hand-set trusts and non-Windows joins, and says a pre-created account still on its lowercase-name default falls instantly while a normal random machine secret would not (Huntress, 2026-11-19).

Reading w32time.dll and netlogon.dll on a fully patched Windows Server 2025 domain controller, Huntress documents two authenticator forms: a 68-byte legacy form with an MD5 MAC, which public tools emit and hashcat cracks, and a 120-byte extended form using HMAC-SHA512, which modern Windows clients send by default and which had no public cracker (Huntress, 2026-11-19). The patched controller answered extended-form requests that asked for the previous key, and Huntress published a reference implementation and a hashcat module for it that awaits a mode number upstream, so an extended-form capture can no longer be read as uncrackable (Huntress, 2026-11-19). Across eleven runs over five hours, with the sensor confirmed live by a control DCSync, Defender for Identity raised no alert on the MS-SNTP traffic; its "Suspicious SAM Account Name Change" alert, which names timeroasting, fires on a sAMAccountName change (event 5136), the fingerprint of the targeted variant, not of the unauthenticated sweep (Huntress, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
Windows domain controllers, which answer MS-SNTP for computer and trust accounts (Huntress tested one patched Windows Server 2025 controller, and Samba AD controllers do not implement the extended form); the accounts at risk are those whose secret is weak, hand-set or never rotated (Huntress, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Network and host telemetry, not authentication logs: the targeted accounts generate no 4768, 4769, 4624 or 4776 events. On the domain controller, Windows Filtering Platform audit event 5156 records w32time accepting the UDP/123 connection when that subcategory is enabled; on any other host, a process other than the time service sending UDP/123 to a domain controller is a high-signal EDR hit (Huntress, 2026-11-19). The rule that holds for both forms and even a single packet resolves the source address to its computer account and flags a request for any other RID; a source asking for many RIDs in a short window is the weaker volumetric fallback (Huntress, 2026-11-19).

Triage: packet size separates nothing on a modern fleet, where members send the 120-byte form as normal time sync and the public tools emit 68 bytes; domain controllers can legitimately request a trust account's RID during hierarchy synchronization, so they need an allowlist (Huntress, 2026-11-19). A machine account that authenticates and then sprays shares is delegation abuse, not timeroasting (Huntress, 2026-11-19).

Defender takeaway
Do not treat Defender for Identity or authentication analytics as coverage; collect UDP/123 telemetry from domain controllers and build the own-RID check, and reset pre-created, image-built and hand-set computer and trust account secrets, since those are the ones a sweep can crack.
research22 Nov 15:08Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Huntress
entries.summary: Huntress reverse-engineered the MS-SNTP signing code on a patched Windows Server 2025 domain controller and reports that timeroasting, an unauthenticated UDP/123 request that makes a domain controller return a password-derived MAC for any computer or trust account, produces no authentication event for the targeted accounts and raised no Defender for Identity alert across eleven test runs. Modern Windows clients send a 120-byte extended authenticator that public tools could not crack; Huntress published a reference cracker and a hashcat module for it. Packet size is not a usable signal: the check that holds is a source host requesting a RID other than its own computer account, with volume as the fallback.

entries.headline: Synology DSM OAuth API flaw lets anyone read or write NAS files; update to 7.4.1-90080-2 or 7.3.2-86009-6
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-120382NATOA2

CVE-2026-120382, Synology DSM OAuth API: an argument injection lets an unauthenticated remote attacker read or write arbitrary files on the NAS (CVSS 3.1 9.8); fixed in DSM 7.4.1-90080-2 and 7.3.2-86009-6, with DSM 7.2.x, 7.1 and BeeStation OS still unfixed

Synology published Synology-SA-26:21 on 2026-11-19 and revised it on 2026-11-20 to update the fix status for DSM 7.3 and 7.4 (Synology, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-120382 is an improper neutralization of argument delimiters in a command (CWE-88) in the OAuth API of DiskStation Manager that allows remote attackers to read or write arbitrary files and conduct denial-of-service attacks; Synology rates it Critical at CVSS 3.1 9.8 with network access, low complexity and no privileges or user interaction (Synology, 2026-11-19). DSM 7.4 is fixed in 7.4.1-90080-2 and DSM 7.3 in 7.3.2-86009-6; DSM 7.2.2, 7.2.1, 7.1 and BeeStation OS 1.5 are marked OnGoing, with an upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6 recommended for the 7.2 lines, while APM, DSM Enterprise and SRM are not affected (Synology, 2026-11-19). The advisory does not mention exploitation. An unauthenticated file write on a network storage appliance warrants action before the regular cycle, because it reaches the data the NAS holds without credentials.

Exposure
A NAS on DSM 7.4 below 7.4.1-90080-2, DSM 7.3 below 7.3.2-86009-6, any DSM 7.2.2, 7.2.1 or 7.1, or BeeStation OS 1.5 whose DSM interface untrusted hosts can reach.
Detection
In DSM web and reverse-proxy logs, requests to the OAuth API from addresses that do not normally use it, and file changes on the NAS outside administrator activity, which follow from the mechanism; Synology names no indicators.
Defender takeaway
Update DSM 7.4 and 7.3 now; where no fix exists, deactivate the OAuth Service package as Synology's mitigation, and for 7.2.x plan the move to 7.3.2-86009-6 (Synology, 2026-11-19).

entries.headline: OptimJack: Optimizely names the exploited signup-flow flaw; Report URI counts 178 organisations, Zscaler 450+ domains
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-132224exploitedupdatedNATOB2

OptimJack: poisoned scripts served by Optimizely, Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly route iPhones to exploit-kit stages, the Optimizely files also carry a crypto clipper and card skimmer, and the University of Basel site loaded a poisoned StorifyMe widget on 2026-11-14

Per Ohey, from 2026-11-13 the scripts served by Kissmetrics and StorifyMe gained a few lines that load a small router script for iPhones, and minute-ly's loader was replaced outright (Ohey, 2026-11-17). Optimizely's customer project files followed on 2026-11-16, when Report URI saw its first injection at 04:21 UTC and counted 188 infected snippets of 178 organisations, a floor (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a flaw in its Web Experimentation account signup flow on 2026-11-16 to impersonate users on targeted customer accounts and insert malicious JavaScript into their projects, that it closed the vulnerability within three hours of detection, that this was not a credentials breach and that fewer than 5% of its customers were affected (Optimizely, 2026-11-18); Zscaler ThreatLabz counts more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the script (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18). Hudson Rock names 21 web properties, among them BBC, Zoom, HSBC UAE and the University of Basel (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16). The Basel capture of 2026-11-14 recorded a poisoned StorifyMe web component (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16). How the Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly files were altered, who operates the campaign and how many visitors loaded them are unknown (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16).

The financial theft sits in the Optimizely files: Ohey says that on 2026-11-16 they switched to a script that swaps copied wallet addresses and skims card numbers in every browser and adds the router only on iPhones and iPads (Ohey, 2026-11-17). Hudson Rock describes the stealer as skimming card number, expiry and CVV from form and fetch POST bodies, and a conditional path that sends readable cookies with a page image only after a recorded wallet address matches (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16). In Hudson Rock's reading the router sends iOS 13 to 17 to a Coruna-associated entry and iOS 18 to 25 to a DarkSword-labelled one (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16), and Ohey states that DarkSword attacks iPhones running iOS 18.4 to 18.7.2 through Safari (Ohey, 2026-11-17); Hudson Rock calls them delivery observations, not demonstrated compromises (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
Any page that loads an Optimizely project snippet, whether from cdn.optimizely.com or from the customer's own host name (Report URI, 2026-11-16), Kissmetrics i.js, a StorifyMe widget or web component, or the minute-ly loader; Hudson Rock's advice is to verify what visitors actually receive (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16).
Detection
Web proxy and DNS telemetry for a vendor script that causes a further script load from a host unrelated to the vendor, payment-form POST bodies sent to an unfamiliar host, and response-body diffs of served third-party bundles; Content-Security-Policy script-src violation reports naming unknown hosts, which Amirul Cyber says stopped the payload on two affected sites (Amirul Cyber, 2026-11-16). After removal, review the provider-side project change history, API credentials and integrations, because the poisoned output does not show how the attacker got in (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16); Zscaler advises customers to review recent changes, user activity, account creation events and administrative access in the Optimizely account (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18).
Defender takeaway
Inventory third-party scripts on public, payment and e-government pages now and verify what each serves; a DNS or network block alone does not remove the poisoned trusted script (Hudson Rock, 2026-11-16), so keep the evidence, remove the file and set an allow-listed script-src policy.
Update18 Nov 2026 04:57 UTCrun 2026-11-18T0356Z-intelactionsbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummary

Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, that it has fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code, and that it secured affected user accounts; that post named no flaw class, CVE or count, and the status entry's later post of 2026-11-18 is described below (Optimizely, 2026-11-18). The status entry covers the Optimizely files only; how the Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly scripts were reached is still unknown.

Report URI's timeline adds that the card skimmer was added to the clipper at 13:43 UTC on 2026-11-16, that a mass clean-up ran between about 20:40 and 21:10 UTC, and that a snippet cleaned and then re-infected shows the writer still had access at that point (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Contradiction on dates: Ohey puts the change to the Optimizely project files at 2026-11-13 together with the Kissmetrics and StorifyMe scripts (Ohey, 2026-11-17), while Report URI's first Optimizely injection is at 04:21 UTC on 2026-11-16; Report URI's logged first-hand record is the better dated one, and the earlier wave through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media is not in the 178 (Report URI, 2026-11-16).

The injected loader came in three forms: a plain script tag, the same address hidden in base64 and decoded with atob(), which a search for the host name misses, and a full inline copy that runs through eval (Report URI, 2026-11-16). Cards entered in hosted payment iframes were out of the skimmer's reach, while cards typed into a site's own form fields were not (Report URI, 2026-11-16).

Update19 Nov 2026 05:06 UTCrun 2026-11-19T0355Z-intelactionsbodyevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniques

Optimizely's status entry now says that on 2026-11-16 an unauthorized third party exploited a flaw in the Optimizely Web Experimentation account signup flow to impersonate users on targeted customer accounts and insert malicious JavaScript into their projects, that it detected the activity the same day, blocked delivery and closed the vulnerability within three hours of detection, that this was not a credentials breach, that the incident was limited to Web Experimentation and that fewer than 5% of its customers were affected; it gives no CVE and no absolute count (Optimizely, 2026-11-18). Zscaler ThreatLabz says the flaw let the attacker edit the project JavaScript field and counts more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script, without stating its vantage point or time window, so the figure is not reconciled with Report URI's 178 organisations (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18). It advises customers to review recent changes, user activity, account creation events and administrative access, to audit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code and to rotate the API tokens, session tokens and integration keys associated with Optimizely (Zscaler ThreatLabz, 2026-11-18).

Update22 Nov 2026 14:54 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditbodysourcessourcing_notesummary

Report URI's update of 2026-11-17 says all infected Optimizely files were clean from 23:11 UTC on 2026-11-16 and stayed clean, and that the main payload and data-collection server was put on a registrar hold (clientHold) at 00:37 UTC on 2026-11-17 and no longer resolves (Report URI, 2026-11-16), which bounds the browser exposure from Optimizely-served pages to 2026-11-16. Ohey reports that the iPhone exploit router is a rental service: its operator rents it by channel code, renters get a console that lists each phone's wallets, keystores, Keychain, messages and photos, Ohey holds 31 renter codes in use since 2026-08-31, and the vendor attack ran on the operator's own channel (Ohey, 2026-11-19). The vendor scripts loaded the router from an address of a seller of hidden backlinks on hacked sites; registrars took that loader down on 17 and 18 November, while nine router hosts still answered on the evening of 18 November (Ohey, 2026-11-19).

Improvement24 Nov 2026 04:29 UTCrun 2026-11-24T0355Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Optimizely's customer incident report, shortened on 2026-11-20 with a link to the full version in its customer portal, says the first malicious code was written at 07:51 UTC on 2026-11-16, detected at 13:34 UTC, the vulnerability closed at 16:10 UTC and the injected code removed from all affected projects by 22:24 UTC, and tells customers the exposure window is 07:51 to 22:24 UTC (Optimizely, 2026-11-20); Report URI logged its first injection earlier, at 04:21 UTC (Report URI, 2026-11-16), and the two accounts are not reconciled. Optimizely says the attacker acted as administrator users without their credentials, so no customer password was stolen, that only Web Experimentation was involved, that the script was meant to take card details typed into the site's own forms and cryptocurrency transfers, and that cards entered in hosted payment iframes such as Stripe or Adyen were not reachable (Optimizely, 2026-11-20).

The vendor's early advice of 2026-11-16 to switch the snippet off has been withdrawn, and re-enabling it is stated to be safe (Optimizely, 2026-11-20). Its customer actions are to confirm which pages ran the snippet in the window, review Content-Security-Policy violation reports and outbound requests to unfamiliar domains, review card and cryptocurrency transactions, keep web server, CDN, WAF, CSP-report and payment logs that cover 2026-11-16, assess legal notification duties, check that a strong Content-Security-Policy is in place, and remove the snippet from payment or crypto pages that run no experiments (Optimizely, 2026-11-20). Report URI counted 68 of the affected sites with no policy, 50 with a policy that still allowed the payload and the data theft, and 24 (15 percent) with one that fully blocked the payload (Krebs on Security, 2026-11-17).

Improvement25 Nov 2026 04:47 UTCrun 2026-11-25T0356Z-intelcvessourcessourcing_notetags

CISA added CVE-2026-132224, an external control of critical state data vulnerability in Optimizely Web Experimentation, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-24, on evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-11-24); the catalogue record points to Optimizely's incident page (CISA, 2026-11-24). Optimizely says it closed the vulnerability exploited on 2026-11-16 in its hosted service (Optimizely, 2026-11-18); the customer actions above are unchanged.

Builds on: DeadTag: expired tag domains send visitors to iPhone exploit kits; opening the page is enough… · APT29-linked watering hole uses n-day iOS and Chrome chains; CISA lists CVE-2024-27834; updated…

entries.headline: N-central: Hotfix 3 fixes 17 more CVEs and blocks the Legacy API; 4EverAble2Shell exploited; upgrade Agents too
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-125883 +24exploitedupdatedNATOB2

N-able N-central: 33 alleged flaws published, and Hotfix 3 (build 2026.4.1.39, 2026-11-16) now fixes 17 more CVE ids and blocks the Legacy API permanently, which 4EverAble2Shell (Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436, exploited on at least 21 servers) and Agent2Shell need; N-able does not say either chain is fixed, and public proof-of-concept code exists for the 17

An independent researcher published what Huntress counts as 33 critical flaws in the N-central appliance, chaining into four exploits, and N-able took its hosted environments offline on 2026-11-09 (Huntress, 2026-11-09).

On 2026-11-10 N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, for which Huntress lists seven CVE ids (N-able, 2026-11-10; Huntress, 2026-11-10; N-able CNA record, 2026-11-10; N-able CNA record, 2026-11-10).

On 2026-11-12 the researcher published a second set. 4EverAble2Shell is unauthenticated command execution as root that requires the Legacy API to be enabled, per BleepingComputer; it chains CVE-2026-90436, an Apache Axis 1.x deserialization flaw for which Apache does not expect a fix, with a root escalation in N-central's maintenance helper (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12; Apache Axis project, 2026-11-06; Huntback, 2026-11-12). Huntback counts at least 21 servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2, in North America, South Africa and Europe but not Switzerland, and Previdian's sensors recorded attempts at the chain (Huntback, 2026-11-12; Previdian, 2026-11-12). Agent2Shell is a set of more than ten issues in how the server talks to Windows Agents and Probes, two chains of which let an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server run commands as SYSTEM on managed endpoints; N-able confirmed it also requires the non-default Legacy API (The Hacker News, 2026-11-12; Huntress, 2026-11-13). N-able has published indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled the Legacy API (Huntress, 2026-11-13). Hotfix 3 of 2026-11-16 fixes 17 more CVE ids, hardens how Agents and Probes authenticate and blocks the Legacy API permanently, without naming 4EverAble2Shell or Agent2Shell or saying either is fixed (N-able, 2026-11-16); Huntress reports public proof-of-concept code for all 17 and no exploitation of them in its partners' environments (Huntress, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
An on-premises N-central server, yours or an IT provider's, below build 2026.4.1.39, and for the second set any build up to Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API, off by default, is on and reachable (Huntress, 2026-11-13); an Agent or Probe not on Hotfix 3 can be impersonated (N-able, 2026-11-16). A compromised server reaches the systems N-central manages (Field Effect, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In N-central's authentication and audit logs from 2026-11-08 onward, unexpected logins, new administrator accounts and changes to stored credentials or API integrations; on managed endpoints, unscheduled software deployments, scripts and remote-control sessions (Huntress, 2026-11-09; Field Effect, 2026-11-09). For 4EverAble2Shell, Huntback names POST requests to the Axis endpoint /dms/services/ServerUI, a symlink at the N-central flag file path, a systemd unit or cron entry relaunching a miner and a hidden miner directory under /tmp or /var/tmp (Huntback, 2026-11-12). Huntress's Agent2Shell indicators are static analysis only: SYSTEM PowerShell with an encoded command spawned by the Agent, where an Agent child PowerShell is common and the command is what matters (Huntress, 2026-11-13).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade on-premises servers to Hotfix 3, then every Agent and Probe, those already on Hotfix 2 included (N-able, 2026-11-16), and confirm the Legacy API is disabled and not internet-reachable, because Hotfix 2 did not stop 4EverAble2Shell, 19 of the 21 compromised servers already ran it (Huntback, 2026-11-12) and N-able does not say Hotfix 3 fixes it; treat a hit as a full compromise and rotate the administrator, service and integration credentials the platform holds where activity looks unauthorised (Field Effect, 2026-11-09). Ask each IT provider managing your endpoints through N-central whether it runs a server on premises and has upgraded it.
Update11 Nov 2026 03:49 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, on 2026-11-10 as a critical security update; hosted servers are already upgraded, on-premises customers must upgrade their own servers, and every customer must upgrade Agents and Probes, Agents first as N-able recommends (N-able, 2026-11-10). Huntress lists seven CVE ids for the fixed flaws and relays N-able's status-page statement that it observed "scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code" but no evidence that any customer environment was successfully exploited; Huntress has seen no exploitation in its partners' environments, and N-able's guidance is to keep on-premises servers offline until the upgrade is complete (Huntress, 2026-11-10). After the hotfix the built-in remote control is temporarily disabled and Take Control still works (N-able, 2026-11-10).

Update13 Nov 2026 03:54 UTCrun 2026-11-13T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagstechniquesaffected_productscvessourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesactionsbody

The researcher's second exploit set, 4EverAble2Shell, published on 2026-11-12, works against Hotfix 2 builds when the Legacy API is turned on and reachable, and no fix exists. It pairs CVE-2026-90436 in the Apache Axis 1.x SOAP engine (Apache Axis project, 2026-11-06) with a separate root escalation (Huntback, 2026-11-12; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12). Huntback counts at least 21 production servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2, mining for one operator (Huntback, 2026-11-12), Previdian's sensors recorded attempts at the chain (Previdian, 2026-11-12), and BleepingComputer relays both (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12). N-able said on 2026-11-12 that it had seen no signs of compromise, had no fix for the new claims and planned a follow-up hotfix (Tenable, 2026-11-12); Huntress says a Hotfix 2 server with the Legacy API disabled is not exposed to this chain (Huntress, 2026-11-12).

Update14 Nov 2026 04:00 UTCrun 2026-11-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The researcher's 2026-11-12 disclosure also includes Agent2Shell, which The Hacker News describes as more than ten zero-day flaws used to run commands as SYSTEM on managed Windows agents, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID (The Hacker News, 2026-11-12). Huntress describes it as a set of more than ten issues in how the N-central server communicates with Windows Agents and Probes, two chains of which let an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server run commands on managed Windows endpoints, including as SYSTEM (Huntress, 2026-11-13). Huntress relays that N-able confirmed Agent2Shell, like 4EverAble2Shell, requires the non-default Legacy API to be enabled, which settles the question Huntress and Tenable had left open on 2026-11-12, and that on 2026-11-13 at 13:40 UTC N-able said it had identified indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled the Legacy API (Huntress, 2026-11-13); the statement that N-able had seen no signs of compromise dates from 2026-11-12 (Tenable, 2026-11-12). Huntress has not observed exploitation of these issues in its partners' environments, and its Agent2Shell indicators come from static analysis of the proof of concept, not from attacks seen (Huntress, 2026-11-13). Tenable adds that N-able has temporarily deactivated the Intune integration for on-premises customers running it (Tenable, 2026-11-12).

Update18 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-18T0356Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3, build 2026.4.1.39, on 2026-11-16 as a critical security update that builds on and supersedes Hotfix 2; it fixes 17 further CVE ids, adds missing authentication and permission checks to server operations, hardens how Agents and Probes authenticate with the server, adds validation to file publishing, path and XML import handling, and permanently blocks the legacy APIs (N-able, 2026-11-16). Agents and Probes that are not upgraded are susceptible to impersonation, and all customers, hosted and on-premises, must upgrade every Agent and Probe to 2026.4.1 HF3 whether or not they already run Hotfix 2 (N-able, 2026-11-16).

The release notes name neither 4EverAble2Shell nor Agent2Shell nor the Apache Axis flaw and do not say they are fixed; what changes is the Legacy API, which N-able itself said both chains need and which is now blocked permanently (N-able, 2026-11-16; Huntress, 2026-11-17). Among the 17 ids, the release notes title CVE-2026-129272 "MMS3 appliance authentication bypass via predictable passcode", CVE-2026-129280 "ServerUI SOAP operations missing authorisation checks" and CVE-2026-129286 "SIS GenericFiles version path traversal leads to RCE", and Huntress counts three critical, eight high and six medium scores, all assigned by N-able as CVE numbering authority (N-able, 2026-11-16; Huntress, 2026-11-17).

Huntress reports that public proof-of-concept code for all 17 CVE ids appeared on the evening of 2026-11-16, shortly after the hotfix, says any unpatched server should be treated as exposed, and has not observed exploitation of them in its partners' environments (Huntress, 2026-11-17). Field Effect reports that technical details on 24 further N-central vulnerabilities were published and are reported to be addressed by Hotfix 3, a count that the 17 CVE ids in N-able's notes do not reconcile (Field Effect, 2026-11-09). Huntress advises confirming the Patch Management Engine is at 2.14.4.5829 or later, rotating secrets embedded in Automation Manager policies on a server that was exposed before patching, not relying on Take Control audit records from an unpatched server, and enforcing MFA on all N-central accounts (Huntress, 2026-11-17).

Update22 Nov 2026 14:52 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditcvessourcestags

CISA added the Apache Axis flaw CVE-2026-90436 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-18 (CISA, 2026-11-18). N-able's own remediation update reads the agent-side risk more narrowly than Huntress: it says the Legacy API is off by default, and that exploiting agent impersonation needs an existing foothold on an endpoint and yields only the information an agent receives and the values an agent can set (N-able, 2026-11-13), while Huntress describes two Agent2Shell chains that let an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server run commands on managed Windows endpoints (Huntress, 2026-11-17).
