entries.headline: Fortinet advisories: FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 8.0 have no fix for a 9.8 JSON API flaw; FortiMail RCE rows too
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-126147 +18updatedNATOA2

Fortinet coordinated security hardening release: the advisories published on 2026-11-10 carry unauthenticated FortiMail, FortiAnalyzer, FortiManager, FortiOS and FortiAuthenticator flaws rated CVSS up to 9.8; FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 8.0 have no fixed build for the JSON API flaw, FortiOS 7.0 and FortiMail 7.2 are left out of the October fixes

Fortinet announced on 2026-10-21 coordinated security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, released on 2026-10-22, and urged customers to treat them as a priority change (Fortinet, 2026-10-21). The 2026-11-10 advisories state no exploitation (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), and NCSC.ch listed the October release's status as unknown (NCSC.ch, 2026-10-22).

Critical rows (CVSS 9.0 or higher) by product: FortiMail: unauthenticated path traversal and command injection that may give code or command execution (CVE-2026-126147 and CVE-2026-126148, 9.8) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), two SQL injections (CVE-2026-126164 and CVE-2026-126263, 9.4) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) and three IBE webmail takeover or access flaws (CVE-2026-126156, CVE-2026-126150 and CVE-2026-126155, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) and an unauthenticated access flaw in other users' secure email accounts (CVE-2026-126157, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager: an unauthenticated GUI flaw that may allow code or command execution only when the JSON API is enabled, which is off by default (CVE-2026-126170, 9.8) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), oftp port SQL injection and SSRF (CVE-2026-126262, 9.3; CVE-2026-126260, 9.0) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), an administrator's access to other VDOMs (CVE-2026-126229, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) and FGFM code execution (CVE-2026-126261, 9.0) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). FortiOS: the OSPF daemon (CVE-2026-126253, 9.3), HA command execution on FGCP, FGSP and autoscale (CVE-2026-126259, 9.0) and iBGP (CVE-2026-126254, 9.6) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). FortiAuthenticator: two authentication bypasses (CVE-2026-126257, 9.0; CVE-2026-126251, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). FortiClient: an origin-validation flaw needing victim interaction (CVE-2026-121529, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10).

The October builds fix most rows: FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9; FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11 (Fortinet, 2026-10-21). Not every row: no 8.0 build fixes CVE-2026-126170 until the upcoming 8.0.3, with rpc-permit none on admin profiles that have the JSON API enabled as the workaround (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10); FortiMail 7.2 awaits 7.2.10 for CVE-2026-126150 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10); FortiAnalyzer, FortiManager and FortiOS 7.0 must migrate (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10; Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). The FortiMail builds also fix the exploited CVE-2026-104286 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-10-01).

Exposure
FortiMail 8.0.0 to 8.0.1, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8 or any 7.2; FortiAuthenticator 8.0.0 to 8.0.3 and 6.6.0 to 6.6.10; FortiOS below the fixed builds and any 7.0; FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 8.0.0 to 8.0.2 or below 7.6.8, 7.4.12 or 7.2.13 (any 7.0), with the JSON API, oftp or FGFM port reachable. FortiClient 7.4.0 to 7.4.7 and, on Windows, 7.2.0 to 7.2.14 are exposed only with the FortiPAM service installed, which Fortinet's workaround removes (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10).
Detection
Fortinet advises watching unusual administrative access and unapproved configuration changes (Fortinet, 2026-10-21); for the new rows, FortiMail web logs for unauthenticated IBE webmail and HA join requests, FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager JSON API, oftp and FGFM connections from unexpected sources, and OSPF advertisements from unexpected hosts and unusual updates from iBGP neighbours.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade FortiMail, FortiAuthenticator and the internet-facing FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer units now; an unpatched FortiMail also carries the exploited flaw. On FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 8.0 apply the rpc-permit workaround until 8.0.3 ships, plan migration off unfixed branches, and keep administrative interfaces, FGFM and oftp off untrusted networks; where an HA segment is shared with less trusted hosts, set the HA password with encryption and authentication on fixed FortiOS builds.
Update11 Nov 2026 03:50 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Fortinet published the advisories it had withheld from the October hardening release on 2026-11-10. They name unauthenticated FortiMail flaws that may allow code or command execution through crafted requests (CVE-2026-126147, CVSS 9.8) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) and through HA join-request packets (CVE-2026-126148, 9.8) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), an unauthenticated SQL injection (CVE-2026-126164, 9.4) that Fortinet remediated in FortiMail Cloud on 2026-10-05 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), and two IBE webmail flaws that let an attacker take over an IBE recipient account (CVE-2026-126156, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) or obtain an authenticated session as one (CVE-2026-126155, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). Two FortiAuthenticator flaws, a hard-coded-password bypass (CVE-2026-126257, 9.0) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) and an incorrect-authorization authentication bypass (CVE-2026-126251, 9.1) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), a FortiOS and FortiSASE OSPF flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the adjacent network broadcast link-state advertisements (CVE-2026-126253, 9.3) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) and unauthenticated code execution through the FortiManager FGFM port (CVE-2026-126261, 9.0) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) are the other rows that page named. The October builds fix most of them but not on every branch (FortiMail 7.2 and FortiOS 7.0 are told to migrate for some rows, as the update below sets out), FG-IR-26-275 lists lower minimum FortiManager builds (8.0.1, 7.6.8, 7.4.6 and 7.2.9) for the FGFM flaw, and none of the 2026-11-10 advisories states exploitation.

Update12 Nov 2026 04:20 UTCrun 2026-11-12T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The advisory pages carry ten more critical rows (CVSS 9.0 or higher), shown above, and the October builds do not fix every row: FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 8.0.0 through 8.0.2 have no fixed build for CVE-2026-126170 until the upcoming 8.0.3 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), FortiMail 7.2 awaits 7.2.10 for CVE-2026-126150 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 7.0 must migrate for CVE-2026-126229, while 7.2 is fixed in 7.2.13 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10), and FortiOS 7.0 must migrate for CVE-2026-126253 and CVE-2026-126259 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10) (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10).

Correction15 Nov 2026 14:55 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditsummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 7.2 do not need to migrate for CVE-2026-126229: Fortinet's advisory lists 7.2.0 through 7.2.12 as affected and fixes them in 7.2.13, and only 7.0 must migrate; the 7.6, 7.4 and 7.2 lines below 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13 are affected as well as 8.0 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). Fortinet revised its advisory for the FortiOS iBGP flaw CVE-2026-126254, a numeric truncation that Fortinet rates as denial of service, on 2026-11-13 to add the virtual patch FG-VD-62507.0day in FMWP database update 26.118 (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). Fortinet's blog dates the FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator builds to 2026-10-21 and the FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer builds to 2026-10-22 (Fortinet, 2026-10-21).

Update17 Nov 2026 04:34 UTCrun 2026-11-17T0355Z-intelcvesevidencebody

Fortinet revised the FortiOS HA advisory on 2026-11-16: FortiGate HA clusters running FGCP, in both active-passive and active-active mode, are also affected on the vulnerable builds, in addition to the FGSP with standalone-config-sync and autoscale deployments named in its summary, but exploitation requires an attack vector adjacent to the HA segment (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). For fixed builds where the HA layer-2 segment is not fully trusted, the advisory adds a hardening configuration: an HA password with encryption and authentication enabled for FGCP and standalone-config-sync, an encryption setting and a pre-shared secret on the standalone-cluster object for FGSP peers, and a pre-shared secret on the autoscale object (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10). The fixed builds are unchanged (8.0.1 or above, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14, with 7.0 migrating) and the revision says nothing about exploitation.

Improvement22 Nov 2026 14:54 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditaffected_productsbodycves

FortiClient is exposed to CVE-2026-121529 only where the FortiPAM service is installed, and Fortinet's workaround is to uninstall that service (Fortinet PSIRT, 2026-11-10).

entries.title: Fortinet coordinated security hardening release: the advisories published on 2026-11-10 carry unauthenticated FortiMail, FortiAnalyzer, FortiManager, FortiOS and FortiAuthenticator flaws rated CVSS up to 9.8; FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 8.0 have no fixed build for the JSON API flaw, FortiOS 7.0 and FortiMail 7.2 are left out of the October fixes

updates.summary: Fortinet's withheld advisories were published on 2026-11-10 and name unauthenticated FortiMail code-execution, SQL-injection and IBE account-takeover flaws (CVSS up to 9.8), two FortiAuthenticator authentication bypasses (9.0 and 9.1), a FortiOS OSPF flaw reachable from the adjacent network and unauthenticated code execution through the FortiManager FGFM port; the fixed versions are unchanged and no exploitation is stated.

Fortinet's advisories of 2026-11-10 carry ten more critical rows than the nine first listed across FortiAnalyzer, FortiManager, FortiOS, FortiMail and FortiClient, and the October builds do not fix every row: FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 8.0 have no fixed build for CVE-2026-126170 until 8.0.3, FortiMail 7.2 awaits 7.2.10 for CVE-2026-126150, and FortiOS 7.0 and FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 7.2 and 7.0 must migrate.

FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager 7.2 are fixed for CVE-2026-126229 in 7.2.13 and only 7.0 must migrate, so 7.2 owners update rather than migrate; the 7.6, 7.4 and 7.2 lines below their fixed builds are affected as well as 8.0. Fortinet added a virtual patch for the iBGP flaw CVE-2026-126254 on 2026-11-13, and FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator are dated to their 2026-10-21 release.

Fortinet revised the FortiOS HA advisory for CVE-2026-126259 on 2026-11-16: FortiGate HA clusters running FGCP, in active-passive and active-active mode, are also affected on the vulnerable builds, though exploitation needs an attack vector adjacent to the HA segment. The advisory adds an HA hardening configuration for fixed builds whose HA segment is not fully trusted; the fixed builds are unchanged.
FortiClient is exposed to CVE-2026-121529 only where the FortiPAM service is installed, and uninstalling that service is Fortinet's workaround.

entries.headline: ARTEX in AWS: CloudWatch log searches for secrets, Cognito self-sign-up for credentials; hunt CloudTrail for both
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

ARTEX against AWS: Datadog sees agent sessions open with anonymous S3 reads, search CloudWatch Logs for secrets with stolen long-term IAM keys, and self-register in public Cognito user pools to obtain AWS credentials

Datadog Security Labs reports that in October 2026 operators of ARTEX, the agentic penetration-testing framework Microsoft ties to Storm-0940, worked against several AWS environments with a focus on financial data, and that every session it reviewed opened with unauthenticated S3 reads, which CloudTrail records with a userIdentity type of AWSAccount and an accountId of anonymous, calling GetObject, ListObjects and similar read APIs (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09). Where S3 hosted a web front end, the agent read build manifests and runtime configuration, and it requested objects named like placeholders just before bursts of key guesses (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09), the habit Wiz saw as a request for a path that should not exist before each fuzzing run (Wiz Research, 2026-10-22).

With a valid long-term IAM access key, the agent's most frequent call was CloudWatch Logs FilterLogEvents, always with a limit of 1,000 events: it first searched log text for the names of cryptocurrency firms, hedge funds and invoicing terms and, in a later session on 2026-10-20, for storage links, internal addresses, database references, passwords and AKIA-style access keys (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Without a key, the agent self-registered in a public Cognito user pool, iterating against a PreSignUp Lambda that checked a tenant domain, then ran InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, GetUser and GetTokensFromRefreshToken and traded the tokens for short-term AWS credentials, which CloudTrail shows under the CognitoIdentityCredentials role session name; some SignUp calls named the tool in the user agent (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09). It then tried read-only discovery calls such as ListBuckets, ListSecrets, DescribeParameters, ListTopics, DescribeLogGroups, GetRestApis, DescribeRepositories and ListFunctions, all of which failed because the identity pool's authenticated role was narrow (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Datadog found hundreds of internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in Mandarin, and says the distributions it analysed do not appear to carry a cloud methodology of their own, so the post-exploitation playbook depends on the model in use; some versions block .gov, .gov.cn, .edu and .edu.cn targets by default (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Exposure
AWS accounts with long-term IAM access keys that may have leaked, applications whose public Cognito user pools allow self-registration with identity pools that vend AWS credentials to authenticated users, and S3 buckets that serve web front ends without authentication.
Detection
In CloudTrail and S3 access logs, anonymous read bursts that include requests for placeholder-named objects; FilterLogEvents calls with a fixed limit of 1,000 from a long-term user key; Cognito SignUp spikes with PreSignUp failures, followed by CognitoIdentityCredentials sessions issuing broad read-only discovery calls that end in access-denied errors; and instance-role credentials used from an address outside AWS, which Datadog lists among the unusual patterns to hunt (Datadog Security Labs, 2026-11-09).

Triage: FilterLogEvents is a routine call for log tooling and engineers; the discriminator is a long-term user key searching log text for credentials, internal addresses or company names at a constant page limit, from an address that key does not normally use.

Defender takeaway
Check which Cognito user pools allow open self-registration and what their identity pools' authenticated roles can read, rotate long-term IAM keys found in code or logs, and hunt CloudTrail for the sequences above; a narrow authenticated role is what stopped the Cognito path in the case Datadog describes.

Builds on: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names… · Elastic: CyberStrikeAI against AWS, six medium or low alerts joined only by source IP; alert on… · Entra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for secrets, an operator reaches MSP clients… · WorkOS breach agent was a researcher's ARTEX test that escaped its sandbox; legacy API, dev…

entries.headline: Linux TCP use-after-free: Sophos hotfix and Ubuntu generic kernels out; WatchGuard, Fortinet have no fixed build
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-98432updatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-98432, Linux kernel IPv4 TCP: a use-after-free in connection setup, present since 4.4, has an Anthropic-built remote root exploit against MPTCP listeners that CloudLinux could not reproduce; Citrix XenServer, XCP-ng, MikroTik, Red Hat, Debian, CIQ, Amazon Linux, Ubuntu's generic kernels for 22.04 to 26.10 and Sophos have fixes, Ubuntu 20.04 and older and some HWE, FIPS, NVIDIA and Azure variant kernels are in progress and WatchGuard and Fortinet have none for their products (CVSS 9.8)

The Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432 on 2026-10-15; the kernel.org CNA scores it 9.8 while upstream rates it 8.1 with high attack complexity (CIQ, 2026-10-30). It is a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP connection setup path, introduced in Linux 4.4 and fixed upstream in 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3-rc7 (Linux kernel CVE team, 2026-10-15). An unauthenticated peer starts it by sending TCP SYN packets that carry IPv4 options, and a retransmitted SYN can then touch the freed option memory (CIQ, 2026-10-30).

Anthropic wrote on 2026-10-27 that Claude produced an exploit that gives a remote attacker root on a Linux server with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener (Anthropic, 2026-10-27), but CloudLinux's kernel team could not reproduce the claim (CloudLinux, 2026-11-02). Akamai is not aware of a public working exploit and says disabling MPTCP alone does not prevent exploitation (Akamai, 2026-11-02), whereas Vates, XCP-ng and WatchGuard say a public exploit exists or circulates (XCP-ng, 2026-11-04; Vates, 2026-11-04; WatchGuard, 2026-11-03). No source reports attacks, and NCSC-NL judges large-scale abuse unlikely given the exploit's complexity (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-30).

Debian, Red Hat, CIQ and AWS have fixed kernels (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-11-03; Red Hat, 2026-11-03; CIQ, 2026-11-01; AWS, 2026-11-02), and Ubuntu's tracker, last updated 2026-11-10, lists 22.04 LTS to 26.10 as fixed (linux 5.15.0-203.213, 6.8.0-149.149, 7.0.0-43.43 and 7.3.0-10.10) while 20.04, 18.04 and 16.04 are still in progress (Canonical, 2026-11-10). Citrix has fixed its XenServer appliances (Citrix, 2026-11-03). XCP-ng released a kernel fix (XCP-ng, 2026-11-04), MikroTik's RouterOS 7.25.1 and 7.24.6 changelogs list the CVE (MikroTik, 2026-11-02; MikroTik, 2026-10-30), Sophos released Sophos Firewall hotfix HF110626.1 on 2026-11-06 and SD-RED firmware 3.0.012 on 2026-11-05 (Sophos, 2026-11-06), and Veeam's KB4966 says its Software and Infrastructure Appliances, workers, helper appliances and recovery media include an affected kernel, fixed through Veeam Updater or a private fix (Veeam, 2026-11-10). WatchGuard lists Fireware OS, AP and Dimension as potentially affected with no fix (WatchGuard, 2026-11-03); Fortinet names no fixed build but added an IPS virtual patch in FMWP database update 26.113 on 2026-11-07 (Fortinet, 2026-11-07).

Exposure
A Linux host on a kernel below the fixed builds that accepts IPv4 TCP connections from an attacker; the demonstrated exploit needs an MPTCP listener, which sudo ss -M -l -n -p -e lists and which Go programs enable on Linux listen sockets by default since Go 1.24 unless the multipathtcp GODEBUG setting or a per-socket option overrides it (Akamai, 2026-11-02; Go team, 2026-10-29). CIQ's testing found that setting net.mptcp.enabled to 0 leaves the plain-TCP path reachable (CIQ, 2026-10-30), and Akamai reports a similar flaw when request-socket migration is on (Akamai, 2026-11-02).
Detection
No source publishes an indicator. Because the trigger is a SYN packet with IP options (CIQ, 2026-10-30) and a lost race only fails the handshake, so the attacker can retry (Anthropic, 2026-10-27), repeated option-bearing SYNs from one source toward a listener in firewall or flow telemetry are the pattern the mechanism implies.
Defender takeaway
Install the distribution kernel and reboot as soon as it ships and confirm the running version afterwards; Ubuntu 20.04 and older and some variant kernels were not out on 2026-11-10. Until then, drop IPv4 TCP packets whose header carries IP options before the TCP stack sees them, tested first on one non-production host because it also drops legitimate option-bearing traffic; disabling MPTCP alone does not remove the path (CIQ, 2026-10-30).
Update01 Nov 2026 13:53 UTCrun 2026-11-01T1312Z-auditactionsbodycvessourcessourcing_notetitle

CIQ released patched kernels on 2026-10-31 for RLC Pro LTS 9.6 and FIPS 9.6 (kernel-5.14.0-570.60.1+27.2.el9_6_ciq), LTS 9.2 and FIPS 9.2 (kernel-5.14.0-284.30.1+45.1.el9_2_ciq) and LTS 8.6 (kernel-4.18.0-372.32.1+40.1.el8_6_ciq); RLC Pro LTS 8.10 and RLC Pro 10 are still waiting, and CIQ says the same fix was backported to the stable series 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56 and 7.2.10 (CIQ, 2026-10-31). Ubuntu's tracker, last updated 2026-10-30, still lists its kernels as vulnerable with fixes in progress (Canonical, 2026-10-30), and Red Hat's page now gives a preliminary CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 (Red Hat, 2026-10-31).

Update03 Nov 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-11-03T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Fortinet published advisory FG-IR-26-188 on 2026-11-02, saying it is investigating the impact on its products and listing FortiOS, FortiProxy, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiWeb and FortiAuthenticator among them, with no fixed build or workaround named (Fortinet, 2026-11-02). CloudLinux's kernel team could not reproduce Anthropic's remote-root claim (CloudLinux, 2026-11-02). AWS says fixed Amazon Linux 2 and 2023 kernels are available, that Network Load Balancer TCP listeners pass client packets, including IP options, to targets, and that Linux targets behind them, Global Accelerator, PrivateLink and VPC Lattice layer 4 need the kernel update or the interim steps themselves, in the bulletin as published on 2026-11-02; its revision of 2026-11-04 says Global Accelerator endpoints are not affected and no longer carries the Network Load Balancer paragraph (AWS, 2026-11-02). Akamai reports a similar flaw when request-socket migration is enabled and lists the stable fixes 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56 and 7.2.10 (Akamai, 2026-11-02). CIQ's table lists patched kernels for RLC Pro 8, 9 and 10 and FIPS 8.6 and 8.10 released on 2026-11-01 (CIQ, 2026-11-01).

Update05 Nov 2026 04:04 UTCrun 2026-11-05T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryentitiesaffected_productscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Citrix's bulletin CTX697256 of 2026-11-03, rated Critical, says an unauthenticated attacker on the management network may compromise a XenServer host and any running Workload Balancing or Conversion Manager appliance; it affects XenServer 8.4 and 9, Workload Balancing before 2026.1.1 and Conversion Manager before 2026.2.0, and Citrix has pushed updates to the Early Access and Normal channels of each XenServer line without naming a build and released Workload Balancing 2026.1.1 or later and Conversion Manager 2026.2.0 (Citrix, 2026-11-03). The bulletin states no exploitation.

Vates's advisory VSA-2026-056, published on 2026-11-03 and updated on 2026-11-04, rates the flaw critical for XCP-ng 8.3 and the Xen Orchestra Appliance, lists the fixed packages kernel-4.19.19-8.0.46.14.xcpng8.3 and, for the appliance, linux 6.1.190-1, requires a reboot, and gives an interim mitigation that drops inbound IP options, because without IP options the vulnerable code path cannot be reached (Vates, 2026-11-04). XCP-ng's post of 2026-11-04 says anyone who can send TCP traffic to the host, for example from its management network, VMs on it included, can attempt the attack, and tells hosts that cannot reboot at once to apply the iptables-based mitigation and not yet the update (XCP-ng, 2026-11-04). XCP-ng says a public exploit exists that relies on MPTCP, which the XCP-ng 8.3 kernel does not have, so it does not work against XCP-ng, while the underlying bug is present and other ways to exploit it cannot be ruled out (XCP-ng, 2026-11-04); Vates says the exploit does not affect XCP-ng and the bug is not specific to MPTCP (Vates, 2026-11-04).

WatchGuard's advisory WGSA-2026-0033 of 2026-11-03 lists Fireware OS, AP and Dimension as potentially affected with no fix, says Fireware OS and AP do not enable MPTCP and are not affected by the exploit chain circulating online, and says it will update the advisory when Ubuntu ships a fix for Dimension (WatchGuard, 2026-11-03). MikroTik's RouterOS 7.25.1 of 2026-11-02 and RouterOS 7.24.6 of 2026-10-30 list the CVE under "improve stability" (MikroTik, 2026-11-02; MikroTik, 2026-10-30). NCSC Switzerland's advisory 13120 of 2026-10-29 rates exploitation unknown with vendor patches available and names MPTCP listeners as the target of the known exploits (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-29). Fortinet's advisory is unchanged: still investigating, with no fixed build, and Known Exploited: No (Fortinet, 2026-11-02).

Update08 Nov 2026 14:01 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditactionsbodycvesheadlinesourcessummarytitle

Ubuntu's tracker, updated on 2026-11-07, lists Ubuntu 26.10 as fixed in linux 7.3.0-10.10, while 26.04, 24.04, 22.04, 20.04, 18.04 and 16.04 remain vulnerable with work in progress (Canonical, 2026-11-07). Sophos released Sophos Firewall hotfix HF110626.1 on 2026-11-06 for v23.0 GA, v23.0 EAP1 and v22.0 MR3, which needs a firewall restart and downloads automatically where automatic hotfix installation is enabled, the default, and SD-RED 20 and SD-RED 60 firmware 3.0.012 on 2026-11-05 (Sophos, 2026-11-06). Fortinet added an IPS virtual patch, "Linux.Kernel.tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock.Use.After.Free.", in FMWP database update 26.113 on 2026-11-07; its advisory still names no fixed build (Fortinet, 2026-11-07).

Update11 Nov 2026 03:55 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-intelentitiesaffected_productssourcesevidenceactionsbodytitleheadlinesummarycvessourcing_note

Veeam's impact statement KB4966, last modified on 2026-11-10, says that every Veeam component that includes a Linux kernel is affected until the kernel is updated: Veeam Software Appliance 13.1, Veeam Infrastructure Appliance 13.1 in any role (backup proxies, repositories including hardened repositories, gateways, mount servers, WAN accelerators and others), workers deployed by the hypervisor plug-ins, the Linux-based helper appliances of Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1 and 12.3, Veeam Recovery Media for the Agent for Linux created before the update, and the public-cloud plug-in appliances; Kasten for Kubernetes is not affected (Veeam, 2026-11-10). The fixed kernel, a CIQ build 5.14.0-570.60.1+27.2.el9_6_ciq, has been in the Veeam repository since 2026-11-02; Veeam Updater checks every 12 hours and, with the default configuration, installs mandatory updates on the nearest Sunday at 14:00 in the backup server's time zone, a restart may be required, Windows-based Backup & Replication servers need a private fix for their helper appliances, and virtual labs and helper appliances that stay deployed must be redeployed (Veeam, 2026-11-10).

Ubuntu's tracker, updated on 2026-11-10, now lists 26.04 LTS (linux 7.0.0-43.43), 24.04 LTS (6.8.0-149.149) and 22.04 LTS (5.15.0-203.213) as fixed alongside 26.10 for the generic linux package, with 20.04, 18.04 and 16.04 and some HWE, FIPS, NVIDIA, Azure and Raspberry Pi variant kernels still in progress (Canonical, 2026-11-10).

Update15 Nov 2026 15:00 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditaffected_productscvessourcesactionsbody

Sophos's advisory, updated to version 5 on 2026-11-12, adds that SD-RED firmware 3.0.012 was released on 2026-11-10 as a manually installed patch for Sophos UTM, which requires UTM 9.724 or later, and that legacy RED models past end of life are affected but will not receive a fix (Sophos, 2026-11-06). Ubuntu's tracker, updated on 2026-11-14, now lists the HWE kernels for 20.04, 22.04 and 24.04, Azure for 22.04 to 26.04, NVIDIA for 22.04 to 26.04 and Raspberry Pi for 22.04 to 26.04 as fixed, while FIPS for 24.04 and 20.04, Azure 7.0 and Azure NVIDIA for 24.04, NVIDIA 6.8 for 22.04 and the generic kernels for 20.04 and older remain in progress (Canonical, 2026-11-10). Veeam's KB4966, last modified on 2026-11-13, adds the helper appliances embedded in Veeam Recovery Orchestrator 13.1, fixed by a private fix, and Recovery Media for Veeam Agent for Linux 6.3, and lists the delivery per component: Veeam Updater for the appliances, an automatic update on launch for workers, a private fix for the helper appliances of Windows-based Backup & Replication and Recovery Orchestrator, and new recovery media (Veeam, 2026-11-10). Debian's tracker lists 6.12.117-1 as the current trixie security build, after the first fixed 6.12.113-1 (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-11-03).

entries.headline: AhsayCBS chain exploited and in CISA KEV: standard releases v9.17.0 and v10.3.6 list a patchset for both flaws
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-105133 +1exploitedupdatedNATOB1

CVE-2026-105133 / CVE-2026-105134, AhsayCBS backup management console: an unauthenticated authentication-bypass and code-execution chain exploited since 7 October to drop webshells and a cryptominer; Ahsay's earlier patches were incomplete, and its standard releases v9.17.0 and v10.3.6 now list a patchset for both flaws

Huntress reports that from 2026-10-07 23:20 UTC attackers exploited two flaws in AhsayCBS, the management console of Ahsay's backup software that managed service providers and system integrators mainly use, to gain unauthenticated remote code execution and deploy webshells on exposed servers (Huntress, 2026-10-08). CVE-2026-105133, an improper-authentication flaw in the checkSysPwd function of the API, is used first to bypass authentication; CVE-2026-105134, in the /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do endpoint of the Replication Receiver component, then gives code execution as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, after which the attacker configured a malicious receiver and dropped a JSP webshell into the directory the application serves (Huntress, 2026-10-08). BleepingComputer reports that the activity targeted at least five organizations on 7 October and that CVE-2026-105133 has a public exploit (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-09).

Follow-on activity, per Huntress: payloads fetched with curl and certutil from cloud object storage, an XMRig Monero miner disguised as a Microsoft Edge binary and run as SYSTEM through a renamed NSSM service that mimics the Edge updater, and a PowerShell script that hides the miner while Task Manager is open (Huntress, 2026-10-08). The earlier patches did not close the flaws: public records had listed AhsayCBS up to 10.3.2 as affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-09), Huntress found on 2026-10-08 that 10.3.4 is also affected (Huntress, 2026-10-08), and Ahsay's release notes for 10.3.4 list no security fix (Ahsay, 2026-08-05).

Exposure
AhsayCBS servers (on Windows a service run from cbssvcX64.exe or cbssvcX86.exe; Horizon3 shows the same chain on the Linux build, where the service runs as root (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14)), whose management web interface is reachable from untrusted networks and that run a v7 to v10 build without the fix (v9.17.0, v10.3.6, or a hotfix from v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70 on), which includes v10.3.4.0 and v9.15.2.59 (Ahsay, 2026-11-12; Ahsay, 2026-11-02; Ahsay, 2026-10-12; Huntress, 2026-10-08).
Detection
Process-creation telemetry with parent lineage: children of the AhsayCBS service process outside its normal startup and maintenance commands, because commands from an uploaded JSP webshell appear as its direct children, and curl or certutil from that lineage writing into a Temp folder; and a service named like the Edge updater running an Edge-named binary from a Temp folder as SYSTEM (Huntress, 2026-10-08). On the server itself, Horizon3 adds new .jsp files under webapps/rps or webapps/cbs that answer 404 unless a specific parameter is supplied, replication receivers created outside a change window (a "Created new receiver" entry in the system log) and system administrator accounts nobody provisioned (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). Huntress's later forensics adds webshells hidden in an uploaded PNG, which leave no command parameter in access logs, a miner relaunched every minute by a SYSTEM scheduled task and Defender exclusions covering the service process (Huntress, 2026-11-09).

Triage: AhsayCBS legitimately spawns its own startup and maintenance commands, so a child process alone is weak; the discriminators Huntress gives are a child of the service that downloads files into a Temp folder, and an Edge-named binary run as SYSTEM from a Temp folder under a service that mimics the Edge updater (Huntress, 2026-10-08).

Defender takeaway
Install v9.17.0 or v10.3.6 (current build v10.3.6.14), whose release notes list the patchset for both CVEs, or the latest partner hotfix v9.15.2.78 or v10.3.4.55 followed by a reboot, on every AhsayCBS server, including those on the earlier patches (Ahsay, 2026-11-12; Ahsay, 2026-11-02; Ahsay, 2026-11-13; Ahsay, 2026-10-27; Ahsay, 2026-10-12); ask your backup suppliers whether they run it, and until it is applied keep the management interface on trusted addresses or a VPN, since the exploit targets the externally reachable web application (Huntress, 2026-10-08); where an indicator of compromise turns up, re-image the host from a trusted backup, since Huntress says attackers hid secondary backdoors for extended persistence (Huntress, 2026-10-08).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:09 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryprioritytagstechniquescvessourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteconfidenceclassificationactionsbody

Ahsay now says its previous patches v9.15.2.59 and v10.3.4.0 "did not fully address" the two flaws, and tells partners to apply the AhsayCBS v10.3.4.45 hotfix on v10 and the v9.15.2.70 hotfix on v7, v8 and v9, both from the partner portal (a valid partner login is required), then to reboot the server (Ahsay, 2026-10-12). The announcement is dated 2026-10-12; Huntress, in an update of the same day to its report, dates the hotfix release to that day and says it independently verified that the v10.3.4.45 hotfix mitigates the initial entry point of the chain, which was still open on earlier v10 versions (Huntress, 2026-10-08).

CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-14 "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-10-14). Bitdefender MDR reports three intrusions through the chain, the first two beginning around 7 to 8 October and a third identified on 14 October; in the first, attackers validated access through JSP webshells, staged PowerShell payloads, tried to stage payloads as command files in C:\Users\Public and tried to establish persistence; in the second they deployed JSP files, tried the same command-file staging, searched for stored credentials, elevated an account to SYSTEM and used obfuscated PowerShell to install and configure OpenSSH, which gives a way back that does not depend on the vulnerable web service, so patching alone does not end the incident; across its incidents the follow-on PowerShell scripts were staged on a subdomain of a public static-site hosting service; it attributes the activity to no named actor, and notes that the file names, tools and binaries differed from one incident to the next, so the dependable signal is how the server behaves after the exploit fires (Bitdefender, 2026-10-15).

Improvement18 Oct 2026 03:34 UTCrun 2026-10-18T0256Z-intelsourcesevidenceactionsbody

Horizon3.ai published a source-level analysis of both flaws on 2026-10-14, working from the Linux installer, and says its proof of concept for the chain, from authentication bypass to a webshell, is on its GitHub (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). For CVE-2026-105133, every action of the JSON API extends a base class whose administrator password check is skipped when the request body carries a FromServlet flag that the caller sets, so the JSON API is reachable without credentials, and the AddSysUser action, which creates a system administrator, never consults the caller (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). For CVE-2026-105134, an authentication-bypassed call creates a replication receiver whose home directory the attacker chooses; the system-folder denylist that screens that directory at creation is not applied to the upload path later built from two attacker-supplied headers, in which only the percent and colon characters are escaped, so a traversal sequence walks the write location into a served web application, and one upload of a .jsp file then runs as LocalSystem on Windows and as root on Linux (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14). Horizon3 says Ahsay released its hotfixes on 12 October 2026 (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14).

Update10 Nov 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-inteltechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Huntress's follow-up covers an organisation whose AhsayCBS servers were exploited between 8 and 11 October 2026, before Ahsay's hotfixes; Huntress verified that 10.3.4.45 blocks the entry point it saw and ties the intrusion to the first campaign by webshell location, an exploit source address and matching files (Huntress, 2026-11-09). The operator planted five JSP webshell families under the console's web application directories (Huntress, 2026-11-09); Huntress reads the Linux-style copies, in directories such as /opt, /usr/local and /home, as showing that the exploit simply tried every likely location (Huntress, 2026-11-09). One family hides an AES-encrypted Java class in the least-significant bits of an uploaded PNG's pixels and runs it in memory, so no command parameter appears in access logs; another is a signed-API shell with command execution and chunked upload and download of up to 4 GB per file, a ready exfiltration channel on a backup host; a third can delete itself and any path it is given, so a missing file does not prove it was never there (Huntress, 2026-11-09).

Huntress also found a second XMRig miner kept alive by a SYSTEM scheduled task with a backdated start time that runs every minute, an embedded Python distribution under the SYSTEM profile started from a Run key whose wrapper only runs if a marker file named for the SHA-256 of the host's MachineGuid exists and which then loads a DLL whose strings are consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS lookups, the tunnelling tools gost and chisel, the remote access tools AnyDesk, Atera and Splashtop, a rogue local account, a Mimikatz package and Microsoft Defender exclusions that include the AhsayCBS service process (Huntress, 2026-11-09). On a Veeam server in the same environment it saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module, a PowerShell script launched through WMI that queried the VeeamBackup database for stored credentials and decrypted them; it cannot say how many credentials were retrieved, has not identified the implant family and cannot say what, if anything, was taken through the webshell's download action (Huntress, 2026-11-09). For any server exposed before the hotfix, Huntress recommends a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotating the credentials stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and in any backup software on the same network (Huntress, 2026-11-09).

Update15 Nov 2026 14:59 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-audittitleheadlinesummarycvessourcesactionsbodysourcing_note

Ahsay released AhsayCBS v9.17.0 on 2026-11-12 as a standard release; its release notes list a security patchset for CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, remote API access disabled by default and the JSP engine disabled to prevent execution of malicious JSP files (Ahsay, 2026-11-12). For v10, the release notes of v10.3.6, dated 2026-11-02, list the same patchset and the same two settings (Ahsay, 2026-11-02), and Ahsay announced v10.3.6.1 on 2026-11-03 (Ahsay, 2026-11-03). Partners who stay on hotfixes have newer builds: Ahsay's advisory of 2026-10-27 tells partners on v7, v8 and v9 to take the v9.15.2.78 hotfix, which adds security hardening, and names v10.3.4.55 as the latest v10 hotfix (Ahsay, 2026-10-27). The current v10 build, v10.3.6.14 of 2026-11-13, lists among its security fixes that the Redirector logged the CBS password in readable form in its access log, so access logs from earlier builds can hold that password (Ahsay, 2026-11-13). The flaw class of CVE-2026-105134 is described two ways: CISA's catalog calls it command injection through the random parameter of the UpdateReceivers.do endpoint (CISA, 2026-10-14), while Horizon3's analysis of the source describes a file-write path traversal that leads to code execution (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-14).

entries.summary: Huntress observed from 2026-10-07 23:20 UTC attackers chaining two AhsayCBS flaws, CVE-2026-105133 (authentication bypass) and CVE-2026-105134 (code execution as SYSTEM through the Replication Receiver API), against internet-exposed servers of the backup management console that managed service providers and system integrators mainly use, dropping JSP webshells and an XMRig cryptominer; Bitdefender MDR investigated three intrusions through the same chain, and CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-14. Ahsay now says its earlier patches v9.15.2.59 and v10.3.4.0 did not fully address the flaws, so servers on them are still exposed; v9.17.0 of 2026-11-12, a standard release, carries Ahsay's patchset for both CVEs and turns remote API access and the JSP engine off by default, the v10 standard release v10.3.6 of 2026-11-02 lists the same patchset, the latest partner hotfixes v9.15.2.78 and v10.3.4.55 of 2026-10-27 remain an option, and a server that was reachable before the fix needs a compromise check.
entries.title: CVE-2026-105133 / CVE-2026-105134, AhsayCBS backup management console: an unauthenticated authentication-bypass and code-execution chain exploited since 7 October to drop webshells and a cryptominer; Ahsay's earlier patches were incomplete, and its standard releases v9.17.0 and v10.3.6 now list a patchset for both flaws

updates.summary: Ahsay says its previous patches v9.15.2.59 and v10.3.4.0 did not fully fix the flaws and names the hotfixes v10.3.4.45 and v9.15.2.70, available only to partners; Huntress verified the v10 hotfix, CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-14, and Bitdefender MDR describes three intrusions through the chain. Hotfixes now cover v10 and v7 to v9, through the partner portal.

Horizon3.ai's source-level analysis of 2026-10-14 gives the root cause of both flaws (a caller-set flag that skips the administrator credential check, and an upload path that escapes the folder denylist), shows the chain runs as root on Linux, and lists server-side hunt artifacts: new .jsp files in served application directories, replication receivers created outside a change window, unexpected system administrator accounts, and requests carrying the bypass field or the receiver upload headers.

Huntress's follow-up on servers exploited between 8 and 11 October, before the hotfixes, describes five webshell families, a second miner and a host-bound Python implant, plus Veeam credential theft on a neighbouring server; it advises a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotation of the credentials the server held or could reach.

Ahsay's standard releases v9.17.0 (2026-11-12) and v10.3.6 (2026-11-02) list its patchset for both exploited CVEs and turn remote API access and the JSP engine off by default, so the fix no longer depends on the partner-only hotfixes, whose latest builds are v9.15.2.78 and v10.3.4.55 (2026-10-27); the current v10 build, v10.3.6.14 of 2026-11-13, also stops the Redirector logging the CBS password in readable form. CISA's catalog calls CVE-2026-105134 command injection, while Horizon3's source analysis shows a path-traversal file write.

entries.headline: XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers: two of 14 flaws exploited, unauthenticated root RCE; password flaws stay unfixed
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-124007 +7exploitedupdatedNATOB2

Dixell/Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors: VulnCheck published 14 CVEs on 2026-11-12, seven scored CVSS 4.0 9.2 to 9.3 (unauthenticated command injection that runs as root, a hard-coded Administrator password, Administrator and root passwords computed from the MAC address and date); VulnCheck sees two of the 14 exploited, the injection flaws are fixed on the current branch and the password flaws will stay unfixed after Copeland ended support on 2026-03-16

VulnCheck, the assigning CNA, describes unauthenticated command injection in XWEB EVO through the password field (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12) and the username field (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12) of its login and API scripts, and through the sh parameter of the setuid xwconsole.cgi (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12), all reaching root; a hard-coded password for the built-in Administrator account that gives a full session in one request (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12); and Administrator and root passwords that can be computed offline from the device MAC address and the date (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12; VulnCheck, 2026-11-12; VulnCheck, 2026-11-12). The cluster holds 14 records, and the seven scored 9.2 or higher are the ones covered here (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-12). VulnCheck says the injection and backdoor-password flaws belong to the pre-2021 builds and are fixed on the current branch, while the predictable-password flaws reach the last firmware, 5.8.8 (VulnCheck, 2026-11-13). Copeland's bulletin says software support ended on 2026-03-16 with no further firmware or security updates (Copeland, 2026-03-16), so those will stay unfixed; its public download pages list EVO packages only up to 5.2.3 of 2018 (Copeland, 2026-11-13).

VulnCheck's canary sensors recorded in-the-wild exploitation of the unauthenticated configuration-file write CVE-2026-124014 (CVSS 4.0 8.8, XWEB EVO 4.3.0 through 5.8.8) from 2026-11-12 22:00 UTC and four root-command probes against CVE-2026-124010 from 2026-11-13 03:41 UTC, from two opportunistic scanners it does not tie to the October refrigeration campaign (VulnCheck, 2026-11-13; VulnCheck, 2026-11-12). Copeland's bulletin of 2026-10-14, carried in the Dixell France guide that CERT-FR links, acknowledges a vulnerability on an end-of-life generation of XWEB EVO controllers and tells operators to remove all XWEB EVO units from the public internet immediately (translated from French) (Dixell France, 2026-10-14); NCSC Switzerland says that guidance addresses end-of-service XWEB EVO systems and that the public information does not confirm exploitation of the Danfoss CVEs it lists (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-06), and BACS lists Copeland and Dixell XWEB as potentially affected (BACS, 2026-11-10). The one compromised-unit log read concerns an XWEB Pro, not an EVO (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
An XWEB EVO unit, sold until October 2023 (Copeland, 2026-03-16), whose login page appears when the site's public address is opened from outside the site network, which is the vendor's own test (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).
Detection
In web or proxy access logs in front of the supervisor, an unauthenticated POST to config.lua or an unauthenticated GET to /cgi-bin/xwconsole.cgi with an sh parameter is VulnCheck's request-level signal (VulnCheck, 2026-11-13). After suspected access the vendor's procedure is to review the user list and profiles and the alarm categories, levels and recipients with a test alarm, and to read product temperatures directly in the cabinets because setpoints or alarm thresholds may have changed; CERT-FR says a factory reset removes persistence but leaves an end-of-life unit vulnerable (Dixell France, 2026-10-14; CERT-FR, 2026-10-16).
Defender takeaway
VulnCheck sees two flaws exploited (VulnCheck, 2026-11-13) and the password flaws will never be fixed, so keep XWEB EVO units off the internet and reach them only through a VPN, install the latest build from Copeland's update page on any pre-2021 unit, and plan the move to the supported XWEB Pro (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).
Update15 Nov 2026 14:53 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-audittitleheadlinesummaryprioritytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

VulnCheck's canary sensors recorded in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-124014, an unauthenticated write of the system configuration file through config.lua that affects XWEB EVO 4.3.0 through 5.8.8 (CVSS 4.0 8.8), from 2026-11-12 22:00 UTC, and four probes running a root command through CVE-2026-124010 from 2026-11-13 03:41 UTC; it added both to its own exploited-vulnerabilities list and reads both sources as opportunistic scanners, not the October refrigeration campaign (VulnCheck, 2026-11-13; VulnCheck, 2026-11-12). The same disclosure says the injection and backdoor-password class was removed in the 2021 rewrite and is fixed on the current branch, so the unfixed exposure is the pre-2021 fleet plus the predictable-password flaws, which reach the last firmware (VulnCheck, 2026-11-13). For CVE-2026-124014 the two VulnCheck sources differ: the blog lists it with the pre-2021 class, while the CNA record gives XWEB EVO 4.3.0 through 5.8.8 as affected (VulnCheck, 2026-11-12). Copeland's guide tells operators to install the latest build for their model from its System Software Update page while they migrate (translated from French) (Dixell France, 2026-10-14).

entries.headline: Chrome zero-day CVE-2026-125350 exploited: update Chrome to 157.0.8103.50 and Edge to 157.0.4341.46 or later
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-125350exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-125350, Google Chrome before 157.0.8103.50: a use-after-free in the XML component is exploited in the wild and listed by CISA; Edge 157.0.4341.46 and Edge for Android carry the fix, other Chromium browsers are still to follow

Google's Stable-channel update of 2026-11-09 moves Chrome to 157.0.8103.50 on Linux and 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Windows and macOS and states "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild" (Google, 2026-11-09). CVE-2026-125350 is a high-severity use-after-free in the XML component, reported by Arni Hardarson (Neonix Security) on 2026-10-12 and by an anonymous reporter on 2026-11-06 (Google, 2026-11-09). The Extended Stable update of the same day, 156.0.8078.96, lists the CVE as well (Google, 2026-11-09). CISA added CVE-2026-125350 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 (CISA, 2026-11-10) and describes it as a flaw that could let a remote attacker execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox through a specially crafted webpage (CISA, 2026-11-10). No source describes the attacks: SecurityWeek, which counts it as the eighth Chrome zero-day of the year, writes that no information appears to be available on them (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-10). NCSC Switzerland rates the flaw as actively exploited (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's Edge release notes state that Edge 157.0.4341.46 of 2026-11-09 and Edge for Android 157.0.4341.53 contain the fix (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Exposure
Chrome desktop below 157.0.8103.50 and Chrome Extended Stable below 156.0.8078.96 (Google, 2026-11-09; Google, 2026-11-09), Edge below 157.0.4341.46 and Edge for Android below 157.0.4341.53 (Microsoft, 2026-11-11), and other Chromium-based browsers such as Opera, which CISA names (CISA, 2026-11-10), until their vendors ship the fix; the build shows in chrome://version or in the managed-browser inventory, and Google rolls the release out over days to weeks, so a pending relaunch leaves a patched machine still running the old code (Google, 2026-11-09).
Detection
Neither Google nor CISA publishes an indicator, so the controls are the browser-version inventory and the browser's own crash and child-process telemetry: a renderer crash followed, for the same user, by a browser-spawned shell or script interpreter, a new scheduled task or a connection to a newly registered domain is the sequence to weigh up.

Triage: renderer crashes are common and benign; the discriminator is what follows them on the same host.

Defender takeaway
Treat the update as out-of-band: force Chrome to the current Stable build (157.0.8103.50 is the first fixed one) and the relaunch on every managed endpoint now, move Extended Stable, Edge and Edge for Android to their fixed builds, and push the other Chromium fixes the day each vendor lists CVE-2026-125350, because the exploit is in use and the sources give no way to tell who is targeted.

entries.action_label: Ransom-ISAC: Gentlemen affiliate, VPN without MFA…
entries.classification_html: NATOC2
entries.headline: Ransom-ISAC: Gentlemen affiliate, VPN without MFA to Domain Admin in an hour; GPO locker likely lost a replication race
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOC2

The Gentlemen affiliate: an SSL-VPN account without MFA, a Windows Server 2003 host and a dormant local administrator gave Domain Admin in under an hour; the GPO locker most likely lost a replication race, so antivirus was disabled estate-wide but only one host was encrypted (Ransom-ISAC)

Ransom-ISAC reconstructs an early-August 2026 intrusion into a small company by a Gentlemen ransomware affiliate from forensic images of two domain controllers, event logs of 41 hosts and firewall logs (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13). Entry was an SSL-VPN account without MFA that succeeded on the first attempt from an unusual country; neither egress address appears in any earlier failed login, so the credential was most likely held beforehand. Within the hour the actor ran an anonymous SMB sweep, three Kerberoast-style service-ticket requests (the KDC logged an RC4 and DES downgrade against an AES-only account) and hundreds of failed SMB logons against a domain controller, then used a dormant, weak-password local administrator on an end-of-life Windows Server 2003 SQL host that allowed null sessions. A Domain Admin session opened on the domain controller less than an hour after the first login; Ransom-ISAC could not prove how and says the credentials were most likely taken from that host. The actor then pushed a Rust credential harvester, which takes the DPAPI domain backup key, and EtherRAT, a Node.js implant that reads its command address from an Ethereum smart contract and never reached it; data left through the VPN tunnel over about two days of a weekend (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

The locker, run on a domain controller in domain-wide mode, built a GPO linked enforced at the domain root and the Domain Controllers container, with eight registry values that disable antivirus and a Preferences scheduled task in SYSVOL. The call that declares the Preferences extension reached a domain controller the GPO had not replicated to, the script suppressed the error and no client read the task: antivirus was off estate-wide but the locker ran on one host, which wiped its logs (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
An SSL-VPN gateway with accounts that lack MFA, and any end-of-life host reachable from the VPN address pool that allows null sessions or keeps dormant local administrators.
Detection
In KDC and authentication logs, RC4 or DES advertised against an AES-only account, bursts of SMB logon failures from one client (expired-password answers show valid credentials) and null-session logons with random sixteen-character workstation names followed by a dormant local account's logon on a legacy host; in directory change records, a new GPO linked enforced at the domain root or a Preferences task file written into SYSVOL outside the management console; on servers, a Run value named like a browser updater, node.exe fed its script on standard input by a node.exe parent, resolution of three or more public Ethereum RPC providers and antivirus preference changes that disable real-time monitoring (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

Triage: scanners and inventory tools also sweep SMB anonymously and legacy applications use null sessions (the finding is a dormant account logging on right after); developers resolve Ethereum RPC providers, so scope that rule to servers; administrators edit GPOs, so correlate with the change calendar (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

Defender takeaway
Ransom-ISAC concludes that the actor needed one credential without MFA and one end-of-life server to reach Domain Admin (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13), so MFA on every SSL-VPN account and retiring or isolating the legacy host with its dormant local administrator each remove a link; Ransom-ISAC advises that a GPO of this shape found in a domain be unlinked and deleted, with its Preferences task file, before hosts are cleaned or credentials rotated (Ransom-ISAC, 2026-11-13).

The locker's GPO disabled antivirus across the estate but the task that runs it most likely never reached clients because of a replication race, so the locker ran on one host; the report names the telemetry at each step. entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Huntress: 2,223 crypto-named fake sessions sit on 118 ScreenConnect servers, likely bait for unpatched technicians
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

ScreenConnect: Huntress finds 2,223 fake guest sessions named after crypto exchanges on 118 self-hosted servers, enrolled from 2026-11-03 and, in its leading hypothesis, bait for technicians whose clients predate 26.6.5; it saw no malicious use and no overlap with SCKit

Huntress counted 2,223 fake guest sessions on 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers across 109 MSP and organisation accounts, enrolled between 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-13: always-online "computers" named after crypto exchanges (an exchange word joined to a role word) with a trading-desktop thumbnail (Huntress, 2026-11-14). An MSP asked about them on 2026-11-12; its own server showed no web shells, suspicious child processes or new accounts, and the first Access installer Huntress examined was publicly downloadable, which ScreenConnect allows without authentication by design, and a guest client needs the server's relay address, which is embedded in that server's guest installer, to register. Huntress saw no malicious activity from the sessions: technicians who opened them mostly stayed under 30 seconds, and in one case a technician used the send-text feature, which ScreenConnect does not log, so Huntress treated it as a possible credential exposure. On 29 servers with complete history the operator revisited every 151 seconds to keep the sessions online (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Huntress's leading hypothesis, which it has not observed, is bait: a technician who connects with a client older than 26.6.5 would let a malicious guest use the file-transfer flaw CVE-2026-84869 to run a file on the technician's workstation, often the MSP's most privileged machine; it cannot rule out capturing what a technician types, and it found no overlap with the published SCKit indicators (Huntress, 2026-11-14). It considers the public suggestion that the sessions are a malware sandbox detonating installers unlikely.

Exposure
A self-hosted ScreenConnect server whose Access guest installer is public or leaked, and every technician host client older than 26.6.5; server session history shows client versions (Huntress, 2026-11-14).
Detection
In the server session database, new guest sessions with ClientType 1 (Windows), an empty guest public key, empty company or site fields and crypto-site thumbnails (guest version 25.3.4.9288 is context, not unique on its own); in web or relay logs, many new Access guests from one external address in a short window; on technician workstations, ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe or msiexec.exe on a file under a Documents Temp folder, which Huntress calls the host-side shape of CVE-2026-84869 exploitation. A fake alone shows reachability, not exposure: compare technician-side with guest-side events (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Triage: a malware-analysis sandbox detonating a ScreenConnect installer also creates guest sessions; per Huntress, a sandbox session sends a key and JPEG screenshots of the analysis VM, while these send no key, reuse seven screenshot families and randomise hardware and OS details (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade technician host clients to 26.6.5 or later, keep Access installer links private and rebuild leaked ones, restrict installer and web access where supported, bar technicians from joining sessions they cannot tie to a customer, and move unfamiliar sessions into a group technicians do not browse; in Huntress's hypothesis the target is a technician client below 26.6.5 (Huntress, 2026-11-14).

Builds on: ScreenConnect clients before 26.6.5 run guest-pushed files unprompted; Huntress confirms… · ScreenConnect SCKit: second wave hits on-prem; disable RMM+, update technician clients to…

entries.headline: Cursor marketplace served a trojanised Claude Code extension for 11 hours; uninstalling leaves the SSH backdoor
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

Cursor marketplace: a tampered Claude Code extension (versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313) planted an SSH key, a reverse tunnel and persistence for about eleven hours on 2026-10-29; uninstalling it does not remove the persistence

Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT on 2026-10-29 (09:27 to 20:35 UTC) a maliciously modified copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for macOS and Windows, was served from the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace; Cursor removed it, rebuilt the marketplace, rotated its keys and had the attacker's server taken offline (Cursor, 2026-10-29). Anthropic told Microsoft its systems were not compromised and that it did not build the package, and Microsoft confirms the packages were never published to the Visual Studio Marketplace or npm (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30). Cursor's report of 2026-11-13 says the attacker wrote the copies onto the marketplace cache with a credential taken through a key exposed at its vendor Fireworks, and that at most 5,000 users potentially received the build (Cursor, 2026-11-13).

The injected loader runs when the extension module loads (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30). It reports host and user data (hostname, username, operating system, directories, Git email, environment-variable names and public IP address), appends an attacker-controlled SSH public key to authorized_keys, tries to enable the local SSH service and open a reverse SSH tunnel, and installs persistence outside the extension: a LaunchAgent on macOS, and on Windows a scheduled task that asks to run as SYSTEM with a Startup-folder fallback, with background scripts retrying the tunnel about every 60 seconds (Cursor, 2026-10-29). Microsoft's analysis adds a user crontab entry for Linux (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30). Because of coding errors, enabling SSH fails unless Cursor was started with administrator privileges, so on most hosts the attacker could not log in through the tunnel, but the key, persistence and host report remained (Cursor, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
Any macOS or Windows host on which Cursor installed or auto-updated Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 inside the window; the code also carries Linux routines though Cursor names only macOS and Windows packages (heise online, 2026-10-30). Extension-install telemetry shows the version. NCSC Switzerland's post of 2026-10-30 places the extension on Open VSX (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-30); Cursor says Open VSX never had it (Cursor, 2026-11-13). Cursor says coding-agent traces from sessions outside Privacy Mode were exposed for fewer than 0.05% of users, all notified, so a user with no notice was not among them (Cursor, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In process-creation telemetry, an editor's extension host starting ssh or autossh with remote port forwarding and no command; in file-write telemetry, an editor process modifying authorized_keys; and, shortly after an extension update, a new LaunchAgent, scheduled task, Startup-folder script or @reboot crontab entry named after system-monitoring components. Phorion advises matching the attacker key's fingerprint rather than the comment string it carries (Phorion, 2026-10-30). Removing the extension does not remove the persistence scripts, which keep running (Cursor, 2026-10-29).

Triage: a running SSH process is not proof the attacker got in, since both ends must allow the connection (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-30); administrators run tunnels too, and what separates this one is an editor extension as the parent process and persistence written to user-writable locations rather than a managed service.

Defender takeaway
Treat a host that ran either version as backdoored whether or not the tunnel connected: remove the key, the persistence and the tunnel processes, rebuild where compromise cannot be excluded, and rotate credentials reachable from it. heise reports a cleaned release, with 2.1.314 as the minimum to install (heise online, 2026-10-30).
Update15 Nov 2026 04:24 UTCrun 2026-11-15T0356Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencetechniquesactionssourcing_notebody

Cursor's incident report of 2026-11-13 says an attacker obtained an access key Cursor had issued to its vendor Fireworks, which Fireworks exposed, and used it to copy a read-only storage bucket of historical coding-agent traces from sessions not in Privacy Mode; a small number of the traces held credentials that had not been redacted, and less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed (Cursor, 2026-11-13). From those credentials the attacker reached select SaaS tools and, through them, archived non-production source code repositories, limited customer support data and credentials users had sent to Cursor support (Cursor, 2026-11-13). On 2026-10-29, "using a stolen credential from the exposed data from our internal system", the attacker placed the malicious copies directly on the cache that serves the marketplace; Cursor says Anthropic did not publish them, that this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product, that Open VSX never had the malware, that at most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions that day potentially received the build, and that the last attacker activity, on 2026-11-01, was blocked (Cursor, 2026-11-13). Where credentials were exposed Cursor emailed team admins a list of the keys to rotate (Cursor, 2026-11-13).

Fireworks' bulletin of 2026-11-09 describes its own intrusion, which it links to a financially motivated group that sells tokens from unauthorized access to language models to illicit routing gateways ("LLMjacking"), and further activity on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-24 after a security incident at a cloud provider that hosted its development machines; it does not mention Cursor (Fireworks AI, 2026-11-09). Neither company names an actor for the extension.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Kaspersky: BlackNevas used vCenter Host Profiles to enable SSH on ESXi, destroyed backups first, then wiped datastores
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky GERT BlackNevas case: credentials from systems outside the virtualisation layer reach both vCenter appliances, a remote-access agent and a VMware-lookalike tunnel service persist, vCenter Host Profile remediation switches SSH on across the ESXi hosts, backups are destroyed first and a wipe of the datastores detonates over ten days, with no vulnerability exploited

Kaspersky GERT describes an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organisation's virtualisation estate over ten days: four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine on them, both vCenter Server Appliances and all connected backup infrastructure (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). No virtualisation-layer vulnerability was exploited: credentials obtained from non-virtualisation systems inside the perimeter reached the appliances, and every action against ESXi ran through legitimate VMware management interfaces (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). The activity is attributed to BlackNevas through the ransom notes (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

The attackers logged in as root over SSH to the vCenter appliance that manages virtualisation disaster recovery, fetched and deployed MeshAgent with a shell script 43 seconds later, and about four hours later returned through MeshAgent to install the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit whose name, description and Restart=always imitate appliance housekeeping (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). They then used vCenter Host Profiles to change the TSM-SSH service state: eleven minutes after the first configuration read SSH was enabled on the target ESXi hosts, and direct SSH to the hosts then came from the vCenter appliance address (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). Payloads went to ESXi over SFTP, a self-test of the executable ran about three hours before the final detonation, and about the first 2 KB of the virtual disk files were overwritten (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). The backup environment fell first: the attacker extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on the backup infrastructure, disabled antivirus there days earlier, then stopped backup services and encrypted the recovery infrastructure, all before ESXi detonation (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
A vCenter and ESXi estate where accounts from systems outside the virtualisation layer can reach the vCenter appliances and where Host Profile remediation can change the SSH service state; the article names no version (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In vCenter events and tasks and in vpxa.log and vobd.log, Host Profile remediation that changes TSM or TSM-SSH from policy-disabled to running outside an approved change window, which Kaspersky rates critical when an SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance to the same host follows within 15 minutes; on the vCenter appliance, a new VMware-looking systemd unit absent from the organisation's list of trusted services; in ESXi shell logs, execution of a newly staged executable under /tmp followed by access to /vmfs; and preserved hostprofiletrace.log (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13). ESXi logs sit in a ramdisk that is cleared at reboot, so Kaspersky says not to begin by rebooting a host (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Triage: each Host Profile step is legitimate alone, so the distinguishing context is authorisation, timing, source account, change window and whether the desired state weakens security; a VMware-looking service is not malicious by default, since custom integrations exist, but one absent from the trusted list is a high-confidence anomaly, and chmod +x is ambiguous alone while execution of a newly staged executable from /tmp is itself a strong indicator (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

Defender takeaway
Treat the vCenter appliances as the control plane to protect: alert on Host Profile changes to TSM-SSH outside change windows and on SSH from vCenter to ESXi that follows them, review VMware-looking services on the appliances against a trusted list, and keep backup-platform credentials and administration separate from the systems that can reach vCenter, because the backup environment was destroyed before the hosts (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-13).

NOTABLECVE-2026-105437 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-105437, GitLab self-managed 19.5.4, 19.4.6 and 19.3.8 critical patch release: a heap overflow in Git's merge code that a user who can open a merge request can trigger for command execution as the git user on the Gitaly node; Git 2.56.1 also fixes CVE-2026-111760, code execution when a malicious repository is cloned with submodules; no exploitation reported

GitLab shipped an ad-hoc critical patch release on 2026-11-10, 19.5.4, 19.4.6 and 19.3.8 for CE and EE, for CVE-2026-105437, a vulnerability in Git that under certain conditions gives out-of-bounds heap writes that could run arbitrary commands in Gitaly's environment; it affects all versions from 16.2 before 19.3.8, 19.4 before 19.4.6 and 19.5 before 19.5.4, while GitLab.com and Dedicated already run a patched version (GitLab, 2026-11-10). GitLab's detection page says any user who can create a project and open a merge request reaches the flaw, which gives command execution as the git operating-system user and read and write access to every repository on that Gitaly node (GitLab, 2026-11-12).

Git 2.56.1 and the backports 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2 of 2026-11-10 fix the same flaw and five others (GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10). The one that matters on workstations and CI runners is CVE-2026-111760: a long path that passes validation is written as .git and replaces a freshly cloned submodule's .git file with a symlink to a directory that holds attacker hooks or configuration, which GitHub says can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone (oss-security, 2026-11-11; GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10). The maintainers believe it is only triggerable with --recurse-submodules and note that such a repository fails fsck, which does not protect downstream users, since an innocuous-looking .gitmodules pointing at it suffices (oss-security, 2026-11-11). GitHub Enterprise Server fixes are in 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4, and GitHub is coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the Copilot app with patched Git (GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10); Git for Windows 2.56.1.windows.1 addresses the issue (Git for Windows, 2026-11-10). No source reports exploitation; GitLab documents a lab reproduction in which opening one merge request left a crash entry within a second and a half (GitLab, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
A self-managed GitLab CE or EE in the affected ranges that lets users create projects and merge requests, or any Git older than the fixed releases on a workstation, CI runner or service that clones or merges untrusted repositories; applications that bundle Git need their own update (GitLab, 2026-11-10; GitHub Blog, 2026-11-10).
Detection
GitLab's rule fires when the error field of a Gitaly event contains merge-tree: signal: followed by anything other than killed or terminated, and a .gitattributes in the target branch that sets an unusually large conflict-marker-size supports a true positive; GitLab says a working attempt is silent, a clean result does not prove the flaw was not used, the rules rest on error wording captured on 19.4.1 only, and many installs do not ship the Gitaly and Sidekiq logs (GitLab, 2026-11-12). On build hosts, hook scripts or shells spawned by git during a recursive clone are the behavior CVE-2026-111760 produces.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade self-managed GitLab to a fixed release and, for a self-compiled install, rebuild both the Git in Gitaly and the Git at git.bin_path or move the distribution Git to 2.56.1 or later (GitLab, 2026-11-10); until then limit who can create projects and sign up, and on a hit treat the instance and every repository on that Gitaly node as compromised (GitLab, 2026-11-12). Servers that cannot upgrade yet can set conflict-marker-size=7 in each repository's info/attributes or turn off the merge checks for untrusted repositories (The Hacker News, 2026-11-11). Update Git on runners and workstations and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories until it is done.

actions: Update every Red Hat Quay registry to its branch's fixed release (3.9.28, 3.10.28, 3.12.24, 3.14.10, 3.15.9, 3.16.7, 3.17.7 or 3.18.3) and, until then, restrict the /keys endpoint at the proxy or load balancer to trusted internal components; on any instance whose /keys endpoint untrusted clients could reach, review audit logs for service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events with a null expiration_date and remove unrecognised approved service keys, because deleting a rogue key is not durable before the fix and resetting passwords or regenerating robot tokens does not revoke it.

entries.headline: Red Hat Quay: anonymous signing-key takeover and cross-tenant token theft; update to your branch's fixed release
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-123710 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-123710 and CVE-2026-110697, Red Hat Quay: an anonymous client can install its own registry signing key and read or overwrite every private image (CVSS 3.1 9.8), and a low-privilege account can steal other tenants' robot tokens (9.9); fixed in Quay 3.9.28 to 3.18.3, no fix for Quay 5 or the mirror registry, no exploitation reported

Red Hat's record for CVE-2026-123710 says an unauthenticated client of Red Hat Quay can obtain an anonymous registry token with an audience it chooses, present it to the service-key rotation endpoint and install its own approved signing key with no expiry (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). NCSC Switzerland summarises the impact as letting network attackers with anonymous or low-privileged access read, overwrite or poison private container images and steal registry credentials, compromising the software supply chain (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13). The condition is that the /keys endpoint is reachable by untrusted clients (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); anonymous access is on by default, and turning it off does not protect, because any valid Quay account can still exploit the flaw (Red Hat, 2026-11-13).

CVE-2026-110697 lets an attacker who creates a namespace containing an underscore match and retrieve robot accounts and their decrypted tokens from other tenants' namespaces; Red Hat says it needs no elevated privileges or victim interaction and that, where Quay is OpenShift's integrated registry, stolen robot credentials can inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines (Red Hat, 2026-11-11).

Red Hat's page for the second flaw lists the fixed builds 3.9.28, 3.10.28, 3.12.24, 3.14.10, 3.15.9, 3.16.7, 3.17.7 and 3.18.3 and says Quay.io is already fixed (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); its CSAF record for the first flaw links eight Quay errata, RHSA-2026:99019 and 99021 to 99027, as its fixes and lists Red Hat Quay 5 and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift 2 as affected with no fix available (Red Hat, 2026-11-13). NCSC Switzerland lists the exploitation status as unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13).

Exposure
A Red Hat Quay registry, standalone, deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift or as the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift, whose /keys endpoint untrusted clients can reach, and for the second flaw a multi-tenant registry where an account can create namespaces (Red Hat, 2026-11-13; NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-13).
Detection
In Quay audit logs, service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events with a null expiration_date and approved service keys nobody recognises (Red Hat, 2026-11-11); for token theft, registry pulls or pushes that do not match expected robot-account usage (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). A planted signing key survives password resets and robot-token regeneration (Red Hat, 2026-11-13).
Defender takeaway
Update to the fixed release of your branch and, until then, restrict /keys at the proxy or load balancer to trusted internal components; a deleted rogue key is not durable before the fix, because the anonymous request can install a new one (Red Hat, 2026-11-11). Where /keys was reachable, treat registry images as unverified until the keys are reviewed and, for the second flaw, restrict who can create namespaces with an underscore and rotate robot tokens of any namespace that collides with one (Red Hat, 2026-11-11).
