entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: PK Softech apparently kept Publica data it had promised in writing to delete; Tamedia says Akira holds about 100 GB
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOA2

PK Softech, software supplier of Swiss pension funds: malware and a data outflow at Publica, with the City of Zurich fund PKZH saying its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Bernese funds BPK and BLVK and Pensionskasse Post also reporting the supplier incident, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office investigating

The Confederation, in a release headlined "data outflow confirmed" (translated from German), says an external software supplier of the federal pension fund Publica detected a cyberattack at the end of September, informed its other customers, and that the Federal Prosecutor's Office has opened an investigation; no other federal office has a business relationship with the supplier (Swiss Federal Administration, 2026-10-08); the supplier, PK Softech AG, says unknown persons used malware to reach part of its IT infrastructure and that it must be assumed data left its systems, with type and scope still under investigation (PK Softech, 2026-10-08). Publica's own page lists name, date of birth, AHV number, address, contact details, salary, civil status, partner details and IBAN as data that could be affected, adding that its investigation indicates personal data of insured persons has presumably left and that it cannot rule out that an individual member's data left (Publica, 2026-10-08). The Bernische Pensionskasse dates the supplier incident to 2026-09-29 and says software that encrypts data (ransomware) was installed (translated from German) (BPK, 2026-10-30); no source names an access vector. The Bernische Pensionskasse names PK Softech AG as its supplier (BPK, 2026-10-30), and the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse (BLVK, 2026-10-08) and Pensionskasse Post (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-09) report the supplier incident too. The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, which has suspended its planned early-2027 move to PK Softech's system (Inside IT, 2026-11-03), says its inquiries indicate that personal data of its insured persons and pensioners, handed over as test data, was stolen (PKZH, 2026-10-15), and Pensionskasse Post says personal data did leave but not yet whether its insured persons' data is among it (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15). Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger reports that the Akira ransomware group holds about 100 GB of compressed pension data on well over 100,000 current and former federal employees, including staff of the security authorities, and demands ransom; as of 2026-10-20 neither the Confederation nor Publica had confirmed the perpetrator or the demand, and Publica said it still had no indication that data was published on the darkweb (Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-20; Inside IT, 2026-10-20; Publica, 2026-10-20). On 2026-11-10 PK Softech said on its homepage that no concrete ransom demand reached it and that it never contacted the attackers (PK Softech, 2026-11-10); Publica's page of the same day says the supplier received general extortion letters immediately after the attack, never made concrete with an amount or payment deadline, and that Publica itself received no demand (Publica, 2026-11-10); the State Secretariat for Security Policy told Keystone-SDA that the federal bodies handling the incident know of no concrete ransom demand to them, that the Confederation paid no ransom, that, as she put it, a demand to the supplier was "not made concrete with an amount or deadline" (translated from German) and that it still has no indication of publication on the darkweb (watson.ch, 2026-11-10). Netzwoche, relaying the same paper, adds that the Federal Council and the security authorities now assume data on practically all current and former federal and federally affiliated staff left (Netzwoche, 2026-10-21).

PK Softech had confirmed in writing to Publica in January 2026 that it deleted the data of the 2019 migration and held no personal data in plaintext, and the Tages-Anzeiger reports that this apparently did not happen, because the data was still on its servers when the attackers got in (Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-21; Inside IT, 2026-10-22). Publica confirmed the sequence: it asked PK Softech to delete all legacy data, including that of the 2019 migration, and received written confirmation in January 2026, and is now clarifying why personal data presumably lay on the servers, while PK Softech did not answer and says it does not comment on individual customer relationships (Inside IT, 2026-10-22). Inside IT, citing Tamedia, adds that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed that data was extracted by the Akira ransomware group, which 20 Minuten words as according to findings so far; the Prosecutor's Office has since confirmed to watson.ch that a notorious extortion gang is behind the attack (watson.ch, 2026-11-03), and Publica's own newsletter of 2026-10-22 also says the Akira group is being associated with the attack while it clarifies whether and whose Publica data left (Inside IT, 2026-10-22; 20 Minuten, 2026-10-22; Publica, 2026-10-22). The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT first said through Corriere del Ticino, relayed by Ticinonline, that potentially all of its insured could be involved (Ticinonline, 2026-10-20); its letter of 2026-10-23 narrows that: its own checks found data of about 1,800 persons among the documents on the attacked server, it has no certain evidence that these data were taken but finds it plausible, and it wrote to all insured because it cannot exclude that more was affected (IPCT, 2026-10-23; Ticinonline, 2026-10-23).

Exposure
A body whose staff are insured with Publica, which insures federal administration and ETH domain staff (watson.ch, 2026-10-08), the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich (PKZH, 2026-10-15), Pensionskasse Post (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15), the Bernische Pensionskasse (BPK, 2026-10-30) or Lehrerversicherungskasse (BLVK, 2026-10-08), the Ticino fund IPCT (IPCT, 2026-10-23), the Pensionskasse der Stadt Zug (Inside IT, 2026-11-09) or a fund that Libera AG manages (NZZ, 2026-10-17), or whose pension administration runs on PK Softech software, whose customers include several further funds (Inside IT, 2026-10-09); each fund's own notice or letter says whether and which of its insured persons' data is affected.
Detection
Publica warns that misuse of the data cannot be ruled out and asks members to watch for unusual e-mails, calls or messages (watson.ch, 2026-10-08), so the telemetry to watch is mail-gateway logs and the helpdesk, HR and payroll call and ticket records of affected bodies for contact that cites an AHV number, a salary, a partner's details or an IBAN.
Defender takeaway
Until the funds report the scope, the AHV number, date of birth, address, salary and IBAN of anyone insured with Publica or any fund named above, whether the fund says data of its insured persons was stolen or only cannot rule it out, should not serve as proof of identity, and a request that quotes them, a request to change a payout account included, deserves a call-back through a known number. An organisation that runs PK Softech software should ask the supplier in writing whether its data was in the environment: the exposed files at IPCT, the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich and, apparently, Publica were project, test or migration data held at the supplier (IPCT, 2026-10-23; PKZH, 2026-10-15; Inside IT, 2026-10-22), so the check to make at any supplier is which personal data it holds outside the productive system and whether its written deletion confirmation is true. Staff should also hear that cantonal police warn that criminals could use leaked personal and financial data for investment-fraud calls (Cybercrimepolice, 2026-10-13).
Update10 Oct 2026 03:48 UTCrun 2026-10-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryprioritysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The supplier's customer base is now partly public and includes cantonal-level institutions. The Bernische Pensionskasse (BPK) states in a notice dated 2026-10-09 that an external software supplier of the BPK suffered a cyberattack at the end of September 2026 (BPK, 2026-10-30), which AWP reports is the same company that counts Publica among its customers (cash.ch (AWP), 2026-10-09); the supplier filed a criminal complaint, informed the relevant federal bodies and its affected customers, various federal bodies are clarifying with it which data is affected, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office has opened an investigation (BPK, 2026-10-30). The BPK says there are currently no indications that its data was stolen but that this cannot be entirely excluded, and that insured persons are being informed (BPK, 2026-10-30). Netzwoche reports that the Canton of Bern's own notice names the BPK and the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse (BLVK) as concretely affected, that the BPK insures canton staff and the personnel of the three cantonal universities (42,145 active insured and 18,321 pensioners on 31 December 2025) and that the BLVK insures 21,417 active Bernese teachers (Netzwoche, 2026-10-08). The BLVK's own notice does not name its supplier; it says the supplier took the affected environment off the network, brought in external specialists, informed the authorities and filed a criminal complaint, and that the supplier and the BLVK are still checking whether and to what extent BLVK data is affected (BLVK, 2026-10-08). Pensionskasse Post, the occupational pension fund of Swiss Post, names PK Softech and says whether and to what extent its insured persons' data is affected is under review; it states that its data at PK Softech is anonymised and holds no particularly sensitive personal data such as IV disability-insurance files, a claim that is the fund's own and not independently verified (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-09). Inside IT lists the BLVK, the BPK, Migros-Pensionskasse, Pensionskasse Post and Syngenta Pensionskasse as customers of the manufacturer "among others" and says some of the funds have already announced that they are checking with PK Softech for a possible data outflow (Inside IT, 2026-10-09). PK Softech says it has been fully available to its customers again since 2 October 2026 (PK Softech, 2026-10-08). The access vector, the actor, which data belongs to which fund and whether a ransom was demanded were not public in any source read as of that date.

Improvement13 Oct 2026 03:38 UTCrun 2026-10-13T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Publica's own page, dated 2026-10-08, lists civil status, details of the spouse or partner and the IBAN among the data that could be affected, besides name, date of birth, AHV number, address, contact details and pension data, and Publica says its investigation indicates that personal data of insured persons has presumably left, while it cannot rule out that an individual member's data left (Publica, 2026-10-08). The AWP report, which relays the software firm's position, says the firm knows that data left but not yet whether personal data is among it, that it could also be business data unrelated to member files, and that the volume is rather small (cash.ch, 2026-10-09). Publica's wording is stronger than the supplier's, and which data left is still open; a request that quotes an IBAN deserves the same call-back as one that quotes an AHV number.

Update15 Oct 2026 03:48 UTCrun 2026-10-15T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactions

The City of Zurich's pension fund has commented, and its position differs from the other funds': the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich (PKZH) says in a notice dated 2026-10-13 that PK Softech was hit at the end of September, that it currently works with another software provider and plans to move to PK Softech's administration system in early 2027, so the attack does not touch the system it uses today, and that it is still clarifying whether, because of tests carried out ahead of that switch, PKZH data is also affected (PKZH, 2026-10-13). It adds that the incident does not affect insured persons' pension assets (PKZH, 2026-10-13). PKZH's concern is that migration tests may have left PKZH data at the supplier; it has not said that they did. Publica's page now carries a status of 2026-10-14 saying that it currently has no indications that data from the attack on its software supplier has been published on the darkweb and that it keeps monitoring the situation; its list of data that could be affected is unchanged (Publica, 2026-10-20). Neither statement says which data left, how the attackers got in or who they are.

Update16 Oct 2026 04:11 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

On the Cybercrimepolice platform, dated 2026-10-13, the cantonal police warn that after a cyberattack on a software provider of a pension fund, criminals could use the leaked personal and financial data to phone those affected and lure them into fraudulent investments of their pension assets (translated from German); the page describes a ransomware attack at the end of September and names no company (Cybercrimepolice, 2026-10-13). SwissCybersecurity.net ties the warning to PK Softech, names the cantonal police of Zurich and Bern as its authors, and reads its conditional wording as meaning no case of actual misuse had been registered yet (SwissCybersecurity.net, 2026-10-15). The police ask pension funds to tell insured persons that knowing someone's personal details or the size of their pension assets is no proof that a caller is trustworthy, and to let them check enquiries through official channels (Cybercrimepolice, 2026-10-13).

The Zurich cantonal fund BVK, which insures the cantonal administration and has bought PK Softech software since 2011, says through its spokesperson that the application runs in the BVK's own data centre independently of the supplier, so it is from today's view not directly affected, and that PK Softech holds only working material from it such as documentation, troubleshooting reports and further-development concepts (translated from German; NZZ, 2026-10-13). PK Softech told the NZZ that it can neither confirm nor rule out that further customers are affected and left the question whether a ransom was demanded unanswered (NZZ, 2026-10-13). Inside IT adds that the Istituto di previdenza del Cantone Ticino is listed on the Simap procurement platform as a PK Softech customer since 2018 and has made no statement on whether its data is at risk (Inside IT, 2026-10-14).

Update17 Oct 2026 03:35 UTCrun 2026-10-17T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich (PKZH), the City of Zurich's pension fund, has moved from checking to confirming. Its notice of 2026-10-15 says its inquiries so far indicate that personal data of PKZH insured persons was also stolen in the attack, and that this data had been used in tests for the planned system switch (PKZH, 2026-10-15); its FAQ adds that data was taken from PK Softech's system, including personal data of insured persons and of pensioners (PKZH, 2026-10-15). Inside IT reports that PKZH currently uses another software provider and plans to move to PK Softech's system in 2027 (Inside IT, 2026-10-16); PKZH's own FAQ says the system it uses to manage assets and pay pensions is not affected and dates the move to the beginning of 2027 (PKZH, 2026-10-15). The page still carries its earlier line that PKZH is checking whether its data is affected next to the confirmation (PKZH, 2026-10-15). It says a switch of this kind has to be tested with data that reproduces the real pension relationships as completely as possible, that PK Softech is contractually bound to protect and keep the data confidential, and that whether it met that duty is being investigated (PKZH, 2026-10-15).

Which data was stolen is still being clarified; in the worst case the fields are first name, name, date of birth, AHV number, address, private and business e-mail and telephone, insured earnings and retirement assets, civil status, partner details and IBAN (PKZH, 2026-10-15). PKZH was told on 2026-10-13 that data of its insured persons might be affected, has filed a criminal complaint and has reported the incident to the data-protection office (PKZH, 2026-10-15). It says a payout needs a signed written request and an identity check and that a change of bank details is checked additionally, so the data alone cannot trigger one, but that criminals can use it to appear credible (PKZH, 2026-10-15).

Pensionskasse Post's notice of 2026-10-15 says the investigation has shown that personal data did leave, and that it remains unclear whether data of its insured persons is affected, though that is possible (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15). It does not repeat its earlier statement that its data at PK Softech is anonymised, and lists name, address, date of birth, AHV number, contact details, e-mail address and pension data as data that could be affected (Pensionskasse Post, 2026-10-15). The access vector, the actor and any ransom demand were not public in any source read as of that date.

Update20 Oct 2026 03:39 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

SonntagsBlick reports that Federal Councillor Karin Keller-Sutter brought information on the supplier incident to the Federal Council's meeting of Wednesday 2026-10-14, and that a confidential information note says the Confederation internally expects "considerable damage", calls the incident "serious" and tells current and retired federal staff to expect longer-term effects (translated from German; Blick, 2026-10-18). The note says the security organs of the Confederation are particularly affected, which Blick glosses as the Federal Intelligence Service (NDB), the Defence Group in the VBS department and the Federal Office of Police (fedpol) (Blick, 2026-10-18). Blick adds, from its own information, that the cantons were also informed because a combination of certain stolen data sets may allow conclusions about Swiss defence capability, and that the Confederation warns internally that some employees could be recognised and questioned by the authorities of another country (Blick, 2026-10-18). The Finance Department confirms only that the Federal Council was informed on Wednesday and says neither the Federal Council nor a department supervises Publica; Publica says it set up a crisis staff and is still establishing which data and how many people are affected (Blick, 2026-10-18). The scenario of matching stolen federal data against entry lists is Blick's reading and an unnamed insider's, not an authority finding.

The NZZ reports that the pension consultancy Libera AG confirmed on Friday 2026-10-16 that it also works with PK Softech and is therefore affected, and that PK Softech first told Libera on 2026-10-14 that personal data had also left, without knowing which; Libera can neither confirm nor rule out that the funds it manages or individual insured persons are affected (NZZ, 2026-10-17). The Bernische Pensionskasse told the NZZ that, contrary to the supplier's earlier information, it must be assumed that personal data left, and PK Softech cannot currently say which of its customers are affected (NZZ, 2026-10-17). Publica concedes that it did not carry out regular on-site security audits at PK Softech, although after the Xplain incident it had old data deleted there (NZZ, 2026-10-17). The access vector, the actor and any ransom demand were not public in any source read as of that date.

Update21 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarytagsentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebodypriority

Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger reported on 2026-10-20 that the Akira ransomware group stole about one hundred gigabytes of compressed pension fund data, that data on well over a hundred thousand current and former federal employees is affected, that special agents and elite soldiers could be identified from it, and that Akira now demands ransom (translated from German; Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-20); the article is paywalled. Inside IT, summarising the investigation, adds that the data sets contain employer details of people who work under a cover identity for fedpol or the Federal Intelligence Service (NDB), that an internal assessment sees a danger to life and limb for individual persons, that the NDB is forgoing certain operations for now without recalling agents from abroad, that the State Secretariat for Security Policy has already seen first fraudulent contact attempts connected with Publica, and that State Secretary Markus Mäder set up a task force under the federal information security officer Anne Rivera (translated from German; Inside IT, 2026-10-20). It says the involved federal bodies assume Akira is responsible and that the group holds the data and threatens to publish or sell it if unpaid, and that at that date neither the Confederation nor Publica had confirmed the perpetrator or an alleged ransom demand (Inside IT, 2026-10-20).

Inside IT recalls that Akira was also behind the attack on a US subsidiary of the state-owned arms company Ruag a year ago, where Ruag paid the ransom, and that the Federal Prosecutor's Office, fedpol and the Federal Office for Cybersecurity warned in October 2025 of stepped-up Akira activity in Switzerland (Inside IT, 2026-10-20). Publica's page, updated on 2026-10-20, says it is still examining whether data left its holdings and whose, still has no indication that data was published on the darkweb, and has updated its list of questions and answers (Publica, 2026-10-20).

Update22 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Netzwoche updated its running story on 2026-10-21, relaying the paywalled article that Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger published on 2026-10-20: the Federal Council and the security authorities now assume that data on practically all current and former employees of the Confederation and of federally affiliated bodies left, among them federal judges, former Federal Council members (the sitting members are said to be spared), intelligence-service staff, elite soldiers and cleaning staff (translated from German; Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-20; Netzwoche, 2026-10-21). According to the paper, an on-site inspection at PK Softech on 2026-10-07 established the outflow of security-relevant federal data, and Publica's letter to its insured persons mentions neither Akira nor the ransom demand (Netzwoche, 2026-10-21). This is one chain of reporting, and the article quotes no confirmation of the actor, the ransom demand or the scope from the Confederation, Publica or PK Softech (Netzwoche, 2026-10-21).

Update23 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-23T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger reported on 2026-10-21 that PK Softech AG had confirmed in writing to Publica that it deleted the data, and that this apparently did not happen: its summary says the company reported in January that it had deleted the information on former Federal Councillors and agents, "but this was false" (translated from German; Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-21); the article is paywalled. Inside IT, working from the Tamedia research, dates the written confirmation to January 2026 and says PK Softech confirmed it held no personal data in plaintext and had deleted the data of the 2019 migration, that Publica confirmed the sequence (after the Xplain case it asked the supplier to delete all legacy data, including that of the 2019 migration, and received written confirmation), that Publica is clarifying why personal data presumably lay on the servers regardless, and that PK Softech did not answer and does not comment on individual customer relationships (Inside IT, 2026-10-22). 20 Minuten reports the same sequence and notes that PK Softech received the data in 2019 in a migration for Publica (20 Minuten, 2026-10-22).

Inside IT also relays, from Tamedia, that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed that data was extracted by the Akira ransomware group, which still threatens to publish or sell it; 20 Minuten writes that according to findings so far Akira stole the data (Inside IT, 2026-10-22; 20 Minuten, 2026-10-22). This is a reported confirmation of the actor by an authority, but it reaches the reader second-hand through the paywalled Tamedia article: the Federal Prosecutor's Office is not quoted directly, and Publica's own page, in its entry of 2026-10-20, still says it is clarifying whether data of Publica left and whose (Publica, 2026-10-20).

The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT says through Corriere del Ticino, relayed by Ticinonline on 2026-10-20, that potentially all of its insured could be involved but that there is no evidence yet that their data was actually taken; it has filed a complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office and is preparing a letter to the insured warning of telephone and e-mail fraud (Ticinonline, 2026-10-20). TicinoNews adds, from its own information, that a folder labelled IPCT with the data of a few hundred insured persons was on the supplier's server, while IPCT, which has about 27,000 affiliated persons, says it has no certainty yet that data of its insured is involved (TicinoNews, 2026-10-21).

Update24 Oct 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelactionsbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT has put numbers on its exposure in a letter of 2026-10-23 to its roughly 17,000 active insured and 10,000 pensioners (IPCT, 2026-10-23). PK Softech told it in the late afternoon of 2026-10-14 that the authorities had established that personal data were taken from the supplier's servers, without saying which funds the data belonged to, and the fund's checks to date found among the documents on the attacked server data of about 1,800 persons, held there for two ongoing projects of spot checks and recalculations (IPCT, 2026-10-23). About 1,700 are persons who left the fund through resignation or death in 2024 and 2025: surname, first name, postal address, date of birth, AHV number and insured number, the exit-benefit amount and the receiving fund with its bank account (IBAN), and the personal IBAN for about 50 who were paid out directly, with no e-mail address or telephone number (IPCT, 2026-10-23). About 80 are insured persons on a disability pension whose passive pension data was being updated: name, date of birth, AHV number, insured number, passive insured salary, passive retirement assets, degree and start of invalidity, with no contact data (IPCT, 2026-10-23).

The fund says it has no certain evidence that these data were taken but that it appears plausible, that savings capital and pensions of all insured are untouched, that the cantonal administration's IT centre hosting the fund's infrastructure was not breached, and that it filed a criminal complaint against unknown persons and was recognised as private plaintiff, while the Federal Prosecutor's Office and the federal police investigate (IPCT, 2026-10-23; Ticinonline, 2026-10-23). It decided to send the letter to all insured because its information is partial, the analyses are still evolving and it may never have certainty, and it asks them to watch for unexpected e-mails, calls and messages over the coming weeks and never to disclose passwords, access data or personal data unless sure of the requester (IPCT, 2026-10-23). The letter names PK Softech's other customers as Publica, large cantonal public funds such as Bern and Zurich and company funds such as Migros and Post, for hundreds of thousands of insured persons in total (IPCT, 2026-10-23).

Update25 Oct 2026 03:37 UTCrun 2026-10-25T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (EDÖB) says PK Softech notified it of the cyberattack on its IT infrastructure on 2026-10-08, that the affected pension funds also reported to it, that it started an informal preliminary inquiry at Publica on 2026-10-14 and that on 2026-10-22 it opened a formal investigation against PK Softech AG on suspicion of data-protection violations (EDÖB, 2026-10-23). Its release states that data of several important occupational pension institutions, Publica among them, was exfiltrated in the attack; the investigation is to give an overall picture of the personal data the funds handed to the software supplier and to clarify the legal framework of those transfers, how they were actually implemented and the scope of the data that left, and the EDÖB gives no further information on pending proceedings (EDÖB, 2026-10-23). Der Bund relays the step and adds that besides Publica the pension funds of Migros, Post and the City of Zurich obtain software from PK Softech (Der Bund, 2026-10-23). The release names neither the actor nor the number of insured persons.

Correction30 Oct 2026 03:55 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Publica's own newsletter of 2026-10-22 says that the hacker group Akira is being associated with the attack, referring readers to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity's description of the group's methods, and that Publica filed a criminal complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office on 2026-10-15 (Publica, 2026-10-22). The same newsletter says Publica must assume that data left the supplier and that whether and to what extent Publica's personal data is among it is still being investigated (Publica, 2026-10-22). The ransom demand and the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmation of the exfiltration by Akira remain press reports.

Update04 Nov 2026 03:32 UTCrun 2026-11-04T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencebodysourcing_note

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich's foundation board suspended the introduction of PK Softech's administration system planned for early 2027 because of the supplier's cyberattack and will keep operating its existing system in 2027; it will decide whether, when and under what conditions to introduce a new system only once the attack and the possible data loss are worked through (translated from German) (Inside IT, 2026-11-03). PK Softech, quoted by watson.ch, says it cannot rule out that non-pseudonymised data was temporarily present in project-related work, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed to watson.ch that a notorious extortion gang is behind the attack and has added the case to its criminal proceeding against the Akira group, open since April 2024 (translated from German) (watson.ch, 2026-11-03).

Correction08 Nov 2026 14:03 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditactionsbodyevidencesourcessummarytechniques

The Bernische Pensionskasse's own notices say it does not know (2026-10-15) and can neither confirm nor rule out (2026-10-30) whether personal data of its insured persons left PK Softech; what it assumes, after the press reports of 2026-10-20, is that more data left the supplier than first thought (translated from German) (BPK, 2026-10-30). The NZZ's report of 2026-10-17 quoted the fund more broadly, as saying personal data must be assumed to have left (NZZ, 2026-10-17). Its notice also dates the supplier incident to 2026-09-29, says software that encrypts data (ransomware) was installed and that the data theft became known on 2026-10-08, and says BPK filed its own criminal complaint on 2026-10-19 (translated from German) (BPK, 2026-10-30). A month after the attack watson.ch found no PK Softech entry on Akira's leak site, so the group's possession of the data and its demand still rest on press reports and the Federal Prosecutor's statement as relayed (watson.ch, 2026-11-03). Inside IT names the supplier's customers in its own voice; the AWP agency is its source only for PK Softech's statement (Inside IT, 2026-10-09).

Update10 Nov 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelsummarysourcesactionsbody

The Pensionskasse der Stadt Zug said on 2026-11-09 that its administration is outsourced to the consultancy Libera AG, which uses software from PK Softech; the fund says it was first informed of the incident in mid-October, believed it was not affected, and received only last week the information that data of its insured persons could be affected, an "elevated risk" that is not yet confirmed (translated from German) (Inside IT, 2026-11-09). It says names, AHV numbers, birth dates, addresses and salary details, in part also phone numbers and e-mail addresses, were stored at the supplier, that it has informed its insured persons and the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, that retirement assets are safe and that particularly sensitive data such as documents on incapacity to work or disability are not affected (Inside IT, 2026-11-09).

Update11 Nov 2026 03:54 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencebody

PK Softech said on its homepage on 2026-11-10, "because of media speculation", that no concrete ransom demand has reached it and that it has at no time contacted the attackers; its investigation continues (PK Softech, 2026-11-10). A spokeswoman of the State Secretariat for Security Policy told Keystone-SDA the same day that the federal bodies handling the incident know of no concrete ransom demand addressed to them and that the Confederation paid no ransom, that, as she put it, a demand to the supplier was "not made concrete with an amount or deadline" (translated from German), and that the Secretariat still has no indication that data from the attack was published on the darkweb; Publica said it also received no demand, is not in contact with the hackers and does not know whether other organisations or individuals are being extorted, which the Federal Prosecutor's Office is investigating (watson.ch, 2026-11-10). This qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom: watson.ch's headline and lead say no demand reached the supplier or the Confederation, while the spokeswoman's wording leaves a non-specific demand to the supplier open, and neither the supplier nor the federal authorities confirm a concrete demand, and the Akira attribution and the data volume remain press-sourced.

Update12 Nov 2026 04:28 UTCrun 2026-11-12T0255Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Publica's own page, in a correction headed "Stand: 10.11.2026", says that according to current knowledge the affected software supplier received general extortion letters immediately after the attack, which have not since been made concrete with an amount or a payment deadline; that the federal bodies involved know of no concrete ransom demand; that Publica received no demand itself and is in no contact with the attacker group; and that it knows of no case of persons demonstrably contacted or harmed and has no indication of publication on the darkweb (Publica, 2026-11-10). PK Softech's own page of 2026-11-10 mentions no extortion letter and does not name the attackers (PK Softech, 2026-11-10). watson.ch reports that PK Softech confirmed on enquiry that it ignores the prompt Akira left in its network to contact it through an anonymous chat and does not want to negotiate a ransom; watson's reading that the denials mean only that nobody opened the link, and that the firm and the Confederation knew early that Akira was behind the attack, is its own inference (watson.ch, 2026-11-11). SRF reported on 2026-11-10, citing several sources, that the perpetrators demanded ransom and threatened to publish or resell the data, while PK Softech and Publica told SRF that no ransom demand reached them (SRF, 2026-11-10).

Correction15 Nov 2026 14:56 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditsourcesevidencebody

That the supplier is the same company that counts Publica among its customers is AWP's report (cash.ch (AWP), 2026-10-09); the Bernische Pensionskasse's notice of 9 October says that an external software supplier of the fund detected a cyber incident at the end of September 2026 but does not name its other customers (BPK, 2026-10-30). Two statements about contacts with insured persons differ in scope: Inside IT relayed on 2026-10-20 a report that the State Secretariat for Security Policy had seen first fraudulent contact attempts connected with Publica (Inside IT, 2026-10-20), while Publica says it knows of no case of a person demonstrably contacted or harmed in connection with the attack (Publica, 2026-11-10); neither names a case.

entries.summary: PK Softech AG, the software supplier of Publica and other Swiss pension funds, says unknown attackers used malware to reach part of its IT and that data must be assumed to have left; the Federal Prosecutor's Office is investigating and has added the case to its criminal proceeding against Akira. Tamedia reports that Akira holds about 100 GB and demands ransom, while PK Softech and the federal bodies say no concrete ransom demand reached them; Publica and several other funds say their insured persons' personal data has presumably left. Cantonal police warn that criminals could use leaked personal and financial data for investment-fraud calls.
entries.title: PK Softech, software supplier of Swiss pension funds: malware and a data outflow at Publica, with the City of Zurich fund PKZH saying its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Bernese funds BPK and BLVK and Pensionskasse Post also reporting the supplier incident, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office investigating

updates.summary: The supplier's customers are now named: the Bernische Pensionskasse (canton of Bern staff and three cantonal universities) says its supplier is the same company that serves Publica, the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse and Pensionskasse Post report the supplier incident, and Inside IT lists Migros-Pensionskasse and Syngenta Pensionskasse among the customers. None of the funds has confirmed which member data left.

Publica's own page of 2026-10-08 lists civil status and the IBAN among the data that could be affected and says its investigation indicates personal data of insured persons has presumably left. The AWP agency relays the software firm's position that it knows data left but not yet whether personal data is among it, that it may be business data, and that the volume is rather small.

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, the City of Zurich's pension fund, says on 2026-10-13 that it currently uses another provider, plans to move to PK Softech's system in early 2027 and is checking whether data from migration tests was affected. Publica's page says as of 2026-10-14 that it has no indications that data from the attack was published on the darkweb.

Cantonal police warn that criminals could use the leaked salary and pension data to phone insured persons with investment-fraud offers, SwissCybersecurity.net ties the warning to PK Softech, and the Zurich cantonal fund BVK says its PK Softech software runs in its own data centre so it is not directly affected; PK Softech can neither confirm nor rule out further affected customers, and the Ticino fund listed as a customer has made no statement.

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, the City of Zurich's pension fund, now says in its notice of 2026-10-15 that its inquiries indicate personal data of its insured persons and pensioners, handed to PK Softech as test data for a planned 2027 switch, was stolen, and that which fields were taken is still being clarified. Pensionskasse Post says in its notice of the same date that personal data did leave and no longer repeats its earlier anonymisation statement, though it is still unclear whether its insured persons' data is among it.

SonntagsBlick reports, from a confidential federal information note, that the Confederation rates the incident as serious and says the security organs of the Confederation are particularly affected, which it glosses as the Federal Intelligence Service, the Defence Group and fedpol, that the Federal Council was briefed on 2026-10-14 and that the cantons were informed; the Finance Department confirms only the briefing. NZZ adds that the pension consultancy Libera AG is also affected, that the Bernische Pensionskasse now says it must be assumed personal data left, and that Publica ran no regular on-site audits at the supplier.

Tamedia reports, and Inside IT relays, that the Akira ransomware group holds about 100 GB of the pension data of well over 100,000 current and former federal employees, with employer details of staff under cover identity among it, and demands ransom; neither the Confederation nor Publica confirms the actor or the demand.

Netzwoche, relaying Tages-Anzeiger, reports that the Federal Council and the security authorities now assume data on practically all current and former federal and federally affiliated staff left, federal judges and former Federal Council members among them, and that an on-site inspection at PK Softech on 2026-10-07 established the outflow of security-relevant data; neither the Confederation nor Publica has confirmed the actor, the demand or the scope.

The supplier's written pledge to delete Publica's 2019 migration data was apparently not kept, Inside IT relays that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed Akira exfiltrated data, though that is second-hand and neither the Confederation nor Publica has itself named the actor, and the Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says all its insured could potentially be involved but has no evidence yet that data was taken.

The Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says in a letter of 2026-10-23 that data of about 1,800 of its insured persons (about 1,700 who left in 2024 and 2025, with exit-benefit amounts and IBANs, and about 80 on disability pensions) sat on the attacked supplier server for two ongoing projects; it has no certain evidence the data were taken but finds it plausible, and it writes to all insured because it cannot exclude more.

The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (EDÖB) opened a formal investigation against PK Softech on 2026-10-22, after an informal inquiry at Publica on 2026-10-14, and states that data of several pension funds, Publica among them, was exfiltrated; the investigation is to establish which personal data the funds handed to the supplier, on what legal basis, and how much left.

The entry said that neither the Confederation nor Publica had named the actor. Publica's own newsletter of 2026-10-22 says the Akira group is being associated with the attack, and that Publica filed a criminal complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office on 2026-10-15; the summary, the sourcing note and the paragraph on the Akira reporting now say so, a population figure was trimmed from the analysis, and the demand and the Prosecutor's Office confirmation still rest on press reports.

The Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich suspended its planned 2027 move to PK Softech's administration system; PK Softech, quoted by watson.ch, cannot rule out that non-pseudonymised data was temporarily present in project work, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office has added the case to its criminal proceeding against the Akira group.

The Bernische Pensionskasse's own notices say it does not know, and can neither confirm nor rule out, whether its insured persons' data left, and it assumes only that more data left the supplier than first thought, while the NZZ quoted it more broadly; its letter also says ransomware was installed at the supplier on 2026-09-29, and watson.ch found no PK Softech entry on Akira's leak site a month after the attack. Inside IT names the supplier's customers in its own voice, citing AWP only for PK Softech's statement, and the September 2025 deletion request is Publica's statement to watson.ch.

The Pensionskasse der Stadt Zug, whose administrator Libera AG uses PK Softech software, said on 2026-11-09 that there is an elevated, not yet confirmed risk that its insured persons' data left the supplier, and has informed its insured persons and the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner.

PK Softech and the State Secretariat for Security Policy said on 2026-11-10 that no concrete ransom demand reached the supplier or the federal bodies, that the supplier never contacted the attackers, that the Confederation paid nothing and that there is still no indication of publication on the darkweb, which qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom.

Publica's own page of 2026-11-10 says the supplier received general extortion letters immediately after the attack, never made concrete with an amount or payment deadline, while PK Softech's page names no letter; watson.ch reports that PK Softech ignores the negotiation-chat prompt Akira left in its network, and SRF's report of a concrete demand with a threat to publish remains unconfirmed by the supplier, Publica and the federal bodies.

The Bernische Pensionskasse's notice PDF no longer resolves, so its citations now point to the fund's notice page, which carries the 9 October notice; that page does not say the supplier is the same company that serves Publica, so that fact is now cited to AWP, which reports it. A Keystone-SDA quote's German original now reads Darknet as the page does, a superseded gloss on the fund's earlier statement was dropped, and the section notes how two statements on fraudulent contacts differ in scope.

actions: Update every non-browser TLS client that keeps its own CA bundle or does not check revocation to a fixed version: standalone Java runtimes, including those already updated on 2026-10-21, to the update of Oracle's Security Alert CVE-2026-114820 or OpenJDK (Oracle Database Server, Autonomous Health Framework and OPatch installations too), Python 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16 or 3.11.18 together with pip 26.2.2 or later, Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, self-managed GitLab to a fixed patch release together with GitLab Runner 19.5.1, and SonicWall Gen7 firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled to SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 or later and Gen8 to 8.2.3-8015 or later; then confirm with curl against the incident tracker's test host that the client rejects the certificate; on managed Macs update to macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3, or where that is not possible remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from /etc/ssl/cert.pem as Apple describes (AAA Certificate Services is optional and can stop tools that read only that file from verifying some unaffected sites).

Replace, by hand where the ACME client does not support ACME Renewal Information, every TLS certificate your organisation holds that chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 or to another of the seven certificates Microsoft removed from the Windows and Edge trust lists, or that was issued by one of the eight RSA G2B and G2C issuing CAs eMudhra revoked on 2026-11-07, because Chrome's removal of the G3 root was due on 2026-10-27 and the Windows change takes effect when the trust-list update reaches a device; deliver the updated Disallowed Certificate Trust List and the trust-list changes Microsoft describes, including its out-of-band update of 2026-10-26, to Windows devices that do not receive automatic certificate-trust updates; do not renew or reissue under emSign Root CA - G1 after 2026-11-16, because Chrome 153 and higher will not trust by default a certificate under it whose earliest SCT is later, and Windows, Edge and WebView2 stop trusting the remaining eMudhra roots on 2026-11-16 as Microsoft's update of 2026-11-10 describes.

Apply Cisco's remediation now for the products its eMudhra advisory (version 1.11) lists with a fix or a procedure available: the CA-trust distrust guide for IOS XE and the guidance for Secure Firewall ASA, FTD and FMC, Secure Email Gateway and Secure Email and Web Manager (run the updatenow command where updates are manual), Duo Access Gateway 3.2.0, Duo Network Gateway 3.4.1, Duo Agentic Authorization Connector 1.0.1 and ThousandEyes Enterprise Agent (Application-hosting Agent 5.2.2).

entries.headline: eMudhra: eight ECDSA CA keys guessable, eight RSA CAs revoked; Windows drops the rest 2026-11-16; update clients
entries.html:

eMudhra: the private keys of eight ECDSA intermediate CA certificates were trivially recoverable, so anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates, and eight RSA intermediates were revoked on 2026-11-07 for key handling eMudhra cannot show compliant; browsers block the eight ECDSA intermediates, clients with their own trust store or no revocation checking need an update (CVE-2026-111943 in Go)

On 2026-10-17 a researcher reported to the Chrome Root Program, and Mozilla received a report the same day, that the private keys of eight eMudhra subordinate CA certificates were compromised: the keys were so weak that anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website against clients that have not removed trust in those CAs; Google describes the cause as insufficient randomness (Google, 2026-10-20; Mozilla, 2026-10-20). BleepingComputer, citing Mozilla's incident report, says all eight were P-384 keys generated in April 2025 with values below 256, so testing 256 numbers recovers a key (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20). eMudhra's incident report of 2026-11-10 says the keys were generated correctly on its hardware module at a ceremony on 2025-04-30 and then passed through a custom Python wrap/unwrap script that truncated the eight ECDSA private values; the keys of eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) stayed intact but were handled in that script's process memory, so eMudhra cannot show compliance with its certification practice statement, and it revoked them on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation after having said on 2026-10-19 that they were not impacted; its G2C issuers had issued end-entity certificates, the last on 2026-11-03, and no source says any RSA key leaked (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10; eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-11). The tracker says it is not known whether attackers used the flaw against other clients (Dennis Jackson, 2026-10-20).

Chrome blocked the intermediates on 2026-10-17, Firefox through OneCRL the same day, Microsoft platforms on 2026-10-20 and Apple products on 2026-10-22, and eMudhra revoked all eight (Dennis Jackson, 2026-10-20; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20). Microsoft went further: an out-of-band Windows update of 2026-10-26 removes seven certificates, six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign, from the Windows trust list, and the same seven left the Edge trust list on 2026-10-27 (Microsoft, 2026-10-26). Google removed the root that signed them, emSign ECC Root CA - G3, from the Chrome Root Store, with the removal expected to reach devices on 2026-10-27 (Google, 2026-10-20). Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 filter chains that contain the intermediates in crypto/x509, tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (Go team, 2026-10-20), and GitLab's release of 2026-10-29 removes trust for the eight intermediates in self-managed CE and EE, with Runner 19.5.1 and the AI Gateway updated separately (GitLab, 2026-10-29).

Oracle's Security Alert of 2026-10-21 for CVE-2026-91403 (CVSS 3.1 9.1, JSSE) provided Java updates that distrust the impacted eMudhra intermediate CA certificates (Oracle, 2026-10-21), and a second Security Alert of 2026-10-24, CVE-2026-114820, removes the impacted root CA certificates and also covers the Java component of Oracle Database Server, Autonomous Health Framework and OPatch (Oracle, 2026-10-30). OpenJDK's guidance tells users of a standalone runtime to act immediately even if they updated in the past few days (OpenJDK, 2026-10-24).

Exposure
Any software that keeps its own CA bundle or does not check revocation keeps trusting the intermediates until updated; Python 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16 and 3.11.18 carry a built-in denylist (Python Insider, 2026-10-26); Apple says the curl, git, python3, ruby, perl and openssl that ship with macOS or the Xcode command-line tools read /etc/ssl/cert.pem, check neither Apple's block nor revocation and keep trusting them until macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3 (Apple, 2026-11-10). SonicOS firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled re-signed the chains with their own DPI-SSL CA, so client browsers could not reject a forged one, until SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 (Gen7) and 8.2.3-8015 (Gen8) (SonicWall, 2026-11-10; SonicWall advisory data, 2026-11-10).
Detection
EMudhra says it found no evidence that the intermediates were used to issue end-user certificates (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20), so a server certificate chain seen in TLS session metadata, proxy or EDR network telemetry that contains one of the eight intermediates or their Sectigo cross-signs, which the tracker lists, is worth treating as a possible forged certificate (Dennis Jackson, 2026-10-20). CT monitoring will not show one, because Google found no certificate chaining to the six TLS intermediates logged before it blocked them (Google, 2026-10-20).

Triage: a site that still chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 failing in Chrome after 2026-10-27, or a certificate that chains to one of the seven certificates Microsoft removed failing in Windows or Edge once the change reaches the device, is the announced root removal, not an attack (Google, 2026-10-20; Microsoft, 2026-10-26).

Defender takeaway
Update trust bundles and toolchains on every non-browser client, rebuild container images that embed an old bundle, and do not rely on revocation or CT for those clients; website operators with certificates chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 need one from another hierarchy now (Google, 2026-10-20), and so does anything issued under emSign Root CA - G1 after 2026-11-16, because Chrome 153 and higher will not trust such a certificate by default when its earliest SCT is later (Google, 2026-11-04). On Macs, update to macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3, which block them in the command-line tools; where that is not possible, remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from that file as Apple describes (Apple, 2026-11-10). From 2026-11-16 Microsoft removes the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2, so a certificate under emSign Root CA - G1 stops validating there too (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). Certificates from the eight revoked RSA G2B and G2C issuers are revoked and eMudhra says its subscribers were migrated (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10), so check inventories for any holder still on them.

entries.summary: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were so weak that anyone could recover them and forge trusted HTTPS certificates for any site, and eMudhra's incident report of 2026-11-10 adds eight RSA intermediates revoked on 2026-11-07 because it cannot show their keys were handled as its policy requires. Browsers and the Apple, Microsoft and Google trust stores block the eight ECDSA intermediates, and Microsoft removes the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2 from 2026-11-16. Software with its own trust store or no revocation checking stays exposed until updated (Go, GitLab, Python, Java, macOS command-line tools, SonicWall DPI-SSL, Cisco IOS XE and ISE), and no exploitation is reported.
entries.title: eMudhra: the private keys of eight ECDSA intermediate CA certificates were trivially recoverable, so anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates, and eight RSA intermediates were revoked on 2026-11-07 for key handling eMudhra cannot show compliant; browsers block the eight ECDSA intermediates, clients with their own trust store or no revocation checking need an update (CVE-2026-111943 in Go)

updates.summary: Standalone Java runtimes keep their own trust store: Oracle's Security Alert CVE-2026-91403 (CVSS 3.1 9.1) and the OpenJDK advisory of 2026-10-21 ship the distrust update, the tracker lists the fixed builds, replacing blocked.certs or enabling revocation checking is the stop-gap, and NCSC.ch lists the exploitation status as unknown.

Oracle's second Security Alert of 2026-10-24, CVE-2026-114820 (CVSS 3.1 9.1), removes four root CAs and lists Java SE builds such as 27.0.1.0.2 as affected, and OpenJDK says even a runtime updated in the past few days needs it, so a standalone Java runtime updated on 2026-10-21 needs the new update or the same stop-gap again; OpenJDK now says Debian, Devuan and Ubuntu packages need the keystore recreated by hand. Python announces a built-in ssl denylist (CVE-2026-115557) without naming a release, so pip 26.2.2 is the Python fix to apply now; Cisco lists the products it has fixes for; and eMudhra is leaving the global TLS business, and standard ACME clients do not replace the affected certificates outside their renewal window unless they support ACME Renewal Information.

Microsoft removed seven eMudhra-hierarchy certificates from the Windows trust list in an out-of-band update of 2026-10-26 and from the Edge trust list on 2026-10-27; Cisco's advisory reached version 1.5 on 2026-10-30 with ISE fixes dated December 2026 and April 2027; GitLab's releases of 2026-10-29 distrust the eight intermediates, with GitLab Runner and the AI Gateway needing separate updates; Python's releases of 2026-10-26 carry the built-in denylist; and Oracle's revision of 2026-10-30 extends the Java alert to Oracle Database Server, Autonomous Health Framework and OPatch. Certificates that chain to the removed roots need replacing, and disconnected Windows devices need the updated trust lists.

Python 3.15.1, 3.14.9 and 3.13.17, which the 2026-10-25 section listed as patched, predate the ssl denylist; the protected releases are 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16 and 3.11.18, and the tracker clause that carried the earlier versions is removed.

Cisco's eMudhra advisory reached version 1.8 on 2026-11-06 with a CA-trust distrust guide for IOS XE and NX-OS and MDS releases listed as impacted without a remediation; Apple's own page confirms that the curl, git, python3 and openssl that ship with macOS keep trusting the intermediates until a future update, and heise reports that macOS 27.2 undid the manual workaround and that Apple's change is not expected before December. Google's post adds that Chrome 153 and higher will stop trusting by default certificates under emSign Root CA - G1 whose earliest SCT is after 2026-11-16, and Apple's page dates its blocks to 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-23.

SonicWall's advisory of 2026-11-10 says SonicOS firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled kept trusting the compromised eMudhra chains and re-signed them for clients; fixed in SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 (Gen7) and 8.2.3-8015 (Gen8), so a Gen7 unit on 7.3.4-7013 is still affected. Apple's macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 now block the certificates in the command-line tools, Microsoft removes the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2 from 2026-11-16, and Cisco's advisory is at version 1.9.

eMudhra's full incident report of 2026-11-10 says eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) were revoked on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation because their keys were handled in the memory of a Python script, so eMudhra cannot show compliance with its policy; it had said on 2026-10-19 that they were not impacted, no source says the keys leaked, and the G2C issuers had issued end-entity certificates.

Microsoft's post now carries an update dated 2026-11-12 whose table adds VS Code 1.147.0 (2026-11-18), Azure CLI 2.93.0 (2026-11-16), which removes two more eMudhra roots, the .NET SDK update in December 2026 and the API Management self-hosted gateway and Microsoft Build of OpenJDK after the Mozilla release of 2026-11-16 to the products that drop the eMudhra roots.

entries.headline: Node-RED flaw in Siemens IoT2050 hit a VulnCheck canary; V4.3.4-1 fixes Industrial OS, Example Image has no fix
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-58115exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-58115, Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced, Basic, M.2 and SM ship a Node-RED interface with no authentication, so one unauthenticated HTTP request runs code with maximum privileges on an OT edge gateway (CVSS 10.0); VulnCheck's canary caught exploitation

Siemens ProductCERT published SSA-834709 on 2026-08-11 for CVE-2026-58115 in SIMATIC IoT2050 devices with Node-RED installed (the current advisory, V1.2 of 2026-11-10, lists the Advanced, Basic, M.2 and SM variants running Industrial OS or Example Image versions): affected devices "do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that are capable of executing system commands on the server", so an unauthenticated remote attacker can create malicious flows and run code with maximum privileges. Siemens scores it 10.0 under CVSS 3.1 and 4.0 (CWE-306), names V4.3.4-1 as the fix for earlier Industrial OS versions and no fix for Example Image versions, and offers uninstalling Node-RED or hardening it per its User Guide as interim mitigations (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-08-11). CERT-FR and NCSC-NL carried the advisory in August and list only the Advanced variant (CERT-FR, 2026-08-12; NCSC-NL, 2026-08-11).

VulnCheck reports that on 2026-10-30 one of its canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115 with a single POST to the Node-RED /flows endpoint: an inject node wired to an exec node ran a base64-wrapped shell command that downloaded a Linux bot into the RAM-backed /dev/shm as a hidden file and started it detached (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01). By 2026-11-01 the same address had produced 16 events against this CVE with further payloads, among them flows that expose an http-in endpoint wired to an exec node as a persistent web shell; VulnCheck did not retrieve the bot, so its function is unknown, and it reads the address as opportunistic mass-scanning infrastructure rather than a campaign (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01). The target was a canary, not a Siemens device, and CISA's catalog did not list the flaw as VulnCheck wrote (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01); The Register relays the finding (The Register, 2026-11-02).

Exposure
A SIMATIC IoT2050 (Advanced, Basic, M.2 or SM) below V4.3.4-1 running Industrial OS, or running Example Image versions, with Node-RED installed and its HTTP interface reachable by an attacker (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-08-11); VulnCheck says Node-RED instances without adminAuth are being found and exploited automatically and that Node-RED is embedded in other ICS and OT products (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01).
Detection
In web or reverse-proxy access logs, POST requests to the Node-RED /flows endpoint from sources that are not engineering workstations, above all bodies that deploy an exec node carrying a base64 string piped into sh, which a filter matching only wget or curl misses; on the host, hidden files started from /dev/shm or /tmp and detached with setsid or nohup by the Node-RED process, and deployed flows with exec nodes or http-in endpoints that nobody built, since the web-shell flows survive the loss of the memory-resident implant (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01).

Triage: legitimate engineering deployments also POST to /flows; the signal is a deployment from a non-engineering address whose exec node carries encoded shell or a download-and-execute chain (an inference from the described mechanism).

Defender takeaway
Update every Industrial OS IoT2050 to V4.3.4-1 or later and, for Example Image units that have no fix, uninstall or harden Node-RED, and take the Node-RED interface of any device off networks that untrusted hosts can reach, because exploitation takes one request and is now observed; on any exposed Node-RED, review the deployed flows for planted exec nodes and http-in endpoints.
Update03 Nov 2026 03:38 UTCrun 2026-11-03T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

VulnCheck says one of its canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115 on 2026-10-30 with a single POST to the Node-RED /flows endpoint that deployed a flow downloading and running a Linux bot, and that the same address produced 16 events against this CVE by 2026-11-01, some deploying persistent http-in web-shell flows; it did not retrieve the bot and reads the traffic as opportunistic mass scanning (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01). The target was a canary, not a Siemens device, and CISA's catalog did not list the flaw when VulnCheck wrote (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01); The Register relays the finding (The Register, 2026-11-02).

Update07 Nov 2026 03:48 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryaffected_productscvesevidenceactionsbodyentities

Siemens revised SSA-834709 to V1.1 on 2026-11-04, describing the change as "Clarified Affected products list. Updated title. Updated summary." (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-08-11). The current advisory lists SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced (6ES7647-0BA00-1YA2), Basic (6ES7647-0BA00-0YA2), M.2 (6ES7647-0BB00-1YA2) and SM (6ES7647-0CA00-1AA2), each in all versions below V4.3.4-1 running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed, with "Update to V4.3.4-1 or later version" as the fix (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-08-11). Owners of the Basic, M.2 and SM variants are therefore in scope for the update and for the exposure and detection points above; the 10.0 scores and the two interim mitigations are unchanged.

Update12 Nov 2026 04:24 UTCrun 2026-11-12T0255Z-intelheadlinesummarycvesevidenceactionsbody

Siemens revised SSA-834709 to V1.2 on 2026-11-10, describing the change as "Added additional affected configuration for SIMATIC IoT2050 family" (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-08-11). For each of the four variants the advisory now lists a second affected configuration, "All versions running Example Image versions with Node-RED installed", for which "Currently no fix is available"; the fix, update to V4.3.4-1 or later, applies only to the Industrial OS configurations, and the two mitigations, hardening Node-RED and uninstalling it, apply to all eight (Siemens ProductCERT, 2026-08-11). The advisory's title and summary still say "with Industrial OS", Siemens does not define Example Image, and the advisory makes no statement on exploitation; VulnCheck remains the only exploitation source (VulnCheck, 2026-11-01).

entries.headline: Certighost AD CS flaw: Kaspersky sees a ransomware group attempting the public exploit; patch every Enterprise CA
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-54121updatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-54121, Windows Server AD CS 'Certighost': a low-privileged domain user forges a DC certificate to DCSync, public PoC since 2026-07-24 and attempted in real intrusions by the Citrus ransomware group (CVSS 8.8)

Researchers H0j3n and aniqfakhrul published a write-up and a public proof-of-concept for "Certighost" (CybersecurityNews, 2026-07-24; Microsoft Defender, 2026-07-31); the flaw, CVE-2026-54121 (CVSS 8.8), is an Active Directory Certificate Services flaw Microsoft describes as "improper authorization in Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) [that] allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network" and fixed in the July 2026 Patch Tuesday cycle (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-14). The vulnerable logic sits in the Enterprise CA's enrollment "chase" fallback: when a request carries the cdc (client DC) and rmd (remote domain) attributes, the CA contacted the requester-supplied cdc host and trusted the identity data it returned without proving that host was a Domain Controller (CybersecurityNews, 2026-07-24).

A low-privileged domain user, using a machine account it can self-register under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota or, per Microsoft, one it already controls (Microsoft Defender, 2026-07-31), stands up rogue LDAP/LSA services, points the chase at itself and receives a certificate carrying a target Domain Controller's identity; that certificate authenticates via PKINIT as the DC, which the reporting says enabled a DCSync of the krbtgt account hash, a single hop from an ordinary domain foothold to full domain compromise (CybersecurityNews, 2026-07-24). Microsoft rated it "Exploitation Less Likely" with no in-the-wild exploitation at patch time (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-14) and said on 2026-07-31 that it had not observed confirmed threat-actor exploitation (Microsoft Defender, 2026-07-31). Kaspersky then reported that the Citrus ransomware group attempted the flaw in real intrusions that began with credentials stolen from contractors' employees and used against VPNs or RDP; it says the victims are Russian companies only and does not say any attempt succeeded (Kaspersky, 2026-11-11).

Exposure
Microsoft lists conditions that must all hold: an Enterprise CA integrated with Active Directory, enrollment through the machine template, a default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota or an attacker-controlled machine account, SMB and LDAP reachability from the CA to the attacker's host, and any valid domain account; the fallback occurs only for templates that require a DNS name and on CAs with the EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC flag (Microsoft Defender, 2026-07-31).
Detection
AD CS auditing is off by default; with the Certification Services subcategory and CA AuditFilter 127 enabled, events 4886 and 4887 show requester, template and outcome, and a certificate for a Domain Controller identity requested through a machine template by a low-privileged principal never occurs normally (Microsoft Defender, 2026-07-31). Kaspersky's attempts left computer accounts named GHOST plus eight random letters and Machine-template requests whose cdc attribute named an attacker-controlled system (Kaspersky, 2026-11-11).

Triage: legitimate cross-domain chase traffic terminates at an address that exists in AD as a real DC computer object; the SERVER_TRUST_ACCOUNT and resolved-SID check the patch enforces is the discriminator a hunt should apply (CybersecurityNews, 2026-07-24).

Defender takeaway
Confirm the July 2026 cumulative update on every AD CS host that runs an Enterprise CA, the durable fix per Microsoft (Microsoft Defender, 2026-07-31); where it is missing, treat the flaw as weaponizable and as already attempted by a ransomware group, enable the auditing above, clear the EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC flag and restart the CertSvc service as a temporary step until the update is applied, after testing in staging because workflows that rely on the chase fallback will break, and re-enabling the flag undoes it (CybersecurityNews, 2026-07-24), and audit ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota (default 10) and whether chase-eligible cross-domain enrollment is needed.
Update12 Nov 2026 04:17 UTCrun 2026-11-12T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodycves

Kaspersky's Citrus report of 2026-11-11 says the group attempted to exploit Certighost with an exploit published on GitHub, requesting a Machine-template certificate on behalf of a newly created account with the cdc attribute pointing the CA at a system it controlled, and that the group later deploys its Go ransomware domain-wide through a malicious Group Policy Object (Kaspersky, 2026-11-11). Kaspersky says that if exploitation succeeds the CA issues the certificate and the domain controller name in it lets the attackers authenticate as the domain controller account, and it never says an attempt succeeded (Kaspersky, 2026-11-11); Microsoft's record has not been revised since 2026-07-14 (Microsoft MSRC, 2026-07-14).

entries.headline: Plone anonymous RCE chain: update or install the 20261110 hotfix, block portal_modifier, check modifier conditions
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOA2

Plone security fix of 2026-11-10: a chain of missing security declarations and opened modules lets an anonymous visitor run code on the server in every supported Plone version and back to 4.3; a working proof of concept exists, no CVE ids yet, no exploitation reported

The Plone and Zope security team says the fixes it released on 2026-11-10 close a chain of several issues that together let an anonymous visitor run code on the server, in all supported Plone versions (6.0, 6.1 and 6.2) and in older ones back to at least 4.3 (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The anonymous entry point is Products.CMFEditions: the conditional modifiers in portal_modifier had no security declarations, so an anonymous visitor could change a modifier's TALES condition and then run it, and the condition is also evaluated when an editor saves versioned content (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). Products.CMFPlone, Products.MimetypesRegistry and plone.batching opened whole modules to restricted code, which let TALES expressions and Python scripts escape the sandbox and reach modules such as os, and plone.restapi opened the json module (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The CMFEditions advisory rates its flaw 9.8 with no privileges required and states that a working proof of concept exists; the team says details are public and that with current AI tools it may not take long to turn them into a working exploit, and no source reports exploitation (Plone, 2026-11-10; Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).

The fixed packages are CMFPlone 6.2.3, 6.1.6 and 6.0.16 with the helper package versions the announcement lists, or the hotfix Products.PloneHotfix20261110, which covers Plone 4.3 to 6.2, and all Zope instances must be restarted afterwards (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10). The team's pre-announcement of 2026-11-02 already gave the workaround, to block any URL containing portal_modifier at the web server at any path depth, which only helps if Zope's own port cannot be reached directly; the team advises keeping it after updating (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-02). After the fix, restricted code can import only the names Plone itself needs from the closed modules, so custom scripts that import others now get an Unauthorized error (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any Plone site reachable by anonymous visitors, on a version below the fixed packages; no source states a non-default setting that the anonymous path needs, and Plone 5.2 and older are out of security support, with the fix released as an exception.
Detection
Web-server access logs for anonymous requests whose path contains portal_modifier; and the stored state, which survives the update: a changed modifier condition stays in the database, so as Manager open @@check-modifier-conditions on the site root, or read the hotfix's startup log line that reports modified versioning conditions, and treat the server as compromised if a condition is not recognised, although defaults have changed over time so a difference alone is not an attack (Plone Security Team, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Update or install the hotfix and restart now on every internet-facing Plone site, keep the portal_modifier block in place, and run the modifier-condition check afterwards, because the fix does not remove a condition an anonymous request already stored.

entries.action_label: Microsoft: GSocket relay clients on exploited Linux…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Microsoft: GSocket relay clients on exploited Linux web servers survive the patch; hunt the host, not the app
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

GSocket on compromised Linux web servers: Microsoft sees several unrelated actors install the open-source relay client after exploiting an internet-facing web application, so access outlives the patch; no inbound listener, no attacker-hosted infrastructure

Microsoft observed several unrelated threat actors deploy GSocket, an open-source remote access tool, on Linux servers after exploiting an internet-facing web application, and says it kept access after the exploited vulnerabilities were remediated (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). The chain starts with command execution as a child of the web server or application runtime, where curl fetches an installation script that bash runs; the script profiles the host, picks a client matching the architecture, stages it as a hidden, executable file in a writable or memory-backed path such as /dev/shm and opens encrypted outbound command and control through the Global Socket Relay Network (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). The client is then disguised with kernel-thread-like process names (bash exec -a), persisted through cron, systemd units, shell profiles, watchdogs and redundant copies, and the staging files are removed (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). In a few incidents the actors afterwards attempted the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-43284, known as Dirty Frag, to reach root; Microsoft gives no success statement and no affected or fixed versions (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Both the compromised host and the operator connect outbound to the public relay, so the host needs no inbound listener, inbound firewall rules do not see the traffic and a shared secret, not an address, pairs the endpoints, which lets the operator reconnect later from any compatible client; Microsoft therefore says that blocking an address or domain is unlikely to cut off access, while egress filtering and outbound monitoring can see it (Microsoft, 2026-11-11). Microsoft's telemetry is concentrated on web applications and hosting; education and research and technology and telecommunications were the largest shares of affected organisations, which Microsoft says reflect exposure more likely than deliberate sector selection (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Exposure
Any Linux web, CMS or hosting server whose internet-facing application was exploited, patched or not, in the months before the patch; Microsoft says the same persistence problem applies when initial access came through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.
Detection
Process-creation telemetry with parent lineage, where a web-server or application-runtime process starts curl and then bash, followed by a long-lived process whose name imitates a kernel thread but whose executable sits in a hidden or memory-backed path; file events in /dev/shm and /tmp; new cron entries and systemd units with plausible service names created in the same window as the download; shell startup file changes; and long-lived outbound sessions to a public relay from servers that have no reason to initiate them. After patching, remove the client, its persistence and staged files, and verify that the outbound relay connections stopped, because persistence is layered and stopping the process alone does not remove access (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Triage: Microsoft notes that the same relay model also serves legitimate remote administration, and says a match must be judged on process ancestry, execution context, persistence changes and related network activity; a client started from a web-service process tree, from a writable or memory-backed path and under a kernel-thread-like name is the pattern it describes (Microsoft, 2026-11-11).

Defender takeaway
Treat every Linux web server whose application was exploited as possibly holding a relay client, not only web shells, and hunt it on the host after patching; Microsoft's hardening steps are deny-by-default egress with monitoring of relay connections, non-executable mounts for temporary and memory-backed directories, and a review of cron entries, systemd units and shell startup files.

Builds on: Dirty Frag: two kernel page-cache write flaws give local root; Microsoft saw su escalation that…

Because the client runs independently of the exploited application, patching does not remove it, and blocking an address or domain is unlikely to cut off access.

entries.action_label: Unit 42: Falcon C2 runs inside the browser, fed by…
