entries.headline: Unit 42: Falcon C2 runs inside the browser, fed by a script tag in government webmail such as Roundcube
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Falcon: Unit 42 describes a browser-resident command-and-control framework planted in government webmail and web applications, with a script tag in Roundcube at a Middle Eastern foreign ministry and a sideloaded 'PDF Viewer' extension elsewhere; it shares its core with PeckBirdy

Unit 42 describes Falcon C2, also called XG and not the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, a NodeJS command-and-control framework whose operator-controlled JavaScript implant runs inside the victim's browser, so the endpoint holds no file for it (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). A script tag placed in a trusted site makes each visit request the implant from the Falcon server, which returns a script obfuscated per browser session, and the implant then holds a TLS WebSocket to the server while the tab is open and runs operator JavaScript through eval (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). Unit 42 identified compromised government entities in one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026, among them ministries and law enforcement agencies, and names no actor (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

In April 2026 a script tag inserted into the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern ministry of foreign affairs let the operator intercept credentials as users signed in and monitor sessions (39 Roundcube instances in that country, none observed elsewhere; how the tag got in is not stated) (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). In May 2026 a module in a Southeast Asian police web application harvested usernames and then showed a fake Adobe Flash Player update prompt to chosen users, which served the Antino implant that uses Microsoft OneDrive for command and control (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). Against a justice-department entity in another country, a Chrome extension named PDF Viewer, sideloaded in developer mode, checked in every 3 to 4 minutes for over three weeks and exfiltrated plaintext credentials for an internal correspondence system and a screenshot of a document the victim was viewing (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). The Jewelbug campaign also used an extension named PDF Viewer (Symantec, 2026-08-13); Unit 42 lists it only as a further resource.

Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy (Trend's JScript framework used by China-aligned actors since 2023) are variants of one core framework; that is code lineage, not who operates Falcon (Unit 42, 2026-11-11; Trend Micro, 2026-01-26).

Exposure
Internal webmail, ticketing and case-management portals whose templates or headers an attacker can edit (Roundcube is the named case), and managed Chrome browsers that allow extensions to be sideloaded in developer mode; Unit 42 does not say how the script tags or the extensions reached their targets.
Detection
Unit 42's four monitoring items, telemetry class first: template and header integrity on webmail, ticketing and case-management portals for a script tag loading a resource from an unfamiliar domain, especially one returning a heavily numeric JavaScript array with a small decoder loop; extension inventory for developer-mode extensions imitating utilities such as PDF viewers with broad permissions; Baidu Analytics-style cookie or local-storage keys on internal government web applications; and OneDrive traffic to tenants outside the organisation's own with repeated small JSON writes (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

Triage: Unit 42's basis for the cookie check is that Baidu Analytics cookies are normal on sites that use that service and anomalous on internal government web applications where it has no reason to appear (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

Defender takeaway
Compare the templates and headers of internal webmail and case-management portals with a known-good copy and list every external script source they load, and inventory the Chrome extensions installed in developer mode on managed browsers; a browser-resident implant leaves nothing on the endpoint for file-based tools to find.

entries.headline: CCB: attackers signed in to Entra ID with an SMS code alone; turn off SMS first-factor sign-in
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOA2

Belgium's CCB warns that attackers abused Microsoft Entra ID SMS first-factor sign-in (phone number and one-time code, no password) to compromise several Belgian organisations; turning off 'Use for sign-in' is the priority step

The Belgian Centre for Cybersecurity (CCB) warned on 2026-11-10 that a trusted partner had observed successful attacks against multiple Belgian organisations in which attackers abused Microsoft Entra ID SMS as a first factor, the sign-in mode in which a phone number and a one-time code replace the password (CCB, 2026-11-10). The warning gives no victim count, sector, actor, date range or attack chain, and it does not say how the codes were obtained; its only statement on the factor itself is that SMS and voice can be phished, intercepted or SIM-swapped (CCB, 2026-11-10). No other source reports the Belgian attacks. Microsoft describes the method as designed for frontline workers, advises enabling it only for them, and says it is different from SMS as a multifactor method, which needs a username and password (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30). Microsoft is disabling first-factor sign-in in tenants with no such traffic in the previous 30 days (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30) and retires its own SMS and voice delivery on 2027-02-01 for all users except Global Administrators and external users, who follow on 2027-07-01; a customer-configured telephony provider can keep the methods working (Microsoft Learn, 2026-09-23).

Exposure
An Entra tenant whose SMS authentication method policy has first-factor sign-in turned on for any user or group; the CCB's path is Authentication methods, SMS, "Use for sign-in", and the Authentication methods activity report shows who actually uses it (CCB, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's how-to calls the same setting "Enable first factor sign-in" and says that leaving it unchecked limits SMS to multifactor authentication and self-service password reset (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30).
Detection
In Entra sign-in logs, look for successful sign-ins that used SMS as the authentication method; in audit logs, for phone-number or authentication-method changes; then for unusual locations or devices and follow-on mailbox rules or application consents, reviewing as far back as log retention allows (CCB, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Disable SMS first-factor sign-in now for everyone who has an alternative and restrict it to the smallest group where it must stay, as the CCB advises; remove SMS and voice for privileged accounts only after each has a working phishing-resistant method, and avoid a blind switch-off, which can lock users out or leave them with a password alone (CCB, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's own clearing reaches only tenants with no first-factor SMS sign-in traffic in the previous 30 days (Microsoft Learn, 2026-10-30), so a tenant that uses the method stays exposed until it acts.

Builds on: Vaud: device-code phishing against Microsoft 365 is running in Romandie; several organisations…

entries.headline: SAP Patch Day: four unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 flaws; Onapsis names ICM2SHELL and the fixed kernel levels
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-120017 +3updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-120017, CVE-2026-89126, CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89103, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP, Web Dispatcher and Gateway: four unauthenticated network flaws rated CVSS 10.0 and fixed on SAP's November 2026 Patch Day; Onapsis, which found three of them, says a working exploit exists and has seen no attacks

SAP's November Patch Day of 2026-11-10 fixes four flaws that SAP scores CVSS 3.1 10.0, each reachable over the network without privileges or user interaction and with changed scope. In the SAML2 service provider of NetWeaver AS ABAP and the ABAP Platform, an unauthenticated attacker could submit crafted data, under certain configurations, to bypass authentication and impersonate arbitrary users, privileged accounts included (CVE-2026-120017, note 3849308) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10). SAP Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager of NetWeaver AS ABAP share a memory corruption that could allow arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-89126, note 3778556; CVE-2026-76964, note 3778530) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10), and SAP Gateway activates its default access control list with high privileges, so an external attacker is treated as an internal application server (CVE-2026-89103, note 3798345) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10).

Onapsis, which found and reported the Web Dispatcher, ICM and Gateway flaws, names the first pair ICM2SHELL: a memory corruption in the shared kernel code that reassembles fragmented WebSocket messages, reachable on the HTTP or HTTPS port with no credentials, and "WebSocket support is enabled by default, whether or not it is used" (Onapsis, 2026-11-10). Onapsis provided SAP a working unauthenticated code-execution exploit that runs commands as the system's <sid>adm user, a single connection crashes the process on every kernel it tested, and it has not observed attacks; NCSC Switzerland lists the exploitation status as unknown (Onapsis, 2026-11-10; NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-10). It affects ABAP systems on kernel 7.40 or higher and every Web Dispatcher, the one in SAP HANA XS included; AS Java alone and kernel 7.22 are not affected, and kernels out of maintenance may get no fix. The fixed patch levels are 7.53 PL 1616 or 1617, 7.54 PL 710, 7.77 PL 914, 7.93 PL 401 or 420, 9.16 PL 111, 9.18 PL 37 and 9.20 PL 11 or 13 (Onapsis, 2026-11-10).

ProxyGate lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access run operating system commands as <sid>adm on the Gateway, and its exploitability depends on the proxy access list: a permissive prxyinfo file, or none with gw/acl_mode_proxy at its default of 0, leaves the system exposed, so "neither a version check nor patching alone tells you whether you are safe"; on most releases SAP's fix combines the kernel patch with gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1, and Onapsis lists the minimum patch level for each kernel release, for example 7.53 PL 1625 and 7.54 PL 718 (Onapsis, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
A system that runs one of the components and lets an untrusted network reach its Web Dispatcher, Internet Communication Manager, Gateway or SAML2 endpoint; the SAML2 flaw applies under certain configurations of the SAML 2.0 service provider (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10).
Detection
Onapsis expects every exploitation attempt against ICM2SHELL to crash the ICM or Web Dispatcher at least once, so unexpected restarts of either process outside maintenance deserve investigation; requests with status 101 in the ICM or Web Dispatcher HTTP log show whether WebSocket is in use before anyone considers disabling it (Onapsis, 2026-11-10). The sources name no indicator for the SAML2 flaw or the Gateway.
Defender takeaway
Patch internet-facing Web Dispatchers and Internet Communication Managers first and every application server and Web Dispatcher after them, set gw/acl_mode_proxy to 1 on every Gateway, and apply note 3849308 where the SAML2 service provider runs; Onapsis calls the notes the only complete fix.
Update11 Nov 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarycvessourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteconfidenceactionsbody

SAP's Security Patch Day page of 2026-11-10 lists 35 new notes and four GitHub security advisories and carries the four CVSS 10.0 notes above (SAP, 2026-11-10). Onapsis published threat advisories for the Web Dispatcher and ICM pair, which it names ICM2SHELL, and for the Gateway flaw, which it names ProxyGate, with the fixed kernel patch levels, the Gateway parameter gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1 and the statement that it gave SAP a working unauthenticated exploit for ICM2SHELL and has seen no attacks (Onapsis, 2026-11-10; Onapsis, 2026-11-10). Five further notes on the page are rated Critical at CVSS 9.1 to 9.9, among them an ABAP application server OS command injection for low-privileged users (CVE-2026-76965, note 3792735) and a code injection in NetWeaver Knowledge Management XML Forms (CVE-2026-109803, note 3809153); they are not covered here (SAP, 2026-11-10).

entries.headline: Barracuda ESG: CISA lists both flaws as exploited, Barracuda reports attacks; update to 9.4.0.029 or later
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-116606 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-116606 / CVE-2026-111560, Barracuda Email Security Gateway: an unauthenticated configuration-import bypass chained with a root command injection, with watchTowr's detection tool public since 2026-11-03 and its full chain since 2026-11-05; patches are out, Barracuda reports exploitation against a small number of organizations and CISA lists both flaws as exploited (CVSS 9.3 and 8.6)

Barracuda's advisory of 2026-11-02 covers two flaws that, chained, give root on the appliance: CVE-2026-116606, a pre-authentication authorization bypass in the Email Security Gateway, and CVE-2026-111560, a command injection that also affects the Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall and Web Security Gateway (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). Barracuda says successful exploitation requires access to the administrative interface and that, in combination, the flaws let an attacker bypass authorization controls and obtain root (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). Mandiant's disclosure describes the first as letting an unauthenticated remote attacker invoke the gateway's configuration-import function and restore a crafted backup archive (Mandiant, 2026-11-02), and the second as shell metacharacters in the timezone configuration field that let an authenticated administrator run commands as root when the crafted value is processed (Mandiant, 2026-11-02). watchTowr Labs showed on 2026-11-05 that the two chain without any account on the gateway: one unauthenticated request reaches the restore function and the restored timezone value reaches the root command injection (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). NCSC Switzerland rated exploitation unknown on 2026-11-03 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-03), and Barracuda changed its advisory on 2026-11-05 to say authentication is not required for CVE-2026-116606, only that the administrative user interface must be accessible to the attacker (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). Barracuda added on 2026-11-09 that it has identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations, without naming the flaw (Barracuda, 2026-11-09), and the Canadian Cyber Centre says open-source reporting indicates CVE-2026-116606 is exploited in the wild (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-11-09). CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 (CISA, 2026-11-10) and marks both for forensic triage (CISA, 2026-11-10).

Barracuda released patches for each product and asks customers to apply any patch not applied automatically and confirm automatic patching is on (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). Its Campus article names firmware 9.4.0.029 or later for the Email Security Gateway (Barracuda Campus, 2026-11-02), while the CVE record lists versions earlier than 9.4.0.030 as affected (Mandiant, 2026-11-02).

Exposure
An Email Security Gateway of any version before the fix, or a Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall or Web Security Gateway for the command injection, whose administrative interface can be reached; NCSC Switzerland puts internet-exposed management interfaces at the highest risk (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-03), and Barracuda says organisations whose administrative interfaces are not publicly accessible from the internet are less exposed to this attack path (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). The installed firmware version is shown under Advanced > Firmware Update (Barracuda Campus, 2026-11-02).
Detection
Barracuda's advisory names no indicators. watchTowr's chain implies, in the interface's web access logs, a POST to /cgi-mod/index.cgi that submits a password change with two different passwords together with a backup file from a session that never logged in, followed by a restored configuration whose timezone value holds shell metacharacters (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05); the mechanism also implies root-owned child processes under the appliance's management service after a restore nobody made. After patching, repeat these checks on any appliance whose interface was reachable before the fix.
Defender takeaway
Take every affected Barracuda appliance's administrative interface off the internet and untrusted networks, update every Email Security Gateway to 9.4.0.029 or later (Barracuda Campus, 2026-11-02), apply the patch listed for each of the other products and confirm that automatic patching is on; Barracuda recommends restricting administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks (Barracuda, 2026-11-05).
Update06 Nov 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-11-06T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryprioritytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

watchTowr Labs published the full chain on 2026-11-05 after comparing firmware 9.4.0.027 with 9.4.0.029 (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). In the login handler a failed password-change attempt returns the login-screen role instead of ending the request, so one unauthenticated POST to /cgi-mod/index.cgi that submits mismatching new and retyped passwords with a backup upload reaches the backup-restore function (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). The restore accepts a backup whose checksum matches, and the checksum is built from the file bytes and a secret that is hard-coded in the product, so an attacker can build a valid archive (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). A restored system_timezone value then reaches an unescaped shell call that runs as root (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). watchTowr shares a Detection Artefact Generator so that owners can test their own appliances, and its post does not claim exploitation in the wild (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). Its README describes a tool that takes a target URL and a command, builds a backup, uploads it to the target and attempts to check whether the target is vulnerable (watchTowr Labs README, 2026-11-03).

Barracuda changed its advisory the same day, 2026-11-05 at 2:30pm EST: the Authentication Required field for CVE-2026-116606 now reads No (Administrative UI Access Required), and the advisory says authentication is not required to exploit it but the administrative user interface must be accessible to the attacker (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). The advisory's entry for CVE-2026-111560 still reads Yes (Administrative Access) (Barracuda, 2026-11-05).

Update10 Nov 2026 03:35 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Barracuda added on 2026-11-09 to its advisory that it has identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations; the advisory does not say which flaw, how many organizations, since when or what the attacker did afterwards (Barracuda, 2026-11-09). The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's update of the same day says open-source reporting indicates that CVE-2026-116606 is exploited in the wild, without naming the reporting (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-11-09). Barracuda's lever is unchanged: organizations whose administrative interfaces are not publicly accessible from the internet are less exposed to this attack path (Barracuda, 2026-11-09), so an appliance whose interface was reachable before patching should also be checked for a restore nobody made and a timezone value that is not a timezone name.

Update11 Nov 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CISA added both CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-11-10). The catalog describes the two as chainable, the first letting an unauthenticated remote attacker restore a crafted backup archive and the second letting an authenticated administrator run commands as root through a crafted timezone value, and marks both for forensic triage (CISA, 2026-11-10). The listing makes CVE-2026-111560 exploited as well; Barracuda's own statement of 2026-11-09 still names no flaw, and no source says how many organizations were hit or what the attacker did afterwards.

entries.headline: Stolen Qubole vendor credentials assumed customers' idle AWS integration roles; a source-IP condition stops it
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB1

Qubole: an attacker used IAM credentials from a vendor-associated AWS account to assume dormant cross-account integration roles in dozens of customer accounts, then harvested secrets and validated Entra ID and Okta client credentials (Wiz and Sentra, 14 to 26 October)

Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, observed a threat actor using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole, a big-data platform, between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-26 (Wiz, 2026-11-09). The actor used two Qubole IAM users to call sts:AssumeRole on the cross-account integration roles that customers had created to trust Qubole's account; "every AssumeRole request we attributed to the threat actor included an External ID, and every one succeeded", most of the roles were otherwise not in use, and the traffic came from a rented hosting server and commercial VPN exits, not the AWS infrastructure where legitimate platform traffic originates (Wiz, 2026-11-09; Sentra, 2026-11-09).

Inside the affected accounts the actor enumerated resources, read Lambda function configuration, Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store, ran TruffleHog to test AWS access keys, Entra ID service-principal client secrets and Okta client credentials it found, and then downloaded S3 data opportunistically, in some cases whole buckets in one session (Wiz, 2026-11-09). Wiz found no tie to other reported activity and judges the targeting opportunistic; how the Qubole IAM users were compromised is not stated. Sentra writes that dozens of Qubole customers were impacted, and BleepingComputer could not find a public Qubole announcement (Sentra, 2026-11-09; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). No Swiss or public-sector victim is named, but the exposure is shared by any account that gave a data or analytics vendor a cross-account role and left it in place.

Exposure
Any AWS account holding an IAM role whose trust policy lets a Qubole account, or any other vendor account, assume it, including roles left from integrations that ended; the roles' trust policies and last-used data show them, and Wiz publishes the vendor account identifier, the two principals and the attacker address ranges for a CloudTrail hunt back to 2026-10-01 (Wiz, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In cloud control-plane audit logs, AssumeRole events into integration roles whose calling identity is the vendor account but whose source address is not AWS infrastructure, and session names with a consistent attacker-chosen prefix; GetCallerIdentity calls from many keys within seconds and Entra ID or Okta sign-ins by service principals or clients right after, as the actor validates credentials; ListSecrets, GetSecretValue, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration reads in bursts. Object reads are absent from CloudTrail management events, so S3 data events or server access logs must be on, and Wiz says missing logs left responders unable to see what was read (Wiz, 2026-11-09).

Triage: legitimate vendor traffic comes from the vendor's own AWS infrastructure; the correct External ID does not discriminate, because it is logged in plaintext and often stored by the vendor, while a vendor role assumed from a consumer VPN or a hosting provider the vendor has never used is the high-signal case.

Defender takeaway
Inventory third-party trust relationships, delete the roles of ended integrations, narrow each trusted principal to the vendor's specific principal and add a source-address or endpoint condition, which Wiz says alone would have blocked every observed assumption; after an incident, revoke the issued role sessions and rotate every secret, parameter, Lambda variable and identity-provider credential the role could read.

Inside the affected accounts the actor listed resources, read Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration, tested harvested AWS, Entra ID and Okta credentials with TruffleHog and downloaded S3 data, in some cases whole buckets; no victim is named, the counts range from more than a dozen to dozens, and how the vendor identities were compromised is not known.

entries.headline: Insikt: GhostFrame implant re-disables ESXi execInstalledOnly every five seconds and steals guest credentials
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

GhostFrame: Recorded Future's Insikt Group finds an ESXi post-exploitation framework (vmhostd-core implant, VM control panel, VMkatz credential theft) used by TAG-218, whose activity overlaps Settra ransomware and which targeted SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet VPN appliances in the US and Europe

Insikt Group describes GhostFrame, a previously undocumented command-and-control and post-exploitation framework for compromised VMware ESXi hosts, which it saw used by TAG-218, a group "whose operations overlap with Settra ransomware" (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Operators must already hold root on the host: the implant, an ELF named vmhostd-core generated from a web operator panel, does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). It copies itself to /opt/vmhostd-core, edits the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh and runs /sbin/auto-backup.sh to keep the change across reboots, masquerades as vmhostd, and about every five seconds disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly control that restricts execution of unsigned binaries, so an administrator who re-enables them is undone (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Its command channel opens simultaneous TCP connections to one address on ports 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443 and 9443, keeps the first that succeeds and retries after a random delay of 5 to 12 seconds, which Insikt notes is a network detection opportunity; the implant is mainly an in-memory shellcode loader (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10).

From the hypervisor the panel can list registered VMs, change power state, create or delete snapshots, enable VNC on a guest, run a SOCKS5 proxy for pivoting, intercept ESXi logins, and run the open-source VMkatz against VM memory snapshots, virtual disks or whole datastores which Insikt says may let an operator obtain NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets and NTDS.dit credentials without deploying malware inside each VM (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Insikt ties TAG-218's victim-facing servers to VPN-appliance targeting across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, "predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices", and says four of those organisations later appeared on the Settra leak site; it assesses that other financially motivated actors are highly likely to adopt the framework, which is an assessment, not an observation (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Unit 42 independently reports that after CVE-2026-0257 exploitation attackers pivot from the VPN gateway directly to the virtualization layer (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
ESXi hosts whose root credentials, SSH or shell, or vCenter are reachable after an edge compromise; no ESXi vulnerability is involved, so patching ESXi does not address it, and an estate that runs both a SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks or Fortinet VPN appliance and ESXi without isolated hypervisor management is in the pattern Insikt describes.
Detection
In ESXi file-integrity and shell-audit telemetry, changes to local.sh, a process masquerading as the host daemon or an unexpected executable under /opt, and repeated firewall-off and execInstalledOnly resets; in network telemetry, six near-simultaneous SYNs from the hypervisor management address to one destination on those ports, and any outbound command traffic from a hypervisor; in vCenter and ESXi logs, snapshot creation or deletion, VNC enablement and power-state changes outside change windows; in datastore telemetry, reads of VM memory-snapshot and virtual-disk files by an identity that is not the backup service.

Triage: administrators legitimately edit local.sh, create snapshots and use VNC; the discriminators are a firewall-off and execInstalledOnly loop, a /opt/vmhostd-core file or vmhostd process where the genuine daemon is vmware-hostd, and snapshot-file reads by a non-backup account.

Defender takeaway
Treat a VPN-appliance compromise as a possible hypervisor compromise and check the ESXi persistence files and the execInstalledOnly state before declaring the incident closed; restrict ESXi and vCenter management to dedicated administration hosts.
Correction15 Nov 2026 15:02 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditbody

Insikt Group gives the persistence file as /opt/vmhostd-core and says the implant presents its process as vmhostd, a name resembling the genuine vmware-hostd daemon; either the file or the process is the indicator it lists (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Its reading of the VMkatz capability is hedged: the capabilities suggest that an operator controlling an ESXi host may be able to obtain credentials from hosted Windows systems without first deploying credential-stealing malware inside each VM (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10).

entries.headline: ESET: Turla's Cereal runs the victim's own Exchange server as C2 and wraps transport agents to collect mail
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Turla's Cereal toolset turns a compromised on-premises Exchange server into the command channel and mail collector at Kazakh and Romanian government bodies, with no attacker infrastructure and no new transport agent registered (ESET)

ESET found a previously undocumented .NET toolset, Cereal, on a Kazakh government organisation's Exchange server on 2025-11-28 and on a Romanian government organisation's Exchange server compromised from 2025-12-23; in Romania the mail-collection module was configured to identify messages to or from NATO and EU institutional addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). ESET attributes Cereal to Turla with high confidence, on the concurrent use of another component publicly linked to Turla and conceptual similarity to older Turla malware, and could not determine the initial access method, although it considers a vulnerability exploit possible because the servers are reachable from the internet (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

The command channel is the victim's own Exchange server. CerealNeuron runs on the compromised server and passively waits for requests on web paths made to look like Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync traffic; a correctly encrypted request is treated as a command and a bad one gets a normal-looking Exchange error page, and ESET found no operator-controlled server and could not identify ingress addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). Each task runs as a small .NET assembly inside a CerealRunner (mailbox retrieval, Active Directory and WMI queries, LSA secrets extraction, file operations) (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealLoader, the only component written to disk in recognisable .NET form, abuses .NET VTable fixups so native code runs before managed code and is placed where trusted processes load it: the System32 wbem directory (ncobjapi.dll, wbemcomn.dll, loaded by WMI) and the .NET native image cache (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealBox, injected into EdgeTransport.exe, wraps the handlers of transport agents already loaded, so "no new agent appears anywhere in Exchange's configuration"; it keeps messages with .doc, .docx or .pdf attachments that match hard-coded sender, recipient, subject or attachment-name lists and stages them compressed and encrypted on disk for exfiltration through CerealNeuron (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any organisation that runs Microsoft Exchange on premises with a role reachable from the internet; ESET names no vulnerable version, so exposure is the deployment model.
Detection
File-integrity telemetry on the Exchange host for DLLs in the System32 wbem directory and .NET native image cache files that do not match the Microsoft originals; module telemetry for non-Microsoft assemblies loaded into EdgeTransport.exe while Get-TransportAgent lists nothing new; web-server logs for requests to the Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync look-alike paths from clients with no matching mailbox flow, whose encrypted bodies return a generic error page; and Exchange Web Services mailbox retrievals made from the server's own context. ReversingLabs adds live HTTP.sys listeners (netsh http show servicestate) and proxy, load-balancer and WAF logs for the look-alike paths, proxy DLLs that mimic system libraries in the service directories, and module loads in WmiPrvSE.exe (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19). With no external C2 and no known entry vector, the check is a compromise assessment of every internet-facing Exchange server.

Triage: third-party anti-spam, data-loss-prevention and archiving products also inject into the transport service, but they are vendor-signed and appear in the transport-agent configuration, which CerealBox does not; the native image cache regenerates legitimately after .NET updates, so only a file that does not match the Microsoft binary is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat internet-facing Exchange servers as top-tier assets, baseline the wbem directory and the native image cache, and run the compromise assessment now, because network-only detection will not find a channel that rides the victim's own web paths.
Improvement20 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-intelsourcesbody

ReversingLabs correlated ESET's published loader samples and says the same files carry different vendor names, CerealLoader at ESET, BlankPage in Microsoft Defender and CerealMood in other engines, so a hunt on a single family name can miss matches; it says the work extends the artifacts defenders can search for and establishes no additional victims or initial-access method (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19). Its hunting guidance (HTTP.sys listeners, proxy-DLL loaders such as version.dll and WTSAPI32.dll, and WmiPrvSE.exe module loads) is in the Detection line (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19).

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Check Point: a Sparrow-framework supplier fronts government watering holes with a fake Chrome certificate warning
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

CopperDragon: Check Point ties three China-nexus intrusion sets to one Sparrow-framework supplier, among them SilentDelivery watering holes on government, shipping, IT and research sites that show a fake Chrome certificate warning (Czech Republic, Germany and France in its telemetry)

Check Point Research's year-long investigation groups three intrusion sets under one malware-supply entity it calls CopperDragon, a possible "digital quartermaster" for China-nexus actors that use the cross-platform Sparrow framework (FamousSparrow and Earth Estries among them); Check Point itself cautions that the use of the same backdoor or C2 infrastructure "does not necessarily mean" the same actor ran two intrusions, so this is a hypothesis (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10).

SilentDelivery, active since early 2026 against Europe and Asia, is the set nearest the constituency. Compromised government, shipping, IT and research websites, one through cross-site scripting in an unsanitised input field, carry obfuscated JavaScript that fingerprints the visitor and replaces the page with a language-localised fake Google Chrome SSL warning urging a "Certificate Fix" utility; the MSI, served from compromised cloud storage buckets, installs the new SquadC backdoor or a SparrowDoor variant (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). SquadC can be set to run only while a browser process is alive, persists through a Run key named WindowsUpdateAssist, and offers file operations, command execution and screenshots. A second route is a spear-phishing RAR whose LNK abuses ftp.exe, with the same C2 (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). Positive Technologies independently documented the same fake-certificate chain, with victims in Taiwan, Germany, Indonesia and the Czech Republic (Positive Technologies, 2026-08-21).

The other two sets show what follows an intrusion. OceanGate in Asia starts from an exploited internet-facing Linux server and moves through trojanised ssh and sshd binaries that log passwords, a Linux backdoor that can load a kernel rootkit, FRP and Chisel tunnels, a hidden local administrator account and an LSA security-package credential interceptor; recent SparrowDoor builds embed the WinDivert driver to share a service port such as 443. DarkWire against Latin American telecom and government bodies uses DLL sideloading of uncommon executables, SoftEther VPN renamed to system-process names, DNS MX tunnelling and WMI lateral movement (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). No Swiss victim is named.

Exposure
Staff of public bodies, shipping, IT and research organisations who browse peer websites, web teams whose sites accept unsanitised input, and Windows endpoints that let a standard user run an MSI from a browser download.
Detection
In endpoint telemetry, a browser followed by msiexec running an installer named like a certificate repair utility and a new Run key value with an update-themed name; in module-load telemetry, DLL sideloading by rarely abused executables, and the WinDivert driver loaded by a process that is not a VPN or firewall product; in account telemetry, a new local administrator account; on Linux, ssh and sshd binaries that differ from the package-manager copy and frpc or chisel binaries; in DNS, MX-query volume from servers that send no mail.

Triage: WinDivert is legitimate in VPN and firewall products, so the signal is a parent that is a sideloaded DLL or backdoor rather than the vendor's signed service; SoftEther running under a system-process name such as vmtoolsd.exe is not legitimate; a genuine Chrome SSL warning is never cleared by installing an MSI.

Defender takeaway
Treat a browser page that offers a "certificate fix" installer as an incident trigger and stop standard users running MSI installers from a browser download; web teams of government and research sites should check for injected third-party script and input-handling flaws, because a compromised site becomes a delivery vehicle for its peers.
Correction15 Nov 2026 15:02 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditbody

The SoftEther discriminator is the name, not the path: Check Point says the operators renamed SoftEther VPN to names such as vmtoolsd.exe and csrss.exe and deliberately placed their tools in existing system directories instead of creating new ones (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10), so a SoftEther binary or configuration under a system-process or VMware Tools name is the signal, wherever it sits.

entries.headline: Synology DSM: pre-auth SQL injection in the Auth API gives file read and write; update to the fixed build of your branch
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-76954 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-76954 and CVE-2026-85101, Synology DSM (SA-26:19): a pre-authentication SQL injection in the Auth API (CVSS 9.8) allows arbitrary file read and write, and an rsync authentication bypass reads and writes files; fixed in DSM 7.4.1-90080-1, 7.3.2-86009-5, 7.2.2-72806-10 and 7.2.1-69057-13, no mitigation

Synology's advisory SA-26:19 of 2026-11-10, severity Critical, fixes two DiskStation Manager flaws that need no credentials and lists no mitigation (Synology, 2026-11-10). CVE-2026-76954 (CVSS 9.8) is an SQL injection in the Auth API that lets remote attackers read or write arbitrary files and cause denial of service; CVE-2026-85101 (8.6) is an authentication bypass in the rsync service that lets remote attackers read specific files, write arbitrary files and cause limited denial of service (Synology, 2026-11-10). DSM is fixed in 7.4.1-90080-1, 7.3.2-86009-5, 7.2.2-72806-10 and 7.2.1-69057-13 (Synology, 2026-11-10; CERT-FR, 2026-11-10). The sources mention neither exploitation nor a public proof of concept.

Exposure
DSM 7.2.1, 7.2.2, 7.3 and 7.4 below those builds with the management interface reachable (and the rsync service enabled for CVE-2026-85101); the build shows under Control Panel, Info Center.
Detection
DSM web and Auth API access logs for SQL syntax or errors in authentication requests, rsync sessions from addresses that are not backup partners, and files in shared folders or system paths that appeared after such requests. After patching, a device that was reachable from the internet needs a check of its scheduled tasks and user accounts, because the file-write primitive can plant persistence.
Defender takeaway
Update every DSM to the fixed build of its branch now and keep the management interface and rsync off the internet until it is installed; Synology offers no other control, and a NAS holds the backups and shares an intruder wants.

entries.headline: Adobe Connect on Windows: five unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 flaws up to 12.12, fixed in 12.12.a; not known exploited
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-121356 +6NATOA2

Adobe Connect (Windows) APSB26-191: five unauthenticated flaws rated CVSS 10.0 and two more unauthenticated rows among 24 fixes in 12.12 and earlier; Adobe knows of no exploitation

Adobe's priority 2 bulletin APSB26-191, published on 2026-11-10, fixes 24 CVEs in Adobe Connect on Windows 12.12 and earlier (Adobe, 2026-11-10). Five of them are scored CVSS 3.1 10.0 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C, so an attacker needs no account and no user interaction: two server-side request forgeries (CVE-2026-121356, CVE-2026-121889), a path traversal (CVE-2026-121351), an incorrect-authorization flaw (CVE-2026-121352) and a CRLF injection (CVE-2026-121353); Adobe describes the impact of all five as privilege escalation (Adobe, 2026-11-10). Two more rows need no privileges either: an SQL injection leading to code execution (CVE-2026-121902, 9.4) and an incorrect-authorization flaw (CVE-2026-121355, 9.1), and a further group of authenticated rows is fixed in the same release (Adobe, 2026-11-10). The fixed builds are 12.12.a, 12.11.i, 12.10.f, 12.9.a and 12.8.a (Adobe, 2026-11-10). The bulletin gives no root-cause detail, names no workaround, and Adobe says it is not aware of exploitation.

Exposure
Adobe Connect on Windows at 12.12 or earlier, the product the bulletin lists.
Detection
The bulletin supplies none, so the signal is behavior at the web tier: unauthenticated requests that return content from administrative or API paths, outbound connections from the Connect server to internal addresses that suggest request forgery, and unexpected files in web-served directories.
Defender takeaway
Patch internet-facing Connect servers to the fixed build of their train now, because five flaws need neither credentials nor a user and the bulletin offers nothing but the update.

entries.headline: Patch Tuesday: Kerberos relay to a DC and Exchange zero-click RCE lead the 9.8 server rows; none exploited
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-85844 +6NATOA2

Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday: seven of the unauthenticated network flaws rated CVSS 9.8, in domain infrastructure and server roles, among them a Kerberos relay to a domain controller (CVE-2026-85844) and zero-click code execution through Exchange attachment indexing (CVE-2026-116928); none exploited or disclosed

Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes seven flaws in domain infrastructure and server roles scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 that need no credentials over the network (the release carries further 9.8 rows, DirectMusic among them, that are not covered here (Microsoft, 2026-11-10)); the only record Microsoft marks as exploited in this release is the Outlook zero-day, which is a separate item, and none of these rows is marked exploited or publicly disclosed (Microsoft, 2026-11-10; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). Two have mechanics that make the timeline short. CVE-2026-85844 is an authentication bypass in Windows Kerberos: an unauthenticated attacker sends crafted Kerberos authentication traffic and relays the resulting authentication to an affected domain controller, with no user interaction (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component that Exchange Server uses: an attacker emails a crafted attachment, Exchange indexes it automatically, so "the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment", and the code runs with the permissions of the processing service (Microsoft, 2026-11-10).

The other five are described more thinly: a double free in Windows DNS (CVE-2026-88218) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10), an out-of-bounds read in Windows DHCP Server (CVE-2026-88243) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10) and a release of an invalid pointer in Windows iSCSI (CVE-2026-88234) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10), each reachable by an in-network attacker calling arbitrary endpoints; an out-of-bounds write in the Windows LDAP service that gives code execution in its context through crafted LDAP calls (CVE-2026-119958) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10); and a heap overflow in SQL Server (CVE-2026-116945) that needs an attacker who controls a network endpoint an integration package connects to, with no credentials or user interaction when the package runs automatically (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). The fixes are the November cumulative updates per release, for example KB5131291 (Windows Server 2016), KB5131085 (Server 2019), KB5131090 (Server 2022) and KB5131080 or KB5131077 (Server 2025), and the November SQL Server updates, for example KB5129299 (2025 CU10) and KB5129300 (2022 CU27).

Exposure
Domain controllers (Kerberos, LDAP, DNS), DNS and DHCP servers, Exchange servers that receive mail from the internet, and SQL Server hosts that run Integration Services packages against endpoints an attacker could control; the installed cumulative update shows in the update history of each host.
Detection
No exploitation is reported, so detection is hardening-grade: crashes or restarts of the DNS Server, DHCP Server and LSASS processes on domain controllers, Kerberos or LDAP bursts from workstation networks toward domain controllers, content-indexing or transport worker crashes on Exchange after inbound mail with unusual attachments, and an inventory of which domain controllers and Exchange servers already carry the November update.
Defender takeaway
Put the November update on domain controllers and internet-facing Exchange servers first; Microsoft's records give an unauthenticated attacker a relay to a domain controller and a mail-borne path to code execution on Exchange, and the DNS, DHCP and iSCSI rows are reachable by an in-network attacker, so keep those services off untrusted segments until they are patched.

entries.headline: Outlook zero-day CVE-2026-124194 exploited: a crafted message file leaks authentication data; install the Office update
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-124194exploitedNATOA1

CVE-2026-124194, Microsoft Outlook: opening a crafted message file makes Outlook reach an attacker-chosen network location without the usual warning and disclose authentication information; exploited as a zero-day, fixed in the November 2026 updates and listed by CISA (CVSS 3.1 6.5)

Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw (CWE-356, the product does not warn the user of an unsafe action) scored CVSS 3.1 6.5, which the Security Update Guide marks as exploited and not publicly disclosed (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's FAQ says an unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted message file and convinces the user to open it, whereupon Outlook may connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, "potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user"; the Preview Pane is not an attack vector, so the file has to be opened (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 (CISA, 2026-11-10), and BleepingComputer counts it as the one actively exploited zero-day of this Patch Tuesday (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). The affected products are Outlook in Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2024 (fixed in 16.0.17932.21140) and Office LTSC 2021 (fixed in 16.0.14334.21048); Microsoft 365 Apps take the fix through the Office security-update channel (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10). BleepingComputer calls it an NTLM credential disclosure flaw: opening the attachment makes Windows connect to an attacker-controlled share and expose the user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be captured and cracked offline (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). No source names the actor or the victims.

Exposure
Every Outlook desktop below those builds; the build shows under File, Office Account, and the delivery path is mail or a download that carries a message file, which the user must open.
Detection
Outbound connections to non-corporate addresses over SMB (TCP 445), WebDAV or HTTPS from OUTLOOK.EXE or from the user's session shortly after a message-file attachment is opened, authentication events carrying the user's identity toward an external address, and mail-gateway logs for message-file attachments from unknown senders. Because the credential material may already have been captured before the patch, the check also covers the weeks before it. The disclosed material is the user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be cracked offline or used to impersonate the user, so also watch for later logons by the account from unfamiliar hosts.

Triage: Outlook legitimately contacts SharePoint, OneDrive and corporate file servers; the discriminator is an external, non-corporate destination preceded by the opening of a message file.

Defender takeaway
Install the November Office update now rather than in the normal cycle, because the flaw is exploited and a patched machine still leaves earlier captured credentials valid; reset the accounts of users whose Outlook reached an external destination.

entries.headline: Xen Orchestra auth bypass is exploited: Admin and root on XCP-ng hosts; update xo-server to 5.213.1 or 5.211.2
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-133469exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-133469, Vates Xen Orchestra (VSA-2026-062): a crafted empty-object login cookie bypasses authentication and is exploited to take over XCP-ng hosts; fixed in xo-server 5.213.1 and 5.211.2 (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

Vates published advisory VSA-2026-062 on 2026-11-10, rated Critical, for Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA), the web management plane for XCP-ng pools; the flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-133469, CVSS 3.1 9.8 (Vates, 2026-11-10; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23). Vates says a threat actor is actively exploiting the flaw, that an adversary can bypass authentication and act with Admin privilege, and that a compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full takeover of XCP-ng nodes as root (Vates, 2026-11-10). The mechanism, per Vates: the REST cookie parser turns an authenticationToken cookie of j:%7B%7D into an empty object, the REST authentication path hands that object to the token provider without requiring a string, the token lookup treats it as unfiltered and returns the first token, and the provider authenticates as that token's owner if the token has not expired; the authenticated token-listing route then returns reusable login token ids (Vates, 2026-11-10). The attacker needs network reach to the interface and an unexpired first token in the Xen Orchestra token store, and no credentials or user interaction; the attacker does not choose which token the lookup returns (Xen Orchestra GitHub advisory, 2026-11-20).

Xen Orchestra before 6.9.2 (stable) and before 6.10.1 (latest) is affected, and the fixes are xo-server 5.211.2 on the stable channel and 5.213.1 on the latest channel; a source install must move to the latest master (Vates, 2026-11-10). The CVE record names the same fixed releases, 6.9.2 and 6.10.1, and states the flaw is actively exploited in the wild (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23); BleepingComputer named 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 as the fixed releases, which the CVE record contradicts (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any Xen Orchestra or XOA instance below those versions whose web or REST port is reachable from an untrusted network; Vates' first mitigation is a dedicated management network, never the internet (Vates, 2026-11-10).
Detection
A successful exploit leaves no Xen Orchestra log, so the signal is on the wire or at a reverse proxy: HTTP requests whose authenticationToken cookie is an empty JSON object in the encoded or the literal form, and Vates warns that a rule written as a regular expression can be bypassed with other encodings (Vates, 2026-11-10). On the XCP-ng hosts Vates lists a VM that sends its serial console to a file, a VM with an unexpected name, cron files written by the actor and the dynamic-linker preload file, and says these cover only the known campaign, so their absence does not prove a clean host (Vates, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Update now and take the interface off any untrusted network; for an instance that was exposed, treat the stack as possibly compromised, rotate every secret it held (backup remotes, the root and pool secrets, user and OTP secrets, mail-server passwords) and reinstall where compromise is confirmed (Vates, 2026-11-10).
Improvement24 Nov 2026 04:29 UTCrun 2026-11-24T0355Z-inteltitlesummaryentitiescvessourcesevidencesourcing_notetagsbody

GitHub, as numbering authority, published CVE-2026-133469 for this flaw on 2026-11-23 with CVSS 3.1 9.8; the record states that it is actively exploited in the wild and fixed in 6.9.2 and 6.10.1, the same releases Vates names, and lists xo-server before 5.211.2 and 5.213.1 as affected (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-23). The project's own advisory, published on 2026-11-20, gives the root cause in the REST cookie parser and the token lookup, and the prerequisite: authentication succeeds only if the token returned first is unexpired and belongs to an existing user, and a successful request returns reusable login token ids (Xen Orchestra GitHub advisory, 2026-11-20). The advisory includes a one-request proof of concept, so the technique is public (Xen Orchestra GitHub advisory, 2026-11-20).

entries.headline: FreeSWITCH: one SIP MESSAGE runs API commands; vendor and CISA say exploited; fixed in 1.11.3
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-116779exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-116779, FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 and earlier: one inbound SIP MESSAGE can select the api chat proto and run FreeSWITCH API commands, the vendor says exploitation has been observed, CISA lists it as exploited, and 1.11.3 fixes it (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

SignalWire's advisory GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p describes CVE-2026-116779: FreeSWITCH's sofia_presence_handle_sip_i_message() splits the To user of an inbound SIP MESSAGE on + and treats the left half as a chat proto name, the mod_dptools module registers an api chat interface that hands its address to switch_api_execute(), and a peer that can deliver a MESSAGE to a profile therefore selects which FreeSWITCH API command the server runs (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The impact is command execution with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process, including arbitrary operating-system commands, disclosure of configuration and credentials and full call control, and where mod_lua is loaded, as the stock configuration does, inline Lua is a second route (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The advisory scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, lists 1.11.2 and earlier as affected and 1.11.3 as patched, and states that exploitation of this path has been observed in the wild without naming an actor or a victim (SignalWire, 2026-10-28); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 (CISA, 2026-11-09). BSI CERT-Bund rated its advisory on the flaw critical and lists versions before 1.11.3 as affected (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-04).

The default posture is exposed: chat handling is on unless a profile sets enable-chat=false, the stock vanilla configuration leaves it on for the internal and external profiles, and the inbound ACL does not cover MESSAGE; where MESSAGE authentication is enforced (the default from 1.10.7) any one account on the profile is enough, and installations that still carry the sample directory user default, which has no password, need no account of their own (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The fix is a per-profile enable-chat-api-proto parameter that is off unless set, so the route is closed by default and a MESSAGE that selects the proto is answered with 403 and logged with the source and the requested command (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). auth-messages alone does not close the path, and disable_system_api_commands=true removes the system API but leaves the route to every other registered API, module loading and call origination included (SignalWire, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A FreeSWITCH of version 1.11.2 or earlier with a SIP profile that accepts inbound MESSAGE from a peer that can reach it, which is the default configuration (SignalWire, 2026-10-28).
Detection
SIP signalling logs, or packet capture at the session border controller, for MESSAGE requests whose To user carries a + with api as the left half, in any letter case; after the upgrade the 403 and the log line with the source and the requested command mark attempts (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The mechanism also implies child processes such as a shell or a downloader started by the FreeSWITCH process, and, where an instance was reachable before the fix, changes to its Lua scripts, dialplan or loaded modules.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 1.11.3, or until then set enable-chat=false on every profile that does not need inbound SIP chat and remove directory users that have no password; on an instance that was reachable by SIP peers, treat its configuration and the credentials it holds as disclosed, because the vendor says exploitation has been observed and CISA lists the flaw as exploited (SignalWire, 2026-10-28; CISA, 2026-11-09).
Improvement08 Nov 2026 14:09 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditsources

The release notes of FreeSWITCH 1.11.3 add the enable-chat-api-proto parameter that gates the api chat proto to mod_verto as well as to mod_sofia (SignalWire, 2026-08-28). SignalWire's advisory describes only the inbound SIP MESSAGE path and does not say whether Verto endpoints reach the same command selector (SignalWire, 2026-10-28), so a deployment that exposes Verto to untrusted clients has a second surface the SIP-profile setting does not cover.

Update10 Nov 2026 04:25 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelsummarytagscvessourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteactionsbodytitleheadline

CISA added CVE-2026-116779 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 "based on evidence of active exploitation" that it does not describe (CISA, 2026-11-09). Until then SignalWire's advisory was the only source of the exploitation claim; the listing adds an authority's assessment, still without a victim, an actor or a count of affected systems. The compromise check in the Defender takeaway applies to any instance that SIP peers could reach before it was upgraded.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: BluePhishing: a consented rogue Entra agent blueprint gives tenant access; Entra users get blueprint rights in November
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

BluePhishing: Proofpoint's proof of concept turns a consent link for a third-party Entra agent blueprint into tenant initial access, with an agent-creation permission that Proofpoint says cannot be revoked

Proofpoint presents BluePhishing, a proof of concept that extends OAuth consent phishing to Microsoft Entra Agent ID. The attacker builds an agent blueprint, the agent analogue of an app registration, in their own tenant with a client secret and permissions set to be inherited, sets its sign-in audience to work across tenants (a setting the Entra portal does not expose, so it takes Microsoft Graph, PowerShell or a manifest edit), and sends the victim a one-time consent link (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09). When a victim consents, a blueprint principal appears in the victim tenant with the AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager permission, which Proofpoint says cannot be revoked from the principal; the attacker then obtains an app-only Graph token for the victim tenant and creates agent identities, up to 250 per blueprint, that inherit the consented permissions (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09). Creating one needs the victim's tenant ID and the object ID of a sponsor user, both obtainable through documented unauthenticated lookups, and Proofpoint's tests used the Graph permissions User.Read.All and Group.Read.All (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09). Proofpoint, citing Microsoft's documentation, says inherited permissions are not visible in the Entra portal or in Microsoft Graph, which limits auditing what an agent identity can do; in its tests silent inheritance appeared only for delegated permissions, those granted through user consent (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).

Proofpoint has identified no in-the-wild activity and says agent consent controls are less mature and less widely deployed than app consent controls; it adds that Microsoft 365 Message Center item MC1506733 says default Entra users will be able to create agent blueprints from November 2026 (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).

Exposure
A Microsoft Entra tenant whose users or administrators can be led to approve a consent link; Proofpoint says the user consent settings that limit third-party app consent also extend to agent blueprints and their agent identities (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).
Detection
Proofpoint says agent and blueprint events surface in the Entra audit log as app consent operations do, the creation of an agent identity blueprint as "Add application" and the creation of an agent identity as "Add service principal", and that the blueprint ID is the same in every tenant that consents to it, so a known malicious blueprint can be searched for across tenants (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).
Defender takeaway
Review the tenant's user consent settings and permission classifications and decide whether default users keep the right to create agent blueprints, which Microsoft's change rolling out through November 2026 grants unless the Users can create agent blueprints setting is turned off (Microsoft 365 Message Center, 2026-10-13), and look in the audit log for blueprint and agent-identity creations that nobody in IT made; no attacks have been reported, so this is a hardening decision, not an incident response.
Improvement15 Nov 2026 15:03 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditheadlinesummarysourcesbody

Microsoft's Message Center item MC1506733 says that starting 2026-11-04 default users will be able to create new agent blueprints unless an administrator turns off "Users can create agent blueprints", with the worldwide rollout beginning in early November 2026 and expected to complete by late November 2026; the setting sits under Entra ID user settings, Default user role permissions, and users assigned the Agent ID Developer role keep the right regardless (Microsoft 365 Message Center, 2026-10-13).

CVE-2026-123218, IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 to 5.0.19: a crafted message bypasses authorization and gives full administrative rights, fixed in 5.0.19 PL1 with no workaround; CISA lists it as exploited two days after IBM's bulletin (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

IBM's bulletin of 2026-11-07 says Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 contains CVE-2026-123218, an incorrect-authorization flaw (CWE-863) in which an authorized user can craft a specific message to bypass user authorization and gain full administrative privileges; IBM scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8 with a vector that needs no privileges and no user interaction (IBM, 2026-11-07). The description speaks of an authorized user while the vector requires no privileges, and the bulletin does not resolve the difference. The fix is Faspex 5.0.19 PL1 on Linux, applied by patching the container images and checking that the faspex-core container image is 5.0.19 (1ce4b13, Fix Pack 1); IBM lists no workaround or mitigation (IBM, 2026-11-07). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09, two days after IBM's bulletin, "based on evidence of active exploitation" that it does not describe (CISA, 2026-11-09). IBM's bulletin does not mention exploitation, and neither it nor CISA's listing gives an actor, a victim or the mechanism of the crafted message.

Exposure
An IBM Aspera Faspex 5 server at 5.0.19 or earlier (IBM lists the fix for Linux), above all one whose portal is reachable from the internet; the tag of the faspex-core container image shows the build (IBM, 2026-11-07).
Detection
Neither source names an indicator or describes the message, so the signal is the outcome: a non-administrator account that acquires administrator rights, new administrator accounts and API keys, and shares or packages created by accounts that did not previously have that access, in Faspex application and web logs. The fix does not undo a takeover that already happened, so the same review applies after patching.
Defender takeaway
Patch Faspex 5 on Linux to 5.0.19 PL1 by patching the container images now, because CISA lists the flaw as exploited and IBM offers no workaround (IBM, 2026-11-07; CISA, 2026-11-09); then review administrator accounts, API keys and shares created since the server was reachable.

entries.headline: SonicWall SSL VPN bypasses SAML MFA and CISA lists it exploited; upgrade Gen7 to 7.3.4-7013, Gen8 to 8.2.3-8015
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-19868 +3exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-19868, SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN: valid credentials for an alternate authentication method bypass SAML and the MFA it enforces; SonicWall investigated a report of exploitation and CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 3.1 7.1)

SonicWall's advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 of 2026-11-06 fixes seven SonicOS flaws on Gen7 and Gen8 firewalls, and one of them, CVE-2026-19868, is an authentication enforcement weakness in the SSLVPN service: a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may bypass the SAML authentication controls, and successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). SonicWall says the flaw only affects SSLVPN when SAML is enabled for SSLVPN logins, and scores it CVSS 3.1 7.1 as a use of single-factor authentication (CWE-308) (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). The advisory says SonicWall PSIRT "has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation" and urges customers to upgrade (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06); its revision of 2026-11-09 adds an interim workaround for SAML deployments that cannot upgrade, to disable or delete every active LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication server on the firewall (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-09); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-06 "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-11-06). SonicWall has not shared details about the reported exploitation (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-06).

The advisory applies one table to all seven flaws: Gen7 hardware firewalls (TZ, NSa and NSsp) and Gen7 NSv up to and including 7.3.3-7015 are fixed in 7.3.4-7013 and higher, and Gen8 hardware firewalls (TZ and NSa) and Gen8 NSv up to and including 8.2.2-8015 are fixed in 8.2.3-8015 and higher (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). It also fixes two management-interface flaws scored 8.8 that in specific conditions could potentially let a remote unauthenticated attacker perform unauthorized operations, and that need user interaction, a pre-authentication heap overflow in the SSL-VPN service that could cause a denial of service, and three lower-severity flaws; no source reports them exploited (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A Gen7 or Gen8 SonicWall firewall or NSv at or below the builds above with the SSL VPN enabled and SAML configured as a login method for SSLVPN; the running SonicOS build is the first check and the SAML setting for SSLVPN the second, the vendor's stated precondition (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06).
Detection
The advisory gives no indicators. From the stated mechanism, compare successful SSLVPN logins on the firewall with the identity provider's sign-in log: a VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in or MFA event, or a SAML-enrolled user who authenticated through another authentication method, is the signal. Patching does not evict an attacker who already holds a session or reuses the credentials, so review VPN sessions since SAML was enabled and reset the credentials of accounts that work through both authentication methods; once the workaround is applied, logins through the removed authentication methods should stop, and any that continue show the change did not take effect or that the session predates it.

Triage: a legitimate SAML sign-in leaves an event at the identity provider; a login through the alternate path does not, which follows from the stated mechanism.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade every Gen7 and Gen8 firewall that serves SAML SSLVPN logins to 7.3.4-7013 or 8.2.3-8015 or later now, because the exploitation evidence is a vendor-investigated report plus CISA's listing; where a firewall cannot be upgraded today, disable or delete its LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication servers as the advisory now says, and expect logins that rely on those servers to stop; then review VPN sessions for logins that skipped the identity provider.
Update10 Nov 2026 03:39 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelsummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

SonicWall revised advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 on 2026-11-09 and added a workaround for CVE-2026-19868: if SAML authentication is in use and upgrading the firmware is not possible, disable or delete any active LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall, through Device, Users, Settings, Authentication and the Configure page of each of the three methods (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-09). The advisory's first version named no workaround (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-06). It still urges upgrading; the workaround removes the alternate authentication methods through which the bypass works, which means any administrator or VPN login that relies on those servers stops working until SAML is the only method (an inference from the mechanism, not a SonicWall statement).

actions: On every musl-based Linux host that runs sshd (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto), install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the distribution's fixed openssh package and restart sshd, because updating the package does not replace the running server, and rebuild container and cloud images from a fixed base; until then set PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config and restart sshd.

On each such host that allowed password logins while reachable, search the sshd log for an accepted password on an account whose password field is *, and check root's and the default alpine user's authorized_keys for keys nobody added and the init scripts for a service nobody installed, because CISA lists the flaw as exploited and GreyNoise saw both persistence steps.

entries.headline: CISA lists the OpenSSH musl password bypass as exploited; update to 10.6p2 or turn passwords off
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-123158exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-123158, OpenSSH Portable before 10.6p2 (*sshole): on Linux with musl libc and no PAM, a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes logs in to accounts whose password field is *; NCSC Switzerland issued an advisory (CVSS 3.1 8.1)

Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 carries what its release notes call a critical security workaround for Linux systems that use the musl libc with PAM disabled (OpenSSH, 2026-11-05). OX Security explains the mechanism: musl's crypt() refuses inputs over 256 bytes and returns the string *, * is also what /etc/shadow holds for an account with no valid password, and OpenSSH reads the two matching values as a successful login; the conditions are sshd on musl without PAM, password logins enabled, an account whose password field is * and at least one other account with a real password, and OX scores the flaw CVSS 3.1 8.1 (OX Security, 2026-11-05). On Alpine's tiny-cloud images the passwordless alpine user can run doas without a password, so the bypass chains to root (OX Security, 2026-11-05), but Alpine says those images are safe on first boot and become exploitable as soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05).

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation, and describes no victim or behavior (CISA, 2026-11-09). GreyNoise says its first successful exploitation came on 2026-11-07 against one of its vulnerable gridpoints and calls the flaw trivial to exploit (GreyNoise, 2026-11-10). Alpine pushed the fix to every branch back to 3.16 (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05), and NCSC Switzerland adds that other software using similar authentication paths may also be affected (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). watchTowr saw botnet and cryptomining use, and GreyNoise says its 16 successful chains are not representative of the broader activity (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-09).

Exposure
Sshd on a musl-based Linux system built without PAM, such as Alpine, OpenWrt and the other musl distributions NCSC Switzerland lists, with password logins enabled (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05) and, per OX Security, an account whose /etc/shadow password field is * (OX Security, 2026-11-05). Containers that do not run an OpenSSH server are not affected (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05).
Detection
Alpine advises looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root or any key-only user) and treating the machine as compromised if a login cannot be ruled out (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05). GreyNoise's gridpoint sessions show what follows a successful login: sshd-session spawning sh -c that runs id, uname and reads /etc/os-release, requests to the AWS, Azure and Alibaba Cloud metadata services, attempts to read root's SSH keys and /etc/shadow through doas, a new key written into the default alpine user's authorized_keys (GreyNoise, 2026-11-10).

Triage: an accepted password login is normal for an account with a real hash; the same event for an account whose password field is * has no benign explanation, because such an account cannot match any password.

Defender takeaway
Install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the distribution's fixed package on every musl-based host that runs sshd and restart sshd, because updating the package alone does not replace the SSH server that is already running, and rebuild container and cloud images from a fixed base (OX Security, 2026-11-05); until then set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, as NCSC Switzerland advises (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). Patching does not remove a key or service planted before it, so review the accepted password logins, the authorized_keys files of root and the default user and the init services on every musl host that allowed password logins before patching.
Update07 Nov 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummarytagscvesevidencesourcessourcing_notebody

Previdian's page for CVE-2026-123158, as read on 2026-11-07, says its sensors observed 15 exploitation attempts from 10 addresses in 8 countries, first on 2026-11-06 and last on 2026-11-07, a live counter, and that these observations do not show that a target was vulnerable or that an attempt succeeded, and its timeline lists public proof-of-concept code from 2026-11-05 17:30 UTC (Previdian, 2026-11-05). The Hacker News, quoting a statement from Previdian's chief executive, reports that Previdian confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH, where the attacker used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran the reconnaissance commands id, uname and hostname in non-interactive SSH sessions, and that the first attempt came less than nine hours after the CVE was published (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06); the honeypot detail is not on Previdian's page, and the article's own total, eight attempts from one address geolocated to Japan, differs from the page's totals. Previdian's page lists the flaw as not in CISA's catalog (Previdian, 2026-11-05).

Alpine's advisory adds that updating the package does not restart a running sshd, so sshd must be restarted, and that on exposed machines the administrator should review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys, treating the machine as compromised if a login cannot be ruled out (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05). No vendor or authority source reports attacks on production systems.

Improvement09 Nov 2026 03:25 UTCrun 2026-11-09T0255Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notesummarybody

SANS Internet Storm Center's Cowrie SSH honeypots independently record the attempts: ISC dates the first genuine sshole attempt to 2026-11-05, with an all-"A" password, from scanners it lists on commercial hosting and telecom networks, and counts long-password attempts at 232 on 2026-11-05, 713 on 11-06, 246 on 11-07 and 51 on 11-08 (the day the page was published) (SANS ISC, 2026-11-08). The honeypots collect only the first 255 characters of a password, which limits what ISC sees; after listing the first scanners, its author expects that quite a few of those login attempts succeeded on its honeypots and promises a follow-up (SANS ISC, 2026-11-08). Two sensor sets, ISC's from 2026-11-05 and Previdian's from 2026-11-06, now record exploitation attempts; Previdian's page, read again on 2026-11-09, shows 20 attempts from 13 addresses in 9 countries, the last on 2026-11-08 (Previdian, 2026-11-05). No source reports a compromised production host.

Update10 Nov 2026 03:36 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CISA added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation, without describing a victim or the behavior (CISA, 2026-11-09); the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security repeats the listing (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-11-09). NCSC Switzerland's advisory, last edited on 2026-11-06, still rates the exploitation status unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). GreyNoise, which holds the telemetry, says its first successful exploitation came on 2026-11-07 at 00:46 UTC against one of its vulnerable gridpoints, and the sessions it records there show reconnaissance, attempts to read root's SSH keys and /etc/shadow through doas, a new key written into authorized_keys, and in some sessions a Python runtime installed with apk and an init-script service for a Python agent that polls an HTTPS server every 150 seconds; on the host it describes, the agent never enrolled and never received a task (GreyNoise, 2026-11-10). GreyNoise's confirmed successes are on its own gridpoints, and no source reports a compromised production host.

Correction15 Nov 2026 14:54 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditsummarysourcesbody

NCSC Switzerland updated its advisory on 2026-11-10 at 09:59 to rate the exploitation status "Actively Exploited, PoC Available", replacing the unknown rating it carried until that morning (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). QNAP's advisory QSA-26-21 of 2026-11-13 states that its system library and account-authentication configurations do not meet the conditions for exploitation, so QTS, QuTS hero and QuTScloud are not affected (QNAP, 2026-11-13).
