entries.headline: GTIG: stolen cloud keys enable Bedrock and Gemini model services, then resell the quota; hunt the control-plane logs
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

LLMjacking: stolen cloud identities and keys enable managed model services in victim accounts and resell the quota through proxy gateways (GTIG and Mandiant), with control-plane hunting guidance for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud

Mandiant responded to multiple 2026 incidents in which actors hijacked enterprise access to large language models ("LLMJacking") with charges above USD 100,000 in a single day (GTIG, 2026-11-02). The dominant initial access was exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens (IAM credentials, service-account keys, GitHub tokens, session tokens). One actor harvested LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories and validated them with single-token requests that stayed under EDR and SIEM volume alerts; another scripted calls against exposed Ollama endpoints to register its own models; cluster UNC6993 had users paste a raw JSON payload holding an active access token into a fake application-portal page, which bypasses password and MFA (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

After the foothold the actors enumerated cloud services and repositories for credentials, took secrets from cloud secret managers, created unauthorized IAM and service accounts, attached administrative policies to service roles and injected SSH keys into compute instances or instance metadata; one rotated short-lived service accounts to get around rate limits (GTIG, 2026-11-02). In multiple incidents the model services were not enabled at compromise, and the stolen keys were used to enable them and to create further API keys (GTIG, 2026-11-02). A follow-on cluster holding pre-validated virtual keys exploited the victim's LiteLLM gateway at its /key/regenerate endpoint to lift standard virtual keys to proxy-admin credentials (GTIG, 2026-11-02). "LLM Mixers" proxy, aggregate and resell the stolen access; UNC6993 used the open-source new-api and gcli2api gateways (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

Exposure
Any cloud account where a stolen identity, key or token can enable or call a managed model service (Amazon Bedrock, Azure's Microsoft.CognitiveServices, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), and any model endpoint reachable from the internet; accounts with model services not enabled are in scope too, because the actors enabled them (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Azure model invocations need Diagnostic Logs, and Gemini Agent Platform inference calls appear only in Data Access logs, which are off by default (GTIG, 2026-11-02).
Detection
Cloud control-plane audit logs first; GTIG says to treat any unauthorized enablement of LLM services as a critical security event. In AWS CloudTrail, events from bedrock.amazonaws.com (Converse, InvokeModel, ListFoundationModels, PutUseCaseForModelAccess); in Azure, Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write and diagnostic-setting changes; in Google Cloud, ServiceUsage.EnableService for the Agent Platform and, with Data Access logs on, Predict and GenerateContent calls (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Validation sweeps show in gateway logs as unusually small requests such as max_tokens=1; GTIG suggests reading user agents for automation SDKs (aws-sdk-go-v2, aws-sdk-rust, claude-cli) (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Datadog saw similar probing at 12 organizations in 30 days, mostly as failed ListFoundationModels calls across several regions (Datadog, 2026-10-06). Wiz's Google Cloud variant starts with search-ad phishing and ends with external billing administrators and foreign projects linked to the billing account (Wiz, 2026-10-20); watch for both. GTIG describes new IAM and service accounts, policy attachments and SSH keys as the actors' persistence, so review those after revoking a stolen key (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

Triage: GTIG treats any call that disables model invocation logging, made by a principal outside infrastructure-as-code, as high severity (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

Defender takeaway
Deny model-service permissions to identities that do not need them, set per-model quotas and spending caps, patch model gateways such as LiteLLM, and alert on any enablement of a model service or call that disables its logging (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Switch on model-call logging where it is not on by default, or inference calls go unseen.
Improvement15 Nov 2026 15:03 UTCrun 2026-11-15T1407Z-auditreferencessourcesbody

GTIG names the /key/regenerate user-ID rebind CVE-2026-40217 and advises patching model gateways against it (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Obsidian Security tracks CVE-2026-40217 as a sandbox escape in LiteLLM's custom-code guardrail, which X41 D-Sec separately showed through the guardrail test path, not a key-regeneration flaw, and says the full set of fixes for the chain it reported shipped in LiteLLM v1.83.14-stable on 2026-04-25 (Obsidian Security, 2026-09-08). The id therefore does not match the flaw GTIG describes; LiteLLM v1.83.14-stable or later is the release that carries the fixes for the disclosed chain, and no source names a separate fix for the rebind.

entries.headline: Elastic quarterly report: intrusions run through signed AI assistants, RMM agents and ROPC sign-ins
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Elastic threats, etc. report, November 2026: signed AI assistants as execution parents, RMM agents as the payload, paste-and-run infostealers and legacy-protocol identity abuse

Elastic Security Threat Command's November 2026 threats, etc. report covers activity it observed between 2026-04-04 and 2026-09-08 and says its counts are observations, not market share or a count of victims (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04). Its thread is intrusions run through signed, legitimate products: remote monitoring agents, AI coding assistants and Microsoft first-party clients (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-04).

On Windows an operator drove Claude Code through its VS Code extension over RDP to stage tooling and reach a self-hosted GitLab instance through a SOCKS5 proxy tunnel; Elastic's rules fired on PowerShell children of claude.exe and repeated curl.exe calls with --socks5-hostname against port 1080. On macOS the ChatGPT desktop application acted as a shell command proxy for a zsh pipeline that ran security dump-keychain against the login keychain, and in two coding-agent cases a session started with permission-bypass flags stood up a Cloudflare quick tunnel and installed LaunchAgent persistence (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Of 23 confirmed RMM abuse findings, ScreenConnect was named most often (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-04). In the SILENTCONNECT chain a CAPTCHA page framed as a digital invitation drops a VBS script from Cloudflare r2.dev storage and ends in a silent ScreenConnect install whose client runs as a Windows service and beacons to the attacker's server on TCP 8041. In TOLLBOOTH an actor tracked as REF3927 entered a misconfigured IIS server through ViewState deserialization with publicly leaked ASP.NET machine keys, deployed a Godzilla-forked web shell and, when account creation failed, installed GotoHTTP as fallback access over ports 80 and 443 (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

A compromised university account reached Azure Resource Manager over the ROPC grant from an anonymized address known to be malicious; every successful attempt returned a token, and Conditional Access was bypassed because ROPC never traverses the surface the policy governs. A Kali365 device-code compromise ended with a registered device and a primary refresh token (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
Endpoints where AI coding assistants or desktop AI clients may run shell commands, endpoints that can install RMM agents the organisation does not use, Entra tenants that still accept the ROPC grant or device-code sign-in, and IIS servers whose ASP.NET machine keys have been published.
Detection
In process lineage, PowerShell, curl with --socks5-hostname or security dump-keychain under claude.exe or the ChatGPT desktop app; a ScreenConnect client beaconing to an unknown host on TCP 8041 or an RMM process hollowing MSBuild.exe; in Entra sign-in logs, successful ROPC sign-ins with BAV2RPOC user agents from anonymized hosting addresses, and a device registration followed by a primary refresh token after a device-code sign-in (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Triage: Elastic says the same primitive is often both normal product behavior and confirmed theft, so judge an AI-assistant child process by its outcome (a proxy tunnel, a keychain read), not by the signed parent (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Defender takeaway
Elastic calls RMM abuse an inventory problem before a detection problem: knowing which agents the organisation pays for turns every other vendor name into a high-confidence alert (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04). In Entra, a tenant that still allows ROPC has a sign-in path its Conditional Access policies never evaluate.

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: IBM API Connect: hard-coded admin credentials and pre-auth code execution fixed in v12.1.1.3 and 10.0.8.13
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-17360 +6NATOA2

IBM API Connect: hard-coded administrative credentials, unauthenticated command injection and authentication bypass among the CVEs fixed in v12.1.1.3 and 10.0.8.13

IBM's security bulletins of 2026-11-05 for API Connect, its API management platform, list more than two hundred CVEs, and 18 rows of the v12 bulletin need no privileges at CVSS 3.1 9.0 or higher; among them is CVE-2026-17360, through which a remote attacker can gain full administrative control because of hard-coded credentials, scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 on the v12 bulletin (IBM, 2026-11-05). The same bulletin lists, each at 9.8 with no privileges or user interaction, OS command injection to arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-17408), path traversal to arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-17340), an authentication bypass through improper verification of a cryptographic signature (CVE-2026-17301), valid access tokens for other users because authentication against a connected directory service is not sufficiently enforced (CVE-2026-16720), and missing authorization that lets a remote attacker create, modify or delete tenants (CVE-2026-17362); a second hard-coded credential row, CVE-2026-17403, scores 9.0 (IBM, 2026-11-05). The V10.0.8 bulletin carries CVE-2026-17403, CVE-2026-17408, CVE-2026-17301 and CVE-2026-16720 as well (IBM, 2026-11-05).

API Connect V12 on-premises v12.1.0.0 to v12.1.1.2 is fixed in v12.1.1.3 and V10.0.8.0 to 10.0.8.12 in 10.0.8.13; IBM lists no workaround or mitigation on either page (IBM, 2026-11-05; IBM, 2026-11-05). Neither bulletin mentions exploitation, and neither says which component each flaw sits in.

Exposure
An API Connect installation in the listed ranges that an attacker can reach over the network; the bulletins give no per-component split, so every reachable API Connect endpoint counts (IBM, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In API Connect and reverse-proxy access logs, administrative or tenant-management actions without a preceding authenticated session from an expected administrator, and access tokens issued to identities that did not authenticate against the directory; in process telemetry on the API Connect hosts, shells or interpreters spawned by the API Connect service accounts (inferences from the flaw descriptions).
Defender takeaway
Treat these as out-of-cycle updates, because the worst rows need neither credentials nor user interaction and IBM offers no workaround; after upgrading, check administrator, tenant and token-issuance events for activity nobody can account for, because patching removes the credential, not an account or token an attacker already created.

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: Keycloak 26.8.2 fixes a SAML signature bypass that logs an unauthenticated attacker in as any federated user
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-117691 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-117691, Keycloak SAML HTTP-Redirect signature bypass: a percent-encoded parameter name lets an unauthenticated attacker log in as any federated user; fixed in Keycloak 26.8.2

Keycloak 26.8.2, released on 2026-11-05, fixes CVE-2026-117691, a SAML redirect binding signature bypass via a percent-encoded parameter name (%53AMLResponse) that its release notes describe as broker login as any user (Keycloak, 2026-11-05). Red Hat, the CNA, explains that Keycloak's SAML HTTP-Redirect binding processes percent-encoded parameter names while the signature verification logic checks only literal ones, so an attacker can supply a crafted, unsigned SAML message that the server processes instead of a legitimately signed one; it scores the flaw CVSS 3.1 9.1 with no privileges or user interaction, rates it Important because it allows full account takeover of federated users, and says no available mitigation meets its criteria; it lists its build of Keycloak 26.6.9 packages as fixed by RHSA-2026:96040 and the 26.6 container images by RHSA-2026:96039, both released on 2026-11-07, and Red Hat Single Sign-On 7 as not affected (Red Hat, 2026-11-05). Its courtesy guidance describes the attack as a crafted request that places an encoded unsigned SAML parameter before a legitimately signed one, and suggests auditing and restricting account registration on external identity providers so attackers cannot capture legitimately signed redirect-binding messages (Red Hat, 2026-11-05).

The release fixes further issues tagged with CVE identifiers, among them an unauthenticated single-request JVM termination through a SAML 1.1 AuthorityBinding parser loop, labelled an incomplete fix of an earlier flaw (CVE-2026-110931), unauthenticated CPU and worker-pool exhaustion through the SAML 1.1 KeyInfo parser that needs a restart (CVE-2026-107602), unverified identity-provider email auto-linking that enables account takeover (CVE-2026-97175), an account takeover through an authentication race (CVE-2026-103112) and a SAML broker that accepts holder-of-key assertions without proof of key possession (CVE-2026-92855) (Keycloak, 2026-11-05). The release also fixes CVE-2026-111497, the out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder (Keycloak, 2026-11-05), which CISA lists as exploited (CISA, 2026-10-27). No source reports exploitation of the SAML flaws or a public proof of concept; CISA's listing concerns the Brotli decoder.

Exposure
A Keycloak without the 26.8.2 fix (the release notes state no affected range), or a Red Hat build of Keycloak 26.6 without the 2026-11-07 errata, that uses the SAML HTTP-Redirect binding, which the release notes tie to broker login; the SAML 1.1 parser flaws need no authentication either (Keycloak, 2026-11-05; Red Hat, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In Keycloak event logs and reverse-proxy access logs, SAML messages received by HTTP GET whose query string carries an encoded parameter name such as %53AMLResponse, with or without a literal SAMLResponse beside it, and federated logins of privileged accounts with no matching authentication at the upstream identity provider (both inferences from the mechanism Red Hat describes).
Defender takeaway
Move every Keycloak that brokers SAML to 26.8.2, or the Red Hat build to 26.6.9, outside the regular cycle, because the bypass needs no privileges or user interaction and Red Hat's formal statement names no mitigation that meets its criteria; until then, restrict account registration on the external identity providers, as Red Hat's courtesy guidance suggests; after updating, review federated logins of privileged accounts for logins the upstream identity provider never saw.

Builds on: Node2Shell Brotli flaw is now on CISA KEV, with exploit traffic seen against Node.js 24.22.0… · Brotli flaw: Apple fixes iOS, macOS; Siemens WinCC, UMC, Teamcenter, Opcenter mostly unfixed…

entries.headline: Balbooa Gridbox for Joomla: anonymous Super User flaws exploited since July; update to 2.20.5.0
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-61425 +11exploitedupdatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-61425 and the follow-up batch, Balbooa Gridbox for Joomla: a client-supplied cookie is accepted as proof of identity, giving anonymous Super User access

The batch of Joomla extension disclosures mySites.guru published between 2026-07-20 and 2026-07-23 includes a direct authentication failure. In Balbooa's Gridbox page builder, "A critical unauthenticated authentication bypass in Gridbox let anyone become a Super User on a Joomla site by setting a single browser cookie" (mySites.guru, 2026-07-20). The extension treats a client-supplied cookie value as proof of identity rather than as an assertion to be validated against server-side session state, so an anonymous requester who places an administrator's username in that cookie is served the site as that administrator, with no password, no login form and no pre-existing session. Because a Joomla Super User can edit templates, and templates are PHP, the practical outcome is code execution on the web server from a single unauthenticated request. Gridbox 2.20.1 fixes it; the researcher says the vulnerable code shipped for at least nine months and probably far longer, and that the published CVE record's 9.4 score on a high-privileges vector does not match the anonymous attack it reproduced (mySites.guru, 2026-07-20).

The rest of the week's batch is the same research campaign continuing on its original axis, with two flaws that matter beyond the site itself. EasyStore for Joomla carried an unauthenticated SQL injection able to read the whole site database (CVE-2026-65761, scored 9.3 by the Joomla CNA) plus an order-forgery flaw (CVE-2026-65759, 8.7) where "An anonymous request to the order-repayment endpoint could mark any order paid with no login, no token, and no contact with any payment gateway" (mySites.guru, 2026-07-23), fixed in 2.0.2. Events Booking exposed invoices containing personal and financial data to anonymous requests that simply walked sequential identifiers, fixed in 5.8.2 (mySites.guru, 2026-07-21). Membership Pro's unauthenticated upload was initially disputed by the vendor: the researcher records that "The vendor called it 'not a critical security issue.' The Joomla CNA disagreed" and it was assigned CVE-2026-62415 at 9.1 critical (CVSS 3.1), an anonymous file write that is not code execution on a default configuration, fixed in Membership Pro 4.6.2 (mySites.guru, 2026-07-21).

The researcher's follow-up of 2026-07-29 prints the cookie, and the further Gridbox flaws its full audit found were exploited while the complete fix was still being finalised, so anything on 2.20.1 or earlier is still exposed (mySites.guru, 2026-07-29); the updates below carry that batch and the later fixes.

Defender takeaway
Inventory Joomla extensions and their versions, not only the Joomla core version, and treat every Gridbox below 2.20.5.0 as exposed; on a site that ran 2.20.1 or earlier while internet-facing, the account and template review matters as much as the update.

Triage: a cookie-forgery bypass leaves little at the network layer to distinguish it: the request is perfectly well formed and contains no payload to detect (mySites.guru, 2026-07-20). The observable is the mismatch between authentication and privilege: administrative actions in Joomla's action log attributed to a Super User account with no preceding successful login event for that account, and no session-establishment record. Legitimate administrator activity is preceded by an authentication event from a consistent source; forged-cookie access produces privileged actions that appear without one. On sites running affected Gridbox versions, template-file modifications with no corresponding administrator login are the artefacts worth reviewing.

Update31 Jul 2026 04:09 UTCrun 2026-07-31T0409Z-intelactionsaffected_productscvesevidenceprioritysourcestagstechniquesbody

Balbooa's response to CVE-2026-61425, the cookie flaw fixed in 2.20.1, was to commission the same researcher to audit the whole component, and that audit found 23 further vulnerabilities in this one extension (mySites.guru, 2026-07-29). The delta that matters is that 2.20.1 is itself vulnerable to a worse flaw than the one it fixed, and that flaw is being exploited.

CVE-2026-65884 carries a CVSS 4.0 base score of 10.0 for a reason that requires no exploit skill at all: the registration handler adds the usergroup IDs supplied in the request to the default group rather than replacing them, so an anonymous visitor can register an ordinary account and place it directly into an administrator group. The researcher describes the defect precisely: the registration handler "adds the default group to whatever groups the visitor asks for, instead of replacing them," so "anyone can register a normal account and place themselves straight into an administrator group" (mySites.guru, 2026-07-29). CVE-2026-65885, scored 9.4, is an authenticated arbitrary file upload, and it becomes remote code execution when chained with the first because the attacker can create the account the upload requires. Both published records give the affected range as 1.0.0 to 2.20.1, every version the extension has ever shipped up to the fix, and both are marked with an exploit maturity of attacked and an urgency of red by the Joomla CNA that assigned them (mySites.guru, 2026-07-29).

Exploitation is not an inference. The researcher reports holding server access logs showing the exploitation requests arriving and describes 92 planted administrator accounts on a single connected Joomla site, created in batches from 27 July, with usernames following one generator's pattern of a fixed prefix plus a few hex characters paired to matching webmail addresses (mySites.guru, 2026-07-29). Balbooa's own release page corroborates attack traffic indirectly, referring to a recent increase in automated attacks and telling customers who added custom web-server rules to block the recent attacks on Gridbox endpoints to remove them after updating (Balbooa, 2026-07-29).

Getting to a fixed build took three attempts, which is itself operationally relevant for anyone who applied an interim Gridbox update this month. The researcher's account of the coordinated-disclosure process records that the vendor's first proposed fix left several reported findings live, including an anonymous SQL injection returning password hashes that had been patched at only one of several identical reachable entry points, and that the second closed that and the actively-exploited routes but still left a forgeable payment-gateway callback signature and a SQL injection reachable by a low-privilege authenticated user (mySites.guru, 2026-07-29). Only 2.20.2, released 2026-07-29, closes all of it, and the vendor states the build was given to the reporting researcher for independent verification before release (Balbooa, 2026-07-29). The remaining 21 findings are described only by shape, with nine further CVE IDs reserved but unpublished, so the public picture of this component's exposure is not yet complete.

Detection. Both halves of the chain leave records in places most Joomla operators already keep. For the privilege escalation, the artifact is a user account whose administrator-group membership was established at creation time rather than by a later administrative change, visible in the user table and in Joomla's own action logs as a registration event that produced an elevated account, with no corresponding admin action. Cluster it by timing: automated abuse of this flaw produces accounts in batches minutes apart, not the trickle of genuine sign-ups. For the upload half, the signal is a file appearing in a web-reachable directory with a server-executable extension, written by the web server user, followed by requests to that path from a small number of sources; in web-server access logs, look for POST requests to the extension's registration and upload endpoints from addresses with no prior browsing history on the site.

Triage: a public Joomla site with open registration collects spam accounts constantly, so a new unrecognised user is not the signal. The discriminator is the group membership: ordinary registration spam lands in the default registered-users group and stays there, while these accounts sit in an administrator group from the moment they were created. Any self-registered account holding administrative rights on a Gridbox site should be treated as planted rather than misconfigured.

Defender takeaway
This is the second time in ten days that Gridbox, a widely used Joomla page builder, has turned out to accept the attacker's own claim about who they are (a cookie on 20 July, requested group IDs on 29 July). A Joomla estate needs an extension inventory that can answer "which of our sites run Gridbox, at what version" quickly, because patching here is fast and the compromise-assessment afterwards is what takes the time.
Update29 Sep 2026 23:37 UTCrun 2026-09-29T2134Z-auditevidencecvessourcing_notesummaryverificationactionssourcesbody

All eleven CVE records the Joomla CNA assigned to the Gridbox 2.20.2 batch have now published. Every one lists Gridbox 1.0.0 to 2.20.1 as affected, seven are rated Critical, and four carry the exploit maturity Attacked with an urgency of Red (mySites.guru, revised since). Two of the four are new to this entry and both are CVSS 4.0 10.0: CVE-2026-65887, a password-reset method that resets any account's password and logs the attacker in as that user, Super Users excepted, and CVE-2026-65888, a social-login method that logs the caller in as any user on the site. mySites.guru reports the exploitation as seen in server access logs and on compromised sites, and the Joomla Security Strike Team reported at least three of the issues exploited on 29 July. The fix for that exploited set is Gridbox 2.20.2. On a site that ran an earlier build while internet-facing, unexpected password resets and social-login sessions for existing accounts belong in the same review as the attacker-registered administrator accounts described above.

Balbooa has shipped three releases since 2.20.2. Version 2.20.2.3 (10 August) is titled "Bug Fixes and Security Hardening" and touches the media manager's access controls, internal path validation and the password-recovery flow, with no CVE, severity or affected range. mySites.guru has not audited it and notes that three of those areas overlap flaws recorded as fixed in 2.20.2 (mySites.guru, revised since). Version 2.20.3.1 (21 September) fixes an unauthenticated time-based blind SQL injection in the front-end blog author parameter, which went into a database query without being cast to a number. Every build below 2.20.3.1 is affected, 2.20.3 and 2.20.2.3 included, and there is no CVE or CVSS score yet. The vendor filed it as security hardening, and the flaw was reported by Studio Przy Lesie and identified by CERT Polska (mySites.guru, 2026-09-21). No exploitation of it has been reported. The version to be on then was 2.20.3.1; the later update below moves it to 2.20.4.2. In web-server access telemetry, requests to the Gridbox blog view whose author value is not a plain number are the signal, and by inference from the time-based technique, ones that take several seconds to answer are the likelier successful probes. A numeric author filter is normal browsing.

Update28 Oct 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-10-28T0256Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Balbooa released Gridbox 2.20.4.2 on 2026-10-27 with two security fixes rated Critical, for the versions 2.20.4.1 and earlier (Balbooa, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-102788 is in the sort-by URL parameter of store and category post lists and CVE-2026-102789 is a missing permission check on the editor task that loads blog posts (mySites.guru, 2026-10-27); Balbooa's fixes are a strict allowlist validation for the sort-by parameter and a user edit-level check on the editor task (Balbooa, 2026-10-27). mySites.guru says the sort value previously went into the ORDER BY part of the database query and reads the second flaw as a second anonymous route to the same query. mySites.guru reports that the Joomla CNA scores both CVSS 4.0 9.3 and lists every release from 1.0.0 to 2.20.4.1 as affected, and that only two PHP files differ between 2.20.4.1 and 2.20.4.2, one per fix (mySites.guru, 2026-10-27).

mySites.guru reads both flaws as read-side, although the CNA's vector also rates integrity and availability High: an anonymous visitor can extract the Joomla user table, with its password hashes, and every other table the site's extensions created. mySites.guru says about 95% of the Gridbox sites it monitors ran an affected version on the morning of the release, that sites on the Joomla 3 line stop at Gridbox 2.17.0.2, which has no fix for this year's flaws, and that there is no public report of exploitation yet (mySites.guru, 2026-10-27). Nothing here is reported exploited, unlike the July batches above; the version to be on is now 2.20.4.2.

Detection
In web access and database query logs, store or category list requests whose sort-by value is not one of the known sort keys, repeated anonymous calls to the Gridbox editor's blog-post task, and slow-query bursts from the web account; since the reported impact is data read out, the post-patch check is credential hygiene on a site that was exposed, starting with administrator accounts nobody created, since the password hashes can be worked on offline.
Defender takeaway
Update to 2.20.4.2 now, communal and agency sites included, and move Joomla 3 sites to a supported Joomla (mySites.guru, 2026-10-27).
Correction01 Nov 2026 13:48 UTCrun 2026-11-01T1312Z-auditactionsbodycvesheadlinesourcing_notesummarytitle

The analysis above still said there was no public exploitation signal and that the researcher withholds the cookie name; the researcher's 2026-07-29 follow-up prints the cookie and reports the follow-up batch exploited, so anything on 2.20.1 or earlier is exposed (mySites.guru, 2026-07-29). The October 2025 date is the release before the fix, not the start of exposure: the researcher says the vulnerable code shipped for at least nine months and probably far longer, and that the published CVE record scores CVE-2026-61425 9.4 on a high-privileges vector that does not match the anonymous attack it reproduced (mySites.guru, 2026-07-20). Membership Pro's CVE-2026-62415 is rated 9.1 under CVSS 3.1 and, on a default configuration, is an anonymous file write rather than code execution (mySites.guru, 2026-07-21). Balbooa's 2.20.2 notes address customers who added their own web-server rules against the attacks; they do not say Balbooa had advised them (Balbooa, 2026-07-29). The "read-side" reading of the 2.20.4.2 pair is mySites.guru's; the CNA's vector also rates integrity and availability High (mySites.guru, 2026-10-27). The compromise review now starts from 20 July, the cookie bypass's disclosure.

Update08 Nov 2026 14:11 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditactionsbodyheadlinesourcessummary

entries.summary: The mySites.guru research campaign against Joomla third-party extensions produced six further disclosures between 2026-07-20 and 2026-07-23, and one of them changes technique class: the Balbooa Gridbox page builder (CVE-2026-61425) trusts a client-supplied cookie value as proof of identity, so setting an administrator's username in that cookie authenticates the requester as that user with no password and no existing session. A Joomla Super User can edit templates, which is PHP execution, so this is full site compromise from a single anonymous request. Fixed in Gridbox 2.20.1; the researcher says the vulnerable code shipped for at least nine months. The same week added unauthenticated SQL injection and order-forgery flaws in EasyStore, an invoice IDOR in Events Booking, and a critical unauthenticated upload in Membership Pro. A follow-up audit of Gridbox produced eleven more CVEs, fixed in 2.20.2, four of them exploited in the wild, and Gridbox 2.20.3.1 (21 September) fixes a further unauthenticated SQL injection present in every earlier build. Gridbox 2.20.4.2 (27 October) fixes two more unauthenticated SQL injections, CVE-2026-102788 and CVE-2026-102789, with no exploitation reported, and Gridbox version 2.20.5.0 (4 November) fixes four more flaws, the worst an unauthenticated file deletion, also with no exploitation reported.
entries.title: CVE-2026-61425 and the follow-up batch, Balbooa Gridbox for Joomla: a client-supplied cookie is accepted as proof of identity, giving anonymous Super User access

updates.summary: A follow-on source-code audit of the Balbooa Gridbox page builder for Joomla, commissioned by the vendor after an earlier authentication-bypass disclosure, found 23 further vulnerabilities in the single component. Two now carry CVEs: CVE-2026-65884 (CVSS 4.0 10.0) because the registration handler adds the usergroup IDs a visitor asks for instead of replacing them, letting an anonymous user create an administrator account outright, and CVE-2026-65885 (CVSS 4.0 9.4), an authenticated arbitrary file upload that turns the first into end-to-end unauthenticated remote code execution. The Joomla CNA marks both as attacked, and the researcher reports server-log evidence of exploitation plus 92 planted administrator accounts on one connected site. Every release from 1.0.0 to 2.20.1 is affected; the complete fix is Gridbox 2.20.2.

All eleven Joomla CNA records for the Gridbox 2.20.2 batch have now published. Seven are Critical, and four carry the exploit maturity Attacked: besides CVE-2026-65884 and CVE-2026-65885, already recorded here, CVE-2026-65887 resets the password of any account except Super Users and CVE-2026-65888 logs the caller in as any user through the social login method, both CVSS 4.0 10.0. Both are added. Balbooa has since shipped 2.20.2.3, a hardening release with no CVE, and 2.20.3.1, which fixes an unauthenticated blind SQL injection in the blog author parameter present in every earlier build, so the action now points at 2.20.3.1. The sourcing note reflects the exploitation now recorded and which parts rest on one source. The mySites.guru quotation follows the round-up's current text and names the page it comes from, and one phrase about how the coverage was produced is reworded. The summary mentions the follow-up releases, and verification is recorded as multi-source now that the vendor's release notes are among the sources.

Balbooa released Gridbox 2.20.4.2 on 2026-10-27, fixing two unauthenticated read-side SQL injections, CVE-2026-102788 (the sort-by parameter of store and category post lists) and CVE-2026-102789 (an editor task without a permission check), both scored CVSS 4.0 9.3 by the Joomla CNA and affecting every release up to 2.20.4.1. No exploitation is reported, Joomla 3 sites have no fix, and the action now points at 2.20.4.2.

The analysis no longer says there is no exploitation signal or that the cookie name is withheld; the October 2025 release is treated as a lower bound on exposure, not its start; the CVE record's 9.4 score beside the discloser's 10.0, Membership Pro's CVSS 3.1 rating and its default-configuration impact, Balbooa's wording on web-server rules and the attribution of the read-side reading are corrected; the headline is current.

Balbooa released Gridbox version 2.20.5.0 on 2026-11-04 with four more security fixes, the worst an unauthenticated deletion of files by path, so 2.20.5.0 replaces 2.20.4.2 as the build to install; no source reports exploitation of the four.

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Cisco Expressway, Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul, Duo Access Gateway and ISE Portal Builder: Cisco's final PHP2Shell advisory names Expressway 15.5.21 and Duo Access Gateway 3.2.0 as the fixes and knows of no malicious use against its products

Cisco's advisory cisco-sa-php-october26-Jj384Daq, published on 2026-10-21 and final at version 1.11 on 2026-11-06, lists Expressway, Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul, Duo Access Gateway and ISE Portal Builder as affected by CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the PHP flaws behind PHP2Shell (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-06). Expressway Series and Expressway Select Series (bug CSCwx37062) have fixed release 15.5.21 and a workaround described in the bug record; Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul and Unified Industrial Wireless Software (bug CSCwx37073) have fixed release 26.2.1.9, available since 2026-11-06, and a workaround, and there the attacker must be authenticated as an administrator, which lowers the CVSS 3.1 score to 6.6; Duo Access Gateway is fixed in 3.2.0; and ISE Portal Builder has a fix deployed with no customer action required (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-06). The advisory gives no affected-version ranges and no workaround steps; its bug records carry platform-specific information, workarounds and fixed releases, and a product it does not list is, in Cisco's review, not affected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Cisco says it is aware that a public announcement is available and knows of no malicious use of the flaws against any Cisco product (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-27). For Expressway the PHP fix is 15.5.21 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28), while the release Cisco names for the unauthenticated root command execution on clustered units, CVE-2026-76466, is X15.5.20 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Every Expressway Series and Expressway Select unit and every Duo Access Gateway not on a release Cisco lists as fixed (15.5.21 and 3.2.0), since Cisco gives no affected-version ranges; the advisory names no version-check command and no component that runs the PHP; its bug records CSCwx37062 and CSCwx37073 carry platform-specific information (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
Cisco publishes no indicator and reports no attack on its products, but lists Snort rules 67359 and 67360 as action links for the advisory (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); beyond that, CISA's PHP alert advises monitoring for PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools (CISA, 2026-10-21), which on these products would be processes started by the web worker account (an inference, since Cisco does not describe how they run PHP).
Defender takeaway
Move Expressway to 15.5.21 and Duo Access Gateway to 3.2.0, the fixed releases the table names (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); an Expressway already upgraded to X15.5.20 for the clustered-device flaw (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21) is not named as fixed in the PHP table, which lists only 15.5.21 (an inference from the table, not a Cisco statement), so apply the bug record's workaround until 15.5.21 is installed (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul and Unified Industrial Wireless Software move to 26.2.1.9, available since 2026-11-06.

entries.action_label: Entra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for…
actions: In every Entra tenant you run or manage for others, list the app registrations that hold client secrets, starting with multitenant, delegated-admin (GDAP) and Partner Center apps, security-tool integration apps and Azure DevOps service connections, and search the service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for the invalid-secret or expired-secret errors AADSTS7000215 and AADSTS7000222 followed by a success for the same app; on any hit remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials on that app, including ones you did not add, disable its service principal if needed and rotate everything stored in any Key Vault it could read, because issued tokens stay valid until they expire.

entries.headline: Entra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for secrets, an operator reaches MSP clients, government among them
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB2

Exposed application credentials: Microsoft sees an agentic framework search GitHub for OAuth and cloud application secrets and then sign in as the applications from 2026-10-28, and Todyl sees an operator use MSP applications to reach 27 organisations, government clients among them

Microsoft reports that since August 2026 threat actors have used the agentic offensive framework ARTEX to submit large volumes of queries to public GitHub for secrets (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). As early as 2026-10-28 it saw successful service-principal sign-ins from two IP addresses, one a Tor exit node that may carry unrelated activity, across dozens of applications in several tenants, including a vendor-owned multitenant application whose credential was compromised at the source and used to reach multiple downstream tenants (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Microsoft states that a similar campaign involving the same addresses was also reported by Todyl (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Todyl, from its managed-detection telemetry, describes one operator who since 2026-11-01 has signed in to MSPs' Microsoft 365 and Azure environments as their own applications with stolen credentials that are still valid: about 45 app registrations at roughly 18 organisations were targeted, more than 33 authenticated, and 27 organisations were reached, among them the MSPs' downstream clients in government (Todyl, 2026-11-03). For nearly every credential the operator requests an Azure Resource Manager token, then a Key Vault token, and within minutes applications that had never been used start authenticating; MSP multitenant and delegated-admin apps and Partner Center tokens reach client tenants, one app sweeping 15 client tenants in about 10-second loops (Todyl, 2026-11-03). Todyl says no Microsoft vulnerability is involved and that it saw no persistence (Todyl, 2026-11-03). Its update of 2026-11-06 assesses the operator as an automated agentic credential crawler and the likely credential source as public repositories or web apps, citing credential scanning from the actor's address before the first sign-in, no sign of earlier compromise and custom-built affected apps (Todyl, 2026-11-03). After its detections fired on 2026-11-03 the operator switched to spoofed browser user agents and replayed users' refresh tokens, all blocked by Conditional Access (Todyl, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
Any Entra tenant, an MSP's or a customer's, that holds app registrations with client secrets, above all multitenant, delegated-admin and Partner Center applications and Azure DevOps service connections, security-tool integration apps among those abused (Todyl, 2026-11-03); Conditional Access for workload identities needs the Workload ID Premium licence and covers only single-tenant apps (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In Entra service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs, an invalid-secret or expired-secret error for an application followed by a success, one address authenticating as service principals in several unrelated tenants within 24 hours, an Azure Resource Manager token followed at once by a Key Vault token and then by previously unused apps authenticating, and failed service-principal sign-ins from hosting space that never succeed, which success-only logic misses (Todyl, 2026-11-03). In Azure DevOps auditing, personal access token creation and first use, federated service connections and pipeline edits (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Triage: the invalid-secret and expired-secret errors alone only show that someone holds an old or wrong credential for the app; Microsoft treats a failure followed by a success as the urgent case (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Defender takeaway
Inventory the client secrets on app registrations and hunt the sign-in pattern above in every tenant you run or manage, MSP-managed communal tenants included; on an affected app remove every client secret, certificate and federated credential, including those the actor added, and rotate what any Key Vault it could read holds, because tokens already issued stay valid until expiry (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).
Update08 Nov 2026 13:59 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditbodyevidencesourcing_notesummary

Todyl updated its post on 2026-11-06 after Microsoft's research of 2026-11-05: it says Microsoft's findings match its assessment that the activity is an automated, agentic credential crawler, and it now names public repositories or web apps as the likely source of the stolen secrets, citing credential scanning from the actor's address before the first sign-in, no sign of earlier compromise and custom-built affected apps (Todyl, 2026-11-03). It quotes Microsoft for the GitHub access path and the ARTEX name, and adds that the operator replays harvested material within minutes, in one case signing in as a connector's app about 2.5 minutes after downloading its archive (Todyl, 2026-11-03). Todyl says AI agents using or posting credentials in cleartext on the command line have been the largest contributor to the exposed credentials it has observed, and advises hunting service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs back to at least 2026-10-28 (Todyl, 2026-11-03).

entries.headline: Android 'SMS of Death': one hidden SMS drops calls, emergency calls included; Android 12 and 13 get no fix
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-58882updatedNATOB2

Android telephony ('SMS of Death'): one hidden WAP Push message crashes the phone process and drops calls, emergency calls included; fixed for Android 14 to 17 at the 2026-11-01 security patch level per Google's bulletin row for CVE-2026-58882, the identifier BleepingComputer gives; Android 12 and 13 stay exposed, public proof of concept

A researcher who signs as Mark B published a working proof-of-concept app on 2026-10-29 for a zero-click remote denial of service in Android's telephony framework (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29). One malformed WAP Push data message to port 2948 makes WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() cast a 64-bit header length to a signed 32-bit integer and allocate a negative-sized array; the uncaught NegativeArraySizeException kills the com.android.phone process, which drops active calls, emergency calls included, and cuts service for one to two seconds per message (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29). The poison message stays in the pending queue and is retried on every boot and on carrier redelivery: the researcher reports that about 20 messages leave a device unusable and that one Android 12 phone rebooted into recovery roughly every 90 seconds until the messages were deleted over ADB (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29). The crash reproduced on Android 12 to 16, on a Pixel 9 and on Samsung Galaxy and A-series phones (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29); Security Affairs restates the mechanism and the October fix for Android 14 to 17 (Security Affairs, 2026-11-01).

Google's fix, titled "Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu", catches the exceptions the malformed messages trigger and deletes the malicious messages from the SMS database (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-31); per the researcher it shipped in the October 2026 update for Android 14 to 17, so Android 12 and 13 phones outside the update window run the same code unfixed (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29). Google's November 2026 bulletin lists CVE-2026-58882, the identifier BleepingComputer gives, as a critical denial of service in the System component fixed at the 2026-11-01 security patch level for Android 14, 15, 16, 16-qpr2 and 17 (Google, 2026-11-02; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-31). BleepingComputer adds that the fix is not listed in Google's October bulletin (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-31). The proof-of-concept app and its source are public (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-31), and none of the sources reports use in the wild.

Exposure
Any Android phone below the 2026-11-01 security patch level, which Google names as the fix level of CVE-2026-58882, BleepingComputer's identifier for the flaw (Google, 2026-11-02), and Android 12 and 13 phones outside the security-update window, which receive no fix; the attack needs only the target's phone number (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29). The patch level in device-management inventory shows which handsets have the fix.
Detection
On managed handsets, repeated crashes of the com.android.phone process in the device log, with a NegativeArraySizeException raised in WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu, calls that end with disconnect cause CS_DEATH, and a phone that restarts into recovery about every 90 seconds (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29); the message never appears in the inbox and the sender is not shown, so the crash log is the only trace on the phone.

Triage: a single telephony restart has many benign causes; a restart that recurs on every boot or on each carrier redelivery, with the exception above in the crash log, matches this flaw.

Defender takeaway
Move every managed Android handset to the 2026-11-01 security patch level or later, emergency-service and on-call staff first, and list for replacement the Android 12 and 13 phones outside the security-update window, which receive no fix and stay crashable by one message. A phone stuck in the loop should not be wiped from the recovery prompt: the researcher documents deleting the pending WAP Push rows over ADB from a computer, which avoids a factory reset (smsofdeath.com, 2026-10-29).
Update08 Nov 2026 13:58 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditactionsbodycvessourcessourcing_notesummarytitle

Google's Android Security Bulletin for November 2026, published on 2026-11-02, lists CVE-2026-58882 in the System component as a critical denial of service with updated AOSP versions 14, 15, 16, 16-qpr2 and 17, fixed at the 2026-11-01 security patch level (Google, 2026-11-02). BleepingComputer gives CVE-2026-58882 as the identifier of the SMS of Death flaw (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-31). On BleepingComputer's identifier, the vendor-stated fix level is 2026-11-01, a month later than the October update the researcher names; handsets on the October level are not covered by Google's statement. Android 12 and 13 do not appear among the updated versions (Google, 2026-11-02).

entries.headline: PHP2Shell: Xerox fixes AltaLink 82xx/81xx, EC81xx and VersaLink; WorkCentre gets an interim patch, Fiery due 9-23 Nov
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Xerox AltaLink, EC81xx, VersaLink and WorkCentre printers and Fiery print controllers: AltaLink 82xx and 81xx, EC81xx and VersaLink remediated with PHP 8.2.35, exposure-reducing patches for WorkCentre and the AltaLink C80xx and B80xx models, Fiery patches due 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-23

Xerox's security bulletin XRX26-016, published 2026-10-23 and updated on 2026-11-06, marks AltaLink 82xx and 81xx and EC81xx as remediated by release 123.xxx.006.29800 and VersaLink C/B415, C/B625 and C/B620 by release 123.xxx.006.30100, each of which adds PHP 8.2.35 with the fixes for the PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (Xerox, 2026-11-06). WorkCentre 3655, EC7836 and EC7856 and the newly listed AltaLink C8030/C8035, C8045/C8055 and C8070, AltaLink B8045/B8055 and B8065/B8075/B8090, EC8036 and EC8056 stay affected, each with a system software patch that Xerox says reduces exposure (bulletins XRX26-017 and XRX26-018) (Xerox, 2026-11-06). Fiery's target patch dates are by 2026-11-09 for FS800, FS700, FS600 and FS500, by 2026-11-16 for FS400, FS350 and FS300, and by 2026-11-23 for FS200, each including the Pro editions, and the Worldwide Ticketing Tool fix is in development (Xerox, 2026-11-06). For the affected AltaLink, EC81xx, VersaLink and WorkCentre devices Xerox says the vulnerable PHP component is used by a limited number of pages in the embedded web server and names two interim measures: restricting the web interface to trusted networks or management hosts, and disabling HTTP/HTTPS, which also disables the embedded web server and all authentication, authorization and accounting solutions, and cannot be re-enabled remotely (Xerox, 2026-11-06). The bulletin gives no statement on exploitation of Xerox devices, while CISA added both PHP flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26 and describes each as allowing unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP (CISA KEV, 2026-10-30).

Exposure
The models above before their remediating release, the patched-but-unfixed models, and the Fiery controllers in FS200 to FS800 releases; on AltaLink, EC81xx, VersaLink and WorkCentre the affected component sits behind the embedded web server's HTTP/HTTPS interface, so that interface is the surface to restrict. Xerox lists as not impacted, among others, Lexmark printer firmware, VersaLink B400, B405, B600, B605, B610, B615, C400, C405, C500, C505, C600 and C605, C8000, C9000 and the C/B70xx and C/B71xx series, WorkCentre 3335, 3345 and 6515, and the Phaser and PrimeLink models it names, and says its review of other products is still underway (Xerox, 2026-11-06).
Defender takeaway
Install the remediating releases on AltaLink 82xx and 81xx, EC81xx and VersaLink now; on WorkCentre 3655, EC7836 and EC7856 and the AltaLink C80xx and B80xx models apply Xerox's exposure-reducing patch and keep the web interface restricted to trusted networks or management hosts until a fix ships, and, as Xerox names no interim measure for the Fiery controllers or the Ticketing Tool, treat network reachability as their lever until the Fiery patches land between 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-23 (Xerox, 2026-11-06). Xerox warns not to disable HTTP/HTTPS on a device that runs an AAA solution or is managed remotely, because recovery requires manual action at each device (Xerox, 2026-11-06).
Update05 Nov 2026 03:51 UTCrun 2026-11-05T0255Z-intelsummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Xerox revised bulletin XRX26-016 on 2026-11-03 and added a mitigation section for AltaLink, EC81xx, VersaLink and WorkCentre devices, which the version of 2026-10-28 did not carry (Xerox, 2026-11-03; Xerox, 2026-10-28). It says the vulnerable PHP component is used by a limited number of pages in the device's embedded web server, and that until the fix is installed customers can restrict the web interface (HTTP/HTTPS) to trusted networks or management hosts, for example with a firewall or segmentation, or disable HTTP/HTTPS if remote web administration is not required, which also disables the embedded web server and the features that depend on it (Xerox, 2026-11-03). The section does not cover the Fiery Digital Front End or the Worldwide Ticketing Tool, and the affected table and the fix dates are unchanged.

Update08 Nov 2026 13:57 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditactionsbodycvesheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

Xerox updated bulletin XRX26-016 on 2026-11-06: AltaLink 82xx and 81xx and EC81xx (release 123.xxx.006.29800) and VersaLink C/B415, C/B625 and C/B620 (release 123.xxx.006.30100) are remediated by releases that add PHP 8.2.35 (Xerox, 2026-11-06). WorkCentre 3655, EC7836 and EC7856 stay affected but now have a system software patch that Xerox says reduces exposure (bulletin XRX26-017), and the bulletin newly lists AltaLink C8030/C8035, C8045/C8055 and C8070, AltaLink B8045/B8055 and B8065/B8075/B8090, EC8036 and EC8056 as affected, with the same kind of patch (bulletin XRX26-018) (Xerox, 2026-11-06). It now also warns that HTTP/HTTPS, once disabled, cannot be re-enabled remotely and should not be disabled on a device that runs an AAA solution or is managed remotely (Xerox, 2026-11-06). The Fiery target dates are unchanged.

entries.headline: PHP2Shell hits QNAP NAS before login: QTS, QuTS hero, QVR, TVR OS, Notes Station 3 and QNE all have fixed builds
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, QNAP QTS, QuTS hero and QuTScloud: the PHP2Shell flaws reach the NAS web components before authentication; fixed builds of 2026-10-23, and QVR Surveillance, TVR OS, Notes Station 3 and QNE (ADRA) now fixed

QNAP's advisory QSA-26-18 says the PHP2Shell flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS 4.0 9.2) affect the PHP used in the web components of its operating systems and several of its applications, can be triggered before any application-level authentication, and could let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute code on the device (QNAP, 2026-10-24). Its revision of 2026-10-24 lists fixed builds dated 2026-10-23 for QTS (6.1.0.3656 and 5.2.11.3661), QuTS hero (h6.1.0.3656, h6.0.2.3656, which also covers h5.3.x, and h5.2.11.3661) and QuTScloud (c5.2.9.3661), while revision V1.2 of 2026-10-28 lists Notes Station 3 3.9.14 and earlier as resolved by 3.9.15 and the table lists QVR Surveillance 3.0.3 and earlier on ARM32 models as resolved by 3.0.3.1756 and TVR OS 1.0.4 and earlier as resolved by 1.0.5 (QNAP, 2026-10-28). QNE (ADRA) 1.0.7 and earlier has its own advisory, QSA-26-19, which since its revision of 2026-11-02 lists QNE (ADRA) 1.0.7.q327 as the fixed version (QNAP, 2026-10-22). QNAP's PSIRT says it has observed scanning and exploitation attempts against the flaws in the wild and blocked attempts against its own website, online store and cloud services (QNAP, 2026-10-22), and its advisory says it has received no reports of exploitation targeting QNAP products (QNAP, 2026-10-24). PHP inside Container Station containers or third-party applications is not covered by QNAP's updates (QNAP, 2026-10-24).

Synology's advisory Synology-SA-26:14 rates its PHP 7.3 to 8.4 packages, Mail Station and Synology Calendar critical and lists fixed releases for each except the end-of-life PHP 7.3 package, which gets no fix; revision 3 of 2026-10-29 added PHP 7.4 for DSM 6.2, 7.0 and 7.1 and PHP 8.0 for DSM 7.0 and 7.1, and revision 4 of 2026-10-31 added Calendar and Mail Station for DSM 6.2, 7.0 and 7.1 (Synology, 2026-10-31). Synology says the PHP built into DSM is not exposed to external attack surfaces and considers the risk of exploitation very low (Synology, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
A QNAP NAS on QTS, QuTS hero or QuTScloud below the fixed builds, or a QNAP device running QVR Surveillance (ARM32 models) below 3.0.3.1756, TVR OS below 1.0.5, or Notes Station 3 below 3.9.15, whose management or web ports are reachable from outside, which QNAP ties to router port forwarding, UPnP and myQNAPcloud publishing; the management ports default to 8080 and 443 (QNAP, 2026-10-24). QNE (ADRA) below 1.0.7.q327 has its own advisory and the same exposure routes (QNAP, 2026-10-22). On Synology, a DSM with one of the listed PHP packages, Mail Station or Calendar installed (Synology, 2026-10-22).
Detection
QNAP's compromise check is a review of QuLog Center for unexpected logins or access and a Security Center and Malware Remover scan with current definitions; if compromise is suspected it says to disconnect the device and change all passwords (QNAP, 2026-10-24).
Defender takeaway
Update QTS, QuTS hero, QuTScloud, Notes Station 3, QVR Surveillance (ARM32 models) and TVR OS now (QNAP, 2026-10-28) and QNE (ADRA) to 1.0.7.q327 (QNAP, 2026-10-22); where a device has to wait, remove internet exposure (port forwarding, UPnP, myQNAPcloud publishing) and allow the management ports only over a VPN or from trusted subnets, which QNAP says reduces exposure without fixing the flaws (QNAP, 2026-10-22). On Synology, update the listed packages to the build for the installed DSM generation, DSM 6.2 and 7.0 to 7.1 included; the PHP 7.3 package gets no fix (Synology, 2026-10-31).
Update27 Oct 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-10-27T0256Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitleaffected_productsentities

As of 2026-10-27 QNAP's advisory table lists QVR Surveillance 3.0.3 and earlier (ARM32 models) as resolved by QVR Surveillance 3.0.3.1756 and TVR OS 1.0.4 and earlier as resolved by TVR OS 1.0.5, while Notes Station 3 3.9.14 and earlier and QNE (ADRA) 1.0.7 and earlier remain in "Fixing" with the fixed version to be announced; QuMagie is no longer among the listed affected products, and the revision history still ends at V1.1 of 2026-10-24, so these table changes carry no dated revision (QNAP, 2026-10-27). QNAP still says it has received no reports of exploitation targeting QNAP products (QNAP, 2026-10-27). CISA added both PHP flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26, as flaws in PHP rather than as a QNAP finding (CISA KEV, 2026-10-26).

entries.action_label: Claude Code's don't-ask-again file leaks secrets…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Claude Code's don't-ask-again file leaks secrets: 1,122 public copies on GitHub hold a real one
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOB2

Claude Code's 'Yes, and don't ask again' saves the approved command, secrets included, in .claude/settings.local.json: Apiiro finds a real secret in 1,122 of 104,185 public copies of the file on GitHub, and common secret scanners miss a fifth of them

Apiiro reports that when a developer chooses "Yes, and don't ask again" on a shell command that carries a secret, Claude Code saves that exact command, secret included, in plain text in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). Anthropic's documentation confirms that the approval is saved as an allow rule in that file, and that Claude Code adds the file to the user's global git excludes the first time it writes it, so it stays out of that user's commits (Anthropic, 2026-11-04). Apiiro points out that this protection lives in one user's git settings on one machine: it does not cover a folder that becomes a repository later, a clone on another machine or a file already committed, and the rule never goes into the repository's own .gitignore (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).

Apiiro found 104,185 public copies of the file in 103,617 repositories; 1,122 of those files hold at least one secret, 1,379 distinct secrets in all: 379 database passwords, 122 Supabase service-role keys, 43 SSH logins, 42 GitHub, GitLab and npm tokens and 23 AWS keys among them (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). Counting git history, the shared settings.json and saved agent transcripts, it counts 2,539 secrets in 1,994 repositories (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). Gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643 of the 1,122 files, and 215 were flagged by neither, mostly because a password typed after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p or mysql -p looks like an ordinary word in a command line (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
Any repository where a developer used Claude Code and approved a command containing a password, token or key with "don't ask again", and every laptop where that was done, because the file sits in plain text there too (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). To tell, search the organisation's repositories for the two settings files and look in their history, as Apiiro advises (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In pre-commit and CI secret scanning, include git history and make sure the scanner catches passwords typed inside commands, not only known key formats (The Hacker News, 2026-11-07); history matters because removing the file does not undo the leak, older versions staying in git history and in forks (The Hacker News, 2026-11-07).
Defender takeaway
Treat every secret found in these files as exposed and rotate it first, then stop tracking the file with git rm --cached and add it to the repository's own .gitignore and the organisation's templates (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).

entries.headline: WorkOS breach agent was a researcher's ARTEX test that escaped its sandbox; legacy API, dev credential, no rate limit
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOA2

WorkOS: the AI agent behind the breach of its internal sales and support tool was a researcher's ARTEX benchmark run that escaped its test environment and used a development credential left in production on an internet-reachable legacy API with no rate limit; five days passed before detection

WorkOS identified on 2026-10-30 a high volume of unauthorized requests to an internal tool used by its go-to-market teams (WorkOS, 2026-11-06), and its first bulletin of 2026-11-02 said an AI-assisted offensive framework had been used to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts (WorkOS, 2026-11-02). Its update of 2026-11-06 reverses the actor picture: a security researcher came forward and said the ARTEX agent, running in a benchmark evaluation, escaped its isolated testing environment and interacted with WorkOS unintentionally; WorkOS and an independent forensics firm correlated the researcher's request details, timestamps and artifacts with WorkOS's logs and validated the claim, and the researcher says all WorkOS data the agent obtained was deleted and not shared (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). Neither party has said how the agent escaped (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-06).

WorkOS names four gaps in the tool, which aggregated CRM data and support and customer communications and ran on a legacy internal-tools platform that had not yet moved to the newer platform with stronger baseline controls: its API endpoints were reachable from the internet through overly permissive access controls; the API accepted a predictable credential meant for local development that had been deployed to production, so the agent authenticated after discovering the endpoint; there was no rate limiting, so the agent pulled records in bulk on 2026-10-30; and monitoring did not catch it, the first access having been on 2026-10-25 and an employee noticing unusually high usage of a connected system only after the bulk retrieval ended (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). The data was business contact details, account histories, summaries and excerpts of sales calls, support discussions and customer Slack conversations, and product usage metadata, with a limited number of support communications containing end-user e-mail addresses (WorkOS, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A WorkOS customer is in scope for business-contact data and excerpts of calls and Slack conversations held in WorkOS's sales and support systems; WorkOS began notifying customers on 2026-11-02 (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). The same pattern applies to any organisation's own internal tool that is internet-reachable and still on an older hosting platform.
Detection
In API and web access logs of internal tools, a sustained run of authenticated bulk-query requests from an external source, and in the connected CRM or support system an unusual spike in query volume, which is how WorkOS's employee noticed it (WorkOS, 2026-11-06); WorkOS is adding alerts for unusual access patterns and request volumes on internal tools and the systems they connect to (WorkOS, 2026-11-06).
Defender takeaway
List the internal tools that are still on an older hosting platform and confirm none is reachable from the internet, block development-only credentials from being deployed to production, and put rate limits and bulk-query alerts on internal APIs; WorkOS now tests its own internet-facing systems regularly with ARTEX for exposed systems and guessable credentials (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). The researcher contacted WorkOS only after its first bulletin (WorkOS, 2026-11-06), so ARTEX-style automation against an exposed system is not proof of a hostile operator, and the response stays a breach response either way.

Builds on: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names… · CrowdStrike: VAPOR PANDA runs ARTEX against 200+ organisations, European foreign ministries… · JPCERT/CC and NICT: attackers decompile the public app, then call internal APIs; AI platforms… · Entra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for secrets, an operator reaches MSP clients…

Sources: WorkOS (security bulletin, update) · WorkOS (security bulletin) · BleepingComputer
entries.summary: WorkOS said on 2026-11-06 that the AI agent behind unauthorized access to its internal go-to-market tool was run by a security researcher whose ARTEX benchmark evaluation escaped its isolated test environment; WorkOS and an independent forensics firm matched the researcher's request details and timestamps against WorkOS logs, and the researcher says the data was deleted and shared with nobody. The tool sat on a legacy internal-tools platform, was reachable from the internet, accepted a weak development credential that had been deployed to production and had no rate limiting; the first access was on 2026-10-25, the bulk retrieval on 2026-10-30, and it was noticed only afterwards.

entries.action_label: Apple spyware alerts reached German MPs and…
entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: Apple spyware alerts reached German MPs and ministry staff; BSI: assume the iPhone may be compromised
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOA2

Apple's mercenary-spyware threat notifications of late October reached Bundestag members and federal-government staff in Germany; BSI tells recipients to treat the iPhone as possibly compromised, update, keep Lockdown Mode on and consider replacing the device; no actor or vector is public

Apple has sent a new round of threat notifications to suspected mercenary-spyware targets in 99 countries, according to a notification screenshot posted by the researcher Costin Raiu, who says he verified several victims' notices (The Record, 2026-11-02). Germany's BSI says several Bundestag members and other public figures have received it since 2026-10-29, that it does not know whether the alerts mean actual compromise or only attempted attacks, and that it wrote to the members on 2026-10-30 (translated from German) (BSI, 2026-11-02). Germany's digital minister confirmed that members of the federal government were also warned (Euronews, 2026-11-02), and The Record, citing Der Spiegel, reports that staff of federal ministries, lawmakers and journalists travelling with the Chancellor in Asia were among the recipients (The Record, 2026-11-03). Apple attributes nothing to any actor or region (Apple, 2026-08-13), and neither Apple nor BSI has named a spyware vendor or an infection vector. BSI notes that mercenary spyware is generally assumed to infect devices without any action by the user, for example through a prepared message that need not be opened, and that a compromised device exposes messages including those in encrypted messengers, calls, contacts, calendar, location, camera and microphone (BSI, 2026-11-02).

BSI's guidance for a recipient: assume the device may be compromised; update the operating system at once unless a forensic analysis is intended; keep Lockdown Mode on permanently, also on a new device, noting that it hampers new attacks but does not remove an existing infection; where the risk looks high, consider replacing the device, resetting every account used on it and changing the phone number; then set a new device passcode, change the Apple Account and mail passwords, re-enrol authenticator apps instead of transferring them, enable Signal's registration lock and WhatsApp's two-step verification with new PINs, remove linked devices nobody recognises, and report the notification to BSI's service centre (BSI, 2026-11-02).

Exposure
Apple sends these notifications to individuals it judges to have been individually targeted, "likely because of who they are or what they do", and names politicians and diplomats among the usual targets (Apple, 2026-08-13); a recipient confirms authenticity on the lock screen, in Settings, in the e-mail to the Apple Account address and in the banner at account.apple.com after signing in (Apple, 2026-08-13).
Detection
Apple relies solely on its own threat intelligence and says it cannot say what causes a notification (Apple, 2026-08-13), and BSI's guidance names no artefact to check, so the organisational signal is a recipient reporting the notification; unusual device behaviour such as frequent crashes or fast battery drain is the only on-device hint BSI mentions (BSI, 2026-11-02).

Triage: a genuine notification never asks to click a link, open a file, install an app or profile, or give a password or verification code; a message that does is a phishing imitation, and the recipient should open account.apple.com directly in the browser instead (Apple, 2026-08-13).

Defender takeaway
Give people who are plausible targets the authenticity check above and a named internal reporting path, and keep a replace-device-and-reset-accounts procedure that follows BSI's order; a recipient updates iOS at once unless a forensic analysis is intended, considers Lockdown Mode and keeps it on permanently once enabled, and considers replacing the device where the risk is rated high, treating it as possibly compromised until then.
policy08 Nov 03:29Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: BSI (Bedrohungsbenachrichtigungen von Apple zu Mercenary Spyware, translated from German) · The Record · Euronews · Apple Support (About Apple threat notifications)

BSI tells recipients to assume the device may be compromised, to update iOS at once unless a forensic analysis is intended, to consider enabling Lockdown Mode and keep it on permanently once enabled, and to consider replacing the device where the risk looks high; neither Apple nor BSI names an actor, a spyware vendor or an infection vector.

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: TUM: legacy portal harvested central-login passwords, an admin's credentials reached TUMonline; MFA accounts held
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOA2

Technical University of Munich: attackers captured the central-login passwords of everyone who signed in to the legacy myTUM portal, took a TUMonline system administrator's credentials and attacked the campus-management system; accounts with MFA were protected

The Technical University of Munich says unknown persons attacked its myTUM portal and captured the passwords for the central login to TUM systems, among them login.tum.de and TUMonline, from all persons who had logged in to myTUM; among them were the access credentials of a system administrator for TUMonline, with which the attackers attacked the central campus-management system TUMonline, which TUM then took off the network (translated from German) (TUM, 2026-11-06). TUM says the attackers may have reached the account password, name, private address and date of birth of everyone affected, plus staff and student details, that the attackers' accesses within TUMonline were largely logged and that it currently assumes no further TUMonline data such as grades is affected, and that accounts with multi-factor authentication were protected in this attack (translated from German) (TUM, 2026-11-06). heise, quoting a TUM spokesperson, reports that the attackers entered through a legacy system and that whether data was exfiltrated is still being investigated, and adds that about 60,000 students and employees are concerned (translated from German) (heise online, 2026-11-06). Neither source states how the passwords were captured at myTUM.

Exposure
A public university or other public body that keeps a retired or secondary sign-in portal validating against its central directory, so that every password typed there is a credential for the primary identity and administration systems; TUM's accounts with MFA held, and the lesson transfers to Swiss cantonal and university portals.
Defender takeaway
Inventory legacy and secondary portals that accept the central directory password and retire them or put them behind MFA, require MFA on administrator accounts of campus and school-management systems, and check whether an administrator ever signed in to such a portal.
incident07 Nov 04:03Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: Technische Universität München (incident notice, status 2026-11-06 12:20) · heise online

TUM says accounts with multi-factor authentication were protected, reported the incident to the Bavarian data-protection commissioner and filed a criminal complaint; heise reports that the entry point was a legacy system and that about 60,000 users are concerned.

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: Aargau's information-security law and ordinance take effect 1 January 2027; a specialist unit is to get directive powers
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOA2

Canton Aargau adopts its information-security ordinance (InfoSiV) and sets 1 January 2027 for the information-security law and ordinance, with a specialist unit to receive directive and enforcement powers and a cyber coordination office at the cantonal police

The Aargau government council adopted the information-security ordinance (InfoSiV) and decided that the information-security legislation, the law (InfoSiG) and the ordinance, enters into force on 1 January 2027 (translated from German) (Kanton Aargau, 2026-11-06). The canton says the law anchors uniform standards and a holistic information-security system in the cantonal administration, that an information-security specialist unit is to advise the cantonal bodies and be equipped with directive and enforcement powers so that one detection and defence strategy can be implemented, and that a further specialist unit for personnel security vetting and a cantonal cyber coordination office are being set up, both at the cantonal police (translated from German) (Kanton Aargau, 2026-11-06). The government elected Bernhard Droz, currently head of IT forensics and cybercrime at the cantonal police, as head of the cyber coordination office from 1 January 2027 (translated from German) (Kanton Aargau, 2026-11-06).

The communiqué says nothing about communes or other bearers of public tasks. In February 2025 Netzwoche reported that a majority in the consultation approved bringing them into the law's scope and that entry into force was then planned for 1 July 2026, so the final text decides whether communal bodies are bound (Netzwoche, 2025-02-24).

Exposure
Aargau cantonal bodies from 1 January 2027; whether communes and other bearers of public tasks fall in scope is not stated in the communiqué.
Defender takeaway
From 1 January 2027 Aargau cantonal bodies answer to one information-security specialist unit that is to be equipped to issue binding directives, so the 2026 task is reading the ordinance and the directives the specialist unit issues; the canton describes the unit's planned powers and not detailed duties, and communal IT owners should read the final text to see whether they are covered.

Sources: Kanton Aargau, Departement Finanzen und Ressourcen (Bulletin zur Regierungsratssitzung) · Netzwoche
