entries.action_label: Oneconsult: a site granted a folder in Chrome or…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Oneconsult: a site granted a folder in Chrome or Edge can steal tokens and plant VS Code and PowerShell persistence
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Oneconsult on the File System Access API: after two clicks a website holds read and write access to folders such as .vscode, .Azure, the public desktop and SMB shares in Chrome and Edge, enough for token theft and persistence without a process on the host

Oneconsult analyses, from the Chromium source and tests on Windows 11 with Chrome and Edge 150.0.7871.101, what a website can reach through the File System Access API once a user selects a folder and grants permission: the handle stays valid as long as the tab is open and is obtained after just two user clicks (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). Chrome rejects blocklisted paths, but a path that is not in its table and not an ancestor of a blocked path is allowed, and the kDontBlockChildren rule leaves the subfolders of listed directories selectable; Oneconsult confirmed .vscode, the Azure token cache, C:\Users\Public and SMB shares as accessible (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

Oneconsult demonstrates these paths. A site can search a granted folder and take files such as cached Azure tokens and .env files. It can drop a fake VS Code extension into .vscode/extensions, which runs inside the normal code.exe process and is unaffected by Mark of the Web because Node.js does not check the Zone.Identifier stream. It can plant PowerShell profile and module backdoors, which work only with the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy because the API stamps every written file with ZoneId=3 and RemoteSigned refuses such files. It can drop files on the public desktop, where they appear for all users and trigger a warning that a certain percentage of users acknowledge. And it can run an interactive file proxy through the still-open tab, where EDR sees only the browser reading and writing files (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). A OneDrive Known Folder Move enabled while Chrome is running leaves a stale blocklist, so the redirected Desktop was writable; Oneconsult notes that the bypass has been reported to Google, which made the issue public, and that Google classed reading a single dragged file from a blocked folder as "not a security issue" (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

Daniel Oz's July write-up of the same technique has a website edit a file the user already holds. He says the user-gesture requirement does not prevent phishing, only automatic picker invocation, and that signed or complex files may fail, be blocked or break in a way that prevents execution (Oz, 2026-07-05).

Exposure
Windows users of Chrome or Edge, above all developer workstations with VS Code, cached Azure tokens or PowerShell on the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy, and estates that enable OneDrive Known Folder Move; the attack needs a user to choose a folder and confirm a second prompt (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).
Detection
File-write telemetry for PowerShell profile paths, PowerShell module folders and .vscode\extensions, and changes to the Zone.Identifier stream there, whose ReferrerUrl and HostUrl fields keep the origin of the page that wrote the file (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). Oz says editing a file does not automatically reclassify it as downloaded, so the stream is a possible marker, not a guaranteed one (Oz, 2026-07-05).

Triage: browsers legitimately read and write files for web editors such as Google Docs and VS Code for Web, as Oneconsult notes; the signal is a browser process writing into a persistence location, not the file activity itself.

Defender takeaway
Restrict file system read and write access with the Chrome Enterprise policies Oneconsult names, FileSystemReadAskForUrls, FileSystemWriteAskForUrls and the respective AskForUrls policies, alert on writes to PowerShell profiles and VS Code extension folders, and treat a website's request to choose a local folder as a social-engineering step (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).
research07 Nov 04:01Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Oneconsult · Daniel Oz (danieloz147)
entries.summary: Oneconsult's analysis of Chromium's Windows blocklist shows that a website granted a folder through the File System Access API after two clicks keeps a handle for as long as the tab is open, and that the blocklist leaves .vscode, .Azure, C:\Users\Public, SMB shares and, after a OneDrive Known Folder Move, the Desktop reachable. The paths it demonstrates are token and .env theft, a fake VS Code extension and PowerShell profile or module backdoors that need the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy, and a file proxy through the open tab that EDR sees only as browser file activity.
entries.title: Oneconsult on the File System Access API: after two clicks a website holds read and write access to folders such as .vscode, .Azure, the public desktop and SMB shares in Chrome and Edge, enough for token theft and persistence without a process on the host

entries.action_label: Kaspersky: ESXi and Proxmox ransomware ran on a…
actions: List every monitoring server, script, scheduled task and connection manager that stores an ESXi, vCenter or Proxmox root password, replace each with a least-privilege monitoring account, and rotate the root passwords that were stored or reused across hosts.
actions_html: List every monitoring server, script, scheduled task and connection manager that stores an ESXi, vCenter or Proxmox root password, replace each with a least-privilege monitoring account, and rotate the root passwords that were stored or reused across hosts.
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Kaspersky: ESXi and Proxmox ransomware ran on a monitoring server's root password and admin notes, no VM escape
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky GERT: two ESXi and Proxmox ransomware cases in which a monitoring server's reused root password and plaintext administrator notes, not a VM escape, gave the attackers the hypervisor

In the first case, Kaspersky's investigation began with BlackNevas ransomware activity on a Windows system in a virtualised domain-controller segment, where the execution of the AnyDesk remote tool and the GMER binary was recorded (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). The environment used PRTG Network Monitor, whose deployment had broad access to the ESXi hosts, and the same root password was reused across several nodes; after obtaining access to the monitoring environment the attacker used the ESXi credential to connect over SSH to the hosts that shared the password (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). On the first host, a file was uploaded during a root SSH session and its first execution failed with "Execution of non-installed file prevented"; the actor then disabled the execInstalledOnly policy with esxcli and ran it, while on a second host in another subnet with the same password the binary ran and the logs were cleared (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).

In the second case, a ransomware incident by The Gentlemen, the actor used information it had collected between initial access and visible impact: on a compromised system administrator's workstation it found Proxmox root credentials and access details in plain-text notes and logged in as root (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). It then activated the VNC web socket through the root account, which gave it control of the Proxmox environment, and used that access to download and run the ransomware in the cluster, encrypting the whole virtual environment (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). Kaspersky says a fully patched hypervisor can still be compromised through a shared password, an overprivileged monitoring account, an open SSH path or an administrator interface reachable from a general server network (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A virtualisation estate where a monitoring, backup or management server stores or can use hypervisor root credentials, where one root password is shared across hosts, where SSH to ESXi is reachable from general server networks, or where administrators keep Proxmox or ESXi credentials in plain-text notes; PRTG, which supports storing VMware credentials at device or group level, is the product Kaspersky names (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
Detection
On ESXi, root SSH logins from addresses that do not normally administer the hosts, a file upload followed by a failed execution of a non-installed file, a change to the execInstalledOnly setting and cleared logs; on Proxmox, root@pam requests to the VNC web socket used to reach other hosts, as the log records Kaspersky shows (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). Kaspersky advises alerting when execInstalledOnly, Secure Boot enforcement, Lockdown Mode, SSH, local accounts or remote logging settings change (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
Defender takeaway
Give each monitoring platform its own least-privilege identity instead of ESXi root, replace stored root passwords with vault retrieval or limited tokens, administer ESXi through vCenter with Lockdown Mode and SSH stopped by default, and keep logs off the hosts so a compromised administrator cannot erase them (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
threat07 Nov 04:00Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Kaspersky Global Emergency Response Team (Securelist)
entries.summary: Kaspersky's Global Emergency Response Team describes two ransomware cases in virtualised estates. In the BlackNevas case a PRTG Network Monitor held ESXi root access and the same root password was reused across hosts, so the attacker connected over SSH, disabled the execInstalledOnly policy with esxcli, ran the encryptor and deleted logs; in the case attributed to The Gentlemen the actor found Proxmox root credentials in plaintext notes on an administrator workstation and used the VNC web socket to encrypt the cluster. Kaspersky stresses that no VM escape was needed.
entries.title: Kaspersky GERT: two ESXi and Proxmox ransomware cases in which a monitoring server's reused root password and plaintext administrator notes, not a VM escape, gave the attackers the hypervisor

entries.action_label: BOSSAI AI agents took emergency-services data…
entries.classification_html: NATOB3
entries.headline: BOSSAI AI agents took emergency-services data through open ports, public APIs and default credentials
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB3

Acronis TRU on BOSSAI: one operator's mesh of 12 AI agents took patient-care records and dispatch case data from Taiwanese emergency services through a legacy open port, a public API and default root credentials, and failed wherever authentication was enforced

Acronis TRU found an open attack workstation holding more than 90,000 files and describes BOSSAI as a mesh of 12 AI agents, nine active, driven by a changing roster of language models, with the operator acting as the bridge between agents and typing commands in Traditional Chinese (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). The agents that executed attacks ran almost exclusively on abliterated open-weight models run locally, after commercial models repeatedly refused offensive requests (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). In the 12 days TRU observed, the operator targeted government emergency services, banks and lenders, universities and military systems in 11 countries, with confirmed exfiltration or system access at roughly ten targets in three countries and about fifteen more attacked without confirmed compromise (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04).

The confirmed emergency-services harm is the part that matters here. A Taipei fire-department patient-care records platform exposed ECG readings, ambulance video and vital signs from 2018, accessible without credentials; a city's 119 dispatch system yielded case records with incident times, response types, status fields and street-level locations across seven districts from the system's API; and a fire-dispatch vendor's database administration panel opened with default root credentials, exposing 18 or more tables (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). In an emergency-management system the agents found a hardcoded AES-256 key in front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, an administrator identity among them, and a partial server-side request forgery path, without confirming a full compromise (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). A brute-force run against a national fire agency's single sign-on portal gave no confirmed access, and the critical Apache flaw that the operator's vulnerability platform reported at a disaster-response centre was fabricated, because the port was filtered (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). TRU says the agents failed where authentication was enforced, where paywalls required valid sessions and where endpoints were properly filtered, and that obscurity no longer protects a system from agents that investigate hundreds of targets at once (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
Emergency-service, dispatch and public-safety systems that expose a record API or a legacy data port without authentication, leave default administrator credentials on a vendor's database panel, or ship secrets in front-end JavaScript; those are the weaknesses the agents turned into data, and TRU reports the patient-care and dispatch records as the gravest confirmed harm.
Detection
TRU names sqlmap, nmap and nikto among the most-used tools, so the traffic is ordinary scanner traffic in web access and authentication logs (an inference from the tool list): bursts of SQL-injection probing, repeated sign-in attempts against a single sign-on portal from one source, and logins to a database administration panel with a default account.
Defender takeaway
Swiss dispatch, patient-care and records systems of emergency services are the same target class, so check them for unauthenticated APIs and legacy ports, default root or administrator credentials on vendor panels, and keys or tokens in front-end code; the agents failed wherever authentication was enforced, so closing those gaps is what stops this tooling.
threat07 Nov 03:59Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Acronis Threat Research Unit
entries.summary: Acronis TRU describes BOSSAI, an agentic campaign it attributes with high confidence to one operator in Taiwan: a mesh of 12 AI agents, nine active, that over 12 observed days targeted government emergency services, banks, universities and military systems in 11 countries, with confirmed data exfiltration or system access at roughly ten targets in three countries. The confirmed emergency-services harm was patient-care records of a Taipei fire department and dispatch case records of a city 119 system; TRU says the agents failed where authentication was enforced and endpoints were filtered.
entries.title: Acronis TRU on BOSSAI: one operator's mesh of 12 AI agents took patient-care records and dispatch case data from Taiwanese emergency services through a legacy open port, a public API and default root credentials, and failed wherever authentication was enforced

entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: CISA lists WordPress core's upgrade-window RCE race as exploited; block wp-content/upgrade before installing 7.1.4
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-119977exploitedupdatedNATOA2

WordPress core 4.7 to 7.1.3: an unauthenticated race in the core update process can lead to remote code execution, fixed in 7.1.4 and backported to every supported branch, listed by CISA as exploited; Wordfence assigned CVE-2026-119977

WordPress 7.1.4, released on 2026-10-28, fixes a weakness in the upgrade process that can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window, and backports follow for every branch that receives security fixes, currently through 4.7 (WordPress.org, 2026-10-28). During a core update with a complete package, the new files are unpacked into a predictable directory under wp-content/upgrade; the temporary copy includes the installer, and an unauthenticated attacker who requests it at the right moment can interact with the staged copy and reach PHP code execution (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Wordfence scores it CVSS 8.1 for versions 4.7 through 7.1.3 and states that the attack complexity is high, because the attacker needs web access to the staging tree and must win a race that lasted only seconds in its lab (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). Patchstack reads the same flaw as needing wp-content/upgrade/ to be reachable over the web and would not call it practical to exploit (Patchstack, 2026-10-28).

Wordfence reports that its new firewall rule matched within nine minutes of deployment and that it recorded more than 18,500 requests for staged setup-config.php installer paths in the first 21 hours (Wordfence, 2026-10-29). CISA lists the flaw as exploited, and no source names a victim or describes a successful compromise (CISA, 2026-11-03). The fix randomises the staging directory, adds an index guard and prevents unsafe promotion of staged configuration data (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
Any WordPress site on 4.7 to 7.1.3 with wp-content/upgrade/ reachable from the internet while a core update runs; the discoverer says the deciding factor is whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed, so the update to 7.1.4 is exposed too, automatic updates included, although a partial package exposes the installer only if it contains the installer files (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06); on 5.9 or later the staging folder name can be predicted, on 4.4 to 5.8 a random suffix hides it unless the site leaks it, and 4.6 and earlier, which Picus counts as affected back to 2.7, get no fix (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). The fixed releases are 7.1.4 and the backport of each branch (7.0.8, 6.9.11 and so on down to 4.7.39) (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).
Detection
In web server access logs, requests under wp-content/upgrade/ and for setup-config.php inside a staging directory, repeated from one source against a few sites as Wordfence saw (Wordfence, 2026-10-29); between updates the directory holds only an index.php (Patchstack, 2026-10-28). Where an unpatched site updated with the directory reachable, check that wp-config.php, which the attack overwrites, still names your database (Picus Security, 2026-11-05) and look for administrator accounts, plugins and PHP files under wp-content/upgrade/ that nobody created (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06).

Triage: a request to a staging path outside an update window finds only an index.php and is probing, not compromise; a successful response from the staged installer during an update is the event that matters.

Defender takeaway
Deny web access to wp-content/upgrade/ at the web server and confirm it answers 403 before the update runs, then confirm that the update completed on every site instead of assuming it, because a firewall that WordPress itself loads cannot block the request: the staged copy loads from its own files (Patchstack, 2026-10-28); Wordfence's blocking rule helps only where its firewall is set up to run before direct PHP requests reach their file (Wordfence, 2026-10-29).
Correction01 Nov 2026 13:52 UTCrun 2026-11-01T1312Z-auditbodycvessourcessourcing_notesummarytitle

The flaw now has an identifier: Wordfence tracks it as CVE-2026-119977, a time-of-check time-of-use race condition scored CVSS 3.1 8.1 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N), affecting WordPress 4.7.0 to 7.1.3 with the same fixed releases as above (Wordfence Intelligence, 2026-10-31). The statement that no source assigns a CVE identifier is withdrawn; scanners and asset inventories can now match the flaw by that ID.

Update04 Nov 2026 03:25 UTCrun 2026-11-04T0256Z-intelcvesprioritytagsheadlinesummarytitlesourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

CISA added CVE-2026-119977 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-03 on evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-11-03), and the Canadian Cyber Centre's advisory of the same day relays the listing for WordPress Core before 7.1.4 (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-11-03). The listing names no victim, attacker behaviour or exploitation method, so Wordfence's probing telemetry above remains the only described activity and Patchstack's high-complexity rating still stands. A site that ran a full-package core update on 4.7 to 7.1.3 while wp-content/upgrade/ was reachable needs the compromise check in the Detection line, not only the update.

Update07 Nov 2026 03:51 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelheadlinesummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Umut Bayram of Picus Security, who found the flaw, shows that the update which installs the fix still unpacks its files with the site's old, unpatched code (Picus Security, 2026-11-05; The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). Picus says the new code's skip of wp-config.php already works in that first update but the randomised folder name does not, so the temporary installer sits at a predictable path on sites running 5.9 or later and, on 4.4 to 5.8, behind a random suffix that hides it unless the site leaks the path; an attacker who reaches it can no longer replace the live configuration but can still set up the temporary copy, log in to it, run PHP and from there read or write files in the live directory (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). Bayram told The Hacker News the deciding factor "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed", and that a partial package exposes the installer only if it contains the installer files; The Hacker News found WordPress.org offering an in-branch move such as 7.1.3 to 7.1.4 as a partial package, automatic updates included, so whether such an update is exposed depends on what that package contains, and only once 7.1.4 or the branch fix is installed do later updates use a random folder (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). WordPress 4.6 and earlier get no fix (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06).

The order matters: Picus advises denying web access to wp-content/upgrade/ in the web server configuration first, confirming that the path answers 403, and only then updating; this does not break updates, because WordPress reaches the folder through the filesystem (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). An .htaccess file placed inside the folder does not work, because the old updater deletes the folder's contents before unpacking, and WP-CLI's wp core update is no substitute because it uses the same updater and folder (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). For sites that stayed on an affected version, Wordfence suggests looking for unexpected requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade, administrator accounts no one recognises, plugins no one installed and PHP files in wp-content/upgrade that no one put there (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06).

Code that its authors describe as an exploit has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week, and whether it works has not been established; WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low, against Wordfence's CVSS 8.1 and CISA's listing as exploited (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). None of these sources reports a compromise through the update that installs the fix; CISA's listing and Wordfence's probing telemetry above are unchanged.

Improvement08 Nov 2026 14:08 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditbody

The configuration check in the Detection line follows from the mechanism Picus describes: an attacker creates a malicious wp-config.php inside the temporary update directory and has the updater copy it over the live configuration, which can redirect the site to an attacker-controlled empty database (Picus Security, 2026-11-05).

entries.headline: Cisco's mail gateway can be rooted by one crafted email; found in a TAC support case, exploitation confirmed
entries.html:
CRITICALCVE-2026-76461 +5exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-76461: Cisco Secure Email Gateway unauthenticated SQL injection in email parsing reaches root command execution, exploited before disclosure (CVSS 9.8)

Cisco's advisory names the mechanism: insufficient validation in the email-parsing logic of AsyncOS lets an unauthenticated remote attacker send a single crafted email containing SQL statements through the device, and "a successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL statements, leading to command execution with root privileges on the underlying operating system" (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14). CVE-2026-76461 (CVSS 9.8) affects every Cisco Secure Email Gateway, physical and virtual, regardless of configuration; Cisco confirms Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not affected by this specific flaw. There is no workaround; the only remediation is upgrading to AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 (re-released on 2026-10-31), 16.0.4-302, or 16.5.0-780, the release Cisco "strongly recommends" migrating to.

Two details in Cisco's own wording raise this above a routine emergency patch. First, Cisco states the vulnerability "was found during the resolution of a Cisco TAC support case" (while the hardening advisory lists the same flaw among those found during internal testing (Cisco PSIRT, hardening-release advisory, 2026-09-14)), and that it has already directly contacted Secure Email Cloud customers on whose devices indicators of compromise were found, having upgraded all Cloud instances itself (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14). Second, CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day and flagged it for Forensic Triage Requirements (CISA KEV, catalogue version 2026.09.14); NCSC-NL's own advisory relays the same exploitation claim: "Cisco reports that successful exploitation of this vulnerability has been observed" (translated from Dutch) (NCSC-NL, NCSC-2026-0368, 2026-09-14).

The same day, Cisco shipped a companion "Security Hardening Release" advisory for the identical product line, bundling five further internally-discovered vulnerabilities that Cisco groups by CWE class: a path-traversal grouping (CVE-2026-76440, CVSS 9.8), an improper-access-control grouping (CVE-2026-76441, CVSS 9.8), an uncontrolled-resource-consumption grouping (CVE-2026-20353, CVSS 9.8), a second injection-class grouping (CVE-2026-76443, CVSS 9.8, in the same weakness class as the exploited CVE-2026-76461) and an input-validation grouping (CVE-2026-76442, CVSS 7.5). Cisco's own table states that "the CVSS score that is assigned to each CVE ID represents the maximum potential severity of the single most impactful underlying vulnerability within that specific CWE category," so the four identical 9.8 scores reflect an assigned ceiling per grouping rather than four independently-confirmed critical bugs. Unlike the exploited flaw, this bundle also affects Secure Email and Web Manager, and Cisco's advisory, revised on 2026-10-14, says two vulnerabilities found in the review are known to be actively exploited: this SQL injection and the separately advised arbitrary file write, which footnotes attach to the injection and path-traversal groupings. Upgrading to 15.5.5-014 or 16.5.0-780 closes the exploited flaw and the hardening CVEs together, while for a 16.0 appliance the hardening advisory names no fixed release and says to migrate (Cisco PSIRT, hardening-release advisory, 2026-09-14), so 16.0.4-302 closes CVE-2026-76461 only (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14).

Defender takeaway
Treat every internet-facing Cisco Secure Email Gateway as potentially already compromised until patched and checked; Cisco's detection guidance and the KEV listing both signal active use against real environments.

Triage: Cisco's own discriminator is the mail_logs pattern COPY.*TO PROGRAM; any hit is evidence of attempted or successful exploitation and warrants incident response, not just a patch, since success implies root-level compromise and possible log tampering; a clean mail_logs result does not rule out the S/MIME injection, which left no such pattern in the module author's reproduction (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22024, 2026-10-16).

Update04 Nov 2026 03:26 UTCrun 2026-11-04T0256Z-intelcvesactionssummarybodyimmediate_actionreferencesheadline

Cisco revised the advisory to version 1.2 on 2026-11-03 with the note "Updated information related to Release 15.5.5-014 in the Fixed Releases table"; its footnote says that, in light of new information related to exploit code that is available online, Cisco released an updated version of the 15.5.5-014 fix on 2026-10-31, and it does not say what the earlier build missed (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14). An appliance on the 15.5 branch that took 15.5.5-014 before 2026-10-31 must run the CLI command retroscannerstatus and confirm that Cisco Retro Remediation Engine runs version 4.0.2 or later, while 16.5.0-780 addresses the flaw regardless of that version and Cisco still recommends that releases earlier than 16.5 migrate to it (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14). Cisco's hardening advisory, in its revision of 2026-10-14, says two vulnerabilities from its internal review are known to be actively exploited, the SQL injection above and the separately advised arbitrary file write (Cisco PSIRT, hardening-release advisory, 2026-09-14). For a 16.0 appliance the hardening advisory's table names no fixed release and says to migrate to one (Cisco PSIRT, hardening-release advisory, 2026-09-14), so 16.0.4-302 closes the SQL injection only (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14). Cisco does not say which exploit code it means.

Update07 Nov 2026 03:49 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummarycvesactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebodytagsimmediate_action

Rapid7's Metasploit framework now carries public exploit modules for two unauthenticated SQL injections on Cisco Secure Email Gateway that end in command execution as root. The first, merged on 2026-11-05, targets an injection in the Email Cloud Scanner URL-retrospective message database and its documentation says "URL Filtering and URL Retrospective Service must both be enabled" (Rapid7 Metasploit module documentation, 2026-10-16), which sits against Cisco's statement that the flaw affects the gateway "regardless of device configuration" (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14); its author says it can only be assessed with medium confidence that this is CVE-2026-76461, the flaw CISA lists, and that of the injections reproduced from the patch diff it was the only one that left the pattern COPY.*TO PROGRAM in mail_logs, the check Cisco's own advisory names (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22024, 2026-10-16). The second targets an injection in the S/MIME public-key harvesting feature, "we have reason to believe this maps to CVE-2026-76443" according to Rapid7's wrap-up of 2026-11-06 (Rapid7, 2026-11-06). The S/MIME module was merged on 2026-10-28; its author tested a gateway on AsyncOS 15.5.1-055 with the S/MIME Public Key Harvesting feature enabled for inbound mail, and the module sends one signed S/MIME email carrying 500 certificate addresses to the gateway's SMTP listener (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22018, 2026-10-15). Its documentation says "Public-key harvesting must be enabled on the inbound mail flow policy for the target to be exploitable" (Rapid7 Metasploit module documentation, 2026-10-15), and the author of the first module calls that feature "a different non-default feature" (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22024, 2026-10-16).

Cisco's hardening advisory lists CVE-2026-76443 with the other grouped CVEs and its fixed-release table gives 15.5.5-014 for 15.5 and earlier, 16.5.0-780 for 16.5 and "Migrate to a fixed release." for 16.0 (Cisco PSIRT, hardening-release advisory, 2026-09-14). A 16.0 appliance on 16.0.4-302 therefore has no named fix for the flaw the S/MIME module most likely uses; moving to 16.5.0-780 closes it. Rapid7 does not report exploitation of the S/MIME module's flaw, and Cisco does not say whether the injection it lists as exploited is the one in either module.

entries.headline: Qilin's October build spreads through vCenter and ESXi, reboots into Safe Mode and prints notes on office printers
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB3

Seqrite: reverse engineering of two Qilin builds shows the October 2026 variant adding a vCenter and ESXi spreading engine, Restart Manager lock release, a Safe Mode reboot loop and ransom notes printed to office printers

Seqrite's reverse engineering of a March 2026 and an October 2026 Qilin (Agenda) sample finds that the Rust code was reworked into a modular workspace of 22 internal crates, that the command line grew from 6 to 42 switches, and that the October build carries subsystems the baseline lacked (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). It uses the Windows Restart Manager API to shut down the processes that lock SQL Server, Exchange and virtual-machine disk files, instead of the brute-force process termination of the March sample, so that the files can be encrypted (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). An embedded PowerShell engine, started with --spread-vcenter, authenticates to vCenter, disables HA and DRS, extracts the ESXi host addresses, opens SSH and SCP sessions, uploads Linux ransomware payloads to /tmp on the hosts and runs esxcli to power off virtual machines and encrypt .vmdk volumes (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

The build also installs the RSAT Active Directory module itself with DISM before enumerating computers, embeds 32-bit and 64-bit PsExec to spread over the ADMIN$ and C$ shares with harvested credentials, and sets a Safe Mode boot with bcdedit plus an AutoAdminLogon registry value so that it reboots into Safe Mode, where EDR drivers do not load (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). A raw-printing module scans local subnets for TCP port 9100 and sends cleartext ransom notes to office printers, and the October binary masquerades as resmon.exe with a forged Microsoft code-signing overlay (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). Seqrite lists healthcare, manufacturing, education and technology as the victim sectors in its telemetry (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
Windows estates with a vCenter and ESXi hosts that a domain-joined host can reach over the network and SSH, since the spreading engine needs a vCenter login and SSH to the hosts; Seqrite names no initial-access route.
Detection
In vCenter audit events, HA or DRS being disabled on a cluster followed by SSH sessions to ESXi hosts and esxcli activity; in process-creation and registry telemetry, bcdedit setting a Safe Mode boot and a Winlogon AutoAdminLogon change outside a change window, DISM installing the RSAT Active Directory component on a host that never had it, and rstrtmgr.dll loaded by a process that is not an installer; in network telemetry, one host sending to TCP 9100 on many hosts of a subnet; and an executable named resmon.exe outside System32 (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

Triage: the Restart Manager and a DISM-installed RSAT component are normal in patching and administration, so each is weak alone; the combination with the print fan-out, the Safe Mode change and the vCenter actions is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat HA or DRS being turned off in vCenter, followed by SSH sessions to ESXi hosts, as an incident, and alert on a Safe Mode boot configured by bcdedit outside change windows, which Seqrite names as a detection point (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

entries.headline: Microsoft Q3 email report: overrides let authentication-failing spoofed mail through; SVG CAPTCHA phishing returns
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Microsoft Email Threat Landscape Q3 2026: tenant and user overrides delivered spoofed business-service mail that failed authentication, SVG attachments return as CAPTCHA-phishing carriers, and Teams impersonators move to ordinary personal names

Microsoft Threat Intelligence's report on Q3 2026 draws four points that matter to a Microsoft 365 defender (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). First, malicious messages that spoof the sender domains of business services, such as document-signing and survey platforms, were often delivered because tenant- or user-level overrides applied, even after the messages failed email authentication and were identified as malicious: in September overrides applied to 63% of messages with a recorded security outcome, most of them tenant-level (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Microsoft says the figures do not show that recipients opened the messages and that an overly broad exception made for a legitimate workflow can weaken protection against messages impersonating it (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Second, CAPTCHA-gated phishing recovered while QR-code phishing kept falling, with SVG attachments central to the recovery: they carried 65% of CAPTCHA-gated attacks in August and 49% in September (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Third, in Teams, ordinary personal-name display names rose from 46% of the observed July sample to 88% in September while explicit help-desk identities fell from 17% to 2%; Microsoft notes a personal name can accompany a help-desk claim while the account address keeps technical wording, and that more targeted attempts used domains resembling the victim organisation's (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Fourth, an August campaign against legal organisations sent a Word document with a personalised QR code that led to a device-code phishing page and the genuine Microsoft device sign-in portal; completing the sign-in would have transferred a valid session token that gave persistent access without exposing the password or re-triggering MFA (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
A Microsoft 365 tenant that has tenant- or user-level allow or override entries covering the sender domains of widely used business services, since a message that fails authentication and is detected as malicious can still be delivered when such an override applies.
Detection
In mail-flow and message-trace telemetry, delivered messages that claim a business service's domain but fail SPF, DKIM and DMARC, together with the override that applied; in mail-gateway logs, SVG attachments that lead to a CAPTCHA page; in Teams audit, first-contact chats and calls from external tenants whose display name is a personal name but whose account address carries help-desk or service wording; in sign-in logs, device-code flow sign-ins.
Defender takeaway
Review the tenant and user overrides in your mail protection for entries that cover well-known service sender domains, because the override, not the detection, decided delivery; Microsoft's own advice is to check its recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

entries.headline: Storm-2603-linked SharePoint intrusion: memory-only VirtualPathProvider shell in w3wp.exe, then Velociraptor and tunnels
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky reconstructs an intrusion through SharePoint ToolShell, attributed to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence, whose implant lived only inside w3wp.exe: an ASP.NET VirtualPathProvider memory shell with a suo5 tunnel, then Velociraptor, several tunnelling mechanisms and Warlock's AV killer

Kaspersky's retrospective analysis of a December intrusion at a customer's on-premises SharePoint server found activity consistent with Storm-2603, with the access and control layer held entirely inside the IIS worker process w3wp.exe and nothing written to disk (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). On December 20 a single request to a SharePoint administrative endpoint tied to the ToolPane component fingerprinted the host for ToolShell (CVE-2025-53770); the full exploit chain ran on December 24 against the same endpoint, and the gap kept the probe from being correlated with it (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The payload was loaded into the ASP.NET runtime and lost when the application pool recycled or IIS restarted (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

The memory shell registers a custom VirtualPathProvider through a non-public method of the ASP.NET HostingEnvironment class, subverts trust controls so that the registration works even in a precompiled application, intercepts requests at the GetCacheKey() hook and stays dormant unless a specific User-Agent header arrives (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). It speaks a custom XOR-obfuscated binary protocol, and the open-source suo5 tool proxies traffic so connections from the command server reach arbitrary hosts inside the network through the SharePoint server (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). It reaches SYSTEM by named-pipe token impersonation adapted from EfsPotato and creates administrative accounts through native SAM RPC calls (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Shortly after the injection w3wp.exe started msiexec.exe to install a remote MSI that was Velociraptor 0.73.4.0, vulnerable to CVE-2025-6264, which the actor used for persistence, discovery, data collection and payload execution and to deploy Zoho Assist unattended access, a VS Code CLI tunnel, Cloudflare Tunnel and a reverse proxy, so access no longer depended on the IIS process (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The actor then uploaded a vulnerable driver that is used to terminate EDR products and sideloaded a DLL that Kaspersky identified as Warlock ransomware's AV killer, possibly meant to use that driver; Kaspersky's endpoint product blocked the ransomware process (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
An internet-reachable on-premises SharePoint Server on which ToolShell (CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771) is exploitable (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In CLR loader telemetry, a dynamically compiled App_Web_toolpane assembly and a Microsoft.GeneratedCode assembly loading in the same application domain after a ToolPane request; in the IIS-Configuration ETW provider, events 25 and 47 for a path without the file-change-monitor events 17, 18, 19 and 21 that a real file produces, checked against an allow-list of legitimate VirtualPathProvider implementations; and memory inspection of w3wp.exe (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Triage: App_Web_* assemblies come from ordinary ASP.NET page compilation and Microsoft.GeneratedCode from legitimate XmlSerializer use, so neither is a signal alone; the signal is the pair in one application domain right after a ToolPane request, and any VirtualPathProvider that is not on the application's inventory (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The December 20 probe came from infrastructure associated with ONYPHE, an attack-surface discovery platform whose vulnerability checks use non-intrusive probes, so a probe alone looks like a benign scanner; Kaspersky's retrospective analysis established the probe as the initial phase of the intrusion that followed on the same endpoint (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Defender takeaway
On a SharePoint host that shows a code-execution exploit, contain the host, hunt the persistence that was installed afterwards, and rotate credentials and the exposed ASP.NET MachineKey; removing the initial shell or known indicators is not enough (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). Hunt for VirtualPathProvider implants with the ETW pattern above on SharePoint farms that were exposed to ToolShell.

entries.headline: Zyxel GS1900: Binarly says the exploit GreyNoise caught works on the June-fixed builds; install the .3C0 builds
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-7273 +1exploitedupdatedNATOB2

CVE-2026-7273 and CVE-2026-107441, Zyxel GS1900 switches: GreyNoise caught a Red Heron-linked actor exfiltrating configurations and hashed root credentials from 996 switches in 48 countries, and Binarly shows its exploit targets a separate flaw that the June fix leaves open; only the .3C0 builds close it

CVE-2026-7273 is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900 series smart-managed switch firmware that Zyxel says lets a LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker execute OS commands through a crafted HTTP request to the web-management interface; Zyxel patched ten models on 2026-06-16, each at its own "…(x).2C0" build (Zyxel PSIRT, 2026-06-16). CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-09-21 (CISA, 2026-09-21), the same day GreyNoise published research on a suspected Chinese-speaking actor whose activity since 7 May 2026 GreyNoise ties to one actor and assesses is the same as or related to Red Heron, which Acronis profiled for rapid n-day weaponisation of a Gitea flaw (Acronis Threat Research Unit, 2026-09-13), based on a shared command-and-control domain, malware family and tradecraft (GreyNoise, 2026-09-21).

Binarly, whose researchers found the Python exploit GreyNoise described in an exposed archive on infrastructure that BleepingComputer ties to Red Heron (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-04), shows that it works without change against all ten "…(x).2C0" builds, because it targets a different flaw: the CGI's request-parameter parser copies a parameter without a size check and never checks the parameter counter before writing (Binarly, 2026-11-03). Zyxel treats it as a separate vulnerability, CVE-2026-107441, which it fixed on 2026-10-22 in the "…(x).3C0" builds of all ten models and disclosed on 2026-11-03 (Zyxel PSIRT, 2026-11-03; Binarly, 2026-11-03). Binarly calls it a zero-day exploited in the wild because the recovered exploit matches the one GreyNoise described; Zyxel's two advisories say nothing about exploitation, CISA's catalog of 2026-11-04 lists CVE-2026-7273 and not the new flaw, and BleepingComputer says it is unclear whether the exploit was built to bypass the June fix (Binarly, 2026-11-03; Binarly, 2026-11-03; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-04; CISA KEV, 2026-11-04).

On or about 17 August 2026 the actor used a PyArmor-obfuscated Python tool with a deterministic single-request mode and an ASLR-brute-force mode averaging roughly 2,048 attempts, and exfiltrated configuration data, networking information and hashed root-level credentials from 996 switches in 48 countries, making the switch's on-device shell fetch a TFTP-delivered collector script and stage the harvested data to a file on the switch (GreyNoise, 2026-09-21). "While the credentials were hashed, 564 of the victims had factory default credentials" (GreyNoise, 2026-09-21). The same actor ran a WordPress chain against at least 49 organizations in 29 countries that cost one unnamed Western government more than 18,000 database records (GreyNoise, 2026-09-21).

Exposure
Every GS1900-8, -8HP, -10HP, -16, -24, -24E, -24EP, -24HPv2, -48 and -48HPv2 at or below its "…(x).2C0" build, which includes every build Zyxel advertised as the June fix (Zyxel PSIRT, 2026-11-03). Zyxel's advisories say the attacker is LAN-based, while Binarly and BleepingComputer say network access to the web interface is enough (Zyxel PSIRT, 2026-11-03; Binarly, 2026-11-03; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-04).
Detection
An outbound TFTP request (UDP/69, or a non-standard high port, as observed here) from a switch's management IP is a strong hunt signal, as is the switch's on-device shell invoking an interpreter against a file just retrieved via TFTP (GreyNoise, 2026-09-21). GreyNoise describes the harvested data staged to a file on the switch and names no implant, so treat any GS1900 whose web interface was reachable on a "…(x).2C0" or earlier build as a candidate for a compromise assessment centred on credential rotation rather than malware removal.
Defender takeaway
Install each switch's "…(x).3C0" build now, not the "…(x).2C0" build the June advisory names, which still carries the flaw Binarly says is exploited (Zyxel PSIRT, 2026-11-03; Binarly, 2026-11-03); move switch management onto a dedicated out-of-band VLAN with ACLs denying general-LAN access to the web-admin CGI port, and rotate any credential that may have shipped as factory-default on a GS1900 switch, regardless of patch status.
Update05 Nov 2026 03:59 UTCrun 2026-11-05T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyclassification

Binarly reports that the Python exploit GreyNoise described, which it found in an exposed archive on infrastructure that BleepingComputer ties to Red Heron (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-04), targets a flaw in the request-parameter parser of the switches' CGI (dispatcher.cgi), not the stack overflow of CVE-2026-7273, and that it works without change against the "…(x).2C0" builds Zyxel advertised as the June fix; Binarly confirmed this against all ten builds on 2026-09-28 (Binarly, 2026-11-03). Zyxel treats the report as a separate vulnerability, CVE-2026-107441, fixed on 2026-10-22 in the "…(x).3C0" builds of GS1900-8, -8HP, -10HP, -16, -24, -24E, -24EP, -24HPv2, -48 and -48HPv2 and disclosed in an advisory of 2026-11-03 that credits Binarly and shows no score or exploitation statement (Zyxel PSIRT, 2026-11-03; Binarly, 2026-11-03). Binarly labels the flaw an in-the-wild zero-day on the strength of the exploit match, scores it 9.8 with a network vector against Zyxel's LAN-based wording, and says it will publish a minimised proof of concept; CISA's catalog of 2026-11-04 lists only CVE-2026-7273 (Binarly, 2026-11-03; Binarly, 2026-11-03; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-04; CISA KEV, 2026-11-04). Switches on the June build are therefore still exposed to the exploit until the "…(x).3C0" build is installed.

Correction08 Nov 2026 14:05 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditactionsbodytechniques

GreyNoise reports that 564 of the exploited switches had factory-default credentials, but not that the actor logged in with them or regained access through them after a rotation (GreyNoise, 2026-09-21); the access it describes is the CGI flaw, followed by a collector fetched over TFTP.

entries.headline: SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier: unauthenticated file read, no fix will ship; replace with NSM
entries.html:
ROUTINECVE-2026-109593 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-109593 and CVE-2026-109594, SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier: an unauthenticated network attacker may read internal GMS files (CVSS 3.1 9.1), and SonicWall says the end-of-life product gets no fix and has no workaround

SonicWall's advisory SNWLID-2026-0019 of 2026-11-03 covers the end-of-life Global Management System: an unauthenticated attacker with network access to GMS 9.5.2 and earlier may be able to read internal GMS files, potentially exposing sensitive information (CVE-2026-109593, CVSS 3.1 9.1), and a post-authentication SQL injection under specific conditions could let an authenticated attacker access or modify data (CVE-2026-109594, 6.8) (SonicWall, 2026-11-03). The advisory lists no workaround and no fixed version, says no remediation or security update will be released because the product has reached end of life, and strongly encourages migration to Network Security Manager (SonicWall, 2026-11-03). End of support was 2026-09-30 (SonicWall, 2025-05-05), and the previous GMS advisory of 2026-08-11 named 9.5.2 as the fixed build for its flaws, so the last fixed build is itself affected now (SonicWall, 2026-08-11). The advisory does not say which files are exposed or whether anyone exploits the flaw, and CERT-FR relays it (CERT-FR, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
A GMS Virtual Appliance or Windows installation on 9.5.2 or earlier that is reachable from a network the operator does not trust; every such installation is unpatchable (SonicWall, 2026-11-03).
Defender takeaway
With no fix and no workaround the levers are reachability and replacement: take any GMS instance off untrusted networks and migrate to Network Security Manager, as SonicWall urges (SonicWall, 2026-11-03).

entries.headline: APT29-linked watering hole uses n-day iOS and Chrome chains; CISA lists CVE-2024-27834; updated devices resist
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2024-27834 +7exploitedNATOB2

Sekoia: an APT29-linked watering hole serves n-day iOS and Android exploit chains through compromised sites, clone domains and a one-week compromise of the Plerdy tracker; CISA lists the Apple WebKit pointer-authentication bypass CVE-2024-27834 as exploited on 2026-11-04

CISA added CVE-2024-27834, a WebKit flaw that lets an attacker with arbitrary read and write capability bypass Pointer Authentication and that Apple fixed on 2024-05-13, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-04, and names no victim or method (CISA KEV, 2026-11-04; Apple, 2024-05-13; Apple, 2024-05-13). The same day Sekoia reported a watering-hole campaign that it assesses with moderate to high confidence to be APT29 or one of its subgroups and in which that flaw is the pointer-authentication bypass of an iOS chain (Sekoia, 2026-11-04); the link between the listing and the campaign is the date alone. Sekoia retrieved three chains from the delivery host, which profiles the visitor and serves a platform-specific exploit without user interaction: an iOS 16.7 chain (CVE-2025-43529, then CVE-2024-27834) that steals the cookies of running apps; a DarkSword-based iOS chain that Sekoia's table labels iOS 18.5 (CVE-2025-43529 with CVE-2026-20700, then CVE-2025-14174 with CVE-2025-43510, then CVE-2025-43520) that harvests the phone; and an Android chain for Chrome 139 to 145 except 143 (CVE-2026-3910, then the Adreno driver flaw CVE-2025-27038) that takes Chrome cookies, saved logins, history and Wi-Fi configuration (Sekoia, 2026-11-04). The payloads exfiltrate data without establishing persistence, and Sekoia says none of the chains contains a zero-day or works against fully updated devices (Sekoia, 2026-11-04).

Delivery used JavaScript injected into legitimate sites, among them a Ukrainian gas producer, a US chemical-industry trade association, a Bulgarian military-related site and an Australian clinic; reverse-proxy clones of high-profile sites; and a one-week compromise, 27 August to 3 September 2026, of the Plerdy SEO tracker script, which Sekoia says exposed hundreds or thousands of sites, mostly Ukrainian (Sekoia, 2026-11-04). Sekoia names no Swiss victim, counts no infected devices and says it is working with national CERTs on victim identification.

Exposure
IPhones and iPads below the builds that fix the six iOS flaws, and Android phones on Chrome before the fix of CVE-2026-3910 or an unpatched Adreno driver. Sekoia's iOS 16.7 chain filters for iOS 16.7 and 16.7.10, and the sources do not establish whether the later 16.7.x builds Apple lists for iPhone 8, 8 Plus, X, iPad 5th generation and the first-generation iPad Pro models, up to 16.7.16 of 2026-05-11, are exploitable (Sekoia, 2026-11-04; Apple, 2026-05-11).

Fixes: iOS 26.2 and 18.7.3 close CVE-2025-43529 and CVE-2025-14174, iOS 26.1 and 18.7.2 close CVE-2025-43510 and CVE-2025-43520, iOS 26.3 closes CVE-2026-20700, and Chrome 146 closes CVE-2026-3910 (Apple, 2025-12-12; Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-03-18; Chrome Releases, 2026-03-12).

Detection
Sekoia names one on-device trace, a marker cookie that the iOS 16.7 chain's script sets as a replay guard so the exploit does not fire twice on a victim; it publishes some indicators and withholds several delivery and exfiltration hosts, so a visit to an injected site shows in web proxy and DNS telemetry from managed phones only against indicators obtained from Sekoia or a national CERT; the dependable check is the OS and Chrome version inventory (Sekoia, 2026-11-04).
Defender takeaway
Bring managed iOS devices to the newest release for each model and Android phones to current Chrome and the OEM patch level, because Sekoia says updated devices resist these chains and CISA lists every flaw they deliver as exploited (Sekoia, 2026-11-04; CISA KEV, 2026-11-04); the devices that cannot go past iOS 16.7.x are the open question.

Builds on: DeadTag: expired tag domains send visitors to iPhone exploit kits; opening the page is enough…

entries.headline: SEPPmail gateway: unauthenticated sender reaches root RCE or file access; fixed in 15.1.1, 15.0.x has no fix
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-114424 +4NATOA2

CVE-2026-114424 and CVE-2026-114425, SEPPmail Secure Email Gateway before 15.1.1: an unauthenticated mail sender can reach root command execution through a replacement rule and root file access through Large File Transfer, with three more flaws fixed in the same release and no fix for the 15.0 branch (CVSS 4.0 9.2)

SEPPmail's revision history lists patch release 15.1.1 of 2026-11-03 with five security fixes in the Secure Email Gateway, all for versions before 15.1.1 (SEPPmail, 2026-11-03). Two are unauthenticated and rated 9.2: in CVE-2026-114424 attacker-influenced replacement text in sender or recipient address-replacement rules is evaluated as Perl code, so a remote sender can run operating-system commands in the mail-processing worker when an active rule uses message-derived replacement data and its search condition matches, and the validated worker context was root (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04); in CVE-2026-114425 a file path supplied in the attachment metadata of an incoming message lets the worker disclose, move or delete an accessible file when Large File Transfer is enabled, also as root (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04). CVE-2026-114426 lets an unauthenticated attacker exhaust workers and disk because the upload interface processed data before checking authentication (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04), and two flaws in the GINA webmail let an unauthenticated attacker take over a created but unregistered account with an empty initial password (CVE-2026-114421) and enumerate email addresses through an unescaped LDAP filter (CVE-2026-114420) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04). The vendor says 15.0.7 of 2026-09-02 is the last release of the 15.0 branch, so the fix for a 15.0.x gateway is the move to 15.1 (SEPPmail, 2026-11-03). None of the sources read reports exploitation.

Exposure
A SEPPmail Secure Email Gateway before 15.1.1; the Home page of the administration interface shows the running version in the System section as "Firmware version" (SEPPmail, retrieved 2026-11-05). CVE-2026-114424 applies where an active rule uses message-derived replacement data, and CVE-2026-114425 where Large File Transfer is enabled (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04).
Detection
No source publishes an indicator. What the mechanism implies, not stated by a source: a child process or shell started by the mail-processing worker after inbound mail whose sender or recipient strings reach a replacement rule, and file operations by the Large File Transfer worker outside its storage area, both running as root.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 15.1.1, moving 15.0.x gateways to the 15.1 branch because 15.0 gets no fix, and until then review which active replacement rules use values taken from the message and whether Large File Transfer is enabled, the two conditions the CNA names (SEPPmail, 2026-11-03). Because the worker runs as root, a gateway that was exposed with such a rule or with Large File Transfer enabled warrants a compromise check.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Sophos RCA: fake interview repo ran BeaverTail via VS Code settings; dead EDR agent, OAuth grant survived revocation
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Sophos's own root-cause analysis of a developer-targeted intrusion: a fake job-interview repository's VS Code workspace settings ran BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret on a Mac whose endpoint agent had not reported since 11 June, and a third-party OAuth authorization outlived the session revocation

On 2026-09-14 a Sophos employee cloned a public repository presented as a job-interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code; a weaponized workspace settings file replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile with a command that downloads and runs a remote script in a loop, delivery relied on the user opening the workspace as trusted, and no exploit or vulnerability was involved (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). Opening a terminal was enough: a shell script fetched a JavaScript component and a package manifest into a hidden directory in the user profile, a package-manager install ran, the JavaScript ran under Node.js and the final-stage backdoor lived in memory only, with no persistence found (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). SophosLabs identified the BeaverTail loader followed by the InvisibleFerret backdoor, able to steal browser-stored credentials, keychain data and SSH keys, and the JavaScript stage sent the process environment to an attacker web endpoint on a cloud application-hosting service (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).

Two gaps lengthened the exposure. The Sophos Endpoint agent was installed but its core services were not running, so it enforced nothing and reported nothing; the device was last seen in Sophos Central on 2026-06-11, the cause is still under investigation, and SophosLabs says a working agent would have blocked the chain at the first dropped file (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). A third-party application authorization on the employee's source-code platform account survived the session revocation and password reset of 2026-09-15 and made 27 read requests against two internal repositories from an address new to the user until it was revoked on 2026-09-16; Sophos found no other host, no cloud activity and no customer impact (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). The analysis names no group; Sophos CTU says the technique matches the tradecraft of NICKEL ALLEY, which it describes as running the Contagious Interview campaign of fake companies, fake recruiters and malicious code repositories (Sophos blog, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
Developer workstations whose users clone and open repositories from outside parties, recruitment pretexts included, in an editor that trusts the workspace; and any managed device that is compliant in identity and device management but does not report to the endpoint console, as Sophos's fleet review found (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).
Detection
In macOS process lineage, the code editor's integrated terminal launching a download-and-run command that a cloned workspace's settings define, followed by a hidden directory in the user profile and a package-manager install run from it (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). In identity telemetry, a device that still signs in but does not report to the endpoint console is a coverage gap; a third-party authorization reading repositories from an address new to the user is the second signal (Sophos blog, 2026-11-04; Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).

Triage: a terminal profile normally launches a shell executable; this one launched a command that downloads and runs a remote script in a loop; it came from the settings of a freshly cloned repository (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).

Defender takeaway
Treat a coding assignment or repository from a recruiter or interviewer as untrusted code, because here the compromise needed only a trusted workspace and an opened terminal. Sophos's lasting controls are to require the endpoint agent for device compliance, to monitor for managed devices that stop reporting, and to revoke application authorizations as part of credential containment, not only sessions and passwords (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).
Correction08 Nov 2026 14:05 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditbodysourcessourcing_note

Sophos's root-cause analysis INC-2026-002 carries the dateline 20 October 2026 (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20); 4 November 2026 is the date of the Sophos blog post that links to it. The facts drawn from the analysis are unchanged.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: SpecterOps: iSCSI Target Server without CHAP lets a host that knows the target and initiator names read shared disks
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

SpecterOps: a Windows iSCSI Target Server set up without CHAP lets any host that knows the target and an authorised initiator name read the shared disks below file permissions, a Hyper-V domain controller's among them

SpecterOps shows that the Windows iSCSI Target Server role, set up as a community cluster guide describes it with the optional CHAP step skipped, accepts a login from any host that knows the target host, the target name and an authorised initiator name (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). The post says the role registers a service principal name on its computer account, so a directory query lists the target hosts, that initiator names are built from the host's DNS name and are therefore predictable, and that in the author's experience the service has no rate limiting or brute-force protection (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). Access is below the file system, so NTFS permissions do not apply, and volume encryption such as BitLocker defeats it (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). The worst case the post shows is a volume that holds a Hyper-V domain controller's virtual disk, from which the local credential stores and the directory database can be taken (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). The author has not tested the technique in production and warns that it can cause outages, and the post cites no Microsoft response.

Exposure
Windows Server hosts that run the iSCSI Target Server role without CHAP, found by the service principal name the role registers and by a listener on TCP 3260 (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04; Pen Test Partners, 2016-05-18). The author's own research puts the common uses with clustered resources such as Hyper-V, SQL Server and Exchange database availability groups, followed by third-party backup products (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04).
Detection
The post names no telemetry. What the mechanism implies, not stated by the post: iSCSI traffic to TCP 3260 on a target host from a source that is not one of its cluster nodes, and a login that presents a listed initiator name from another source address, because the access list keys on initiator names that an impersonator can present (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04).
Defender takeaway
Enable CHAP on every iSCSI target, and isolate iSCSI traffic with segmentation and host-based firewalling, which the post calls arguably the most effective step; the post says IPsec mitigates network sniffing, and BitLocker or similar volume encryption makes the stolen disk unreadable (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). Treat the disks of any domain controller that sat on an unprotected target as exposed.

The attacker then reads the shared disk below file-system permissions; where it holds a Hyper-V domain controller's virtual disk, the directory database and local credential stores are exposed. CHAP, network segmentation and volume encryption are the levers.

entries.headline: Vaud: device-code phishing against Microsoft 365 is running in Romandie; several organisations already affected
entries.html:
HIGHNATOA2

Canton Vaud warns of a device-code phishing campaign against Microsoft 365 accounts running in French-speaking Switzerland, with several organisations already affected

The canton of Vaud said on 2026-11-04 that a phishing campaign is currently running in French-speaking Switzerland and that several organisations have already been affected (translated from French) (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04). The messages can appear to come from a company or a known contact and invite the reader to view an invoice, open a document or verify information through a link; the campaign uses device-code phishing, which gets the victim to type a code on a genuine Microsoft authentication page and so gives the attackers fraudulent access to the Microsoft 365 account (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04). The links printed in the notice combine a company-style name and a portal word on a workers.dev subdomain whose second label starts with a cloud-storage word and an identifier, and the canton says other addresses can be used too (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04); workers.dev is the route assigned to every Cloudflare Worker (Cloudflare Docs, 2026-09-22). The notice names no actor, kit, count of organisations, sector or start date.

Exposure
Any Microsoft 365 tenant whose users can complete the device code flow, which Microsoft describes as meant for devices without local input such as shared devices or digital signage and as a high-risk method that phishing can use (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24).
Detection
Mail, web proxy and DNS telemetry for links to workers.dev subdomains of the structure above; in the Entra sign-in logs, device code events found with the authentication protocol filter (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24). Microsoft says protocol tracking persists through token refreshes, so later sign-ins in the same session can fall under an authentication-flows policy, and it records an original transfer method property in the activity details of the Conditional Access sign-in logs (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24).

Triage: Microsoft documents device code sign-in for shared devices and signage; a device-code sign-in by a user who has no such device, soon after that user received a mailed link, falls outside that use (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24).

Defender takeaway
Where the tenant has no documented need for device code flow, Microsoft recommends blocking it with a Conditional Access policy, testing in report-only mode and auditing existing use first (Microsoft Learn, 2026-04-07). Tell users never to enter a Microsoft login code at a third party's request, and that anyone who has entered a code or validated an authentication request must call IT support at once, which is the canton's own instruction (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04).

Builds on: FBI PSA260521, Kali365 OAuth device-code PhaaS bypasses M365 MFA without credential capture · Huntress: stolen post-MFA M365 tokens replayed within minutes; a password reset leaves planted…
