entries.headline: Drupal Commerce Core access bypass is exploited in the wild; update to 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41 and audit orders
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-118539exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-118539, Drupal Commerce Core: an access bypass in routes and entity fields is exploited against online stores, fixed in 3.3.13 and 8.x-2.41 (Drupal risk 21 of 25)

Drupal's advisory SA-CONTRIB-2026-254 of 2026-10-28 says Commerce Core "doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor" and that the flaw is being actively exploited in the wild (Drupal Security Team, 2026-10-28); The Hacker News carries the same wording (The Hacker News, 2026-10-30). The Drupal security team scores it 21 of 25, which SecurityWeek reads as exploitable without authentication whatever the module's configuration, and Drupal's statistics put the module on more than 42,000 sites (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30). The affected releases are Commerce Core 3.0.0 up to but not including 3.3.13 and earlier releases before 8.x-2.41 (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30). Drupal has not said how the bug is exploited, by whom, how many sites were targeted or whether it was exploited before the fix (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30); NCSC Switzerland's advisory of 2026-10-30 describes the impact as unauthenticated manipulation of order-related data with financial loss for the shop operator (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-30).

Exposure
Any Drupal site running Commerce Core below 3.3.13 on 3.x or below 8.x-2.41 on earlier releases, including shops built on the module's decoupled APIs rather than its own cart and checkout (The Hacker News, 2026-10-30); a public body that sells goods, permits or fees through such a site is in scope. The same day's batch holds 38 further Drupal advisories for 21 contributed projects, nearly a dozen rated critical, among them code execution, account takeover and Commerce orders marked as paid through Stripe without payment (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30).
Detection
Drupal's own guidance is an order audit for inconsistencies (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-30); checking each order's state, totals and payment status against the payment provider's records is the obvious test, an inference since no source names a method. The sources name no routes, parameters or request patterns; the web-server access log of the shop's API and checkout routes is the other record to review, an inference since nothing describes the requests.
Defender takeaway
Update Commerce Core to 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41 now and audit orders; the flaw needs no login and the upgrade is the only mitigation the sources name. Check the other contributed modules the site runs against the advisories of 2026-10-28.

entries.html:
CRITICALCVE-2026-102764exploitedupdatedNATOB1

CVE-2026-102764, BeyondTrust Remote Support: an unauthenticated file-operation flaw exploited as a zero-day since late August by a suspected China-nexus actor that left a web shell and boot-time sudo persistence (CVSS 4.0 9.3)

BeyondTrust's advisory BT26-05 of 2026-10-15 fixes CVE-2026-102764, an improper origin validation (CWE-290) in an internal messaging component of Remote Support that lets a remote attacker perform file operations on the appliance without authenticating; every version up to 26.2.3 is affected (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15). Google's Threat Intelligence Group found in an incident response that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor it formerly tracked as UNC5221, exploited the flaw as a zero-day in late August 2026 (GTIG, 2026-10-15); BeyondTrust dates the exploitation of one hosted instance and one self-hosted appliance to 2026-08-29 (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15). GTIG warns that ARMORY CASTLE and others have historically exploited broadly once a flaw is public (GTIG, 2026-10-15); BeyondTrust lists government among the actor's documented targets (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15). On 2026-10-30 Rapid7 published a root-cause analysis in which one forged message makes an internal file-transfer service write a PHP file into the site's public directory, run as the site's operating-system user, and says a Metasploit module now implements the chain (Rapid7, 2026-10-30).

After the exploit GTIG saw SAWFLY, a lightweight PHP web shell that evaluates attacker-supplied code as the appliance's unprivileged site account; the actor then made a root-owned SUID copy of the system shell, tried to dump the appliance's native secrets vault, and persisted through a boot-time script that adds a passwordless-sudo line to the sudoers template, so the escalation survives reboot and configuration reset (GTIG, 2026-10-15). It deleted appliance logs throughout, raised an account's Jump Item and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator, and exposed BARECLAW, a custom SOCKS5-over-WebSocket tunneler, by editing the HAProxy configuration (GTIG, 2026-10-15).

Exposure
Self-hosted Remote Support appliances on any version up to 26.2.3 without the BT26-05-RS patch; apply the patch manually unless the instance is subscribed to automatic updates in its /appliance interface, and a build older than 24.3.1 must be upgraded first (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15). SaaS tenants were patched by 2026-10-09 (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15); BeyondTrust says its patch was built and tested for Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access, though its advisory names only Remote Support as impacted (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15).
Detection
The actor deletes on-appliance logs, so use other copies: forwarded syslog for user changes that raise a Jump Item or Team role to Administrator and for account or API-account changes without a change ticket; authentication logs for administrative /login success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space; reverse-proxy or WAF logs for unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from non-support addresses; file transfers by accounts whose roles changed (GTIG, 2026-10-15). Rapid7's successful request was an extensionless URL, since the web server answers a direct .php request with 404, so a rule that matches only .php requests misses it (Rapid7, 2026-10-30). Patching does not evict the actor, so GTIG advises redeploying any appliance of confirmed or unknown status from a clean, fully patched image and rotating credentials in dependency order (GTIG, 2026-10-15).

Triage: an administrator changing Jump Item roles or signing in from a new network under a change ticket is routine; BeyondTrust's signal is a privileged session from a residential or VPN address tied to no administrator or ticket (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15).

Defender takeaway
Patch every self-hosted appliance now, then treat each one that was internet-reachable on an affected build since late August as potentially compromised until reviewed, and redeploy from a clean image any whose status is confirmed or unknown (GTIG, 2026-10-15).
Update31 Oct 2026 03:39 UTCrun 2026-10-31T0256Z-intelheadlinesummaryimmediate_actionsourcesevidenceactionsbody

Rapid7 published a root-cause analysis on 2026-10-30 and says a Metasploit module now implements the chain, with PHP and Unix Command targets (Rapid7, 2026-10-30). An anonymous customer session, started through the public customer connection, sends a message whose source address carries a reserved local router ID; the appliance's customer worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component, which exposes an internal file-transfer service with its native filesystem provider. Rapid7 used it to write a PHP file into the site's public directory and ran it as the site's operating-system user (Rapid7, 2026-10-30). The successful request was an extensionless URL, because the web server answers a direct .php request with 404 and maps an extensionless URL to the existing file, so detection that only searches for requests ending in .php would miss it; the appliance's thin-scc logs record file-transfer stream creation and rejected requests (Rapid7, 2026-10-30). Rapid7 tested Remote Support 24.1.2 and says other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established (Rapid7, 2026-10-30); BeyondTrust's advisory remains the reference for affected and fixed versions (BeyondTrust, 2026-10-15).

entries.headline: Ivanti Connect Secure chain: root step patched 29 Oct, CISA lists three flaws; 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 fall short
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-104935 +2exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-104935, Ivanti Connect Secure: an authentication bypass chained to code execution is exploited as a zero-day, the root-escalation step was patched on 2026-10-29 and CISA lists all three chain flaws (CVSS 8.6)

Ivanti disclosed a Connect Secure flaw on 2026-10-13 and says it is aware of limited exploitation in the wild (Ivanti, 2026-10-13); Rapid7 describes it as CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker run commands, CVSS 8.6 (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and CISA listed it in KEV the same day (CISA, 2026-10-13). Volexity tracks the operator as UTA0576 and dates exploitation of a fully patched 22.8R2.4 appliance to 2026-10-03 (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

The chain has three steps. A request to the public login script welcome.cgi names a protected script in an X-DSCGI-PATH header, which passes the authentication check and picks the destination. The upload script wu.cgi writes a file to disk before checking that it is a ZIP, and parallel requests run a Perl script before it is deleted. A root escalation then abuses the dsinvoked service's trust in the shared DSCache configuration store (Volexity, 2026-10-13). Volexity says Ivanti tracks the first two steps under CVE-2026-104935 (Volexity, 2026-10-13) and the root step is CVE-2026-111357 (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15); Volexity's update banner says Ivanti patched it on 2026-10-29 (Volexity, 2026-10-13). CISA listed it and a third chain flaw, CVE-2026-118527, on 2026-10-30 and says each can be chained with the other two (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-30); Ivanti's CVE record of 2026-11-03 describes CVE-2026-118527 as predictable filenames that let a remote authenticated attacker upload attacker-controlled files to a known location on disk (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03), and CERT-FR relays Ivanti's statement that all three flaws are actively exploited (CERT-FR, 2026-11-02).

The exploit leaves no web shell and patches library code in memory only, so Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool does not detect it, and Volexity found log entries removed. The operator then went after the Active Directory service account stored on the appliance: LDAP queries for LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys and password attributes, password spraying, and packet capture of plaintext LDAP, HTTP Basic and NTLM traffic (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
25.1.1.1 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior and 22.8R2.4 and prior are affected by CVE-2026-104935 and 22.7.x and below are not (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). The Canadian Cyber Centre's bulletin, updated 2026-10-30, lists every version before 25.1.1.3, 25.1.3.1 and 22.8R2.6 as affected (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-10-13), which takes in 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5, the builds of 2026-10-13. No cited source maps each fixed build to CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357 separately.
Detection
The appliance's own logs were tampered with, so start upstream: web proxy, load balancer or WAF logs for many requests to welcome.cgi, above all with an X-DSCGI-PATH header or one whose script differs from the URL path. On domain controllers, look for LDAP queries from the appliance's service account for LAPS, BitLocker recovery and password attributes, and spraying from the appliance's address. Patching does not evict an attacker who is already in: check /tmp for post-exploitation files and run network and memory forensics, because the Integrity Checker may not identify a compromise (Volexity, 2026-10-13).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 25.1.1.3, 25.1.3.1 or 22.8R2.6 now, then treat every appliance that was exposed on an affected build as a compromise-assessment target and rotate what it could reach. Where compromise cannot be excluded, isolate the appliance and preserve its memory and logs before any reset, because CERT-FR knows of lateral movement using the LDAP and Active Directory secrets stored on it (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:10 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelsummaryimmediate_actioncvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CERT-FR's alert of 2026-10-14 says Ivanti reports the vulnerability as actively exploited and that CERT-FR itself is aware of lateral movement using the LDAP and Active Directory secrets stored on the appliance (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). It puts the response in an order: fully isolate the appliance from both the internet and the internal network, snapshot the file system and memory of a virtual appliance, avoid powering it off so that traces survive, place the logs under seal and analyse the appliance with the Volexity indicators, and only then, on compromise, factory-reset it, upgrade and reset the secrets (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). Its list of secrets to treat as compromised is wider than a password reset: the LDAP and Active Directory secrets, every certificate on the appliance (machine, user-authentication, code-signing and the TLS certificate of the exposed interface), the administration password, stored API keys, the passwords of local accounts including the service accounts used for authentication servers, the Kerberos tickets and other authentication material of those service accounts, and the licence-server authentication (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). CERT-FR adds that running Ivanti's external Integrity Checker Tool needs physical access to the appliance and can interrupt service, and that some threats survive a factory reset (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). Its affected-systems list names the 22.8Rx builds before 22.8R2.5, the 25.1.1.x builds before 25.1.1.2 and the 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 and, in its text of that date, did not list a 25.1.2.x line; by counting 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 as affected it includes 25.1.3.0, a build that Rapid7's table lists as resolved (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14).

Improvement17 Oct 2026 03:34 UTCrun 2026-10-17T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryimmediate_actioncvessourcesevidencebody

The root-escalation step of the chain now has its own identifier, CVE-2026-111357, published on 2026-10-15 and rated High on GitHub's advisory database as GHSA-fhw5-mpvj-x89m (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15). Its description reads "Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 mishandles the manner in which the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, leading to privilege escalation to root, as exploited in the wild in October 2026." (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15), the same step Volexity describes as abusing the dsinvoked service's trust in the shared DSCache store (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

The record names only 22.8R2.4 as affected and states no fixed build; Volexity wrote that Ivanti was working on a fix for release in the coming weeks (Volexity, 2026-10-13), and no source read says whether any build now fixes it. The Canadian Cyber Centre's bulletin on the Ivanti advisory, updated 2026-10-16, adds that open-source reporting indicates CVE-2026-111357 is being exploited in the wild (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-10-13). A scanner, SIEM enrichment rule or ticket can now follow the unfixed step by this ID, and an appliance that was exposed still needs the compromise check above.

Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:20 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Ivanti's own description of CVE-2026-104935, as the numbering authority, reads "Authentication bypass by spoofing in ICS before version 25.1.3.0 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands" (ENISA EUVD, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 relays that, according to Ivanti, a portion of the flaw was found through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0, and that exploitation occurred while Ivanti was backporting the fix to the other supported versions (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). CERT-FR's text of that date still listed 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 as affected (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14), so 25.1.3.1 remained the build to reach on that line; its text updated on 2026-11-02 lists 25.1.2.x before 25.1.3.1 instead.

Update31 Oct 2026 03:37 UTCrun 2026-10-31T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryimmediate_actioncvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Volexity's report now carries an update banner saying Ivanti published a patch on 2026-10-29 for the privilege-escalation step, which is tracked as CVE-2026-111357 (Volexity, 2026-10-13). CISA added CVE-2026-111357 and a third chain flaw, CVE-2026-118527, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-30 (CISA, 2026-10-30). The catalog describes CVE-2026-118527 as a generation-of-predictable-numbers-or-identifiers flaw that lets a remote authenticated attacker upload files with attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk, and says it can be chained with CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357 (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-30). The Canadian Cyber Centre's bulletin on Ivanti's advisory, updated 2026-10-30, now lists the Connect Secure versions before 25.1.1.3, 25.1.3.1 and 22.8R2.6 as affected (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-10-13), a range that takes in 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5, the builds of 2026-10-13; CISA's alert, updated the same day, lists versions 25.1.1.2 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior and 22.8R2.5 and prior as affected by the three chain CVEs (CISA, 2026-10-13). Ivanti's advisory page could not be read, so which build carries which CVE's fix is not confirmed, and CVE-2026-118527 had no public CVE record, affected range or fixed build at that date.

Improvement01 Nov 2026 13:46 UTCrun 2026-11-01T1312Z-auditbody

Volexity's compromise-assessment guidance applies after patching as well: check the appliance's /tmp directory for evidence of post-exploitation actions and, where compromise is suspected, conduct network and memory forensics, because the Ivanti Integrity Checker may not identify a compromise (Volexity, 2026-10-13). Volexity says Ivanti tracks the authentication bypass and code execution steps under CVE-2026-104935 (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

Improvement04 Nov 2026 03:29 UTCrun 2026-11-04T0256Z-intelcvessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Ivanti's own CVE record for CVE-2026-118527, published on 2026-11-03, describes predictable filenames in Connect Secure before 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6 that let a remote authenticated attacker upload files with attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-03). CERT-FR's advisory of 2026-11-02 relays Ivanti's statement that CVE-2026-104935, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 are all actively exploited, lists Connect Secure 22.8Rx before 22.8R2.6, 25.1.1.x before 25.1.1.3 and 25.1.2.x before 25.1.3.1 as affected, and says Ivanti states that the 25.1.3.x releases are not affected by the last two (translated from French) (CERT-FR, 2026-11-02). The target builds and the compromise check above are unchanged.

entries.headline: HPE ClearPass 6.14, 6.12 and 6.11 are affected by PHP2Shell; a hotfix patch exists for each train
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, HPE Networking ClearPass Policy Manager: bulletin HPESBNW05171 lists the 6.14, 6.12 and 6.11 trains as affected by the PHP2Shell flaws and names a hotfix patch for each (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

HPE Networking's bulletin HPESBNW05171, released on 2026-10-22 and revised on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-29, covers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the PHP flaws behind PHP2Shell, in ClearPass Policy Manager and scores each CVSS 3.1 9.8 with network access, no privileges and no user interaction (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). Its affected-products note lists ClearPass 6.14.0 and earlier in the 6.14 release train and 6.11.15 and earlier in the 6.11 train, while its machine-readable record also lists the 6.12 train and gives 6.14.1, 6.11.16 and 6.12.8 as the boundaries; the bulletin does not reconcile the two (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). The fix is a hotfix patch for each train, 6.14.1, 6.12.8 (added in revision 3, which HPE says "exceptionally" includes 6.12.8) and 6.11.16, downloadable from the HPE Networking Support Portal; versions past end of maintenance are presumed affected and are not covered, and HPE has not assessed versions past end of support, which it says should be considered potentially impacted (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).

HPE recommends confining the CLI and web management interfaces to a dedicated layer 2 segment or VLAN, or controlling them with firewall policy at layer 3 and above, and asks customers to consider removing guest portals and all management interfaces from public access until the affected ClearPass instances have been upgraded (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). Other HPE Networking products and software versions it does not list are not known to be affected, and for Mist products the bulletin points to a Juniper reference advisory (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29). CISA added both PHP flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-27); the bulletin itself says nothing about exploitation of ClearPass (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
Every ClearPass Policy Manager on the 6.14, 6.12 or 6.11 train without the hotfix patch; the guest portal and the management interfaces are the surfaces HPE asks to take off public access (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).
Detection
HPE gives no indicator and no post-patch check; CISA's PHP alert advises monitoring for PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools (CISA, 2026-10-21), which on a ClearPass node would be processes started by the web worker account (an inference, since HPE does not describe how ClearPass runs PHP).
Defender takeaway
Install the hotfix patch for 6.14.1, 6.12.8 or 6.11.16 on every node now, the remediation HPE's bulletin names, and take any guest portal or management interface reachable from untrusted networks off public access, as HPE asks (HPE Networking, 2026-10-29).
Update30 Oct 2026 03:53 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytitle

entries.headline: GitLab's CVSS 10.0 CI regex RCE is now on CISA KEV; the public PoC needs push access to a public project
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-97229exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-97229, GitLab CE/EE: an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler allows code execution on self-managed servers; exploited, fixed in 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8 (CVSS 10.0)

GitLab's critical patch release of 2026-10-12 (19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8) fixes CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler that, "under certain conditions", could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration; GitLab scores it CVSS 3.1 10.0 with no privileges required (GitLab, 2026-10-12). Affected are self-managed CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5 and 19.4 before 19.4.2. The 19.4.1 release of 2026-09-23 fixed two related flaws in the same component (GitLab, 2026-09-23) but is still affected (GitLab, 2026-10-12). Rapid7 reproduced the code execution on 19.4.1 and published a proof of concept on 2026-10-13 (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29 on evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-10-29), and NCSC Switzerland updated its advisory the same day to active exploitation, citing Alpine Linux (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-29). Alpine says a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to its GitLab 19.3.4 on 2026-10-20 and 21, crashing worker processes eight times, four of them partway through the exploit; it found no evidence that code ran, could not rule it out and rebuilt the instance (Alpine Linux, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
Self-managed GitLab CE or EE on 19.2.x below 19.2.8, 19.3.x below 19.3.5 or 19.4.x below 19.4.2; GitLab's table for this flaw starts at 19.2 (GitLab, 2026-10-12), but the sibling CVE-2026-110264 reaches every version from 7.0 (GitLab, 2026-10-21). The Ruby project says the underlying engine bugs are reached by any application that compiles a regular expression from attacker-controlled input (Ruby, 2026-10-23). Rapid7 found the conditions: an attacker must first commit a malicious CI/CD configuration file and a repository path containing UTF-8 characters to a branch in a public project, which an ordinary account can do by creating a public project where the instance allows it (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and on instances where new users can self-register and create projects that constraint is removed (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). An instance with open sign-up, or with public projects that untrusted users can write to, is the case to prioritise.
Detection
GitLab's release page lists six detections for exploitation attempts on self-managed instances (GitLab, 2026-10-12). Alpine saw the attack as crashes of GitLab worker processes after crafted CI configurations from a newly registered account, with 502 errors and failed CI jobs, and notes that a successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs (Alpine Linux, 2026-10-28); in process-creation telemetry, shells, interpreters or network tools started as children of the GitLab application server processes are the sign of success, and a server where that turns up needs its CI/CD variables, runner registration tokens and deploy keys treated as exposed.

Triage: ordinary CI jobs run shells under the runners; only a shell spawned by the GitLab application server processes themselves matches this flaw, not one started inside a runner job.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 now (GitLab, 2026-10-12), or better to 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6 or 19.2.9, or on older branches the backports 19.1.9, 19.0.10 and 18.11.13, the builds of 2026-10-21 that also fix a second CVSS 10 regular-expression compiler flaw, CVE-2026-110264 (GitLab, 2026-10-21), internet-facing instances first as CERT-EU advises (CERT-EU, 2026-10-12), then instances where new users can self-register and create projects, which removes the push-access constraint Rapid7 found (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); the fix is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and images, so an installation with its own Ruby, from source or in a self-built image, needs Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9 as well, and Alpine's GitLab on 19.3.6 with standard Ruby stayed vulnerable (Alpine Linux, 2026-10-28). CISA lists the flaw as exploited and NCSC Switzerland reports active exploitation, so an instance reachable on an affected version needs a compromise assessment as well as the upgrade; Rapid7's interim controls (restrict anonymous access to public projects and stop untrusted users creating or writing to public projects) reduce exposure only to the path it demonstrated (Rapid7, 2026-10-13).
Update14 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Rapid7 reports that it independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on the official GitLab CE 19.4.1 image with address space layout randomization enabled, that the same input did not execute on the patched 19.4.2 image, and that it found no confirmed exploitation in the wild (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). Its testing shows the unauthenticated label needs a qualifier: the attacker must first push a malicious CI/CD configuration and a UTF-8 repository path to a branch in a public project, which an ordinary account can do where users may create public projects (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); the proof of concept then triggers it with a request without credentials (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). A proof of concept went public the same day; its README says the included offsets were tested only against the 19.4.1 CE Linux amd64 image, that other builds need adjusted offsets, and that the generated payload is slightly larger than 2 GiB, needing about 9 GiB of memory on the test host (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). The affected and fixed versions are unchanged.

Update30 Oct 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-10-30T0255Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinereferencessourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

CISA added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29, "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-10-29), and NCSC Switzerland edited its advisory the same day to add reports of exploitation attempts, moving the exploitation status to active exploitation (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-29). The report behind it is Alpine Linux's: on 2026-10-20 and 21 a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to its GitLab instance, which still ran 19.3.4, crashed the worker processes eight times and got partway through the exploit in four of them; the attacker returned on 2026-10-25 and 26 and failed, Alpine found no evidence that code ran but could not rule it out, and it rebuilt the instance (Alpine Linux, 2026-10-28). Alpine's upgrade to GitLab 19.3.6 on 2026-10-22 did not close the flaw, because the fix is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab applies only in its official packages and images, so an installation that runs its own Ruby needs Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9 or later as well (Alpine Linux, 2026-10-28). GitLab's release page now says its security team has released six threat detections for self-managed instances (GitLab, 2026-10-12). GitLab's release of 2026-10-21 (19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9) also fixes a second CVSS 10 regular-expression compiler flaw, CVE-2026-110264, so those builds are the better upgrade target (GitLab, 2026-10-21). Rapid7's statement of 2026-10-13 that it saw no confirmed exploitation predates all of this.

Improvement01 Nov 2026 14:03 UTCrun 2026-11-01T1312Z-auditbodysourcestitle

GitLab's notes of 2026-10-21 give the sibling flaw CVE-2026-110264 a wider range than this one: every GitLab CE/EE version from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9 and 19.2 to 19.5 before their October 21 builds, with the fix backported to 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9 and 19.2.9 (GitLab, 2026-10-21). An instance on a branch older than 19.2 is therefore not out of scope and has a fixed build to move to. The Ruby project says the regular-expression engine bugs behind these CVEs are reached whenever an application compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls, fixes all of them in Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13, and advises avoiding compiling regular expressions from untrusted input where an upgrade is not possible (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

entries.headline: privatim cloud guidance v3.02: public bodies keep their own keys for sensitive data; big-vendor SaaS mostly out
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOA2

privatim revises its cloud guidance for Swiss public bodies (Merkblatt v3.02, 2 October 2026): sensitive data stays under the body's own keys, SaaS from Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP is in most cases inadmissible for secrecy-bound data, and top management signs the residual risk

privatim, the conference of the Swiss data-protection authorities, dates version 3.02 of its guidance "Cloud-specific risks and measures" to 2 October 2026 (privatim, 2026-10-02); it replaces the version of 3 February 2022 (DCOD, 2026-10-27). For particularly sensitive personal data the public body must encrypt, the keys may be available only to it, and outsourcing such data, or data under a statutory duty of confidentiality, to SaaS from large international providers, with Microsoft, Google, AWS and SAP named, is in most cases inadmissible because of the untenable risk (privatim, 2026-10-02). Keys may stay with the provider only where no untenable risk follows and the provider is bound by contract to use them only with the body's express consent and to log every access (privatim, 2026-10-02).

The body, or its top management, is to confirm in writing that it has understood the risks and accepts the residual risk, and data the cloud services generate about their users, such as telemetry and logging data, is to be treated with the same care and contract terms as the content data (privatim, 2026-10-02). The five risk areas are contract design, places of processing including foreign authority access, confidentiality with encryption and key management, user data, and sub-processors (privatim, 2026-10-02).

Defender takeaway
The guidance addresses public bodies subject to Swiss data-protection law; a body that runs or plans SaaS from the named providers for sensitive or secrecy-bound data is advised to keep its own encryption keys, to have top management sign the residual risk, and to hold provider telemetry and logs about its users to the same contract terms.

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Lumen: Volt Typhoon's Silent Train relay chains fronted zero-days against SD-WAN, N-central and KACE
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Silent Train: Lumen's Black Lotus Labs describes the rotating relay network Volt Typhoon used for one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against management and control-plane platforms (Quest KACE, Versa Director, N-able N-central, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator)

Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reports that Volt Typhoon used a covert framework it calls Silent Train, first seen in late 2023, for the phases that need protection: exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration and continued access to victims (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). A session starts from a virtual private server outside the US, passes through compromised non-US SOHO and IoT devices and leaves through a compromised US device before the victim; more than 27 device classes were enrolled, from TP-Link routers and Netgear Orbi devices to Fortinet appliances and CyberPanel servers, and the enterprise platforms stayed in chains for one to three months as final hops (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The operators exploit exposed web interfaces on the relay devices and deploy only what chained SSH needs, namely temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files and living-off-the-land utilities, with reverse tunnels over open-source proxies in later variants; sessions averaged about four hours, and at the end the operators removed all artifacts and dismantled the chain (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28).

Lumen says its monitoring helped identify one likely and four confirmed zero-day campaigns against endpoint and network management platforms and SD-WAN orchestrators: Quest KACE, where the activity looked like an undisclosed flaw, affected more than 30 victims and fell after Quest's October 2025 updates (a moderate-confidence assessment); Versa Director in 2024; the N-able N-central flaws CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876; Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN through CVE-2026-20127, exploited by late 2025 and after Cisco's February 2026 disclosure; and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator through the zero-day later designated CVE-2026-16812 (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). Post-incident analysis found in-memory webshells, credential harvesting and abuse of native platform features such as endpoint control and remote file transfers, and in several cases erased or altered logs (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The victims it names are US government, telecommunications, defence-industrial, managed-service and critical-infrastructure organisations, concentrated in Hawaii, California and Texas, and it names no European or Swiss victim (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28). The Hacker News carries the same findings from a report Lumen shared with it (The Hacker News, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
Internet-reachable management and control-plane platforms (endpoint management, SD-WAN controllers and orchestrators, out-of-band administration), and edge devices with exposed web interfaces, which can be enrolled as relay hops without any data of the owner being the target.
Detection
Telemetry classes are administrative logins, API calls, remote file transfers and configuration changes on management platforms outside normal administration hours or workflow, in-memory web shells that leave no file on disk, and, on edge devices, temporary SSH services, unfamiliar keys and outbound reverse tunnels to unfamiliar upstream hosts (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28).
Defender takeaway
Restrict the administrative interfaces of management and control-plane platforms to a VPN, jump host or management network and prioritise their patching, as Lumen advises, and treat an edge device that shows temporary SSH services or reverse tunnels as a possible relay in someone else's intrusion chain.

entries.classification_html: NATOB3
entries.headline: CrowdStrike: VAPOR PANDA runs ARTEX against 200+ organisations, European foreign ministries among them
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB3

VAPOR PANDA: CrowdStrike reports a China-nexus actor running the ARTEX agent framework against more than 200 organisations from 17 October, among them foreign ministries in Europe and a Greek government entity, and deploying the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor

CrowdStrike OverWatch reports that from 2026-10-17 a single ARTEX controller linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure directed exploitation against entities in at least 14 countries over 11 days, and that the campaign reached more than 200 organisations, including foreign ministries in Europe (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). One engagement focused on a single European country, its foreign ministry, presidency, prime minister's office and defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities, and another targeted 19 US organisations in pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, defence, nuclear and finance (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine organisations and password spraying and credential scanning against at least 12 more, among them government entities in Europe (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). CrowdStrike states that the campaign is separate from the Storm-0940 ARTEX activity Microsoft reported and is VAPOR PANDA's first observed use of AI-driven tooling (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29).

The framework ran mainly on the DeepSeek model, with a human operator steering the agents at decision points while they pursued web, cloud, container, Active Directory, mail and VPN paths in parallel (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). In transcripts at a US pharmaceutical company the agent chained an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity flaw to query the cloud instance metadata service and obtain a role that could issue administration commands to thousands of instances; at a second it deployed web shells, abused an unauthenticated orchestration service for root in a container environment, read LAPS passwords and abused resource-based constrained delegation (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). Against a Greek government entity the operator supplied a 2022 directory export from the mail server whose authentication keys had likely not been rotated; the agent forged an administrator token, read mailboxes and used VPN configurations from a user's sent mail, with a VPN client key the operator described as coming from a May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). The operator also told the agents to find domain Windows hosts without the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). At a Middle East interior ministry and a Latin American foreign ministry the actor loaded the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor through a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe that loads a malicious DLL (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29). No Swiss target is named.

Exposure
Government, mail, identity and VPN estates where a directory export or backup holding authentication keys has never been rotated, SAML service providers that accept unsigned assertions, and cloud instances that still allow instance metadata service version 1; CrowdStrike names foreign ministries and government entities in Europe among the targets (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29).
Detection
Telemetry classes are authentication logs (password spraying and credential scanning against many accounts, an administrator token minted outside the identity provider, VPN logins that use a configuration or key from an old mailbox or leak), cloud control-plane audit (administration commands issued to many instances through the cloud systems manager, instance metadata queries from an application), process lineage (a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe loading a malicious DLL) and endpoint inventory queries for hosts without the security agent; CrowdStrike lists ARTEX-named command-line parameters, cloud roles and a directory under ProgramData as hunt markers (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29).
Defender takeaway
Rotate keys held in old directory exports and backups, require signed SAML assertions and IMDSv2, and hunt authentication and cloud audit logs for the parallel, many-target pattern an operator-steered agent produces; CrowdStrike expects China-nexus actors to keep adopting agent frameworks (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-29).

entries.headline: Talos IR Q3: public administration tied for most targeted; vishing into RMM and EDR killing mark the ransomware cases
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOB2

ANNUAL REPORT: Cisco Talos Incident Response trends Q3 2026: public administration tied with finance as the most targeted sector, help-desk vishing into remote-management tools, and ransomware operators uninstalling and killing EDR

Cisco Talos Incident Response reports that in Q3 2026 financial organisations made up 18 percent of its engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Phishing was the leading initial-access technique at 37 percent of engagements and exploitation of public-facing applications second at 33 percent; the phishing cases include numerous actors who phone the victim as the IT help desk to get remote access allowed through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Ransomware and pre-ransomware cases were 27 percent of engagements, with The Gentlemen, Qilin, Rhysida and the closed group Interlock among the families and a new variant, VYPR, that Talos calls operationally immature: it had no leak site when seen, reused leaked Conti-derived source code and exfiltrated over several days (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

The VYPR intrusion began with a vishing call that had the user start a Microsoft Quick Assist session; the actor then used RMM software that ran PowerShell to download and install an MSI from a remote address, with MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, an IP scanner and mstsc as tools, and disabled EDR with several vulnerable drivers (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Interlock operators repeatedly tried to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint, used PsExec and taskkill to end security services and integrity checkers, turned off Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared event logs (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29). Talos names insufficient logging (over 40 percent of engagements), weak credential and secret handling, and absent or incomplete MFA as the most common weaknesses, and recommends centralised logging with at least 90 days of retention (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-29).

Exposure
An organisation whose help desk or staff can be reached by phone and whose endpoints permit Quick Assist or an unapproved RMM agent; Talos names public administration among the most targeted sectors in its caseload.
Detection
In process-creation and software-install telemetry, an RMM or Quick Assist session started after an inbound call, followed by PowerShell run under the RMM agent that downloads an installer from an external address; in endpoint and service-control telemetry, attempts to uninstall the EDR agent, PsExec or taskkill ending security services, Defender real-time protection switched off, vulnerable kernel drivers loaded, and event logs cleared.
Defender takeaway
Treat a remote-support session that nobody at the help desk started as the vishing signal and inventory which RMM tools and Quick Assist are permitted on endpoints; alert on EDR uninstall and security-service termination as a ransomware precursor; and centralise logs with the 90-day minimum retention Talos recommends, because actors delete logs on the endpoint.

entries.headline: Cisco ASA and FTD SSL VPN reload flaw is exploited and on CISA KEV; fixes in every branch, no workaround
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-76418exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-76418, Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: a crafted request to the remote access SSL VPN reloads the device when a tunnel group uses secondary authentication; Cisco reports active exploitation and CISA lists it (CVSS 3.1 8.6)

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-28 describes CVE-2026-76418, a logic error in the remote access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure FTD: an unauthenticated, remote attacker who sends a crafted request while connecting to the SSL VPN makes the device reload, and a successful VPN login is not required to reach the affected processing path (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026 and names no actor or victim (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-29 (CISA, 2026-10-29), and CERT-FR restates the advisory (ANSSI / CERT-FR, 2026-10-29). The stated impact is a reload and denial of service, scored CVSS 3.1 8.6 with availability as the only impact; no code execution or data access is described (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

The first fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104 (for 9.16 and earlier), 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, 9.24.1.27 and 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11 (for 7.0 and earlier), 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco lists no workaround; its mitigation is to remove secondary authentication from the tunnel group, which lowers the security posture of the remote access VPN, or, where DefaultWEBVPNGroup does not use secondary authentication, to disable the tunnel group list with no tunnel-group-list enable (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco confirms that Secure FMC, Cloud-delivered Firewall, cdFMC and Secure Access are not affected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An ASA or FTD unit below the first fixed release of its branch whose running configuration has webvpn enabled on an interface and secondary-authentication-server-group on any tunnel group; the default tunnel group DefaultWEBVPNGroup counts even when the tunnel group list is disabled. On FTD, read the deployed remote access VPN policy and the resulting configuration in FMC or FDM (Devices > VPN > Remote Access) (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
Neither Cisco nor CISA publishes an indicator. The mechanism points at device availability telemetry: unexpected reloads, HA failover flaps, uptime resets and crash files on units that terminate the remote access VPN, read against VPN authentication logs for connection attempts from external addresses that never complete a login.

Triage: a reload also follows upgrades, HA events and hardware faults; a reload that coincides with unauthenticated SSL VPN connection attempts from an external address is the pattern the stated mechanism produces.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade the units that terminate remote access SSL VPN with secondary authentication this week, perimeter units first; Cisco states denial of service as the only impact, so patching leaves no further step, and removing secondary authentication as a stop-gap trades an outage risk for a weaker VPN login.

Builds on: Cisco confirms exploitation of an unauthenticated ASA/FTD VPN denial-of-service flaw; hardening… · Cisco Expressway root RCE is exploited (CISA KEV, F6 incident): upgrade clustered units to…

entries.headline: Public root exploit for a Linux page-cache write past the Dirty Frag fix; AlmaLinux kernels carry the fix, no CVE yet
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Linux kernel ZDI-CAN-33367: a public local root exploit for an skb_zerocopy page-cache write that gets past the Dirty Frag fix, with no CVE and no mainline fix, among six reports Trend Micro's ZDI copied to public lists, two of them ksmbd flaws scored CVSS 9.0

On 2026-10-21 Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative sent five Linux kernel reports and copied public mailing lists on every one, several with no fix in any released kernel; none of the six reports, the five kernel ones and a ConnMan report, has a CVE (Sysdig, 2026-10-24). ZDI-CAN-33367 matters most: skb_zerocopy() moves shared page-cache pages into a new socket buffer without the marker the Dirty Frag fix added, so IPsec ESP decrypts in place and an unprivileged local user writes attacker bytes into the cached copy of a read-only file, which gives root through a setuid binary or /etc/passwd; the public exploit needs unprivileged user namespaces and networking modules such as nlmon and act_pedit (Sysdig, 2026-10-24). TuxCare reproduced a root shell on AlmaLinux 8 to 10 (Dirty Frag fix installed), CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 (AppArmor user-namespace restriction bypassed) (Sysdig, 2026-10-24). A reviewed patch from the netdev list is now in the kernel's networking tree but not in mainline, and a kernel with only the fix for CVE-2026-90049, a bug in the same function, is not covered (Sysdig, 2026-10-24; TuxCare, 2026-10-27). AlmaLinux has put fixed kernels into production (4.18.0-553.178.1.el8_10, 5.14.0-687.60.1.el9_8, 6.12.0-211.69.1.el10_2), and TuxCare's rebootless patch is out for EL9 and EL10, with EL8 ready and Debian and Ubuntu in progress (AlmaLinux, 2026-10-28; TuxCare, 2026-10-27).

Two reports concern ksmbd, the kernel's own SMB server, not Samba. ZDI-CAN-33774 is a pre-authentication race in the SMB1 or SMB2 handler choice: its public proof of concept leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel, ZDI labels it remote code execution, nothing public shows code execution, and a fix is queued in ksmbd-for-next (Sysdig, 2026-10-24; Phoronix, 2026-10-22). ZDI-CAN-33549 is an SMB Direct integer underflow that needs an RDMA interface, a writable share and an SMB Direct client, and its proof of concept crashes the kernel (Sysdig, 2026-10-24). ZDI scores both 9.0, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux does not include ksmbd by default (The Hacker News, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
A Linux host where a local user or workload can run code and unprivileged user namespaces are on (shared hosting, CI runners, container nodes, login nodes) on the distributions above. For ksmbd, look for the ksmbd module, the ksmbd.mountd daemon and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445 (Sysdig, 2026-10-24).
Detection
The exploit is one unprivileged process that unshares into new user and network namespaces and writes sysctls, brings up an nlmon interface, installs XFRM state over netlink, adds an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attaches a tc pedit action with a redirect and then calls splice() into a socket on the loopback address; Sysdig says nothing legitimate does all of that from one unprivileged process, so syscall-level runtime telemetry sees it (Sysdig, 2026-10-24). The write lands in the page cache, not the file, so a disk-content integrity check does not show it.
Defender takeaway
Restrict unprivileged user namespaces where nothing depends on them (Sysdig says user.max_user_namespaces=0 should block the public exploit, untested by TuxCare, and breaks rootless containers and some build tooling), do not rely on Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction, set seccomp RuntimeDefault on Kubernetes pods and install the fixed kernel where your distribution has shipped it; unload ksmbd where unused and keep TCP 445 to trusted networks where it must stay (Sysdig, 2026-10-24).
Update29 Oct 2026 05:00 UTCrun 2026-10-29T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryupdated_atsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

AlmaLinux says its fix for ZDI-CAN-33367 is now in the regular kernel updates in the production repositories for every supported release: kernel-4.18.0-553.178.1.el8_10 for AlmaLinux 8, kernel-5.14.0-687.60.1.el9_8 for 9 and kernel-6.12.0-211.69.1.el10_2 for 10, installed with a metadata refresh, an upgrade and a reboot; the earlier testing-repository kernels also carry the fix (AlmaLinux, 2026-10-28). TuxCare's status of 2026-10-27 adds that the upstream fix has been accepted into the kernel's networking tree but not mainline, that no CVE exists and no exploitation has been reported, that its rebootless patch is out for EL9 and EL10 on AlmaLinux, CloudLinux, RHEL, Oracle Linux and Rocky Linux with EL8 ready for release, and that Debian and Ubuntu work is in progress (TuxCare, 2026-10-27).

actions: In every Entra tenant you or your MSP administer, disable without deleting the seven ConnectWise application identities that ConnectWise lists by client ID (Cloud Backup is 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae; the other six are in ConnectWise's advisory), dormant connections included, and keep them disabled, because ConnectWise's restoration of 2026-10-28 has partners consent a new application, “ConnectWise Cloud Backup for M365”, in each tenant, so take its details only from the instructions on ConnectWise's Trust Center; where Graph activity logs were enabled, review them for these apps until at least 90 minutes after you disabled them, because a token issued before the disable stays valid for up to 90 minutes, and preserve the sign-in and audit logs promptly without delaying containment, because Entra ID Free keeps only 7 days.
In the same tenants list the apps owned by the ConnectWise tenant (ID 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7), and disable each that you do not use or cannot verify as safe.

In the same tenants review every enterprise application and app registration, MSP management and security tools first but none skipped (Huntress saw the secrets planted on apparently random applications, in one tenant on some of the least privileged ones), for client secrets, certificates and federated credentials added since 2026-10-13 and remove any you did not create; also check the directory roles, owners and consent grants held by ConnectWise and SkyKick service principals, Conditional Access exclusions for them, and mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rules and delegated access, because disabling the vendor applications does not remove access planted through them.

entries.headline: ConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+ Microsoft 365 tenants; disabling it does not undo planted access
entries.html:
HIGHexploitedupdatedNATOA1

ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick): the vendor's Microsoft 365 application credential was used to sign in to customer tenants, with directory-role self-assignments in about 50 tenants and, Huntress reports, added credentials in two

ConnectWise says it identified unauthorized access to application identities within its Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) environment; on 2026-10-17 it disabled seven application identities, suspended the service, says the shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid, and warns that disabling does not reverse changes already made in a tenant (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). As of ConnectWise's update of 2026-10-19 01:15 UTC, Cloud Backup, SaaS Security and Cloud Management remained suspended with no confirmed restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19), and its status page of 2026-10-28 says partners can now re-authorize Microsoft 365 backup and restore through a new application (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28); ConnectWise reports no successful threat activity in the environments it monitors since it implemented mitigations (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19) and says it cannot independently determine whether a given partner or customer tenant was affected (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Huntress and Todyl report that on 2026-10-15 the app's identity signed in to customer Microsoft 365 tenants from one hosting-provider address and received app-only Microsoft Graph tokens; the credential sits in the vendor's own tenant, so no user, MFA prompt or user Conditional Access was involved, and the app's consent covers read and write access to mail, files and Teams chats (Huntress, 2026-10-16; Todyl, 2026-10-15). Huntress confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants by 2026-10-16 and later counted almost 1,000 tenants with sign-in activity from that address, over 300 successful, after password spraying against four law-firm tenants on 13 and 14 October, and a separate failed wave targeted 16 tenants in policy and national-security sectors (Huntress, 2026-10-16). In about 50 of its tenants, ConnectWise Cloud Management apps assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator; in one the Teams app added itself to Global Administrator and client secrets were added to an MSP management application and to Huntress's own application within about five minutes, the credential additions from private Azure space (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Huntress later identified a second tenant with the same sequence, the application granting itself Global Administrator and then planting a new secret on a small number of other applications, within two minutes of the first around 03:45 UTC on 2026-10-15, with the choice of applications apparently random (Huntress, 2026-10-16). It says the unauthorized sign-ins with the credential were bunched across the morning of 2026-10-15 UTC, that the last successful one it observed was at 08:44 UTC that day with only failed attempts afterwards in the tenants where it can read sign-in logs, and that in the two tenants it reviewed it found no mailbox or file manipulation and no user or policy changes (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Microsoft Threat Intelligence, as BleepingComputer relays it, called it an active supply-chain attack and assessed likely abuse of existing permissions including Directory.ReadWrite.All (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-17). Microsoft Threat Intelligence later assessed that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, was responsible, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). How the credential was obtained and what was read remain unknown (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-17).

Exposure
Every Entra tenant, including each customer tenant an MSP manages, in which a ConnectWise or SkyKick Cloud Backup or Cloud Management app was ever consented, dormant connections included; ConnectWise lists seven application client IDs, among them Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), and says to match on client ID (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Todyl identifies the application as "ConnectWise Cloud Backup" (formerly SkyKick Backup), app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae; SpecterOps hunts for applications owned by the ConnectWise tenant (ID 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7) and notes that older tenants may list them under SkyKick names (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17).
Detection
Entra service-principal sign-in logs for these apps from any address outside Microsoft and Azure ranges, which misses the credential additions, made from private Azure space (Huntress, 2026-10-16); the sweep of sign-ins itself, which Sophos saw come from a single virtual private server in strictly ascending tenant-ID order with Python HTTP-library user agents (Sophos, 2026-10-19); directory audit events Add member to role, Update application and Add service principal credentials initiated by a ConnectWise or SkyKick app (Huntress, 2026-10-16); Graph activity logs (Entra ID P1 or P2, not retroactive) for per-request source addresses (Todyl, 2026-10-15); and mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rule and delegation changes (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Huntress notes that Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no audit record, so a clean audit log does not rule out reads of the directory (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Disabling the apps does not remove credentials, roles or consents already planted, and revoking user sessions does not end this access (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; Todyl, 2026-10-15). Disabling an app stops new tokens only: a token issued before the disable stays valid for up to 90 minutes (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17), and ConnectWise says that after its own certificate revocation previously issued tokens may remain usable until they expire (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). The service-principal sign-in log records an application's authentication (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19), while per-request use of a token appears in the Graph activity logs named above (Todyl, 2026-10-15), so the review of that period belongs there. Microsoft asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, and to search by application ID rather than display name (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). As of 2026-10-19, any alerting a tenant took from ConnectWise SaaS Security was out of service while that service was suspended (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).

Triage: the vendor's apps sign in from Azure addresses with a .NET SDK user agent, while the credential additions used a Python user agent; Python and curl are common in administration, so Huntress says the combination of actor, operation and user agent is the signal (Huntress, 2026-10-16). Role self-assignments carrying the vendor's own user agent are not proven benign, since Huntress has not confirmed vendor automation (Huntress, 2026-10-16).

Defender takeaway
Where any ConnectWise or SkyKick app is consented, disable it by client ID without deleting it, keep it disabled (ConnectWise's restoration works through a new application that each tenant consents separately), and review credentials, roles, owners, consents and Conditional Access exclusions since 13 October (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19; Huntress, 2026-10-16). An MSP should review its own management and security tools first, since a foothold there can reach its customers, but the review covers every application, because Huntress saw secrets planted on apparently random ones (Huntress, 2026-10-16). ConnectWise cannot independently determine whether a given partner or customer tenant was affected, so the answer for a tenant has to come from its own sign-in and audit logs (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).
Improvement19 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-19T0256Z-intelactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

ConnectWise's update of 2026-10-18 01:00 UTC took SaaS Security and Cloud Management offline in addition to Cloud Backup, which had been suspended since 2026-10-17, so ConnectWise SaaS Security monitoring and alerting is out of service as well, and the update of 2026-10-19 01:15 UTC still gives no restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). Disabling an app stops new tokens only: Todyl and SpecterOps each state that tokens already issued stay valid for up to 90 minutes, and ConnectWise says that after it revoked the Cloud Backup certificates previously issued tokens may remain usable until they expire (Todyl, 2026-10-15; SpecterOps, 2026-10-17; ConnectWise, 2026-10-19). SpecterOps hunts for applications owned by the ConnectWise tenant, noting that older tenants may list them under SkyKick names (SpecterOps, 2026-10-17).

Update20 Oct 2026 03:57 UTCrun 2026-10-20T0256Z-inteltitlesummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Huntress's update of 2026-10-19 13:30 ET identified a second tenant with post-compromise activity, a tenant Huntress did not originally protect, where it got deployed to collect telemetry (Huntress, 2026-10-16). In both tenants the activity was fast and scripted, within two minutes of each other around 03:45 UTC on 2026-10-15: the application granted itself Global Administrator and then planted a new secret on a small number of other applications to keep a foothold (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The choice of applications appeared random: the same flow picked two different sets, one application present in both was backdoored in only one, and in one tenant the applications that received secrets were among the least privileged in the environment while far more powerful ones were untouched (Huntress, 2026-10-16).

Huntress says the unauthorized sign-ins with the credential were tightly bunched across the morning of 2026-10-15 UTC, the last confirmed successful sign-in it observed was at 08:44 UTC, and it saw only failed attempts afterwards in the tenants where it can read sign-in logs (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, which leave no audit record, and in the two tenants Huntress reviewed it found no evidence of mailbox or file manipulation or of user or policy changes (Huntress, 2026-10-16). The check for planted credentials therefore has to cover every application registration and enterprise application in the tenant, and a clean audit log does not exclude directory reads. ConnectWise's latest readable update (2026-10-19 01:15 UTC) gives no restoration time (ConnectWise, 2026-10-19).

Improvement21 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Sophos X-Ops independently observed the token requests: on 2026-10-15 a single virtual private server authenticated as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application and requested app-only Microsoft Graph tokens for about 96 minutes, from 07:11 UTC, in strictly ascending tenant-ID order, one to six minutes apart, using Python HTTP-library user agents, and the sweep included tenants with no active backup subscription (Sophos X-Ops, 2026-10-19). Sophos found no hands-on-keyboard activity and no evidence that the application created new secrets, applications, consents or role assignments in the tenants it reviewed, which differs from the role grants and added secrets Huntress reports in other tenants; Sophos says it is unclear how the credential was obtained and what was done with the tokens (Sophos X-Ops, 2026-10-19). The two vendors' sweep timings differ: Huntress puts the first app sign-ins at 06:13 to 08:34 UTC on 2026-10-15 with tenants taken in sorted GUID order a few seconds apart (Huntress, 2026-10-16), where Sophos gives about 96 minutes from 07:11 UTC, one to six minutes apart; the vantage points differ, so both are reported as stated.

Update22 Oct 2026 03:46 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelbodyentitiesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, was responsible for the compromise. It says AI agents running the ARTEX framework kept signing in to customer tenants as the ConnectWise applications, without an interactive user sign-in, and in multiple tenants went on to Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to change privileges (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). It counts attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants and links the activity to an automated cross-tenant password spray between 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-14 against 327 accounts at eight organizations, from the same network range and including an address that ConnectWise's advisory later listed among its indicators; the spray peaked on 2026-10-11 at 2,900 failed logons a minute and produced no successful authentication (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Microsoft warns that the application credential changes can remain active as a backdoor after the vendor application is remediated, and asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, together with the Entra audit trail for credential additions, role assignments, consents and owner changes (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Expel, which analysed the activity separately, relays the attribution, notes that ConnectWise's fix leaves secrets planted on other applications in place and that Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record, and says Huntress has not tied its Global Administrator observation to the same operator (Expel, 2026-10-21). ConnectWise itself says that, based on the evidence available to it, including threat intelligence shared by Microsoft, it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and used an openly available agentic AI framework (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21). It began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21, expects it to take several days, says the start of restoration does not mean all capabilities are available, and tells partners to keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to their service, while noting that its actions do not remove unauthorized access already established in individual customer tenants (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21; heise online, 2026-10-21).

Correction25 Oct 2026 13:43 UTCrun 2026-10-25T1308Z-auditbodyevidence

The update of 2026-10-22 attached a rate of 2,900 attempts a minute to the ARTEX sign-ins against more than 2,250 tenants. Microsoft gives no rate for those sign-ins: 2,900 a minute is the peak of failed logons in the separate password spray of 10 to 14 October, reached on 11 October (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). The figure now sits with the spray.

Improvement27 Oct 2026 03:46 UTCrun 2026-10-27T0256Z-intelevidencesourcessourcing_note

Huntress published its analysis of what drove the 2026-10-15 activity on 2026-10-26, working from Entra sign-in and directory audit logs in the tenants it monitors. It says its telemetry aligns with Microsoft's Storm-0940 and ARTEX account without independently confirming it, that it is highly confident an operator, a person or an LLM, adapted the tooling between runs, and that its confidence that an LLM was involved in the escalation tooling is low to medium on its own telemetry and medium to high once Microsoft's attribution is included (Huntress, 2026-10-26). Its evidence for adaptation: a certificate upload that failed on a thumbprint mismatch ended one run with no retry, and the next run 55 seconds later retried the same error with growing waits until it worked; in a second tenant that refused removal of the Global Administrator role, the actor granted a different role to a sibling principal and the original service principal was then deleted (Huntress, 2026-10-26). Microsoft Graph reads are not recorded in the Entra audit log and no victim Huntress knows of had Graph activity logging enabled, so a clean audit log does not show that no Graph access took place (Huntress, 2026-10-26). Huntress recommends alerting when a service principal assigns itself Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator, deletes itself, or when one vendor principal grants a role to a sibling, and turning on Graph activity logs where licensing allows (Huntress, 2026-10-26).

Update29 Oct 2026 04:59 UTCrun 2026-10-29T0255Z-intelupdated_atsourcesevidenceactionsbody

ConnectWise's status page announced on 2026-10-28 at 17:09 UTC, after restoration in controlled phases had begun on 2026-10-21, that it is beginning phased restoration for partners, starting with Microsoft 365 backups and restores through a new, security-hardened application, with other features returning in phases over the coming days (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28). Partners must re-authorize each Microsoft 365 tenant using the new application, “ConnectWise Cloud Backup for M365”, to resume backup and restore operations, and ConnectWise points to its Trust Center for the detailed instructions (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28). Before that, from 2026-10-26, it had said it would first enable a process to restore data from existing backups and then phased re-enrollment, and it still told partners to keep affected connections disabled until instructions applied to their service (ConnectWise status page, 2026-10-28).

entries.summary: ConnectWise says it identified unauthorized access to application identities of its Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) service; Huntress and Todyl report that from 15 October the app's credential was used to obtain app-only Microsoft Graph tokens in customer Microsoft 365 tenants; Huntress alone confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants by 16 October and saw ConnectWise Cloud Management apps assign themselves directory roles in about 50 tenants and, in two tenants, a scripted Global Administrator self-grant followed by new client secrets planted on apparently random applications. ConnectWise disabled seven application identities and suspended the service on 17 October, but says disabling does not reverse changes already made in a tenant, so every tenant that ever consented a ConnectWise or SkyKick app needs the apps disabled and its application credentials, directory roles and consents reviewed. Microsoft assesses that the China-state aligned actor Storm-0940 is behind it, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework, and says it attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants; how the credential was obtained and what data was read are not public.

Huntress's update of 2026-10-19 reports a second tenant with scripted post-compromise activity (the application granting itself Global Administrator and planting a secret on other applications, the choice of applications apparently random), bounds the sign-in activity to the morning of 2026-10-15 UTC with the last successful sign-in at 08:44 UTC, and says Graph directory reads leave no audit record; the secret check therefore has to cover every application.

Sophos X-Ops reports the same token sweep from its own telemetry, from a single server in ascending tenant order and including tenants with no active backup subscription, and found no planted secrets, applications, consents or role assignments in the tenants it reviewed, unlike Huntress's two tenants.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, was responsible for the compromise, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants after an automated password spray from the same network range, and warns that credential changes planted in tenants can persist after the vendor application is remediated. ConnectWise itself says it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21.

Corrects the 2026-10-22 update: Microsoft's 2,900-a-minute figure is the peak of failed logons in the separate 10 to 14 October password spray, not the rate of the ARTEX sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants.

Huntress's analysis of 2026-10-26 reads the activity as scripted tooling steered by an operator, rates LLM involvement low to medium on its own telemetry, adds a detection for service principals that assign themselves or a sibling a directory role, and notes that Graph reads leave no Entra audit record.

The text on the vendor tenant is corrected: the name 'ConnectWise S-K LLC' and the claim that Todyl says all SkyKick apps come from one vendor tenant are removed.
