entries.headline: Oracle's October CPU: six unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 rows, two WebLogic 9.8 flaws; EBS decoys probed on 27 Oct
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-87337 +11updatedNATOA2

Oracle October 2026 Critical Patch Update: six unauthenticated network CVSS 10.0 rows in Access Manager, SOA Suite, E-Business Suite and JD Edwards, and WebLogic CVSS 9.8 flaws reachable over HTTP and T3/IIOP

Oracle's Critical Patch Update advisory of 2026-10-20 contains 1295 new security patches (Oracle, 2026-10-20). Its risk matrices score 112 rows at CVSS 3.1 9.0 or higher, and 90 of those, covering 73 distinct CVE ids, are marked as remotely exploitable without authentication with a network attack vector (Oracle, 2026-10-20). Six rows score 10.0: CVE-2026-87337 in the Access Manager Authentication Engine (HTTP), CVE-2026-91231 in the SOA Suite Adapters (HTTP), CVE-2026-91216 and CVE-2026-91221 in the SOA Suite Fabric Layer (T3 and IIOP), CVE-2026-101809 in the E-Business Suite Workflow Notification Mailer (HTTP, 12.2.3 to 12.2.15) and CVE-2026-91299 in the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Orchestrator security component (HTTP, 9.2.0.0 to 9.2.26.5) (Oracle, 2026-10-20). WebLogic Server 12.2.1.4.0, 14.1.1.0.0, 14.1.2.0.0 and 15.1.1.0.0 carry CVE-2026-91323 (HTTP) and CVE-2026-83399 (T3 and IIOP) at 9.8 and CVE-2026-87302 (HTTP) at 9.1; Identity Manager's End User Self Service has CVE-2026-91408 (T3 and IIOP, 9.8) and Access Manager's SAML path CVE-2026-87251 (9.8) (Oracle, 2026-10-20). The advisory states no exploitation for any row and carries only Oracle's standing sentence that it receives reports of attempts to exploit already-patched flaws (Oracle, 2026-10-20); for CVE-2026-101767, Defused's decoys have since recorded exploit attempts, described in the update below. Oracle points to My Oracle Support documents for patch availability (Oracle, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
A WebLogic, SOA Suite, Access Manager or Identity Manager server whose HTTP, T3 or IIOP listener, or SAML endpoint, answers from a network that is not the management network; an E-Business Suite 12.2.3 to 12.2.15 web tier with the Workflow Notification Mailer, or whose URL firewall allows the Thin Client Framework servlet, as the default configuration does (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-20); a JD Edwards EnterpriseOne 9.2 server with the Orchestrator. The product version comes from the product's own version command or the inventory.
Detection
Oracle names no indicator. For the E-Business Suite flaw CVE-2026-101767, Horizon3 lists unauthenticated POST requests to the Thin Client Framework servlet followed by backend database activity, SQL reconnaissance shortly after unauthenticated web requests, and the oracle account spawning a shell through the Concurrent Manager (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-20). Otherwise watch web and application-server access logs and the WebLogic and SOA server logs for requests to the affected components from untrusted sources, T3 and IIOP connections from unexpected networks in flow or load-balancer logs, and Java process-creation events where the middleware process spawns a shell, an interpreter or a download tool.
Defender takeaway
Apply the October 2026 update to the six 10.0 components first wherever they are reachable beyond the management network, together with any E-Business Suite web tier exposed to CVE-2026-101767, whose chain Horizon3 has described, then to the WebLogic and Identity Manager rows; where a patch cannot go in at once, remove the Thin Client Framework servlet from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict the EBS web tier to trusted networks (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-20). Oracle's next scheduled update is the Critical Security Patch Update of 17 November 2026 (Oracle, 2026-10-20).
Improvement25 Oct 2026 14:09 UTCrun 2026-10-25T1308Z-auditcvestechniquessourcessourcing_notebody

Horizon3, which reported CVE-2026-101767 to Oracle on 2026-07-24, described the chain on release day, without publishing exploit code. An unauthenticated SQL injection in the Thin Client Framework servlet of E-Business Suite 12.2.3 to 12.2.15 (Application Object Library, Core component, CVSS 3.1 9.8), which the default EBS URL firewall configuration permits, gives SQL execution as the APPS database user and then operating-system commands as the EBS application account (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-20). Until the update is in, Horizon3 advises removing the servlet from the URL firewall allowlist and restricting the web tier to trusted networks, measures that reduce exposure but do not replace patching (Horizon3.ai, 2026-10-20). Oracle scores the row 9.8, unauthenticated over HTTP (Oracle, 2026-10-20).

Update29 Oct 2026 04:56 UTCrun 2026-10-29T0255Z-intelheadlinesummaryupdated_atsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Threat-intelligence firm Defused reported that its Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploit attempts against CVE-2026-101767 on the morning of 2026-10-27, one week after the October update (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-28; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-28). BleepingComputer notes that Oracle has not tagged the flaw as exploited and that Shadowserver tracks more than 670 internet-exposed E-Business Suite instances, without saying how many are decoys or already patched (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-28). SecurityWeek adds that there have been no other reports of in-the-wild exploitation; the attempts hit decoys, and neither article describes a compromise of a production system (SecurityWeek, 2026-10-28).

entries.headline: VMware vCenter's pre-auth Syslog RCE is exploited; patch it with the auth bypass and VMXNET3 escape, no workaround
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-59309 +4exploitedupdatedNATOA1

VMSA-2026-0006, VMware vCenter: unauthenticated Directory Service auth bypass and Syslog traversal RCE (both CVSS 9.8), plus a VMXNET3 guest-to-host escape

Broadcom published VMSA-2026-0006 on 2026-07-29, covering five vulnerabilities across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation and Fusion, and stating that they "were privately reported to Broadcom" with updates available to remediate them (Broadcom, 2026-07-29). Three national CERTs picked it up immediately: NCSC-CH on 2026-07-29 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-07-29), NCSC-NL on 2026-07-29 (NCSC-NL, 2026-07-29), and BSI CERT-Bund, whose advisory is dated 2026-07-28 with a 2026-07-29 revision (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-07-29).

Two of the five sit on vCenter and need no credentials. CVE-2026-59309 (CVSS 9.8) is an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service, and Broadcom's own attack-vector text is unambiguous about the prerequisite: "a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system" (Broadcom, 2026-07-29). CVE-2026-59310, also CVSS 9.8, is a directory-traversal flaw in vCenter's Syslog server that reaches arbitrary code execution through manipulated file and directory paths (Broadcom, 2026-07-29). vCenter is the control plane for an entire virtual estate: an unauthenticated path into it is a path to every workload it manages, which is why an anonymous network-reachable bypass warranted out-of-cycle handling even though no exploitation had been reported at first publication. CVE-2026-59310 has since been exploited in the wild, as the updates below record.

The third flaw crosses the isolation boundary in the other direction. CVE-2026-47876 (CVSS 9.3) is an out-of-bounds write in the VMXNET3 virtual network adapter, and Broadcom scopes it precisely: "a malicious actor with local administrative privileges on a virtual machine with VMXNET3 virtual network adapter may exploit this issue to execute code on the host. Non VMXNET3 virtual adapters are not affected by this issue" (Broadcom, 2026-07-29). That precondition is the useful part of the triage: exposure is determined by adapter configuration rather than by ESX version alone, so the inventory question is which guests run VMXNET3 and how much you trust whoever administers them.

Two lower-severity issues complete the advisory. CVE-2026-41703 is an out-of-bounds read that Broadcom scores differently by product: 7.6 on ESX, where it says a denial of service of the host process is the more likely outcome than information disclosure, against 2.7 on Workstation and Fusion, where it restricts the impact to information disclosure (Broadcom, 2026-07-29). CVE-2026-41709 is insufficient logging on ESX that allows an administrator to act without the action being recorded (Broadcom, 2026-07-29); CrowdStrike says WARP PANDA exploited it as a zero-day and CISA lists it as exploited, so ESX audit logs are not a complete record of administrator activity.

Two further product families are in scope: Broadcom lists VMware Telco Cloud Platform and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure as impacted, with their own knowledge-base fix path rather than the vCenter and ESXi build numbers below (Broadcom, 2026-07-29).

Fixed builds differ per flaw and per track. vCenter takes 9.1.0.0300, 9.0.2.0100, 8.0 U3k or, on the U2 branch, 8.0 U2f, with Cloud Foundation 5.x served by an async patch to 8.0 U3k; the VMXNET3 escape is fixed in ESXi-9.1.0.0200, ESXi-9.0.2.0100, ESXi80U3k and ESXi80U2f, and the 7.0 lines are served only under Broadcom extended support (Broadcom, 2026-08-19). Broadcom records no workaround for any of the five, which removes the usual option of mitigating while the maintenance window is arranged.

At first publication nothing here was reported exploited. Broadcom states the vulnerabilities "were privately reported to Broadcom" and credits Atredis Partners, Nguyen Hoang Thach of STARLabs SG working with Pwn2Own held by the Zero Day Initiative, Maxim Suhanov, and CrowdStrike (Broadcom, 2026-07-29), and none of the three national CERTs reported in-the-wild activity. What earned this out-of-cycle attention at publication was the reachability profile rather than an exploitation signal: two anonymous network paths into a virtualization control plane, with no interim control available. CVE-2026-59310 and CVE-2026-41709 have since been reported exploited, as the updates below record.

Detection on the vCenter side means watching the two named services rather than the appliance generally: authentication events from the Directory Service, where a successful bind that no operator session accounts for is the signal, and Syslog-server request logging, where path-traversal sequences in a requested file or directory path have no legitimate counterpart. For the guest-to-host escape the telemetry is host-side: hypervisor crash and process-fault records on ESX hosts running VMXNET3 guests, since a failed escape attempt is far more likely to surface as an anomalous fault than as a clean compromise. On hardening, NCSC-NL is the source that spells out the architectural control: access to ESX and vCenter should be made available only from a separated management environment and not reachable directly from the internet or external networks (NCSC-NL, 2026-07-29). Broadcom's own advisory offers no hardening section and records "Workarounds: None" against every one of the five.

Update13 Aug 2026 04:58 UTCrun 2026-08-13T0412Z-intelactionscvesevidenceregionssectorssourcestagstechniquesbody

One of the five VMSA-2026-0006 flaws, none of which was reported exploited at disclosure, has now been confirmed in use against real estates.

QUIRSO, a German security firm, reports that an incident-response engagement gave it visibility into an exploitation campaign against internet-accessible vCenter systems using CVE-2026-59310, the CVSS 9.8 directory traversal in the vCenter Syslog server that reaches arbitrary code execution from network access alone (QUIRSO, 2026-08-10). The timeline is the part that should reset patch priorities: "Compromised systems identified by QUIRSO were found to first establish contact with the attacker's domains on August 3, five days after Broadcom publicly disclosed the flaw" (The Hacker News, 2026-08-12). QUIRSO records 361 unique victim IP addresses across 47 countries, with Germany, the United States, Turkey, Iran and France the most affected and 185 of the 361 addresses in those five countries; it is explicit that an address does not correspond to an organisation, since some belong to hosting providers and shared infrastructure. By 5 August, 343 of the 361 addresses had already appeared: the campaign reached roughly 95 per cent of its observed footprint within three days of starting (QUIRSO, 2026-08-10). QUIRSO assesses that while the attacker might have had prior knowledge of the flaw, the correlation with disclosure suggests the advisory itself was the campaign's starting point.

Switzerland's NCSC updated its own VMSA-2026-0006 advisory on 12 August, setting "Current exploitation status: Actively Exploited" and citing QUIRSO's report (NCSC-CH, 2026-08-12).

What the attacker does after landing. The chain reported is path-traversal activity consistent with the flaw, "followed by the deployment of a malicious cron job to establish persistence on the host using reverse_ssh" (The Hacker News, 2026-08-12), an open-source SSH-based reverse-shell framework whose legitimate penetration-testing features include automatic connect-back, port forwarding and file transfer. The choice is a deliberate one about direction of travel: the control channel is established outbound from the appliance, which sidesteps controls built to stop unsolicited inbound access (QUIRSO, 2026-08-10). QUIRSO says a follow-up publication examining the attacker's tradecraft, infrastructure and post-exploitation activity is planned, and that further detection content is being released in coordination with law-enforcement partners.

A second, separate signal sits alongside it and should not be merged with the first. The Hacker News reports Defused Cyber observing a spike in scanning against vCenter (version probes and walks of the single-sign-on flow) that it associates with CVE-2026-59309, the unauthenticated Directory Service authentication bypass from the same advisory. QUIRSO's co-founder Denis Szadkowski told the outlet there is not enough evidence to correlate that scanning with the intrusion set behind CVE-2026-59310, adding that "the forensic evidence strongly points toward CVE-2026-59310 as the initial access vector" for the compromises QUIRSO investigated (The Hacker News, 2026-08-12). Two flaws in one advisory are drawing attention independently; only one has confirmed compromises behind it.

Detection concepts, telemetry class first. The behaviours worth hunting are all unusual for a management appliance rather than unusual in general. In egress and flow records, an SSH-protocol session initiated from a vCenter appliance to an external destination inverts the normal direction of vCenter traffic, which is inbound administrative access and outbound management of hosts. In configuration and scheduling state on the appliance, cron or scheduled entries that no platform-engineering change record accounts for are the persistence artefact reported here. In process telemetry, execution lineage descending from the Syslog service is the exploitation artefact. QUIRSO's own framing of the tool is the right calibration and applies to any dual-use binary: "The presence of reverse_ssh should not, by itself, be treated as proof of malicious activity." and "In combination with unauthorized installation, unexpected outbound connections or execution on a vulnerable vCenter appliance, however, it is a high-priority indicator requiring investigation." (QUIRSO, 2026-08-10)

Triage: administrators do legitimately place scheduled jobs on appliances and do run SSH from jump hosts, so neither artefact alone resolves. What separates this activity is the appliance being the SSH client toward an external network, a scheduled entry created outside a change window and not present in the platform team's configuration baseline, and either appearing on a vCenter whose build predates the VMSA-2026-0006 fixes. On an appliance patched before 29 July none of the three should be present at all.

Defender takeaway
VCenter is a single control point over an entire virtual estate, and this flaw needs nothing but network reach to it. Broadcom offers no workaround, so version state is the only preventive control; but for any appliance that was reachable and unpatched between 29 July and now, the five-day disclosure-to-exploitation gap and the three-day saturation curve mean an upgrade closes the door without answering whether anyone already walked through it. Treat that window as a compromise-assessment scope, not a patching backlog item.
Update28 Aug 2026 05:20 UTCrun 2026-08-28T0409Z-intelcvestagstechniquessourcesevidencebody

CISA added CVE-2026-59310 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-18, a jurisdiction-agnostic confirmation of active exploitation, independent of any US-FCEB remediation deadline, layered on top of NCSC-CH's own actively-exploited determination already recorded above.

QUIRSO's continued work on the campaign now attributes the activity to a suspected China-nexus actor and reports that Babuk-derived ransomware was deployed against ESXi hosts in at least one investigated case (The Hacker News, 2026-08-17). Infosecurity Magazine had reported only QUIRSO's earlier assessment that "a suspected advanced persistent threat (APT) actor was responsible" (Infosecurity Magazine, citing QUIRSO GmbH, 2026-08-13). The ransomware deployment is assessed by QUIRSO as plausibly a smokescreen rather than the operation's goal: the deployment of "the locker", the Babuk-derived payload, "may not have been the primary objective of the campaign" (The Hacker News, paraphrasing QUIRSO's assessment, 2026-08-17), plausibly intended to encrypt ESXi log files and hinder forensics rather than for extortion.

Both findings warrant the same caveat as the CVE-2026-59309 scanning correlation: every outlet surveyed (The Hacker News, Infosecurity Magazine, and further security-press pickup) cites QUIRSO's own Medium write-ups as the sole source for the China-nexus attribution (built on a UTC+08:00 activity pattern, Chinese-language code artefacts, and reuse of a Chinese security publication) at QUIRSO's own stated moderate confidence, and for the ransomware finding. Two outlets reporting one firm's conclusion is wide distribution of a single assessor's work, not independent corroboration of it: the attribution and the ransomware-deployment finding should be read as QUIRSO's own assessment, not as cross-verified intelligence; the multi-CERT corroboration covers the vulnerability and initial-exploitation facts only.

Nothing in this update changes the remediation guidance already given above: patch every internet-reachable vCenter to the fixed builds, and treat any instance that was internet-reachable and unpatched between 29 July and 3 August as a compromise-assessment candidate rather than a patch-and-close item; that assessment should now explicitly include a check for Babuk-derived encrypted files on any ESXi hosts the appliance manages, alongside the reverse_ssh persistence and cron-entry artefacts already described.

CVE-2026-59310, the vCenter Syslog traversal, has been exploited in the wild since before the update of 2026-08-13, and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-18 (CISA KEV). The patch guidance is unchanged, and the compromise check in the actions applies to any vCenter that was exposed and unpatched.

The Directory Service authentication bypass may not be far behind. On one compromised vCenter appliance that QUIRSO analysed, the evidence shows malicious activity consistent with exploitation of CVE-2026-59309 as early as 2026-08-01, followed by the creation of an administrative account on vCenter, with no login events for the legitimate administrator account used to create it (The Hacker News, 2026-08-17). That is one appliance and a "consistent with" finding, and CVE-2026-59309 is not in CISA's KEV catalog, so its status here stays patch-available. On an exposed vCenter, an administrative account created without a matching administrator login is the signal to look for.

entries.summary: Broadcom's VMSA-2026-0006 (2026-07-29) fixes five flaws across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation and Fusion, and NCSC-CH, NCSC-NL and BSI CERT-Bund all carried it across 2026-07-28 and 2026-07-29. CVE-2026-59309 (CVSS 9.8) is an authentication bypass in vCenter's Directory Service reachable with nothing but network access to vCenter, and CVE-2026-59310 (CVSS 9.8) is a directory traversal in vCenter's Syslog server that reaches arbitrary code execution. CVE-2026-47876 (CVSS 9.3) is an out-of-bounds write in the VMXNET3 virtual network adapter that lets a guest administrator execute code on the ESX host, affecting only VMs using that adapter. No workaround exists for any of the five, so patching is the only control. All were reported privately to Broadcom, one of them through Pwn2Own, and CVE-2026-59310 has since been exploited in the wild and was added to CISA's KEV catalog on 2026-08-18; CISA also listed the ESX logging flaw CVE-2026-41709 as exploited on 2026-10-28, the day CrowdStrike said the actor WARP PANDA used it as a zero-day.

updates.summary: CVE-2026-59310, the CVSS 9.8 directory-traversal-to-code-execution flaw in the VMware vCenter Syslog server that Broadcom fixed in VMSA-2026-0006 and that this pipeline covered on 2026-07-30 as reported unexploited, is under active exploitation. German firm QUIRSO, working an incident-response engagement, identified 361 unique victim IP addresses across 47 countries whose first contact with attacker infrastructure came on 3 August (five days after public disclosure) with persistence established through a cron entry launching the open-source reverse_ssh tool for an outbound control channel. Switzerland's NCSC updated its VMSA-2026-0006 advisory to actively exploited on 12 August. No workaround exists; patching is the only remediation, and an unpatched internet-reachable vCenter now warrants a compromise assessment rather than an upgrade alone.

CISA added CVE-2026-59310 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-18. QUIRSO's continued investigation of the exploitation campaign this entry already tracks now reports a suspected China-nexus attribution and, in at least one case, deployment of Babuk-derived ransomware against ESXi hosts, but both findings trace to QUIRSO's own investigation alone; no independent assessor has corroborated either, and they are recorded here as QUIRSO's assessment rather than established fact.

The summary still said none of the five flaws was reported exploited; CVE-2026-59310 has been exploited in the wild since before the 2026-08-13 update and was added to CISA's KEV catalog on 2026-08-18. entries.headline: F5 BIG-IP is affected by PHP2Shell: fixes are in 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4; APM data plane and TMUI exposed
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, F5 BIG-IP: the PHP2Shell flaws reach the Configuration utility of every module and the APM and SSL Orchestrator access profiles on 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0, and F5's cumulative critical releases 17.1.3.7, 17.5.1.11 and 21.1.0.4 carry the fix

F5's release notes for BIG-IP 17.1.3.7, 21.1.0.4 and 17.5.1.11, each updated on 2026-10-24, list K000163821 as the reference for the fix of the PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and describe each build as a critical release whose only new changes are PHP vulnerability fixes and which is cumulative and includes earlier hardened and critical releases (F5, 2026-10-24; F5, 2026-10-24; F5, 2026-10-24). NCSC-NL records F5 as confirming that BIG-IP 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 and 21.1.0 are vulnerable through the Configuration utility control plane in all modules and, for APM and SSL Orchestrator, through the access-profile data plane, and that earlier affected releases stay vulnerable until updated (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-26). CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited since 2026-10-26; nothing found reports an attack on BIG-IP (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A BIG-IP on 17.1.0 to 17.1.3, 17.5.0 to 17.5.1 or 21.1.0 whose Configuration utility is reachable from a network the attacker can reach, or that publishes an APM or SSL Orchestrator access profile (NCSC-NL, 2026-10-26).
Detection
F5's article on exploitation and mitigations could not be read and no indicator is published in the sources found. The telemetry to review on an exposed system is access to the Configuration utility and the access-profile web paths from untrusted sources, and shells or downloads started by the web service; this is an inference, not an F5 statement.
Defender takeaway
Move to the cumulative critical release of your train and read K000163821 in a browser for F5's own mitigation list; until then keep the Configuration utility off untrusted networks, and treat an APM or SSL Orchestrator system that was exposed and unpatched as needing a compromise check.

entries.headline: SafeDep and JFrog: the testmetest npm worm now runs on import, so --ignore-scripts does not stop it; 42 repos armed
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

testmetest: an npm worm in the Miasma and Shai-Hulud family now starts when an application imports the package, so install with --ignore-scripts no longer protects, and JFrog finds 42 third-party GitHub repositories already armed with its publisher

SafeDep counts 19 npm packages from the same operator between 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-27, eight of them published through four npm accounts, that carry a worm sharing code with the June Miasma worm and adding the token-revocation wiper of Mini Shai-Hulud; SafeDep has not confirmed the lineage, and JFrog says its evidence does not establish that the original Miasma operators are responsible (SafeDep, 2026-10-27; JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26). The install trigger has changed twice: first a command expansion in a binding.gyp file, with no install script; then a postinstall script that loads a native addon which decodes and starts the worm; and, since SafeDep's update of 27 October, an addon that runs when an application imports the package, so a hardening step that disables install scripts does not stop it (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).

The payload exits on CIS locales and in known analysis sandboxes. It steals SSH keys, registry and Git credentials, .env files, browser logins, AI-tool, cloud, Vault and Kubernetes secrets and GitHub Actions secrets read from runner memory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). It exfiltrates by committing encrypted data, with the victim's encrypted GitHub token, to a new public repository in the victim's own account, injects a GitLab CI job that requests npm and PyPI OIDC tokens, adds its loader to the victim's npm packages and publishes new patch versions, republishes to PyPI and RubyGems, commits a fake CodeQL workflow and AI-agent configuration files that infect the host again, and copies itself over SSH to the hosts in known_hosts (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). A persistence service checks the stolen GitHub token every 45 seconds for 48 hours and on an authentication failure deletes the home directory (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). JFrog found 42 armed third-party GitHub repositories of 11 legitimate owners with hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, and says the payload blobs were large enough to evade GitHub's search and API paths (JFrog Security Research, 2026-10-26).

Exposure
Any developer endpoint, build agent or CI runner that installed or imported one of the operator's packages, and any GitHub or GitLab account whose token such a host held (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Detection
In package metadata, a binding.gyp whose sources field runs node in a package with no C or C++ sources, a postinstall that requires a .node file and discards errors beside a large high-entropy file, and prebuilt addons with no native source; on endpoints and CI runners, a node process that downloads or finds and runs the Bun runtime and a child node process started from a temporary path named after its process ID; in GitHub and GitLab audit logs, a new public repository in a developer's own account with a generic project description, commits with a fixed automated-sync message, commits that add AI-assistant configuration files (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .vscode tasks, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md), an injected CI job that requests OIDC tokens, and unexpected patch releases of your own packages (SafeDep, 2026-10-27).
Defender takeaway
An install that ran with scripts disabled is not clean once the package has been imported; for an affected host SafeDep's order is to disconnect it, remove persistence first, rotate all credentials, check the accounts for the repositories and commits above and reinstall the operating system (SafeDep, 2026-10-27). Because the wiper is triggered by the token's revocation, the host is isolated and cleaned before the GitHub token is revoked.

entries.headline: ESET: an emailed RAR ran code on MDaemon servers via ClamAV's UnRAR; fixed in MDaemon 26.0.4, ClamAV 1.4.6 and 1.5.4
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2025-8088exploitedNATOB2

MDaemon mail server below 26.0.4 and Windows ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3: a crafted RAR emailed to any address runs code on the server through the bundled UnRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088, and ESET saw Russia-aligned attackers use it in Ukraine to deploy the HELLAGE and HELLTAG backdoors

ESET reports an active campaign in Ukraine in which Russia-aligned attackers exploited MDaemon mail servers and deployed two backdoor families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). MDaemon uses ClamAV to scan attachments of incoming mail; old ClamAV versions carry CVE-2025-8088, the WinRAR path-traversal flaw ESET uncovered last year, which ESET says was fixed in ClamAV's source on 27 July 2025 (the release notes below date the fixed ClamAV builds 2026-08-07), while MDaemon kept shipping an old libclamunrar.dll until MDaemon 26.0.4 of 2026-08-25 (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). The chain ESET describes: a crafted RAR archive is mailed to any address at a vulnerable server, MDaemon invokes ClamAV to scan it, and the exploit writes a malicious DLL to the server's file system with no user interaction, so the message carries no lure (ESET Research, 2026-10-28). CERT-UA names the backdoors: HELLAGE steals email messages and other data, talks to a hardcoded server and can deploy more malware, and HELLTAG takes commands, transfers files and does reconnaissance through a hardcoded Telegram bot; ESET cannot attribute the campaign to a known Russia-aligned actor (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

The exposure is wider than MDaemon. ClamAV's release notes of 2026-08-07 say it adopted the upstream UnRAR fix for CVE-2025-8088, which rejects path separators in NTFS alternate data stream names so that extraction cannot leave ClamAV's temporary scan directory on Windows, and that the issue affects ClamAV 0.101.0 through 1.5.3 with the fix in 1.4.6 and 1.5.4 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07). CISA has listed CVE-2025-8088 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 2025-08-12 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
An MDaemon server on Windows below 26.0.4 that accepts inbound mail (ESET Research, 2026-10-28), and any other Windows host that scans mail or files with ClamAV 0.101.0 to 1.5.3 (ClamAV, 2026-08-07).
Detection
Because the attack needs no lure, the mail log shows an ordinary message with a RAR attachment. The telemetry that matters is file creation of a DLL by the ClamAV or mail-service scanning process outside ClamAV's temporary scan directory, inbound RAR attachments whose member names carry alternate-data-stream syntax with path separators, and the mail service process starting unexpected children or connecting to Telegram's bot interface; these follow from the described chain and are not an ESET detection list. An update does not remove a DLL or backdoor that was already written, so check the server after patching.
Defender takeaway
Patch the mail scanning path first on any internet-facing Windows mail server, then look for unexpected DLLs and persistence and treat stored mail as exposed, since HELLAGE steals email (ESET Research, 2026-10-28).

NOTABLENATOB2

Huntress: phished MDM enrolments in Hexnode and Rippling give attackers a management path that brings ScreenConnect back after it has been removed

Huntress reports several recent incidents in which attackers used legitimate mobile-device-management platforms, not flaws in them, as a trusted management path, naming Hexnode and Rippling as the two it saw and noting the list is not definitive (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the first case, proposal-themed emails led a user to download an MSI named like a DocuSign installer that installed Hexnode components (gateway, agent and PostgreSQL components); ScreenConnect followed shortly after and connected to an attacker relay, the managed-service provider removed it, and it came back several hours later to the same relay while the Hexnode client was still installed (Huntress, 2026-10-28). In the second, a receptionist clicked a link in an email about tax planning that led to a fake Teams calendar page; about a minute later a Rippling enrolment registry key appeared, the agent was downloaded into a SYSTEM profile path and installed with SYSTEM rights, and about 35 minutes after that the attacker used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A managed Windows endpoint whose user can run an installer or follow an enrolment link, in an organisation without an inventory of its authorised MDM tenants, agents and RMM instances (Huntress, 2026-10-28).
Detection
The chain Huntress describes as a stronger signal is social engineering, then a new MDM enrolment, then an RMM installation, then outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay, correlated across identity, MDM, endpoint and network telemetry; in endpoint telemetry that is an MSI run from a browser download folder that installs an MDM agent, an enrolment registry key on a device nobody enrolled, a new SYSTEM-level agent in a vendor directory shortly after a click, and an RMM installed by that agent (Huntress, 2026-10-28). A repeat of the same RMM relay after the RMM was removed, as in the Hexnode case, points to a remaining MDM client as a possible source (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Triage: a corporate enrolment started by IT looks similar in process telemetry; the discriminators are a tenant that is not in the authorised inventory, a trigger that is an emailed link or a user-run installer instead of IT's enrolment workflow, and an RMM install within minutes (an inference from Huntress's two cases).

Defender takeaway
Treat an unexpected MDM enrolment as a security event and keep an inventory of authorised tenants; after removing a rogue RMM, unenrol the device from the unauthorised tenant, disable accounts the attacker created, revoke sessions and tokens, reset credentials and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed, as Huntress advises (Huntress, 2026-10-28).

Huntress says the products are not at fault and that removing the RMM does not remove the management architecture behind it.

entries.headline: Machelen municipality: foothold from a website's misleading instructions, 22 days to detection; Rhysida lists its files
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOA2

Machelen (Belgium) municipality: its own timeline shows a foothold through misleading instructions on an external website on 2026-08-20, found 22 days later after a high-privilege user was reached, with personal data confirmed stolen and Rhysida now listing municipal and social-welfare files

Machelen's own timeline records that on 2026-08-20 attackers gained access to an internal laptop through misleading instructions on an external website, explored it extensively from 24 August to 1 September, and on 10 September had access to a user with high access rights and other IT systems; the municipality found the incident on 11 September, isolated all systems, reported to the Belgian CCB-CERT, restarted part of its systems from a backup of a safe date on 14 September and recorded the first evidence of leaked data on 17 September (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22). It confirms that personal data was leaked and says the scope is still being investigated (Municipality of Machelen, 2026-09-22); the mayor had said on 14 September that no personal data appeared to be affected, and ITdaily reports that this proved wrong (ITdaily, 2026-09-23). Ransomware.live recorded on 2026-10-27 that Rhysida listed Machelen on its leak site, describing the listing as municipal and social-welfare file servers of about 1.3 million files, with client files that include passports and identity cards, nursing-home medical files and civil-status records, which are the group's own claims (Ransomware.live, 2026-10-27).

Detection
The timeline puts 22 days between first access and detection, with the first laptop explored from 24 August to 1 September; it names neither the website nor the commands, so the telemetry to review includes endpoint process creation after a user followed instructions on a web page and later use of a high-privilege account from that workstation, which is an inference from the timeline.
Defender takeaway
Treat a user who followed instructions from a website on a work laptop as a possible intrusion that can sit unseen for weeks; review high-privilege account activity from the user's workstation for the weeks after the event, not only the day it is reported.

entries.headline: Moldova: unauthenticated e-government services queried for about one million ID numbers; data on 750,000 extracted
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOA2

Moldova's government digital services: attackers used flaws in services reachable without authentication to query about one million national identification numbers and extract data on about 750,000 of them between 19 and 23 October, and the Prime Minister says AI allegedly helped find the flaws

Moldova's Electronic Governance Agency (AGE) reported on 2026-10-27 that between 19 and 23 October attackers queried about one million national identification numbers (IDNPs) through state digital services and that, on preliminary estimates, data sets for about 750,000 of them were extracted; MOLDPRES had put the access requests at about 11 million on 2026-10-24 (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27; MOLDPRES, 2026-10-24). AGE's technical explanation is that the attackers exploited vulnerabilities in services reachable without authentication and then used the data they obtained for further extractions; the first attacks hit an electronic service that logged the legal basis of processing incorrectly, which is why citizens saw entries for civil-status document requests and driving-licence issue in the data-access history of the EVO app (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27). Data that may be affected, not every category for every person, includes name, date and place of birth, first-degree relatives, insured status, family doctor, social benefits, pensions, disability, driving licence, photograph, vehicles and companies owned or run, IBAN, tax debts and payment history; AGE says card data is not held on the platform and it found no unauthorised change to state registers (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27).

AGE stopped the extraction on 23 October at 11:30, reviewed 82 digital services and suspended the exposed ones, and its timeline says 82 public services and more than 30 information systems and administration panels were disconnected as a precaution on 23 October; it blocked further attempts on 25 and 27 October, and the Prime Minister's account is that 30 of the 82 services were disconnected (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27; MOLDPRES, 2026-10-28). The Prime Minister says the incident is not isolated, that foreign state actors are being investigated and that the attackers automated the extraction, with the use of artificial intelligence allegedly facilitating the identification and exploitation of the vulnerabilities (MOLDPRES, 2026-10-28). Moldova has not attributed the attack to any country or group (The Record, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A public e-service of a federal, cantonal or communal administration that returns person data for an identifier without authentication, or whose output feeds other registers, since AGE says the extraction chained from unauthenticated services into further data (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27).
Detection
Citizens noticed the abuse because the data-access history in the EVO app showed processing for civil-status document requests and driving-licence issue that they had not made, so a data-subject-visible access log is a detection channel (Moldova Electronic Governance Agency, 2026-10-27). On the server side the relevant telemetry is per-service request volume and sequential or bulk identifier lookups from one source; the sources give no breakdown of the request pattern, so that is an inference from about 11 million requests against about one million numbers.
Defender takeaway
List the public services that answer for a person identifier without authentication and check what each one returns, whether it feeds other registers and whether its access log records the true purpose; rate limits and alerts on bulk lookups belong in front of every such service.

Builds on: An attacker defeated Switzerland's cantonal vehicle-registry rate limits at scale, and two…

The Prime Minister says foreign state involvement is being investigated and that AI allegedly helped find the flaws; Moldova has not attributed the attack, and the agency took 82 services under review and disconnected exposed services and more than 30 systems.

entries.headline: WatchGuard fixes three feature-dependent unauthenticated flaws scored 9.2 in Fireware OS; no exploitation known
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-93866 +6NATOA2

WatchGuard Fireware OS 2026.4, 12.12.4 and 12.5.22: seven of 17 fixed Fireware OS flaws are scored 9.0 or higher, among them unauthenticated memory-corruption and missing-authentication rows in the Access Portal, the SIP proxy and the FireCluster sync daemon; WatchGuard knows of no exploitation

WatchGuard's advisory listing of 2026-10-27 opens with 18 rows, 17 for Fireware OS and one for Mobile VPN with SSL Client for Windows, and seven of the 17 are scored 9.0 or higher (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). The fixes are in Fireware OS 2026.4, 12.12.4 and, for T15 and T35 models, 12.5.22. Three of the seven need no authentication but a specific feature. CVE-2026-93866 (9.2) is an integer overflow in the WebSocket handling of the Access Portal that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker write beyond the bounds of a heap buffer while the Access Portal is enabled (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-93857 (9.2) is a stack buffer overflow in the SIP proxy that gives remote code execution when a SIP proxy is configured on the Firebox (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-93865 (9.2) is missing authentication in the FireCluster synchronization daemon: a remote unauthenticated attacker invokes privileged administrative actions with a crafted request to the FireCluster management IP when clustering is enabled (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).

The other four need a network position. CVE-2026-112709 and CVE-2026-112710 (9.2 each) are heap overflows in the authentication service that give denial of service and possibly code execution to an attacker who controls or intercepts traffic to the configured Active Directory server and returns a crafted response (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-103594 (9.5) is a stack overflow in WireGuard configuration processing for a man-in-the-middle with TLS-decrypted access between a Firebox that acts as a FireCloud Gateway and WatchGuard Cloud (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). CVE-2026-103593 (9.1) is a stack overflow in the logging service that gives root code execution to a network-adjacent attacker who impersonates or intercepts traffic to the log server with a crafted certificate, in FIPS mode (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27). Six rows affect Fireware OS 2025.1 up to before 2026.4 and 12.0 up to before 12.12.4, T15 and T35 up to before 12.5.22, the WireGuard row starts at 2026.2 and 12.12, and each page states that WatchGuard is not aware of exploitation in the wild (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
A Firebox on a Fireware OS release inside those ranges with at least one of the listed features: the Access Portal, a SIP proxy policy, FireCluster membership, an Active Directory authentication server, the FireCloud Gateway role, or FIPS mode with an external log server; the three unauthenticated rows are reachable by any host that can reach the Access Portal, the SIP proxy policy or the cluster management address (WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27; WatchGuard PSIRT, 2026-10-27).
Detection
WatchGuard publishes no indicator and no workaround. For the three unauthenticated rows, connections to the cluster management address from hosts that are not cluster peers, WebSocket upgrade requests to the Access Portal from unexpected sources, SIP traffic from outside expected carriers, and restarts of the portal, SIP or sync services on the Firebox are the telemetry to review; this is an inference from the stated mechanisms.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed release on appliances with the Access Portal, a SIP proxy or clustering first; where an upgrade has to wait, turn off a feature that is not used and keep the cluster management address off untrusted segments.

entries.headline: Veeam fixes an unauthenticated 9.1 authorization bypass on 13.x servers, a VB365 SQL injection and a ONE MFA bypass
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-108142 +5NATOA2

CVE-2026-108142, Veeam Backup & Replication: an unauthenticated authorization bypass on the CDP Coordinator Service of 13.x backup servers (CVSS 4.0 9.1), fixed in 13.1.2 and 13.0.3, with a Backup for Microsoft 365 SQL injection to code execution and a Veeam ONE MFA bypass fixed the same day

Veeam published three advisories on 2026-10-27. In Backup & Replication, CVE-2026-108142 (CVSS 4.0 9.1, critical) lets an unauthenticated attacker bypass authorization on the CDP Coordinator Service of Windows-based Backup & Replication and of the Veeam Software Appliance; it affects 13.1.1.18 and all earlier 13.1 builds and 13.0.2.29 and all earlier 13.0 builds, is fixed in 13.1.2 (build 13.1.2.57) and 13.0.3 (build 13.0.3.63), and does not affect 12.x (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). The same advisory fixes two medium path-traversal flaws that need the Restore Operator role plus control over the contents of a backed-up NAS share and that write attacker-controlled files to an arbitrary path on the backup server, and a local privilege escalation in Veeam Agent for Linux version 13.1.1.4 and earlier that applies only to agents managed by a Backup & Replication server (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). Veeam Backup for Microsoft 365 8.5.0.1014 and earlier carry CVE-2026-106076 (9.0, critical): an authenticated organization-transfer peer injects SQL into the source server's configuration database, which gives cross-tenant read and write of configuration data and remote code execution as the PostgreSQL service account; the fix is 8.6 (build 8.6.0.1102), as it is for CVE-2026-106077 (8.3), which lets a user with the Backup for Microsoft 365 Administrator role read arbitrary files on the backup server as LocalSystem; two further flaws, an unauthenticated REST API authentication bypass with a forged federation token (6.9) and an installer file-write (4.3), need 8.6 Patch 1 (build 8.6.0.5011) (Veeam KB4957, 2026-10-27). Veeam ONE 13.1.0.7233 and earlier let an attacker with valid Administrator credentials disable multi-factor authentication globally before completing MFA verification (8.5, high; fixed in 13.1 P1, build 13.1.0.7940) (Veeam KB4951, 2026-10-27).

NCSC Switzerland relayed the Backup & Replication and Veeam ONE advisories on 2026-10-28, lists the exploitation status as unknown with the vendor reporting no evidence of active exploitation, and gives the prerequisite for the critical flaw as network access to the backup server's CDP Coordinator Service (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-28). heise adds that backup servers are a favourite target of ransomware groups (translated from German) (heise online, 2026-10-28), and Veeam itself says attackers will likely try to reverse-engineer a disclosed patch to exploit unpatched deployments (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
A Veeam Backup & Replication or Veeam Software Appliance on a 13.x build below 13.1.2 or 13.0.3 whose CDP Coordinator Service accepts connections from a network the attacker can reach; 12.x is out of scope (Veeam KB4948, 2026-10-27). Veeam Backup for Microsoft 365 version 8 below 8.6 Patch 1 (Veeam KB4957, 2026-10-27) and Veeam ONE 13.1 below Patch 1 (Veeam KB4951, 2026-10-27) are the other affected builds.
Detection
Veeam publishes no indicator. The telemetry that bears on this flaw is authentication and authorization events and service-account activity on the backup server, and new or changed backup jobs, repositories, stored credentials and restore operators; this is an inference from the described flaw, not a Veeam statement. For Veeam ONE, an MFA setting switched off followed by an Administrator sign-in is the sequence the flaw describes.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed builds on every backup server first, since backup infrastructure is what ransomware groups try to reach before encrypting, and keep backup servers off networks that untrusted hosts can reach; where a backup server was reachable and unpatched, review its jobs, repositories and credentials for changes nobody made.

entries.headline: Talos: UAT-11473 implants KeyDrift in Cisco SD-WAN controllers through CVE-2026-20127 to collect data-plane keys
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-20127exploitedNATOB2

KeyDrift: Talos reports UAT-11473 exploiting CVE-2026-20127 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN controllers to run an implant inside the control-plane daemon that collects data-plane keys, with infrastructure overlapping Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network

Cisco Talos reports that UAT-11473 exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass in the peering authentication of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28), and then installed a custom framework it calls KeyDrift (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). CISA has listed the flaw in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 2026-02-25 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-28). Cisco's advisory (CVSS 10.0) says an unauthenticated remote attacker can log in as an internal high-privileged non-root user and reach NETCONF to change the SD-WAN fabric configuration, and that there is no workaround (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Cisco's advisory, revised on 2026-10-28 to link Talos's post, says its PSIRT is aware of limited exploitation (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). Lumen's Black Lotus Labs reported on 2026-10-28 that Volt Typhoon had exploited the flaw since late 2025 and after Cisco's February disclosure (Lumen Black Lotus Labs, 2026-10-28), and Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473's operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

KeyDrift runs inside the control-plane daemon. The actor edits the runit launchers of sshd and of a look-alike aaamgr service and remounts /rootfs.rw executable: the sshd launcher starts a script that injects the PolyFlame library into every running vdaemon process by ptrace, and the aaamgr launcher runs a packed PolyFlame loader directly (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). PolyFlame is tasked in-band over the control-plane traffic and offers a command, file-write and file-read backdoor and an intermediate command relay; Talos recovered no hardcoded address, port or domain (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). A second component, LittleFilch, hooks SSL_read in vdaemon and collects peer system addresses and 32-byte values Talos assesses to be OMP-distributed IPsec data-plane keys, writing them RSA-encrypted to /var/tmp (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). Talos lists observed targeting as space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research, calls the activity historical and does not say how many controllers were affected (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
Every Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager and Validator regardless of configuration, on-premises or in Cisco's hosted clouds, on a release below the first fixed one in the advisory's table; Cisco says controllers with ports exposed to the internet are at risk (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).
Detection
On the controller's authentication log, Cisco says to audit /var/log/auth.log for accepted public-key logins of the vmanage-admin account from addresses that are not among the configured System IPs, and to validate control-connection peering events, those of peer type vmanage first, against maintenance windows and asset inventory (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28). On the host, Talos names modified runit run scripts that remount the overlay root executable and start a background script, an aaamgr service that runs a compiled, packed ELF, extra libraries mapped into vdaemon with ptrace activity against it and encrypted staging files under /var/tmp (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28). Cisco asks for admin-tech files and a TAC case when compromise is suspected (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-28).

Triage: an aaamgr service that runs as a compiled ELF is the discriminator, because the legitimate component is a Python package and does not normally appear that way (Cisco Talos, 2026-10-28).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to the fixed releases and restrict the control components' management ports, then treat any controller that was internet-reachable on a vulnerable release as a compromise-assessment target, because Lumen dates exploitation of the flaw to late 2025, before Cisco's February disclosure, and the implant runs in the process that handles the fabric's control sessions.

Builds on: A netadmin user on Cisco SD-WAN can become root through a crafted upload file; Mandiant saw…

entries.headline: DeadTag: expired tag domains send visitors to iPhone exploit kits; opening the page is enough on vulnerable iOS
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

DeadTag: re-registered domains of defunct analytics and advertising tags redirect visitors of thousands of sites, among them to a page that serves the Coruna and DarkSword iPhone exploit kits, which compromise a vulnerable device when the page opens

Report URI and iVerify describe a campaign they name DeadTag: attackers buy the expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that thousands of websites still load, so every page that still carries the tag runs the operator's script without the site owner changing or noticing anything, and the operator sells the visitors those tags bring in (Report URI, 2026-10-22). Report URI has identified more than 660 re-registered domains still embedded on thousands of sites and cautiously estimates 135 million visits a month (Report URI, 2026-10-22). The script is about 2 KB, does nothing for search engines, scanners and other bots, asks the operator's server what to do with each visitor and redirects the chosen ones, and Report URI found that the operator stopped answering when it probed from data-centre addresses or returned too often from residential ones; destinations include scam pages, a fake VPN pop-up and, for iPhones, a page that serves two exploit kits (Report URI, 2026-10-22).

One chain ends at a fake prediction-market page that picks the kit by the visitor's iOS version, Coruna for iOS 13 to 17.2.1 and a modified "P7" variant of DarkSword for iOS 18.4 to 18.7; both attack the browser itself, so opening the page is enough to compromise a vulnerable device, and the spyware they install steals keychain passwords, crypto-wallet app data and device and account information and reports to one server; Report URI notes that Coruna and DarkSword are separate exploit kits that have been seen in different campaigns, and that here both send their stolen data to the same server, which it reads as one operator running both (Report URI, 2026-10-22). iVerify reads DeadTag as mostly focused on European domains rather than .com (iVerify, 2026-10-21), and saw the P7 variant reach an employee's device at a customer organisation through a malicious Instagram ad while the employee was scrolling in the app (iVerify, 2026-10-21). The kit operator does not rely on DeadTag alone: Report URI found DarkSword loaders on hundreds of online shops on one e-commerce platform, PrestaShop (Report URI, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
Any public website that still loads a script from a third-party domain whose provider no longer operates it, where the browser fetches nothing useful and the page looks normal, and any iPhone on iOS 13 to 17.2.1 or 18.4 to 18.7 that opens such a page (Report URI, 2026-10-22).
Detection
Inventory the external script references of each public site and flag any whose domain has been re-registered or no longer belongs to its provider; Report URI recommends script monitoring that shows when a new script or domain appears on a page, and a Content Security Policy that controls which domains a site may load code from (Report URI, 2026-10-22). A security scanner usually sees only an empty response from the malicious script, because the operator answers only selected visitors.
Defender takeaway
Remove dead third-party tags from every site you run, enforce a Content Security Policy and keep iPhones on the current iOS, with Lockdown Mode for people who may be targeted; for an iPhone that may have opened an affected page, Report URI advises restarting it, changing the passwords stored in its keychain and moving crypto assets to a new wallet (Report URI, 2026-10-22).

entries.headline: PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356): Magento upload flaw attacked since March, fixed in July, CISA lists it as exploited
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-48356exploitedNATOB2

CVE-2026-48356 (PolyShell), Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source: an unauthenticated file upload attacked since March 2026, fixed for supported lines in July, and listed by CISA as exploited on 2026-10-27

Sansec named the flaw PolyShell: a missing validation in Magento's REST API that lets unauthenticated attackers upload executable files to a store, using a polyglot (code disguised as an image) to pass the image check (Sansec, 2026-03-17). It reports that its Shield service has blocked exploitation attempts against 79.5% of the Magento stores it protects since 2026-03-16, with first attacks observed on 2026-03-19, and that the vulnerable code has existed since the first Magento 2 release (Sansec, 2026-03-17). On 2026-03-30 a mass wave uploaded webshells, spread backdoor scripts across several directories and injected a JavaScript loader into the CMS pages of 471 stores within one hour (Sansec, 2026-03-30).

Sansec dates a fix in Magento 2.4.9 to 2026-05-12, without a backport to the supported 2.4.8 and 2.4.7 lines, and the backport to those lines to 2026-07-14, in bulletin APSB26-73 (Sansec, 2026-03-17). That bulletin rates the flaw Critical at CVSS 3.1 9.6, lists 2.4.9 among the affected versions, names the 2026-jul builds, 2.4.9-2026-jul included, as the fix for Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source, and still says Adobe is not aware of any exploits in the wild (Adobe, 2026-07-14). CISA added CVE-2026-48356 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-27 on evidence of active exploitation and gives no detail (CISA, 2026-10-27; CISA KEV, 2026-10-27). Sansec's research of 2026-10-24 shows the operator behind the March wave still active: its newest loader domain, registered on 2026-10-06, sits in the CMS blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which already carried an earlier loader, and one of them, on Magento 2.4.7-p1, still lacks APSB26-73 and holds PolyShell webshells disguised as images (Sansec, 2026-10-24).

Exposure
Every Magento Open Source and Adobe Commerce store without the 2026-jul fix, 2.4.9 included (Adobe, 2026-07-14); the anonymous guest-cart item routes need no credentials, and the upload becomes code execution on stock nginx for the oldest 2.x lines, on any non-stock nginx that hands every .php file to the PHP handler, and on Magento before 2.3.5 running on Apache without the engine switch set for that directory (Sansec, 2026-03-17).
Detection
Sansec calls any .php, .phtml or .phar file in the custom-options upload directory a strong indicator of compromise, and the uploaded file stays on disk even where execution is blocked (Sansec, 2026-03-17); also look for requests that add items to guest carts with embedded file data from unfamiliar sources (Sansec, 2026-03-17), script tags in the CMS block table and administrator accounts nobody created (Sansec, 2026-10-24).
Defender takeaway
Install the fix now, and treat a store that ran an unpatched build while internet-reachable since March as possibly compromised until its upload directory, CMS blocks and administrator accounts are checked, because an uploaded file stays on disk even where execution is blocked (Sansec, 2026-03-17), so the fix does not remove a shell already written (an inference), and deleting a loader script does not remove the access behind it (Sansec, 2026-10-24).

entries.action_label: Inside IT: SafePay published about 49 GB from a…
entries.classification_html: NATOC3
entries.headline: Inside IT: SafePay published about 49 GB from a Bernese wastewater association; the association declines to comment
entries.html:
ROUTINENATOC3

ARA-Region Lyss-Limpachtal (canton Bern, communal wastewater-treatment association): SafePay has put about 49 GB into the darknet, which Risikomonitor's analysis, relayed by Inside IT, finds holds personal records, bank statements, weak passwords and a third party's monitoring credentials; the association declines to comment

The tracker DeXpose recorded on 2026-09-15 that SafePay had claimed an attack on ARA Lyss, the wastewater-treatment association at ara-lyss.ch, posting that the full leak would be published soon unless a company representative made contact (DeXpose, 2026-09-15). Inside IT reported on 2026-10-27 that SafePay has put the stolen data into the darknet, about 49 GB in the case of the Bernese association ARA-Region Lyss-Limpachtal, that the security firm Risikomonitor analysed it, and that the association's management declined to comment (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). Risikomonitor's analysis, relayed by Inside IT and not verified independently, finds about 3,200 e-mail addresses and data on more than 1,200 identifiable persons; user folders and a data store with content up to March 2026 that hold 255 password hits, 195 of them very weak; bank statements and a transaction list with more than 100 payments by private persons with name and address; the full login data to the monitoring portals of the photovoltaic plants of another company's customers, stored on the same server; and a 2015 applicant list with birth dates, civil status, former employer and interview notes that was never deleted (Inside IT, 2026-10-27).

BACS told Inside IT that SafePay, which relies on double extortion, is among the more active ransomware groups in Switzerland and, together with The Gentlemen, the third most active in 2026 after Akira and Payload, that it has no clear focus on Switzerland, and that it was first observed there in May 2025 (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). No source says how the attackers got in or that data was encrypted at the association.

Defender takeaway
A communal body or association should look for credentials, bank statements and applicant files on its own file servers before an attacker does: Risikomonitor found 255 password hits in files, another company's portal logins and a 2015 applicant list that had never been deleted, and those are what a published dump gives fraudsters (Inside IT, 2026-10-27).

entries.action_label: IDCF Cloud ransomware began with an open-source…
entries.classification_html: NATOA2
entries.headline: IDCF Cloud ransomware began with an open-source flaw in the customer portal's login system; no server data left
entries.html:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOA2

IDC Frontier: ransomware stops four zones of IDCF Cloud for 495 companies and local governments; the provider's seventh report traces it to an open-source flaw in the customer portal's authentication system and says no server data left

IDC Frontier says a ransomware attack that began around 3:40 a.m. on 2026-10-07 stopped four zones of IDCF Cloud East Japan Region 1, affecting 495 companies and local governments, and has suspended customer management consoles in every region; no source names the actor or the ransomware family (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-07; IDC Frontier, 2026-10-08; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-08). The provider's seventh report of 2026-10-27 gives the route: a flaw in open-source software used in the customer portal's authentication system was exploited, and the attacker then obtained administrator rights on the virtualisation platform through the management console, stopped customers' virtual servers and encrypted them; the software is not named (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-27). The lesson is supplier concentration: local governments sat behind one provider whose recovery first depended on copies the customers held, until the fifth report made the provider's own snapshot backups retrievable for 194 of the 495 (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-14) and for 206 by 2026-10-20 (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
Customers of IDCF Cloud; IDC Frontier lists IDCF Cloud TypeS and its private-cloud offering as outside the incident (translated from Japanese) (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-08). For any other body, the condition is a website, mail or form service whose hosting and recovery copies depend on one provider.
Defender takeaway
Check where the recovery copies of hosted websites, mail, forms and line-of-business systems live: IDC Frontier first expected restoration only from copies customers hold themselves (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-08), and its own snapshot backups became retrievable for 194 of the 495 customers only a week into the outage (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-14), and for 206 by 2026-10-20 (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-27); the attacker's console message claims it wiped 554,153 snapshots, which the provider's report does not confirm (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-08). A copy in the provider's own environment is not one to count on for the recovery window. Ask a hosting or cloud supplier in writing how its customer portal authenticates and whether the open-source components behind that login are inventoried and patched, because here the path to the virtualisation platform ran from the portal's login system through the management console; the supplier's own remediation, a rebuilt portal, an external identity provider, access limited to customer IP addresses with mandatory multi-factor authentication and a company-wide software inventory matched automatically against vulnerability data, is the checklist (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-27).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:12 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

IDC Frontier's fifth report of 2026-10-14 says that, with an external security firm, it confirmed the backup data is safe, so the 194 of the 495 affected customers that used its snapshot function can retrieve it, and that it found no trace of customer data in the affected zones being queried or carried out, so it judges that none left those servers, while confirming improper queries of the registration data of 48 customers in its cloud portal with no trace of it being taken (translated from Japanese; IDC Frontier, 2026-10-14). This replaces the third report's expectation that data could be restored only from customers' own backups; the report does not state the intrusion route.

Update28 Oct 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-10-28T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebodyclassificationverification

IDC Frontier's seventh report of 2026-10-27 says its investigation with an external security firm is complete and names the cause: a third party exploited a vulnerability in open-source software used in the authentication system of the IDCF Cloud Portal, the portal customers use to start virtual servers and check billing, and so entered that system (translated from Japanese; IDC Frontier, 2026-10-27). The attacker then obtained administrator rights on the virtualisation platform through the management console, stopped customers' virtual servers and encrypted them; the software is not named. The provider finds no trace of customer data leaving the virtual servers, says the improper queries of portal registration data reached up to 71 customers, up from 48, that up to four customer login passwords were improperly changed and have been reset, and that backups are retrievable for 206 customers. It is rebuilding the portal in a new environment, replacing the affected authentication system with an external identity provider and limiting portal access to customer IP addresses with mandatory multi-factor authentication.

entries.action_label: Camping.Care booking data stolen: TCS and a second…
entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Camping.Care booking data stolen: TCS and a second campsite warn of WhatsApp fraud; PHP link not vendor-confirmed
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Camping.Care booking system (TCS Camping): customer and booking data stolen in connection with the PHP flaws, with real reservation numbers already used in WhatsApp fraud and 15,000 guests warned as a precaution

TCS Camping is warning about 15,000 guests as a precaution because the provider of its booking system, Camping.Care, suffered a data theft; TCS confirmed to the SRF consumer programme Espresso on 2026-10-26 that fraudsters could steal customer and booking information, and SRF reports the case in connection with the worldwide PHP security hole (SRF, 2026-10-26). Blick describes Camping.Care as a Dutch company whose booking system handles reservations for all campsites of the Touring Club Schweiz, writes, citing SRF, that the hackers used the critical PHP flaw to steal customer and booking data and that Camping.Care is not the only software supplier hit (Blick, 2026-10-26). No source names the CVE identifiers, the entry point, the date of the intrusion or an actor, and TCS says the hole has since been closed (SRF, 2026-10-26). The stolen data already in criminal use includes, among other data, names, telephone numbers and reservation numbers: guests received fraudulent WhatsApp messages that refer to existing reservations (SRF, 2026-10-26). TCS says account details and IBANs were not affected and that credit card data is not stored in the booking system (SRF, 2026-10-26). A second customer, Campingplatz Hüttenberg in canton Thurgau, told its guests in a notice (page date 2026-10-23) that Camping.care had informed it of WhatsApp messages to guests of several campsites that contain real booking information and a link, that Camping.care is investigating the cause and that booking data must be assumed to have been used without authorisation; the notice does not mention PHP, and Netzwoche points out that it does not say whether the attackers used one of the PHP flaws (Campingplatz Hüttenberg, 2026-10-23; Netzwoche, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
The guests who booked through the TCS campsite booking system, about 15,000 of whom TCS has warned, and any other customer of the Camping.Care platform, one of which, Campingplatz Hüttenberg, has warned its own guests; Blick says Camping.Care is not the only software supplier hit (Blick, 2026-10-26; Netzwoche, 2026-10-27).
Detection
The only signal the sources describe is on the recipient side, unsolicited WhatsApp messages that quote a real reservation with the correct name, telephone number and reservation number; no source gives intrusion telemetry from the supplier's systems (SRF, 2026-10-26).

Triage: TCS Camping sends no automated booking details, payment requests or reservation links over WhatsApp, so a WhatsApp message of that kind that quotes a genuine reservation is the fraud, however accurate its details (SRF, 2026-10-26).

Defender takeaway
For a booking, ticketing or citizen-portal application that a supplier runs on PHP, ask the supplier in writing whether its runtime was updated to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 (CISA, 2026-10-26) and whether customer data was accessed before that, because SRF, Blick and a TCS spokesperson tie this theft to the PHP flaws (SRF, 2026-10-26; Blick, 2026-10-26; watson.ch, 2026-10-26), although a customer's notice says the supplier is still investigating the cause (Campingplatz Hüttenberg, 2026-10-23) and no source says how the intrusion happened; and tell the people whose data the supplier holds that a message quoting their real booking details is no proof that it comes from you.
Update28 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-28T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Netzwoche reported on 2026-10-27 that a second Swiss Camping.Care customer, Campingplatz Hüttenberg in canton Thurgau, has warned its guests of WhatsApp messages about existing bookings that contain real booking information and a link; the campsite's notice carries the page date 2026-10-23 (Netzwoche, 2026-10-27; Campingplatz Hüttenberg, 2026-10-23). The notice says Camping.care informed the campsite of the messages, that Camping.care is investigating the cause and that booking data must be assumed to have been used without authorisation; it does not mention PHP, and Netzwoche points out that it does not say whether the attackers used one of the PHP flaws. The link to the PHP flaws therefore rests on SRF, Blick and a TCS spokesperson's statement to Keystone-SDA (watson.ch, 2026-10-26), not on the supplier.

entries.action_label: Inside IT: SafePay published about 30 GB from…
entries.classification_html: NATOB3
entries.headline: Inside IT: SafePay published about 30 GB from Manno, social-assistance files with AHV numbers; no commune statement
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB3

Swiss commune Manno (TI) confirms a cyberattack that encrypted part of its servers on 4 August 2026; SafePay has now published about 30 GB, which Risikomonitor reads as social-assistance decisions with AHV numbers, naturalisation files and a near-complete address book

The Ticino commune of Manno stated in a signed notice dated 2026-09-16 that on 4 August 2026 part of its servers suffered an attack that encrypted data (Comune di Manno, 2026-09-16). The commune isolated the affected server immediately and, per the notice, restored data and operations from existing backups in the course of the afternoon (Comune di Manno, 2026-09-16). It reported the case to the competent authorities, filed a criminal complaint against persons unknown, and told residents to distrust unexpected letters or e-mails that demand urgent payments or personal or financial data and to verify through official channels (Comune di Manno, 2026-09-16). The notice names no actor, no intrusion vector, and does not say whether data left the network; Inside IT's article of 2026-09-29 calls it a ransomware attack and says a backup allowed a quick return to normal operation (Inside IT, 2026-09-29).

On 2026-09-28, 55 days after the encryption, Ransomware.live recorded that the ransomware group SafePay had listed manno.ch on its leak site (Ransomware.live, 2026-09-28). Inside IT reported on 2026-10-27 that SafePay has put the stolen data into the darknet, about 30 GB in the case of Manno, and that the security firm Risikomonitor analysed it (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). Risikomonitor's reading, relayed by Inside IT and not verified independently: files with about 5,300 e-mail addresses and more than 2,000 identifiable persons; social-assistance decisions with name, address, monthly amount, AHV numbers and health insurer from 2014 to December 2025; debt-enforcement register extracts, naturalisation dossiers from 2018 and payment orders against tax debtors; employees' bank statements with IBANs; and mass letters, a youth-protection survey and a list of property owners with parcel and water-meter numbers that together give a near-complete address book of a commune of 1,381 inhabitants (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). Asked by Inside IT, the commune said it will make no statement on the publication (Inside IT, 2026-10-27).

Defender takeaway
A clean restore did not close the data-theft question here: the leak-site listing appeared 55 days after the encryption and the data has since been published, so a communal response to an encryption attack should keep its data-theft assessment open and plan for notification of affected persons, residents on social assistance first, and for the fraud that published AHV numbers, addresses and payment histories enable. The resident-fraud warning the commune issued belongs in the same response plan.
Update28 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-28T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagstechniquessourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteclassificationbody

Inside IT reported on 2026-10-27 that SafePay has put the data stolen from Manno into the darknet, about 30 GB, and that the security firm Risikomonitor analysed it (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). Risikomonitor's analysis, relayed by Inside IT and not verified independently, finds files with about 5,300 e-mail addresses and more than 2,000 identifiable persons, social-assistance decisions with name, address, monthly amount, AHV numbers and health insurer from 2014 to December 2025, debt-enforcement extracts, naturalisation dossiers from 2018 and payment orders against tax debtors, and information on the whole population of 1,381 inhabitants (Inside IT, 2026-10-27). The commune told Inside IT it will make no statement. The claim as Inside IT reported it on 2026-09-29 named no dataset (Inside IT, 2026-09-29).
