entries.headline: NetScaler's PHP2Shell fix is out: 14.1-73.49, 13.1-64.32 and FIPS builds; restrict management access until installed
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, NetScaler ADC and Gateway: the PHP2Shell flaws reach the management GUI on the NSIP, management-enabled SNIPs and the cluster IP of every supported version; fixed in 14.1-73.49, 13.1-64.32 and the FIPS and NDcPP builds

NetScaler Product Security says NetScaler is affected by the two PHP memory-safety flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 because the NetScaler Management Portal uses PHP and that all supported software versions are affected; the post, last updated on 2026-10-27, now says Citrix has released fixes for all supported versions (NetScaler Product Security, 2026-10-21). Citrix describes both as critical flaws in PHP that could let an unauthenticated attacker execute code in the context of the affected PHP process, each rated 9.2 under CVSS 4.0: CVE-2026-109618 is memory corruption when PHP handles an out-of-memory condition during request processing, and CVE-2026-109619 is stale request state that persists after memory is released and is reused by a later request (NetScaler Product Security, 2026-10-21). The affected surfaces are the NSIP GUI, any SNIP configured to permit management access and the cluster IP GUI in a cluster; NetScaler Console (service and on premises) and NetScaler SVM are not affected (NetScaler Product Security, 2026-10-21).

Citrix's bulletin CTX697263, revised on 2026-10-27, now urges customers to install NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.49 or later, 13.1-64.32 or later of 13.1, ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.49 FIPS or later, and ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1.37.286 or later, and lists NetScaler Console as not impacted (Citrix, 2026-10-22); CERT-FR's notice of 2026-10-27 gives the same first fixed builds (CERT-FR, 2026-10-27). Citrix tells customers to restrict GUI and API access on those addresses to trusted administrative hosts or narrowly scoped management networks, to keep management interfaces off the internet behind jump hosts or tight ACLs, and to review every address that permits GUI or API management and verify that it is not broadly reachable (NetScaler Product Security, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Every NetScaler ADC and Gateway on a supported version whose NSIP, a management-enabled SNIP or the cluster IP answers on its GUI or API from a network that is not a trusted administrative one; a SNIP or VIP can also carry application traffic, so Citrix tells customers to scope ACLs to management protocols and ports (NetScaler Product Security, 2026-10-21).
Detection
Connections to the management GUI and API from addresses that are not the administrative hosts, which is also the test of whether the ACLs hold; Citrix's post publishes no detection guidance and does not say whether NetScaler has been attacked (NetScaler Product Security, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed builds now, appliances whose management addresses are reachable from outside the administrative network first; the PHP project's own fixed releases do not help an appliance owner, because the fix ships in Citrix's package. Until a build is installed, apply the management ACLs and keep a recovery path such as console access in case a rule blocks administration (NetScaler Product Security, 2026-10-21).
Update27 Oct 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-10-27T0256Z-intelcvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytags

CISA added both PHP flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26, as flaws in PHP rather than as a NetScaler finding (CISA KEV, 2026-10-26). No source reports an attack on NetScaler through them. Citrix's bulletin CTX697263, whose revision history ends on 2026-10-22, still lists NetScaler ADC and Gateway as impacted, points to the Tech Zone post for mitigation and names no fixed build (Citrix, 2026-10-22), so the management-interface restriction stays the control until Citrix lists a fixed build.

CERT-FR's notice of 2026-10-27 lists the same first fixed builds for ADC and Gateway (CERT-FR, 2026-10-27). Neither page says NetScaler has been attacked, and no source reports an attack on it.

entries.headline: Gheist abuses stolen GitHub tokens to dump secrets through Actions; GitHub's hold covers public repositories only
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

Gheist: stolen GitHub tokens plant a secret-dumping workflow in every repository they reach; GitHub's July approval hold stops it on public github.com repositories but not on private ones or GitHub Enterprise Server

Wiz Research has tracked since 2026-09-15 a campaign it calls Gheist, after the user agent on its API calls, that uses stolen GitHub access tokens to create a branch and commit a workflow named sync-check in every repository each token can reach: more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, from personal projects to private enterprise repositories (Wiz, 2026-10-25). Wiz traces the tokens to infostealer logs and earlier supply-chain compromises (Wiz, 2026-10-25). The push triggers the workflow, which prints the repository's secrets, and those of any deployment environment, into its own run log; GitHub masks secret values only when they appear verbatim, so a base32-encoded value prints in full, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later, and because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API there is no attacker domain or connection to block (Wiz, 2026-10-25). In enterprise organizations the tool cycled through the tokens of several users and automation accounts within minutes and cloned private repositories before planting the workflow; hours later cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager (Wiz, 2026-10-25). Around 2026-10-19 the second variant added a job for repositories with a self-hosted runner that searches the host, and through the Docker socket its root filesystem, for tokens, private keys, environment files and Terraform state; Wiz calls the job buggy (Wiz, 2026-10-25).

Since 2026-07-28 GitHub holds potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories until a collaborator approves them, and every public Gheist run Wiz checked stayed held; the hold applies to public repositories on github.com only and not to GitHub Enterprise Server (Wiz, 2026-10-25; GitHub, 2026-07-28). In private repositories and GitHub Enterprise environments Wiz saw runs on the attacker branches complete and be deleted, and cloud audit logs showed the organizations' own workflows running on those branches and assuming AWS roles (Wiz, 2026-10-25). As of 2026-10-24 Wiz called the attack ongoing and distinct from the earlier GhostAction campaign (Wiz, 2026-10-25).

Exposure
Organizations whose developers or automation accounts hold GitHub tokens that an infostealer or earlier compromise could have exposed, above all with private repositories, GitHub Enterprise Server, cloud OIDC workflows or self-hosted runners (Wiz, 2026-10-25).
Detection
In GitHub audit logs, workflow runs on a branch named ci-sync- plus six random characters that were deleted within a minute of completing, and API activity with the user agent gheist; in cloud audit logs, role assumptions whose OIDC subject names such a branch, which shows Actions ran on an attacker branch even where GitHub logs are not collected; on self-hosted runners, the helper files Wiz lists (Wiz, 2026-10-25).

Triage: the planted commit is unsigned but authored as the token's owner, so the author name alone proves nothing; one new workflow file with a fixed commit message on a branch the owner did not create is the pattern (Wiz, 2026-10-25).

Defender takeaway
Rotate every secret available to a repository where a planted branch exists, revoke the tokens that pushed the commits and check their owners' devices for infostealers, treat a self-hosted runner host and its instance role as compromised if a planted branch ran there, and scope OIDC trust to protected branches or environments with required reviewers on environments that hold production secrets (Wiz, 2026-10-25).

Builds on: GhostAction: fake security workflows now harvest whole git histories; rotating Actions secrets…

entries.headline: Apple's exploited CoreGraphics zero-day is now fixed for iPhone XS, XS Max, XR and iPad 7th generation (iOS 18.7.11)
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-86950exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-86950, Apple iOS, iPadOS and macOS CoreGraphics: out-of-bounds write exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack on targeted iOS users, CISA KEV-listed (CVSS 8.8)

CVE-2026-86950 is an out-of-bounds write in CoreGraphics, the graphics component shared by iOS, iPadOS and macOS, and processing a maliciously crafted file can lead to arbitrary code execution (Apple, 2026-09-28). Apple states that it "is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27" (Apple, 2026-09-28). The fix, "improved bounds checking", ships in iOS and iPadOS 26.7.1 (Apple, 2026-09-28), in iOS and iPadOS 18.7.11 for iPhone XS, XS Max, XR and iPad 7th generation (Apple, 2026-10-26), macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 (Apple, 2026-09-28) and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 (Apple, 2026-09-28); Meta Product Security is credited with the report. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-09-29 (CISA, 2026-09-29). ENISA's vulnerability database scores it CVSS 3.1 8.8, network vector with user interaction required (ENISA EUVD, 2026-09-29). The macOS advisories repeat Apple's iOS-scoped exploitation sentence, so Apple does not claim exploitation on macOS.

Nothing about the attack itself is public: Apple gave no details on how many people were targeted, whether any attempt succeeded, or when exploitation began (The Hacker News, 2026-09-29), and no delivery mechanism is stated. SecurityWeek reads the component's role in 2D graphics and PDF rendering as meaning a file could arrive through web pages, email attachments or messaging apps, where automatic previews could allow zero-click exploitation; that is SecurityWeek's inference, and it also notes Meta would not say whether WhatsApp was involved (SecurityWeek, 2026-09-29). It also says iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate 27 do not appear to be affected. No indicators or behavioural detections have been published by Apple, Meta or CISA, so version compliance is the only measurable lever: device-management inventory of iPhones and iPads below iOS or iPadOS 26.7.1 (below 18.7.11 on iPhone XS, XS Max, XR and iPad 7th generation), and of Macs on Tahoe or Sequoia below the fixed builds.

Defender takeaway
Apple describes an attack on specific targeted individuals, so the staff an adversary would single out are the first whose devices need the update. A device that ran a vulnerable build is not evidence of compromise, and no published signature exists to check for one.
Update02 Oct 2026 09:11 UTCrun 2026-10-02T0404Z-intelsummarytagscvessourcesevidencebody

Researchers at Calif published a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-86950 on 2026-09-30, built from a public binary comparison of iOS 26.7 and 26.7.1: a PDF with a crafted TrueType font that triggers a controlled out-of-bounds write in CoreGraphics and crashes unpatched iPhones and Macs, with generation scripts and a sample PDF in a public GitHub repository (The Hacker News, 2026-10-01). Calif demonstrates a crash and a controlled write to two adjacent 16-bit values, not code execution, did not obtain the in-the-wild sample and cannot say how the attacker completed the chain (The Hacker News, 2026-10-01). The harness reaches the flaw through the ImageIO thumbnail path an app uses to preview a received attachment (The Hacker News, 2026-10-01). Calif pointed to new font-checking code in WhatsApp's attachment scanner as circumstantial evidence of a possible delivery path; the published analysis does not describe or test that path, a WhatsApp sentence in the first version was removed after publication, and WhatsApp has published no advisory linking the flaw to its products (The Hacker News, 2026-10-01).

Correction11 Oct 2026 13:46 UTCrun 2026-10-11T1307Z-auditcvesbody

CISA's catalog record for CVE-2026-86950 does not set the forensic-triage flag that it sets for some other recent listings; the 2026-09-29 listing carries only the catalog's standard required action (CISA, 2026-09-29). The analysis had said CISA attached its forensic-triage requirements to the listing.

Update27 Oct 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-10-27T0256Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessummary

Apple's security content for iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11, released 2026-10-26, lists CVE-2026-86950 as fixed for iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR and iPad 7th generation and repeats Apple's statement that it is aware of a report of exploitation in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27 (Apple, 2026-10-26). The notes for iOS and iPadOS 26.7.1 of 2026-09-28 list the fix for iPhone 11 and later and for iPad models from the iPad 8th generation, and the CISA catalog record for the flaw names no other Apple document, so in the documents these sources name the fix reaches those four device families four weeks after the others (Apple, 2026-09-28; CISA, 2026-09-29). SANS Internet Storm Center says this round delivers the corresponding iOS 18 patches for a flaw patched a month earlier and that no new vulnerability is marked as already exploited (SANS ISC, 2026-10-27).

entries.headline: JPCERT/CC and NICT: attackers decompile the public app, then call internal APIs; AI platforms scan exposed web apps
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOA2

Japan's wave of personal-data theft from web systems: JPCERT/CC and NICT describe attackers who decompile the published Android app to find internal APIs, drop JSP web shells as .war files on application servers, and run AI penetration-testing platforms against exposed web applications and WSUS servers

JPCERT/CC's alert of 2026-10-08, updated on 2026-10-23, says that around September 2026 Japanese organisations disclosed a run of personal-data leaks through unauthorised access, and singles out an attack type that may be increasing: systems the operator never expected strangers to reach, such as business-intelligence tools and staff-management systems, were hit alongside public apps (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23). It does not tie them to one method and groups them in five: per-target scanning for known flaws and exposed configuration and backup files; unauthorised calls to application management APIs; the Metabase SQL injection CVE-2026-72898; .war files carrying a JSP web shell that runs commands passed in query parameters, placed on application servers reachable from the public web server; and, added on 2026-10-23, attempts through AI penetration-testing platforms it names as Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX, including against exposed WSUS servers (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23).

In the API case the attackers analyse the published smartphone app to find endpoints and keys, then attack internal APIs the app screens cannot reach: changing user rights, creating accounts, toggling a header or sending malformed tokens to compare responses, and blind NoSQL injection to find account data; some use API keys stolen elsewhere (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23). NICT calls this an app-to-backend attack: the app need not be vulnerable, and backend authentication, authorisation or input-validation faults leak data (NICT, 2026-10-13). On attack servers JPCERT/CC found Android packages, reverse-engineering tools and a Python script that answers requests with HTTP 302 redirects and appears to have been used to test for server-side request forgery (JPCERT/CC Eyes, 2026-10-21).

No source names an actor. JPCERT/CC says it confirmed that the attackers used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and attack through APIs (JPCERT/CC Eyes, 2026-10-21), while Macnica could not confirm AI use (Recorded Future, 2026-10-22). API-attack access also arrives through Tor exit nodes and residential proxies (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23).

Exposure
An organisation that publishes a mobile app with a backend API, runs internet-facing web applications, or leaves BI tools, staff-management systems or WSUS servers reachable from the internet (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23); NICT asks operators to inventory public APIs and servers and check their access logs (NICT, 2026-10-13).
Detection
In API and web access logs, calls to internal or management endpoints from clients that never load the app screens, role-change and account-creation calls outside the admin console, one endpoint called in sequence with and without a header or with malformed tokens, blind NoSQL-injection-style probing of account lookups, and use of API keys extracted from the app; in web server telemetry, scans for exposed configuration and backup files and .war deployments to application servers (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23).

Triage: the app's own User-Agent proves nothing, because JPCERT/CC saw attack requests carrying it; the endpoints called and the sequence (header toggling, malformed tokens, role changes) discriminate, and a TLS fingerprint that matches a generic Python client does not identify the attacker alone (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23).

Defender takeaway
Treat the published app package as public and test the backend for authorisation gaps on internal endpoints (IDOR and BOLA), server-side request forgery, remote code execution and SQL injection (NICT, 2026-10-13). JPCERT/CC's measures are per-endpoint and per-method access control including non-public APIs, expiring least-privilege API tokens with fast revocation, rate limits on login, password reset, SMS and search, no long-lived secrets in apps, and no management functions on the internet (JPCERT/CC, 2026-10-23; JPCERT/CC Eyes, 2026-10-21).

Builds on: Metabase Cloud was breached through its own 0-day; self-hosted instances stay vulnerable until… · FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names… · Three off-the-shelf AI agents ran almost the entire card-theft campaign, from discovery to…

entries.headline: Three configuration-dependent NGINX heap flaws (CVSS 9.2) are fixed in 1.30.6, 1.31.7 and Debian trixie, not bookworm
entries.html:
NOTABLECVE-2026-15176 +4updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-15176 / CVE-2026-93479 / CVE-2026-97205, NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus: three unauthenticated heap-corruption flaws rated CVSS 4.0 9.2, reachable only in specific configurations and fixed in 1.30.6 and 1.31.7

nginx's change log for 1.30.6, dated 14 October 2026, lists five security fixes, which nginx.org's advisories page ties to 1.30.6 (stable) and 1.31.7 (mainline) (nginx.org change log, 2026-10-14; nginx.org, 2026-10-14); three of them are CVE-2026-15176, a heap buffer overflow in the core module that CCB describes as reachable where a location uses alias together with rewrite and a set or return directive referencing $request_filename, or where $request_filename appears in an access-log format; CVE-2026-93479, a heap buffer overflow in script evaluation that affects configurations whose regex map captures are referenced in root or an access-log format before the map's output variable, or that use a non-cacheable variable in a string expression; and CVE-2026-97205, a use-after-free when asynchronous file I/O is enabled, which Daily CyberSecurity relays from F5 as triggered by an SSI page with include virtual commands (Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19; Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14). Each is scored CVSS 4.0 9.2 and reachable by an unauthenticated network attacker, the first two under conditions beyond the attacker's control, with CCB's warning and vector covering the first two and Daily CyberSecurity all three (Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19; Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14). F5's CNA text says the overflow may restart the worker process and that attackers can execute code where ASLR is disabled or can be bypassed (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-20). Daily CyberSecurity reports that F5 has confirmed no public proof of concept for any of the three, and no exploitation is reported (Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14). Help Net Security reports that VulnCheck flagged exploitation attempts against an earlier NGINX flaw, CVE-2026-42945, three days after the flaw and its proof of concept were public (Help Net Security, 2026-05-18). The other two are CVE-2026-95101 (with HTTP/3, part of an unknown frame might be treated as the request body, bypassing client_max_body_size or injecting data into the proxied request) and CVE-2026-97629 (with TLS session ticket key rotation, one key was left uninitialised, which might allow forging a session) (nginx.org change log, 2026-10-14); nginx.org rates all five medium (nginx.org, 2026-10-14).

Exposure
Nginx 0.1.29 to 1.31.6 depending on the flaw, with branches older than 1.30 outside the range of CVE-2026-93479, and NGINX Plus R33 to R36 and 37.0.0 to 37.1.0 for the first two (nginx.org, 2026-10-14; Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19). A build is affected only if its configuration matches one of the patterns above, which nginx -T prints with every include; the version string alone is not enough, because distribution packages carry their own fixes. Debian fixed trixie with DSA-6575-1 (trixie-security 1.26.3-3+deb13u10) (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-25), while its tracker still marks bookworm (1.22.1-9+deb12u10) vulnerable (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-20).
Detection
F5 says the overflow leads to a worker restart, so process-supervision and error-log telemetry for unexpected worker exits and respawn bursts, matched against the unauthenticated requests to the affected locations in the access log, is the signal (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-20). Patching does not remediate a compromise that already happened (Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, 2026-10-19).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 1.30.6 or 1.31.7 (NGINX Plus 37.0.5.1 or 37.1.0.1), starting with internet-facing instances whose configuration matches a pattern above; until a package is fixed, F5's workarounds are aio off or ssi off for CVE-2026-97205, named captures confined to the matching block for CVE-2026-93479, and no alias in the affected locations or no $request_filename reference for CVE-2026-15176 (Daily CyberSecurity, 2026-10-14).
Update25 Oct 2026 14:03 UTCrun 2026-10-25T1308Z-auditheadlinesummarysourcessourcing_noteactionsbody

Debian fixed the five flaws in trixie with DSA-6575-1, which ships nginx 1.26.3-3+deb13u10 in trixie-security (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-25). Bookworm's package, 1.22.1-9+deb12u10, is still marked vulnerable, so Debian has not shipped a bookworm fix (Debian Security Tracker, 2026-10-20).

entries.classification_html: NATOB2
entries.headline: Required LDAP and SMB signing did not stop NTLM relay: a re-authenticated session kept the attacker's key
entries.html:
NOTABLENATOB2

NTLM relay past required signing: SpecterOps and Blackfield re-authenticate a signed LDAP or SMB session with a relayed victim identity, and Microsoft fixed it in the September and October 2026 updates

SpecterOps and Blackfield show that NTLM relay to a server that requires signing works again when the attacker first owns a signed session and then re-authenticates it with the victim's identity, so the session keeps the attacker's signing key. For LDAP, the attacker signs a session to a domain controller with valid credentials or, where accepted, an anonymous NTLM context, coerces a victim over SMB, and sends the victim's relayed authentication with a malicious LDAP modification in one SASL record signed with the attacker's key; the controller checks the signature once, switches to the victim's identity and runs the modification with the victim's rights (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23). The tested controller enforced LDAP signing and channel binding and the attack still worked over 389/TCP; the demonstration writes the resource-based constrained delegation attribute, and relaying a domain controller's machine account to another controller leads to DCSync and domain compromise (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23). Blackfield shows the SMB counterpart: a server keeps the original signing key on re-authentication without checking that the identity matches, so on any host that requires SMB signing, domain controllers included, a relayed privileged authentication yields a privileged session still signed with the low-privilege key, provided the attacker can capture or coerce that authentication (Blackfield, 2026-10-21).

SpecterOps reported the LDAP flaw to Microsoft on 2026-10-06, received no response, and says the fix shipped in the 2026-10-13 cumulative update, KB5126646, while the SMB variant was patched quietly in September 2026 (KB5122882) (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23). KB5126646 is the October update for Windows Server 2025 and KB5122882 the September update for Windows Server 2022 (Microsoft, 2026-10-13; Microsoft, 2026-09-08), so each release needs its own cumulative update of the month. Blackfield found no CVE or KB note for the SMB change, says similar changes seem to have reached the other supported versions in the following weeks without having traced every build, and warns that one or two end-of-life versions may never receive it (Blackfield, 2026-10-21). Both publish tooling; neither reports use in attacks (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23; Blackfield, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Windows Server domain controllers and SMB servers without the September 2026 (SMB) or 2026-10-13 (LDAP) cumulative update of their release; SpecterOps tested Server 2016 domain controllers and above and says every Server 2022 and 2025 domain controller it tested accepted the relay with LDAP signing required (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23). The LDAP variant needs a signed session the attacker controls, a victim coerced to authenticate over SMB and LDAP reachable on 389/TCP (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23).
Detection
Neither researcher publishes detection guidance. The demonstration ends in an LDAP modification of msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the victim's own computer object, and msDS-KeyCredentialLink (shadow credentials) is the other write (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23), so directory-service change auditing on computer objects for those two attributes is where it surfaces, attributed to the victim's own computer account while the connection comes from the attacker's host. Patching does not remove values a relay already wrote.
Defender takeaway
Confirm that every domain controller runs the 2026-10-13 cumulative update of its Windows release and every Windows server the September one, because required signing did not stop this relay before them. SpecterOps also advises enforcing LDAP signing and channel binding together, restricting LDAP on 389/TCP where possible and reducing NTLM; Blackfield says SMB signing stays necessary but is not sufficient (SpecterOps, 2026-10-23; Blackfield, 2026-10-21).

Microsoft fixed the SMB variant in September 2026 and the LDAP variant in the 2026-10-13 cumulative update; SpecterOps reports no reply to its report and Blackfield found no CVE for the SMB change; public tooling exists and neither researcher reports use in attacks.

entries.action_label: Stolen UpdraftCentral keys install backdoor plugins…
actions: On every WordPress site your organisation, its web agencies or its hosting suppliers run with UpdraftPlus, free or premium, including old municipal, campaign and project sites, check for an UpdraftCentral key (wp option get updraft_central_localkeys, or Settings > UpdraftPlus Backups > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral) and delete every key even if nobody remembers using UpdraftCentral, then update to 1.26.13 or 2.26.13 or later; deleting a key stops remote management only, and backups keep working.

On any site where a plugin, must-use plugin or Editor account holding manage_options appears that nobody created, delete the UpdraftCentral key first, then restore the site from a backup taken before 17 October, rotate every administrator and UpdraftCentral password, the teamupdraft.com account password (which UpdraftPlus Premium can leave stored in the site database and its backups) and end all sessions.

entries.classification_html: NATOB1
entries.headline: Stolen UpdraftCentral keys install backdoor plugins on WordPress sites; the plugin update alone does not evict them
entries.html:
HIGHupdatedNATOB1

TeamUpdraft breach: stolen UpdraftCentral connection keys are used to push backdoor plugins to connected WordPress sites, with no flaw in UpdraftPlus and no CVE; deleting the keys is the fix

TeamUpdraft says unauthorised access to teamupdraft.com on 17 and 18 October and that it believes its customer database was accessed, which holds connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone; it says UpdraftPlus plugin files and downloads were not affected, that the attacker used a compromised key to access its site, and that there is no evidence the attacker still has access, and it suspects, from exploit speed and faulty first plugins, that AI accelerated the attack (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). Patchstack reports that an attacker holding valid UpdraftCentral dashboard keys has been installing backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites since 2026-10-18 at 15:32 (the page gives no time zone), and that this is not a vulnerability in UpdraftPlus: the UpdraftCentral client ships inside every copy of the plugin and executes any command signed with the dashboard's private key once the site holds a key (Patchstack, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20).

The attacker sends a signed plugin.upload_plugin command as an ordinary POST to the site root and WordPress installs and activates the plugin; each delivered plugin wakes on a secret URL parameter carrying a 32-character token, creates an account with a hardcoded password, gives it the Editor role and then the manage_options and install_plugins capabilities, and logs the visitor in with a cookie, which bypasses the login form, two-factor authentication and login-protection plugins (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). The account stays after the plugin is removed, and early samples crash the site with an HTTP 500 and must not be repaired, because fixing the error switches the backdoor on (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). Nethemba adds a variant that logs the attacker in as an existing administrator without a database trace (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

A site holds a key if it was connected to UpdraftCentral or if a teamupdraft.com account was logged in from the plugin, where the option to add the site to UpdraftCentral is ticked by default, and keys do not expire (Patchstack, 2026-10-19); on UpdraftPlus 1.26.4 or 2.26.4 and earlier an attacker needs no key at all, through CVE-2026-10795, fixed in 1.26.5 and 2.26.5 (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). BleepingComputer reports an estimate of up to about 400,000 sites (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20; Nethemba, 2026-10-19). TeamUpdraft says UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 and 2.26.13 disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 13:07 BST (12:07 UTC) on 18 October; Nethemba says 1.26.12 and 2.26.12 deleted none and that 1.26.13 does not delete keys created on 18 October between 12:07 and 21:00 UTC, which have to be deleted by hand (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19; Nethemba, 2026-10-19). Nethemba saw the attacker send UpdraftCentral commands to two of its sites on the morning of 2026-10-21, after 1.26.13 had shipped, blocked by Nethemba's own blocking plugin, with the keys already deleted, and says sites that neither run 1.26.13 or 2.26.13 nor have deleted the key by hand remain at risk (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

Exposure
A WordPress site running UpdraftPlus, free or premium, that holds an UpdraftCentral key; wp option get updraft_central_localkeys prints it, including on sites whose owners never used UpdraftCentral (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). Self-hosted UpdraftCentral is not affected (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19).
Detection
Web server access logs for POST requests to the site root carrying an UpdraftCentral command whose user agent lacks the library version and URL that genuine dashboard traffic carries, and for GET requests with a short underscore-prefixed parameter and a 32-character token, which mean a backdoor was used; the UpdraftCentral log on the site for plugin.upload_plugin and plugin.delete_plugin commands without a matching administrator action; the user table for an Editor that also holds manage_options (Patchstack, 2026-10-19; Nethemba, 2026-10-19); and the plugin and must-use plugin directories (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). TeamUpdraft asks users to look at the sites listed under their UpdraftCentral account for any they did not knowingly connect since 2026-10-19 and says it is seeing a pattern of unexpected Editor roles (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). The backdoor account stays after the plugin is removed (Patchstack, 2026-10-19).
Defender takeaway
Delete the UpdraftCentral key on every site first, then update; if a backdoor is found, delete the key before removing it or the attacker pushes a replacement, and treat the site as compromised (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). IP blocking is not a control, since Patchstack saw the source addresses rotate within a day (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). On UpdraftPlus Premium sites Nethemba reads the code as leaving the teamupdraft.com account password stored in the database, and so in backups, until add-ons are claimed with a token, although the vendor says it is removed after the first connection, a reader found it on all three of their premium sites and in backups going back to 2022, and Nethemba has not found the samples it analysed reading it; changing that account password is therefore part of the cleanup (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelactionsbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

TeamUpdraft's updates of 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22 say the attacker used a compromised key to access its site, that there is no evidence the attacker still has access, and that the speed of the exploits and the initially faulty backdoor plugins suggest AI was used to accelerate the attack, which is the vendor's inference and comes with no technical evidence (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). It asks users to look at the sites listed under their UpdraftCentral account for any they did not knowingly connect since 2026-10-19, says it is seeing a pattern of unexpected Editor roles, and stresses that UpdraftPlus Premium users should check for unexpected plugins and new administrators even if they never used UpdraftCentral (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19).

Nethemba reports that the attacker kept going after the fix: on 2026-10-20 it tried the secret triggers of already removed backdoors on at least six sites of four administrators, and on the morning of 2026-10-21 it sent UpdraftCentral commands to two of Nethemba's sites after 1.26.13 had been released, blocked by Nethemba's own blocking plugin, with the keys no longer existing (Nethemba, 2026-10-19). A site that has a stolen key and neither updated nor deleted it by hand therefore stays exposed, and a removed backdoor is still probed. Nethemba also reads the code of UpdraftPlus Premium as storing the teamupdraft.com account password in the site database as entered and deleting it only after add-ons are claimed with a token, so it can stay in the database and in backups; a reader found it on all three of their premium sites and in backups going back to 2022, and Nethemba on one of its three, while the vendor says it is removed after the first connection and Nethemba has not found the samples it analysed reading it (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

Improvement25 Oct 2026 14:01 UTCrun 2026-10-25T1308Z-auditbody

TeamUpdraft bases its suspicion that AI accelerated the attack on the speed of the exploits after the breach and the initially faulty backdoor plugins, and publishes no technical evidence beyond that; its own guidance includes checking the plugins list, the Must-Use tab included, for anything not recognised (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19).

actions: Find every host, build agent and container that installed litellm 1.107.0 from PyPI between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC on 2026-10-21, or pulled the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest or main-stable tag of the official GHCR or Docker Hub LiteLLM images between 11:46 and 14:20 UTC; treat each as compromised, inspect it with tooling that does not start Python in the affected environment, rebuild it from a reviewed artifact pinned to 1.106.2 or an image digest, and rotate every cloud, Kubernetes, registry, SSH, database and AI-provider credential it could read, including the provider keys stored in a LiteLLM proxy database.

entries.classification_html: NATOB1
entries.headline: LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI and in the official images stole cloud and AI credentials; removing the package does not stop it
entries.html:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

LiteLLM 1.107.0: the PyPI wheels and the official Docker images carried a credential stealer and a dormant remote-code loader that Python starts at every launch, published through the maintainers' own release workflow with stolen developer tokens

Socket reports that LiteLLM 1.107.0, an open-source LLM gateway, carries malicious Python startup files in all seven wheels, and that Upwind found the same payload in the published images (Socket, 2026-10-21). A startup hook and a second startup module in the Python library directory run at every Python start without the application importing LiteLLM: the first collects cloud, Kubernetes, CI, registry and database credentials, SSH, GPG and TLS private keys, browser stores, AI-tool credential files, environment variables and, where configured, the credentials saved in a LiteLLM proxy database; the second forks a detached loader that polls a file in a GitHub repository for a domain and would execute Python downloaded from it with no signature or hash check, though at 13:01 UTC the pointer returned an empty body, which stops the loader before its download stage (Socket, 2026-10-21).

The payload is not in the git tag: a packaging setting in an untagged commit pulls it into the wheel, and the container build provenance records a source repository named Berri-AI/litellm, one hyphen away from BerriAI/litellm (Socket, 2026-10-21). The maintainers' root-cause post of 2026-10-23 traces the chain to a configuration file committed on 2026-05-27 to a public repository with the administrative key of an experimental internal agent service; a follow-up commit deleted the file about three hours later, but the original commit stayed in the repository's public history until 2026-10-22 and the key was never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-10 the attacker used that key against the service's API, which returned the GitHub CLI OAuth token of an organization owner, not a service account and not scoped down, and from then on the attacker held owner-level access to every repository; such CLI tokens are post-2FA and exempt from GitHub's re-authentication for sensitive actions (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). With it the attacker pushed throwaway branches whose workflows posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint, yielding the CLI tokens of two maintainers, and deleted the workflow runs minutes later (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Socket found secret-exfiltration workflows running in the repository on 2026-10-10 from its Actions performance metrics, eleven days before the release attack, says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access and does not claim that the 2026-10-10 theft produced the access used on 2026-10-21, while LiteLLM says its audit logs tie the token stolen on 2026-10-10 to the approval of the release (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 a push to the private release-orchestration repository with a maintainer's token was rejected by branch protection, and the owner's token then overrode it so that the build could be pointed at the look-alike repository; the owner's token dispatched the staging build, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate, a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, and the owner's token force-pushed the history clean, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). PyPI quarantined 1.107.0 and the images were pulled the same day (Aikido, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
An environment that installed litellm 1.107.0 from PyPI between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC on 2026-10-21, or pulled the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest or main-stable tag of the official images from GHCR (until about 13:51 UTC) or Docker Hub (until 14:20 UTC); lockfiles, caches, build logs and running image digests show which (Socket, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In the cloud audit logs of every account the host could reach, a caller-identity check followed by a Bedrock model listing and IAM enumeration, made with an instance-role credential harvested from CI runners or Kubernetes nodes from an address outside your estate, which Wiz saw from 16:20 UTC on 2026-10-21 (Wiz, 2026-10-21); on hosts, startup hooks and sitecustomize modules in a Python library directory that your tooling did not install, a detached Python process holding a lock file, and an encrypted archive posted to a path labelled as a health check (Socket, 2026-10-21). In the GitHub organization audit log, short-lived throwaway branches that add a single workflow file, workflow runs deleted minutes after they ran, and branch-protection and force-push-block overrides made with an owner's token; the log records a hash of the token behind each action, which tied the stolen maintainer token to the release approval (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Starting Python or pip in an affected environment can run the payload again, and removing the package directory does not remove the startup files or stop a running loader (Socket, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Rotate every credential the host could reach (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21), because removing the package does not remove the startup files (Socket, 2026-10-21) and stolen cloud credentials were in use within hours (Wiz, 2026-10-21); rebuild from a reviewed release and pin container digests (Socket, 2026-10-21), and move to 1.106.2 or an explicit earlier version as the maintainers advise (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21). For your own pipelines, the root cause was a key whose file was deleted from a public repository while the commit stayed in its history and the key was never revoked, and an organization owner's CLI token held by an automation service; the maintainers call it an illustration of the risk of failing to rotate a potentially exposed key (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniques

The maintainers published a root-cause post on 2026-10-23 that supersedes the earlier hypothesis that the tokens were read from the logs of an internet-exposed internal deployment: their request logs show the first token came from a different service, an experimental agent platform whose administrative key had been committed to a public repository on 2026-05-27 and never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The attacker used the key on 2026-10-10 to obtain an organization owner's GitHub CLI token, so access began eleven days before the release, and the same day throwaway branches in two repositories ran workflows that posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint and were deleted minutes later, yielding the tokens of two further maintainers (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

Socket found the same activity independently from the repository's Actions performance metrics, including a second run on 2026-10-12 that took 14 further secrets, and says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 three credentials did different jobs: the owner's token overrode branch protection and later force-pushed the history clean, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate and a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The maintainers say they are revoking every token tied to every internal system and vendor platform, and that the attacker's activity on other systems focused on upstream inference API tokens (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

Microsoft advises isolating affected hosts and investigating them from a known-clean system without running python, pip or other commands that invoke the affected interpreter, confirming that the malicious startup files are gone from the library path rather than assuming that deleting the litellm directory removed them, and it treats Python-launched OpenSSL public-key encryption of files staged in a temporary directory as a behavioural lead (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-23).

entries.headline: Metabase Cloud was breached through its own 0-day; self-hosted instances stay vulnerable until manually upgraded
entries.html:
HIGHCVE-2026-72898exploitedupdatedNATOA1

Metabase CVE-2026-72898: an unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day gave attackers administrator access to BI instances, exploited since at least 2 August, with VenariX counting fifteen downstream victims

Metabase, an open-source business-intelligence platform run both self-hosted and as a managed cloud service, disclosed on 2026-08-06 that its own Metabase Cloud environment had been attacked by someone using an unknown vulnerability affecting versions 1.58 and above, and that it blocked the endpoints used in the attack before identifying and patching the flaw (Metabase, 2026-08-06). The mechanism matters more than the platform: an unauthenticated caller injects arbitrary SQL against the Metabase application database, and that yields administrator access to the instance, from which the attacker can change the application configuration, steal the stored credentials Metabase holds for the databases it connects to, read anything reachable through those connections, and export it (Metabase, 2026-08-06; Metabase GitHub advisory, 2026-08-06). VenariX places the injection at the /api/session/reset_password endpoint (VenariX, 2026-08-10); the vendor's stated interim workaround for anyone who cannot upgrade immediately is to block that endpoint outright, and its published attack pattern runs through the same route (Metabase, 2026-08-06). BleepingComputer, quoting the associated security advisory, reports it is rated critical at CVSS 10.0 with active exploitation confirmed, and that no CVE identifier had been assigned (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07). The flaw is now tracked as CVE-2026-72898 (Metabase GitHub advisory, 2026-08-06), and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-11 (CISA, 2026-08-11).

The exposure split is the part defenders need to act on. Metabase Cloud customers were upgraded and patched by the vendor, while self-hosted instances remain vulnerable until an administrator upgrades them by hand (Metabase, 2026-08-06). The minimum safe point releases are 0.58.24, 0.59.21, 0.60.17, 0.61.11, 0.62.9 and 0.63.5 for their respective branches, and anything on a lower point release of those branches is still vulnerable; installations below version 58 are not affected (Metabase, 2026-08-06).

Two organisations have confirmed data theft from their own instances. Framework, the laptop manufacturer, told customers that the attackers stole full names, email addresses, login IP addresses, billing and shipping address details, phone numbers and company names, with VAT, EIN and billing email address additionally in scope for its business customers, and said Metabase notified it on 6 August that its instance had been vulnerable and was accessed on 3 August (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07). Tally, an online form builder, notified users that its Metabase analytics environment was compromised on the same date and that the attackers reached email addresses and password hashes, while its forms and the responses submitted to them are stored separately and were not reached (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07). VenariX's tracker has since counted fifteen downstream incidents, set out in the updates below.

Detection is unusually well specified for a flaw that went its first week without a CVE, because the vendor published the request sequence rather than indicators. The attack shows up as a call to POST /api/session/reset_password returning a 400 status code followed by a call to GET /api/user/current returning 200, and Metabase states that finding that pattern in application logs or in Metabase server ingress logs means the instance was likely compromised (Metabase, 2026-08-06). After upgrading, the vendor's own follow-up steps for any instance whose reset endpoint was publicly reachable are to revoke every active session by deleting all rows in the core_session table, review and delete unrecognised API keys, check administrator accounts for unexpected changes, rotate the credentials for every connected database, and review both data-warehouse logs and Metabase's own activity and query history for unauthorised access (Metabase, 2026-08-06).

Defender takeaway
The reason this deserves attention beyond the patch is what a BI platform holds. Metabase sits in front of production data warehouses with standing credentials for each one, so administrator access converts directly into read access across every system it was ever pointed at. Any self-hosted instance that was internet-reachable on an affected point release before the upgrade needs the credential rotation and the log review, not just the version bump. The week without a CVE is a process lesson worth naming internally: while exploitation was already under way, an asset patched on the strength of CVE feeds, KEV listings or scanner findings got no signal for this at all.

Triage: a 400 on the password-reset route is ordinary, users mistype addresses and reset flows reject malformed requests all day, and on its own the 400 means nothing. The discriminator is what follows it from the same source: an unauthenticated client that is genuinely failing a password reset has no session and cannot then get a 200 from /api/user/current, so it is the ordering and the success of the second call that separate exploitation from noise (Metabase, 2026-08-06).

Update12 Aug 2026 04:46 UTCrun 2026-08-12T0411Z-intelactionscvesevidenceregionssectorssourcestagstechniquesbody

The entry on Metabase's unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day closed on the observation that no CVE identifier had been assigned, so a purely CVE-driven patch process would not surface the exposure at all. That gap is now closed in both directions. GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-vwf4-m7j8-wcjf assigns CVE-2026-72898 with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 10.0 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), and Metabase's own advisory text states that "Metabase has confirmed active exploitation of this vulnerability" and that the flaw "allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to inject arbitrary SQL into the Metabase application database, which can give them administrator access to the instance" (Metabase, 2026-08-06). CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-11 (CISA, 2026-08-11).

The second half of the delta is the affected-version matrix, which the vendor's original blog post did not carry in this form. The advisory lists the affected ranges per release line as >= x.58.0 < x.58.23, >= x.59.0 < x.59.20, >= x.60.0 < x.60.16, >= x.61.0 < x.61.10, >= x.62.0 < x.62.8 and >= x.63.0 < x.63.3, and names the patched versions separately as x.58.24, x.59.21, x.60.17, x.61.11, x.62.9 and x.63.5; note the two lists do not meet, so a build sitting between an affected upper bound and its patched release is not described either way and should be treated as needing the named patched version (Metabase, 2026-08-06). That turns "upgrade Metabase" into a query an asset inventory can answer, and it is what a scanner needed in order to report anything at all.

Nothing here changes the exposure of an instance that has not been upgraded; the exploitation window has been open since at least 3 August per the earlier coverage, and the interim control is unchanged: block the /api/session/reset_password endpoint if an upgrade cannot happen immediately. What changed is visibility, and that is the operationally useful part. An organisation whose vulnerability management runs off CVE identifiers, SBOM matching or KEV feeds got no signal on this flaw for over a week while it was being exploited; the same tooling will now produce a finding on the next scan cycle. The advisory's post-upgrade guidance also stands and is worth re-reading against what an attacker with administrator access would already have taken: revoke active sessions, audit API keys and administrator accounts, and rotate the stored credentials for every connected data source, because those credentials are what an instance-level compromise reaches.

Update19 Aug 2026 05:02 UTCrun 2026-08-19T0410Z-intelactionscvesevidencesectorssourcestagstechniquesbody

The count of downstream victims is now the story. VenariX's tracker, first published 2026-08-10, lists n8n, Framework, Tally and Kilo Code from the first wave, followed by Stocksy United Co-op, ShipMonk, Checkly, Cypress.io and Bits of Gold (VenariX, 2026-08-10). The earlier entries covered the flaw itself: an unauthenticated SQL injection reachable at the password-reset endpoint, CVSS 10.0, exploited, catalogued as such on 2026-08-11.

The mechanism behind the growing list is a property of business-intelligence tooling rather than of this bug. Metabase stores the connection configuration, including credentials, for every external database and warehouse it queries; an attacker who reaches administrative context in the application can therefore read those stored credentials and query or export whatever they reach (VenariX, 2026-08-10). The blast radius of any given instance is set entirely by what it was wired to; VenariX's own framing is that a deployment connected only to a restricted reporting database is a materially different incident from one connected to a production warehouse, which is the assessment question a defender should be answering first.

The victim disclosures show the range. n8n's update of 11 August breaks its 136 accessed records down: 7 with cloud usernames and email addresses and 5 that also held bcrypt-hashed n8n Cloud passwords were confirmed accessed, 62 with names and email addresses may have been, and the remaining 62 held nothing sensitive (n8n, 2026-08-08). Framework confirmed customer data was stolen including names, email addresses, phone numbers, login IP addresses and billing and shipping addresses, and Tally's exposure covered email addresses and password hashes while form content was stored separately and unaffected (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07). Kilo Code says a subset of its users or organizations may have had partial or full prompts or user data such as name, email address, billing address and location exposed (Anaconda, 2026-08-07). Of the newly added names, Bits of Gold separately disclosed on 2026-08-16 that an attacker gained unauthorized access to a third-party data analytics network and obtained names, national ID numbers and emails for roughly 200,000 customers (DataBreaches.net, 2026-08-17); the company describes the platform class, not the product, and it is VenariX that places the incident in this campaign.

The operational point is the one most likely to be got wrong in a remediation ticket. Metabase's own guidance, as VenariX relays it, is that "Credential rotation is especially important if exploitation is suspected, because patching the application does not invalidate credentials that may already have been exposed" (VenariX, 2026-08-10). An estate that upgraded Metabase and closed the ticket has fixed the injection and left the attacker holding working warehouse credentials. Metabase's fuller recommendation set for potentially exposed instances is to revoke active sessions, review administrator accounts and API keys, rotate credentials for connected databases, and review both Metabase and warehouse logs; where an immediate upgrade is impossible it recommends temporarily blocking access to the reset-password endpoint.

Detection has an unusually crisp anchor for a SQL-injection flaw, because the vendor published one. Metabase identified a recurring two-request pattern associated with exploitation (a POST to /api/session/reset_password returning HTTP 400, immediately followed by a GET to /api/user/current returning HTTP 200) and "Metabase states that this pattern in application or ingress logs indicates that the instance was likely compromised" (VenariX, 2026-08-10). Beyond that, the investigative surface is Metabase's own query history, database and warehouse audit logs, administrator accounts, API keys, and any unexpected use of the stored connection credentials; the last being where a compromise that started in the BI tier becomes visible in the warehouse tier.

Triage: a failed password reset followed by a session check is not by itself unusual in a web application's logs, which is exactly why the ordered pair matters rather than either request alone; a genuine failed reset does not produce an authenticated /api/user/current success on the same session immediately afterwards. Downstream, the discriminator for warehouse activity is whether queries arriving under the Metabase service credential match the dashboards and questions that credential is actually used for: bulk selects against tables no saved question references, or access at hours the reporting schedule does not run, are the signal, while high query volume under that identity is normal by design.

Update27 Sep 2026 04:38 UTCrun 2026-09-27T0404Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The downstream count grows again, through a further intermediary. Shipup, a French platform used by more than 700 e-commerce brands to send delivery-tracking notifications and post-purchase communications, ran a Metabase instance whose compromise Cyberattaque.org links to the campaign against Metabase, with unauthorized access possible between 31 July and 17 August 2026, a window that starts earlier than the "since at least 3 August" the earlier coverage had established for the campaign (Cyberattaque.org, 2026-09-26). Carrefour notified some customers in early September, after Cyberattaque.org had already reported Micromania and Easypara exposed through the same Shipup compromise (Cyberattaque.org, 2026-09-26), and French Breaches notes similar incidents at Printemps, Citadium and Aroma-Zone (French Breaches, 2026-09-27). The exposed categories match the pattern this campaign has shown throughout: names, email addresses and phone numbers; Carrefour states no banking data or passwords were affected, and Cyberattaque.org reads nothing in its communication as suggesting that its site, customer accounts or internal systems were compromised, consistent with the exposure being limited to data it had shared with Shipup for delivery notifications. Carrefour has not disclosed the exact number of customers affected or confirmed whether the exposure window matches Shipup's own 31 July-17 August dates.

Shipup is a new entry in this campaign's chain of intermediary vendors, distinct from the data warehouses and analytics platforms this entry's earlier coverage described (n8n, Kilo Code and the others connected directly to a compromised Metabase instance): here, the retail brands are themselves downstream of a vendor that was downstream of the Metabase flaw, a second hop the credential-rotation and log-review guidance in this entry's original analysis already covers, since it applies to any instance that was reachable and unpatched during the exploitation window regardless of how many contractual layers separate the ultimate data subject from the compromised application.

Correction27 Sep 2026 13:28 UTCrun 2026-09-27T1308Z-auditbody

The Shipup paragraph above stated that the 31 July to 17 August 2026 access window matched the exposure window this entry had already established for the campaign. It does not. This entry's earlier coverage places exploitation "since at least 3 August", so the Shipup window opens three days earlier and widens the campaign's known exposure period rather than corroborating it. For a defender scoping a log review against a Metabase instance or a downstream vendor relationship, the earlier start date is the operative one, and the sentence now says so.

Update29 Sep 2026 22:50 UTCrun 2026-09-29T2134Z-audittitlesummarytagsentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

VenariX's tracker has grown from nine confirmed downstream incidents to fifteen. The additions to the nine named in the update of 2026-08-19 are Privy, Paradigm Connect Asia, Statista, Dodo Payments, Marsello and LEGO Certified Stores South Africa (VenariX, 2026-08-10, revised since). The Shipup compromise and its retail clients, covered in the update of 2026-09-27, are not on that list, so the real total is higher still.

The larger change is who is using the flaw. VenariX says it has confirmed that Dire Wolf, a ransomware and data-extortion group, exploited CVE-2026-72898 in at least two incidents against self-hosted Metabase deployments, at Statista and Dodo Payments, and suspects the group targeted fourteen more companies the same way. It is explicit that it has no evidence Dire Wolf discovered the zero-day or is behind the other confirmed incidents (VenariX, 2026-08-10, revised since). Dodo Payments, a payments company, confirms the vector without naming an actor: an unauthorised party exploited CVE-2026-72898 in a self-hosted Metabase instance used for internal reporting, viewed and queried the reporting datasets that system could reach, and the company contained it within hours of learning of it on 16 August (Dodo Payments, 2026-08-17). A dark-web listing dated 16 August, reviewed but not verified by MediaNama, claims about 60.8 GB and 39.3 million rows from four ClickHouse analytics databases, including tables it labels API keys, one-time passcodes and identity-provider credentials, where Dodo says API keys and credentials were not in the affected system (MediaNama, 2026-09-01).

For a defender this moves the self-hosted exposure from opportunistic data theft to an extortion operator's target list. The dispute over what left Dodo's warehouses is the point this entry has made since August: the reach of a compromised Metabase instance is whatever its stored connections reach, and the vendor's statement of what the BI tool itself held does not bound it. An instance that was internet-reachable on a vulnerable build between late July and its upgrade should be scoped as a warehouse compromise, not an application one.

Update21 Oct 2026 03:48 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0256Z-intelregionssectorssourcesevidencesourcing_notebodytitle

Republik, a Swiss online magazine, reported that an unauthorised access that had been going on since August ended on Wednesday 2026-10-14, when one of its analysis tools stopped working and it took its own Metabase installation offline; its statement says the vulnerability had been known since 6 August and that the magazine failed to take countermeasures in good time (swissinfo.ch, 2026-10-16). Netzwoche quotes it saying it had not subscribed to the manufacturer's security warnings and had no automatic check that reports a known gap in the software it runs (translated from German; Netzwoche, 2026-10-19).

The attackers certainly retrieved the records of all registered users, at least names and email addresses and in part date of birth and gender, and demonstrably sampled postal addresses, comments and votes; Republik reported the incident to the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner on 2026-10-15 (Netzwoche, 2026-10-19; swissinfo.ch, 2026-10-16). Republik believes it was a broad automated wave in which the attackers first looked for what every Metabase installation holds, such as login details and keys for AI services that could be resold, and says nothing indicates anyone targeted the magazine specifically (swissinfo.ch, 2026-10-16). It will use Metabase again only when it is updated and no longer reachable from the open internet, and says the stolen data had not surfaced online (Netzwoche, 2026-10-19).

Correction25 Oct 2026 14:07 UTCrun 2026-10-25T1308Z-auditsummarytechniquessourcesbodytitle

Several statements went beyond their sources and are corrected where they stand. No source says Framework and Tally were the first victims: 2026-08-03 is when Framework's instance was accessed (BleepingComputer, 2026-08-07), n8n disclosed in the same days (n8n, 2026-08-08), and so did Kilo Code, which dates the incident at its Metabase instance to 2 August, a day earlier (Anaconda, 2026-08-07). For Shipup, Cyberattaque.org links the compromise to the campaign against Metabase and says unauthorized access was possible, not confirmed, between 31 July and 17 August 2026 (Cyberattaque.org, 2026-09-26). The statement that Carrefour's own site, accounts and systems were not compromised is that outlet's reading of Carrefour's notice, not Carrefour's words (Cyberattaque.org, 2026-09-26). Bits of Gold disclosed its breach on Sunday 2026-08-16, the day before DataBreaches.net reported it (DataBreaches.net, 2026-08-17).

entries.summary: Metabase disclosed on 2026-08-06 that its Metabase Cloud platform was attacked through a previously unknown vulnerability in versions 1.58 and above: an unauthenticated attacker injects arbitrary SQL against the application database and obtains administrator access to the instance, from which they can rewrite configuration, steal the stored credentials for every connected database and export the data those connections reach. The only interim workaround the vendor offers is to block the /api/session/reset_password endpoint, which is also where its published attack pattern runs. Cloud instances were patched by the vendor; self-hosted deployments stay vulnerable until manually upgraded to 0.58.24, 0.59.21, 0.60.17, 0.61.11, 0.62.9 or 0.63.5. Laptop maker Framework and form builder Tally confirmed customer data was taken from instances accessed on 2026-08-03. The flaw had no CVE identifier at disclosure; it is now tracked as CVE-2026-72898, which CISA added to its KEV catalog on 2026-08-11. VenariX now tracks fifteen publicly confirmed downstream incidents and ties two of them, at Statista and Dodo Payments, to the Dire Wolf extortion group working against self-hosted instances.
entries.title: Metabase CVE-2026-72898: an unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day gave attackers administrator access to BI instances, exploited since at least 2 August, with VenariX counting fifteen downstream victims

updates.summary: Metabase's unauthenticated SQL-injection zero-day, covered here on 2026-08-09 when no CVE existed, has been assigned CVE-2026-72898 in GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-vwf4-m7j8-wcjf at CVSS 3.1 10.0, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-08-11. The advisory publishes affected ranges per release line and confirms active exploitation in Metabase's own words. For self-hosted instances nothing about the exposure changed, but the flaw is now visible to every scanner, SBOM pipeline and CVE-keyed patch process that could not see it a week ago.

A tracker maintained by VenariX, updated 2026-08-17, now counts nine publicly confirmed organisations whose compromised Metabase environments were used to reach connected data warehouses, n8n, Framework, Tally and Kilo Code, joined on 2026-08-17 by Stocksy United Co-op, ShipMonk, Checkly, Cypress.io and Bits of Gold. This pipeline covered CVE-2026-72898 on 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-12 as an exploited CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated SQL injection in the password-reset endpoint; the delta is the downstream pattern. Because Metabase stores the credentials for every database it connects to, administrative access to the application yields those credentials, and Metabase's own guidance is that patching does not invalidate credentials already exposed. Metabase also published a two-request log pattern that indicates a given instance was compromised.

The downstream victim list grows again through a further intermediary: Shipup, a French package-tracking platform used by 700+ e-commerce brands, was compromised through the same vulnerability, and at least six of its retail clients, including Carrefour, Printemps, Citadium, Aroma-Zone, Micromania and Easypara, have since notified their own customers of exposed contact data.

The Shipup section claimed the 31 July to 17 August access window was the same one this entry's earlier coverage had already established for the campaign. It was not: the earlier coverage says "since at least 3 August", three days later, so the Shipup window widens the campaign's known exposure period rather than confirming it. The sentence now states that difference instead of asserting agreement. Recorded for the audit trail and not otherwise fixable: the changelog record of the same day declared a change to the evidence list that its commit did not make.

VenariX's tracker now counts fifteen publicly confirmed downstream incidents, up from nine, adding Privy, Paradigm Connect Asia, Statista, Dodo Payments, Marsello and LEGO Certified Stores South Africa. It attributes two of them, at Statista and Dodo Payments, to the Dire Wolf ransomware and extortion group exploiting self-hosted Metabase, and suspects fourteen more targets. Dodo Payments' own disclosure confirms a self-hosted Metabase instance breached through CVE-2026-72898. The title, the summary and the main analysis no longer describe the flaw as having no CVE or Framework and Tally as its only victims.

A Swiss victim: Republik, a Swiss online magazine, says attackers used the Metabase flaw against its own installation from August until the tool failed on 2026-10-14, retrieved the records of all registered users and reported the incident to the federal data protection commissioner; it had not subscribed to the vendor's security warnings.

Corrects statements beyond their sources: Framework and Tally are no longer called the first victims, Kilo Code dates its incident to 2 August (the title now says exploited since at least 2 August), Shipup's access window is stated as possible rather than confirmed, the statement about Carrefour's own systems is attributed to the outlet that made it, and Bits of Gold's disclosure is dated 2026-08-16.

actions: Patch every PAN-OS GlobalProtect portal and gateway to the fixed build in Palo Alto's advisory for its minor release (users then re-authenticate once, because the fixed firewall regenerates the override cookie), or until then disable Authentication Override or give the cookies a certificate that no other feature uses.

entries.headline: Qilin and Inc ransomware exploit the GlobalProtect bypass; one intrusion pivoted to vCenter and ESXi past in-guest EDR
